World.title: Ukraine Envoy: Russia ‘Not Interested’ in Peace Talks, African States Urged to Reject Recruitment Drive
World.content:
Mr. Oleg Kobzystyi, Chargé d’Affaires of the Ukrainian Embassy in Dakar, Senegal./Credit: Ukrainian Consulate in Dakar, Senegal.

As Ukraine marks its Independence Day on Monday, August 24, the Chargé d’Affaires of the Ukrainian Embassy in Dakar, Senegal, Mr. Oleg Kobzystyi, speaks to the Liberian media on a wide range of issues, including the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war and the state of Liberia-Ukraine relations. Below is the full interview.

Q. How do you assess the current state of affairs on the battlefield? Do you have any thoughts on when the war might end?

Mr. KOBZYSTYI: The Armed Forces of Ukraine defend our State every day and thwart the enemy’s plans. In particular, the President of Ukraine recently announced the complete liberation of the Dnipro region from the Russian occupiers. In addition, despite the permanent false statements of representatives of the Russian military corps, as of the end of August 2026, the Russian occupiers have not been able to completely capture Donbas.

This indicates Russia’s inability to advance further. They hide this inability behind the daily terror of the civilian population, because they know that there is nothing to catch on the battlefield. Every day, the Russian Federation launches dozens of ballistic missiles at peaceful neighborhoods of Ukrainian cities. What kind of readiness for the end of the war can we talk about?

We will be able to talk about when the war will end, when the fighting will cease. As you know, the Ukrainian side has repeatedly proposed holding negotiations on neutral grounds – in Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Qatar. However, Russia is not interested in negotiations, which is why every time they find new excuses not to accept President Zelensky’s proposals. Russia is only interested in capturing, killing, raping and stealing.

Unfortunately, this is exactly what the documented crimes of the Russian Federation in Bucha, Irpin, Olenivka, Kherson and a number of other Ukrainian cities testify to. People were killed, tortured, raped – all this solely because they are Ukrainians…

Q. How important is the mediation of other countries in the humanitarian issues of this war? Do you see the potential for involving Africa in the negotiation process on the humanitarian track?

Mr. KOBZYSTYI: We are grateful to all those who, to varying degrees, are joining in helping Ukraine and its citizens. This applies to both the states located on the same continental shelf with Ukraine, such as the states of the European Union, Norway, North Macedonia and others, and the United States of America, Canada, the states of South America, as well as Qatar, the UAE, Japan, and South Korea.

At the same time, we are convinced that the potential for involving African states in the humanitarian track in this regard is more than significant. First of all, we are talking about assistance in the return of Ukrainian children and the Coalition of the same name – unfortunately, the issue of abduction of children, their loss of ties with their family and homeland – many African states have gone through these trials and their experience in resolving complex humanitarian issues is extremely important right now, when thousands of Ukrainian children were illegally taken away by Russia and placed in foster families in the Russian Federation, which is one of the most egregious crimes of this war unleashed by the Russian Federation.

Q. How do you assess the current state of Ukrainian-Liberian relations?

Mr. KOBZYSTYI: Liberia is a friend and ally of Ukraine in the West African region in particular and on the African continent as a whole. Official Monrovia shares the same postulates as official Kyiv – respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states, as well as for human dignity and freedom, and this is what allows our countries to develop a mutually beneficial partnership.

At the same time, we are sure that we still have something to offer each other in a significant number of areas. For example, Ukraine remains open to students from African countries and Liberia in particular – the high quality of Ukrainian education is a well-known factor in African students choosing Ukraine as the country where they prefer to acquire new skills and competencies.

Currently, a simplified online system for submitting documents to Ukrainian higher education institutions is operating. We already have a significant number of students from West Africa who have received permits to enter Ukraine and are preparing for the start of the new academic year. We are convinced that the educational component is a solid foundation for the development of further cooperation.

In addition, we believe that the potential for cooperation in the field of agriculture remains untapped. Ukraine has unique experience and expertise, primarily in the context of crop management systems, GPS monitoring of equipment and precision agriculture. Moreover, all of the above is currently functioning during the period of active hostilities on the territory of Ukraine, which indicates the stability of the Ukrainian development system to external factors and the possibility of its implementation in states interested in the development of the agricultural sector.

Another important direction is the digitalization of state databases and systems for providing public services. Ukraine has something to offer in this regard, in particular in the light of the automation of the provision of certain consular services to Ukrainian citizens abroad (approximately 7-9 million people – ed. note), access to online state registers, etc.

Q. How does the Russian Federation operate in Africa? Have you encountered cases of disinformation directed against you?

Mr. KOBZYSTYI: The Russian Federation does not have a strategy specifically allocated to the African continent – Russia has always pursued the same policy towards everyone with whom it considers it necessary not to cooperate, but to exploit.

This is exactly how Russia cooperates with African states – it does not offer solutions, it sows discord and, in fact, does not hide it.

For example, almost on a monthly basis, we receive new information about African students who went to the Russian Federation to study, but ended up in the combat zone against their will – they are forced to sign a contract drawn up in Russian, that is, a language they do not even speak sufficiently. If they are lucky, they manage to surrender to the Armed Forces of Ukraine and not die. Unfortunately, such cases are rather an exception to the rule, because for the most part, those whom Russia uses as cannon fodder die in the first days of entering the front line – they are thrown into battle after a week of training.

From open sources, we know about cases of criminal recruitment by the Russian Federation in Kenya, Uganda, South Africa, and Zambia. In our region, citizens of Senegal, Gambia, Guinea, Sierra Leone, and Ghana have become victims of Russian manipulation. Fortunately, there is currently no information about citizens of Liberia who have become victims of Russian recruitment. We hope that this trend regarding Liberia will continue in the future, because it is very important to make it clear to the Russian Federation that, unlike Russia itself, people are not expendable in other countries.

Citizens of African countries should weigh all the risks when they come into contact with Russians. If there are any doubts, victims of Russian recruiters have repeatedly highlighted the nature of the Russian Federation’s attitude towards people (Malik Diop (Senegal), Richard Kanu (Sierra Leone), etc.). Think twice before signing up for certain death – until a contract with the Russian Armed Forces is signed, you will not find yourself on the battlefield. As soon as the contract is signed, you automatically become a war criminal who violates the territorial integrity and sovereignty of another state and falls under the relevant norms of international law. There is no way back.

As for disinformation, just as Russia hides its inability to advance on the battlefield in Ukraine, Russia hides its crimes behind manipulations and lies in the media. Ukrainian Embassies in Africa are constantly accused of recruiting local citizens, assembling drones right in the Embassies, looking for sorcerers who would poison Putin and his henchmen… This style is nothing new – Ukraine has coexisted and fought against Russia for survival for centuries, so we know very well how Russia seeks to eliminate rivals. But readers should be very careful with such narratives – our African partners have repeatedly debunked Russian lies (for example, in Ghana, when an agent of Russian influence placed Nazi literature on a shelf with Ukrainian books, or in Côte d’Ivoire, when the Russians invented a story about “assembling drones at the Ukrainian Embassy in Abidjan”), which indicates an increasingly better understanding by African countries of the deceitful nature of the Russian Federation.

Q. Turning to the prospects of bilateral relations between Liberia and Ukraine, what, in your opinion, should be the next steps on both sides for the further development of mutually beneficial interstate dialogue?

Mr. KOBZYSTYI: Ukraine and Liberia are partner countries. Countries that value and respect each other. And this is not only within the framework of international organizations, as I said above. In the bilateral direction, among other things, we are working on agreeing on the draft Agreement on the Establishment of a Joint Commission on Economic and Trade Cooperation between the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine and the Government of the Republic of Liberia, on the Memorandum of Understanding between the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine and the Ministry of Education of the Republic of Liberia on cooperation in the field of education, as well as on other equally important draft bilateral documents.

In addition, we continue to work on the possible organization of an official visit of the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Liberia, Ms. Sara Beysolow Nyanti, to Ukraine, within the framework of which both states could sign these documents and agree on other specific steps, as you say, of mutually beneficial cooperation between Ukraine and the Republic of Liberia.

These elements of the contractual and legal framework could form the basis, as you ask, of a new stage on the track of Ukrainian-Liberian relations.

World.title: The Inalienable Right to Justice: Embracing a Universal Ethos in Liberia’s Legal System
World.content:
Austin S Fallah: “Justice is not a slogan to be shouted in the streets or a weapon to be used against political opponents. In a nation governed by law, justice requires patience, evidence, due process, and respect for the courts. Liberia must learn to let the law speak louder than empty political rhetoric.”

Austin S Fallah: “The inalienable right to justice belongs to every Liberian, friend or foe, government official or ordinary citizen. We can not demand justice for ourselves while denying it to others. A truly democratic Liberia must embrace one universal standard of justice for all.”

Austin S Fallah: “When allegations arise, responsible citizens should seek truth through lawful institutions, not replace evidence with slogans or judgment with political excitement. Liberia’s strength will not be measured by how loudly we accuse one another, but by how faithfully we allow the law to take its course.”

Austin S Fallah: “Patriotism is not the reckless condemnation of another Liberian before the courts have spoken. Patriotism is respecting the Constitution, trusting due process, and demanding accountability without abandoning fairness. Let justice be pursued with courage, but also with restraint and dignity.“

Austin S Fallah: “A new Liberia cannot be built on rumor, political vengeance, or empty declarations of guilt. It must be built on the universal principle that no one is above the law and no one is beneath its protection. Let us replace slogans with substance, anger with wisdom, and accusations with evidence, and allow justice to take its rightful course.”

In the kaleidoscopic realm of social justice, where the principles of equality and equity contend for dominance, one question reverberates with alarming urgency: If justice is truly impartial, should feminism and gender sympathy inform its execution?

As a resurgent Liberia stands at the proverbial crossroads—with President Joseph Boakai, Vice President Koung, and the coalition government steering the ship —an opportunity looms that must not be squandered.

This moment, situated in the second quarter of the 21st century, is a call to arms for a modern understanding of justice that transcends the constraints of class, gender, and political influence.

It requires a vision of justice that flows unfettered across the vast expanse of our motherland, a vision as relentless and boundless as the Atlantic Ocean itself.

What is justice, if not an unyielding commitment to uphold the rights of every individual, regardless of their societal standing?

It is fundamentally an aporia to assert that laws should only serve the downtrodden.

To segment justice into comfortable compartments risks undermining its very essence.

True justice must be enshrined in the belief that it serves a pluralistic society; it should not be a mere balm for wounds but rather a clarion call for collective responsibility and universal dignity.

Thus, it is not sufficient for justice to cater only to specific groups, be they feminists, the economically disadvantaged, or marginalized communities, while ignoring the broader landscape of humanity.

Justice must resonate with everyone, transcending the divides engineered by economic disparity or social standing.

The contemporary challenges that Liberia faces necessitate a comprehensive re-evaluation of its legal framework.

Under the enlightened leadership of President Boakai, the effort to craft a just society is indeed a salutary ambition that can bear fruit if pursued with sincerity and introspection, as it has been in recent times and will continue.

Laws must be created to encompass all citizens, ensuring that justice does not become a mere playground for tribalism, partisan politics, sectionalism, or countyism.

Such barriers incite division among the citizenry, diluting the purpose of justice and turning it into a vitriolic tool weaponized by political maneuvering and power struggles, as has been done in the past.

The concept of justice as more than a partisan game must be deeply ingrained in Liberian consciousness.

Justice can not simply masquerade as an instrument for political advancement; it must be perceived as a stabilizing force in society.

This idea rejects the notion of selective justice, a concept that appears temporary and transient, more performative than substantive, as Liberians saw in the past.

Liberians must rally around the principle that true justice is devoid of favoritism, empty political slogans, good-for-nothing rhetoric, or partiality, becoming a bulwark against oppression and tyranny in all its forms.

Liberians must examine the dynamic relationship between feminism and justice.

While feminism must amplify women’s voices and address systemic gender inequalities, it must also be framed within universal justice.

A justice system informed by gender sympathy is vital; however, to assign it a singular and exclusive role risks alienating other marginalized experiences that co-exist within the socio-justice landscape.

It is a delicate balance that requires pursuing justice for oppressed demographics while avoiding apathy toward the struggles others face.

Achieving this is no simple undertaking, and it requires courage and commitment from leaders and society at large.

They must act not as arbiters of selective justice but as facilitators of equity for all.

The coalition government under the leadership of President Boakai and Vice President Koung has an invaluable opportunity to establish a judiciary that safeguards the rights of women and men, youths and elders, rich and poor alike, which they are doing.

The winds of change blowing through Liberia’s legal landscape are rife with potential, provided they are harnessed effectively and cascaded through policies and practices that reflect an earnest dedication to neutrality and fairness.

Moreover, the fight against drug trafficking and its criminal networks within Liberia exemplifies the urgency and necessity of an impartial justice system.

The drug cartels that have seeped into the fabric of society are a visceral reminder of the degenerative forces that threaten to undermine the nation; therefore, anyone criminally involved must be held to account.

To confront this challenge, Liberians must collectively confront these entities’ manipulation of justice.

A justice system that is equal for all citizens must approach crime through a lens of unwavering scrutiny.

Drug traffickers and their accomplices must reckon with the full weight of Liberian jurisprudence, uninhibited by questions of social hierarchy or political association.

Liberia stands poised to redefine its narrative, to be something more than a historic victim of division and strife.

By nurturing a contemporary legal framework, one that exists above the fray of commonplace prejudices, Liberians embrace a future rooted in justice that is both restorative and transformational.

Justice should not be an abstract ideal whispered within academic circles; it must permeate citizens’ everyday lives, reinforcing the bonds of community and kinship.

The pursuit of justice in Liberia must also encompass compassion and understanding, recognizing that pontificating ethics can not fill the void created by injustice.

It must push the boundaries of empathy and extend beyond superficial engagement.

The legal system must be as multi-faceted as the challenges Liberians face.

It requires every air-breathing Liberian at home and in the diaspora to engage dialectically, acknowledging and integrating diverse perspectives that repeatedly clash in the society.

In doing so, they cultivate a justice that is informed by the complexities of their lived experiences.

To expound on the notion of dual citizenship, both in terms of legal status and moral obligation, is essential when discussing this new dawn of governance.

Emphasizing mutual accountability encourages each citizen to uphold the civic principles of justice while remaining vigilant and proactive against injustices they witness.

Engaging through community outreach initiatives that foster dialogue among diverse segments of the population can mitigate the fears and grievances that often surface in the collective psyche.

Embracing this new wave of justice under the leadership of President Boakai and Vice President Koung demands more than a superficial commitment; it necessitates action.

Each citizen must also see themselves as a steward of justice, a guardian of their neighbors’ and compatriots’ well-being.

To cultivate a legal environment conducive to true justice requires a long-term investment in education, positive advocacy, and unremitting diligence.

The very fabric of justice in Liberia hangs in the balance.

It can become a tool for selective justice or a profound catalyst for unity and equity.

The opportunity to forge a new path has emerged at a critical juncture in our history.

Let us champion a justice system robust enough to encompass individuals from all walks of life, unraveling the chasms formed by tribalism and systemic oppression and promoting a collective sense of responsibility.

Together, everyone must see justice flow like the bountiful tides of the Atlantic Ocean, limitless, unyielding, and impartial, until it envelops the very essence of the nation and identity.

Only then can Liberians truly dare to call ourselves a society committed to justice for all.

World.title: Stakeholders welcome National Carbon Registry launch
World.content:
BioCarbon Partners Chief Executive Officer Nic Mudaly, says the launch of Zambia’s National Carbon Registry will strengthen transparency, accountability and confidence in the country’s growing carbon market.

Mr Mudaly told the media that a robust national registry will provide greater visibility of carbon projects and credits being developed in Zambia, helping to build confidence among project developers, communities, buyers, investors and other stakeholders.

He noted that the registry is also critical towards supporting the integrity of Zambia’s carbon market by improving coordination and transparency across the sector.

He pointed out that Zambia’s developing carbon market presents an opportunity to mobilise climate financing at scale and channel investment, into projects that deliver measurable benefits for both people and nature.

“As Zambia seeks to attract increased climate finance, the regulatory and institutional framework must continue evolving to support high-quality carbon projects, protect environmental integrity and ensure benefits reach local communities,” added Mr Mudaly.

He also said a well-functioning National Carbon Registry will be an important component of Zambia’s broader climate and development ambitions, while providing greater confidence to international carbon-credit buyers.

Mr Mudaly has since welcomed the continued development of Zambia’s carbon market and pledged to work with government and other stakeholders to strengthen systems that can unlock the potential of climate finance for the country.

Meanwhile, Environmental Activist Conwell Hakapya says the establishment of Zambia’s National Carbon Registry will strengthen the regulation and standards governing carbon trading in the country.

Mr Hakapya said that the Registry is an important intervention that will bring proper regulation and oversight to Zambia’s growing carbon market, which has operated without a comprehensive national registry for some time.

He said the Registry will also contribute to climate action by ensuring that carbon trading activities are properly monitored and managed, while supporting environmental protection.

Mr Hakapya having a national framework for carbon trading would help Zambia maximise the benefits of the carbon market, while ensuring that environmental considerations remain at the center of such activities.

“Zambia needs to strengthen its preparedness for a possible El Niño weather phenomenon. The country has an opportunity to improve on its preparedness by drawing lessons from previous El Niño experiences and adopting strategic measures to respond to climate-related risks,” he added.

He suggested that preparedness should include strengthening climate-risk awareness and adaptation measures across key sectors to enable the country to respond quickly to changing climatic conditions.

Mr Hakapya further called for continued investment in climate resilience and diversification of energy sources to reduce the impact of climate-related shocks on the country.

The Ministry of Green Economy and Environment, recently launched the National Carbon Registry, marking a major historic milestone in Zambia’s efforts to regulate carbon trading, strengthen climate action and attract climate finance through a transparent and accountable carbon market.

World.title: PIDACC boosts Mwinilunga mechanisation
World.content:
Government through the Program for Integrated Development and Adaptation to Climate Change (PIDACC) with support from the African Development Bank (AfDB) has over the last one year handed over an assortment of agriculture mechanisation equipment to three wards in Mwinilunga District of North-western Province.

The equipment which include three tractors, three rippers with calter and crumbler, three maize shellers, three Boom sprayers, three multicrop planters and three trailers have been procured at the cost of overK5.1 million.

District Agricultural Coordinator Lewis Chiwele said the agricultural equipment has been distributed to Chibwika, Ntambu and Kakoma wards to support farmers and build resilience against the effects of climate change.

Mr Chiwele explained that the equipment has brought about agricultural efficiency as farmers are now able to prepare their fields, harvest and shell their crop within a short period of time while implements such as trailers are being used to transport their farm produce to markets and satellite depots.

“This program has proven that this support can improve the efficiency of our farming operations, most of our farmers have had challenges to prepare their land, to harvest, to shell, now with this support our farmers are able to save time” he said.

He said the program is equally critical in contributing to the government’s target of 10 million metric tonnes of annual maize production by 2031 adding that farmers in the three wards are eager to utilize the equipment to increase their agricultural productivity.

Boaz Mukanzu a farmer in Kamfumbu area of Chibwika ward thanked the government for implementing the PIDACC project stating that it has afforded him efficiency and reduced production cost.

Mr Mukanzu said using the machinery, he was able to cultivate over three hectares within a day and shell his maize on time which previously took him months to do.

“We thank the government because this project has significantly reduced our manual labour and we now can shell maize or cultivate as much as three hectares in a day,” he said.

The PIDACC project targets to build resilience in farmers that are vulnerable to effects of climate change through mechanisation in communities along the Zambezi river basin.

World.title: Greece, Rwanda congratulate President Hichilema on re-election
World.content:
Presidents of Greece and Rwanda have congratulated President Hakainde Hichilema on his re-election as President of the Republic of Zambia.

President of the Hellenic Republic (Greece) Constantine Tassoulas expressed confidence that the bilateral relations between Greece and Zambia will be further strengthened to the mutual benefit of the two peoples.

And in a separate congratulatory message, Rwandan President Paul Kagame has congratulated President Hichilema on his re-election and commended the government and people of Zambia on the successful conduct of the general elections.

This is according to statements made available to the media.

The messages from the two Heads of State, add to local and international congratulatory messages extended to President Hichilema following his re-election on August 17, 2026.

World.title: Over 9,400 Cattle vaccinated against CBPP in Northern Province
World.content:
The Department of Veterinary Services in Northern Province has vaccinated 9,404 cattle against the Contagious Bovine Pleuropneumonia (CBPP), in Mbala and Senga Hill Districts.

The ongoing exercise represents a 41.5 percent coverage of the department’s total target of 22,655.

Mbala District Veterinary Officer, Goliath Zulu, told the media in an interview that the department received 23,000 doses of the CBPP vaccines for the operation.

Dr Zulu, revealed that the exercise commenced on August 9 and is expected to conclude during the third week of September 2026.

“Northern Province received 23,000 doses of CBPP vaccines for Mbala and Senga Hill districts, and the vaccination exercise commenced on August 9, 2026.So far we have vaccinated 9,404 cattle achieving 41.5 percent coverage against 22,655 target,” Dr Zulu explained.

He clarified that the annual exercise is only targeting high risk areas which are the two districts.

The Veterinary officer stated that the exercise aims to prevent animal disease outbreaks, noting that the province remains free of any current outbreaks and is on track with preventive measures.

Dr Zulu urged farmers to cooperate with extension officers by bringing their animals for the activity and encouraged them to report any animal health challenges.

World.title: Inauguration preps underway
World.content:
Rehabilitation works at the National Heroes Stadium in Lusaka are expected to be complete, in readiness for the inauguration ceremony for President—elect Hakainde Hichilema.

Ministry of Youth, Sports and Arts Principle Public Relations Officer Nchimunya Ng’andu disclosed that the government is procuring a turf protector from South Africa, to safeguard the grounds, indicating that works are progressing well.

Mr Ng’andu confirmed this to journalists at the National Heroes Stadium in Lusaka, shortly after a delegation led by Deputy Secretary to the Cabinet Oliver Kalabo inspected the facility and were impressed with works done so far.

The PPRO highlighted that the works on the project which is being implemented through a multi-sectoral approach began in June, this year in preparation for the inauguration.

He further revealed that Secretary to the Cabinet Patrick Kangwa is expected to inspect the facility on Friday, August 28th, 2026 .

World.title: Mufulira earns walkover win over Diggers
World.content:
The Zambia Rugby Union (ZRU) has controversially awarded National League leaders Mufulira a 21-0 walkover win over Kitwe giants Diggers after the latter failed to provide a venue for their rescheduled match.

The decision has sparked debate in rugby circles with the league now past its mid-point.

According to ZRU Director of Rugby, George Funga, Diggers were unable to host the game at their home ground and did not secure an alternative.

“Diggers said they were unable to host the match. We told them to find an alternative venue after learning that their home ground was not available for this game,” Funga said.

As a result, the union awarded *free points to defending champions Mufulira.

However, Diggers Chairperson Sam Lukonde has described the ruling as “strange”, arguing his club was not properly informed.

“There was nothing on the fixture relating to that game,” Lukonde said.

The walkover has strengthened Mufulira’s grip on top spot.

Mufulira now leads the National League with 35 points from eight matches, seven points clear of second-placed Red Arrows.

Diggers remain 5th on 14 points from eight games.

In the other rescheduled fixture, former league champions Red Arrows edged Buffaloes 26-22.

Arrows’ points came from two tries, three penalties, one drop goal and two conversions.

Buffaloes responded with one converted try and five penalties.

The Soldiers, who have a game in hand, sit on 22 points after seven games.

With the 2026 league campaign now at the mid-point, the title race is shaping up between Mufulira and Red Arrows, while Diggers will look to recover ground amid the controversy.

Co-Presidents of the Republic of Nicaragua, Daniel Ortega Saavedra and Rosario Murillo, have congratulated President Hakainde Hichilema on his re-election as President of Zambia.

The Nicaraguan leaders have said that President Hichilema’s re-election reaffirms the confidence that the Zambian people have in President Hichilema’s leadership and guidance of the country.

World.title: Lesotho, Eswatini congratulate President Hichilema
World.content:
The governments and people of Lesotho and Eswatini have congratulated President Hakainde Hichilema on his re-election as President of Zambia.

The government and people of the Kingdom of Lesotho, through its Embassy in Addis Ababa, congratulated the people of Zambia for exercising their democratic right and wished President Hichilema success as he assumes the renewed responsibility of leading the country.

The Embassy expressed confidence that President Hichilema’s second term will further deepen the fraternal relations between Zambia and Lesotho for the mutual benefit of the two peoples, stating that the strengthened relations will also contribute to regional integration, peace, stability and sustainable development in Southern Africa.

The Embassy noted that Zambia and Lesotho share longstanding bonds of friendship, solidarity and cooperation, anchored on the two country’s common membership of the Southern African Development Community (SADC), African Union (AU) and other multilateral institutions.

Meanwhile, King Mswati III of Eswatini, who is the current Chairperson of the SADC Organ on Politics, Defence and Security Cooperation (Troika), has also congratulated President Hichilema on his re-election.

In a message conveyed on behalf of the King and people of Eswatini, King Mswati III extended heartfelt congratulations to President Hichilema and the people of Zambia on the electoral victory.

The King expressed confidence that Zambia will continue to enjoy peace and tranquility under President Hichilema’s leadership.

He said Eswatini was ready to strengthen the bonds of friendship between the two countries for the mutual benefit and enrichment of their peoples.

King Mswati III also wished the people of Zambia continued progress and prosperity.

World.title: Congo-Brazzaville: Congo's Wealth Is Not Yet Power
World.content:
guest column

Across Africa, the decisive economic contest lies between raw material and finished product. For cotton, it is the distance from fibre to fabric. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, it is the distance from mineral and hydropower wealth to electricity, industrial capacity and productive work. The sectors differ, but the development question is the same: who captures the value created between extraction and the final product?

The Democratic Republic of Congo contains a startling share of the raw materials on which the modern economy depends. It is the world’s leading producer of cobalt. It has vast copper deposits, one of the planet’s great river systems and a population of roughly 100 million people, most of them young. On a map of the energy transition, the country appears indispensable.

On a map of lived prosperity, it looks very different. Only about 21 per cent of Congolese people have access to electricity, according to the World Bank. Poverty remains deep, insecurity persistent and the state distant or predatory for many citizens. The country’s most important economic question is therefore not how much wealth lies beneath its soil or runs through its rivers. It is whether that wealth can be converted into power, production and broadly shared opportunity.

That distinction separates endowment from development. Congo has never lacked resources. It has lacked the durable institutions and infrastructure that allow resources to become public value.

An extractive inheritance

The origins of that failure reach back to the formation of the state itself. Under King Leopold II, the Congo Free State became synonymous with forced labour and brutal extraction. Coercive labour practices persisted after Belgium assumed direct colonial rule in 1908, and a genuinely free labour market emerged only slowly before independence in 1960, according to academic research cited in the original manuscript.

The colonial economy was designed to remove value and administer territory, not to cultivate a broad Congolese political, managerial and technical class. At independence, the country inherited immense land and mineral wealth but little indigenous administrative capacity. A World Bank historical assessment cited in the manuscript describes both the shortage of trained Congolese personnel and Belgium’s effort to retain influence through technical advisers placed alongside key officials.

The crisis that followed independence, the assassination of Patrice Lumumba, Mobutu Sese Seko’s long authoritarian rule and the Congo wars deepened those institutional weaknesses. Mobutu did not invent the extractive state, but his personalised system entrenched it: institutions weakened, patronage expanded and public resources served political survival. Later conflicts and regional interventions fragmented authority further and allowed armed groups to flourish.

This history matters not because it condemns Congo to failure, but because it explains why geology alone has proved such a poor development strategy. Resources create possibilities. States, markets and public institutions determine who captures them.

From quarry to factory

The scale of the opportunity is nonetheless exceptional. The US Geological Survey estimated that in 2024 the DRC accounted for about 75 per cent of global cobalt production and roughly 55 per cent of global reserves. It was also the leading producer of tantalum and among the leading producers of copper, diamonds, tin and other strategic minerals.

These materials sit inside the energy, electronics, telecommunications, defence and manufacturing supply chains that are reshaping global commerce. Yet the familiar model remains one in which the highest-value activity occurs elsewhere. Minerals are extracted in Congo; more sophisticated processing and manufacturing take place abroad.

The policy choice is often described as one between exporting minerals and exporting products. But moving from one to the other requires more than declaring an industrial ambition. Copper processing, battery materials, electrical equipment, construction inputs, machinery and chemicals all require dependable electricity, transport, skills, capital, enforceable contracts and access to markets.

The real transition, then, is not simply from “quarry” to “factory”. It is from an extractive system to a productive one. The measure of success is not how many tonnes leave the ground, but how much capability, employment and domestic value are created before they leave the country.

The river and the grid

Congo’s most consequential industrial asset may be the one that flows through it. The Congo River and its tributaries give the country extraordinary hydropower potential. The Inga site alone has an estimated capacity of about 42,000 megawatts, which the World Bank describes as one of the world’s largest hydropower opportunities.

That number is dazzling. The national power deficit is sobering. With electricity reaching only about one in five people, the first claim on Congo’s hydropower future must be domestic: households, schools, clinics, farms and businesses that cannot develop without reliable power. The country’s National Energy Compact aims to raise access to 62 per cent by 2030, potentially reaching about 82 million people, according to the World Bank.

Power is also the bridge between Congo’s mineral base and its industrial ambitions. A processing plant cannot run on geological promise. Mines, smelters, factories and cities need generation connected to functioning transmission and distribution networks. The Inga opportunity therefore cannot be judged only by installed capacity. It must be judged by whether electricity reaches Congolese users reliably and affordably.

Regional trade could extend the value of that system. The DRC participates in the Southern African Power Pool, and electricity from Inga has historically been supplied to countries including South Africa and Zimbabwe. The World Bank has identified stronger transmission links between Inga, Zambia and the wider southern African market as strategically important.

The proposed Inga 3 project illustrates both the promise and the uncertainty. World Bank analysis cited in the manuscript places its possible generation between 2 and 11 gigawatts, depending on the final design. Congo’s position could eventually allow power to move across southern, central and eastern African pools. But “could” is the operative word. Regional electricity trade depends on finance, transmission lines, credible contracts, regulatory alignment and political confidence—not capacity estimates alone.

World Bank/ Ai Generated Congo at the centre. Country and river geometry: Natural Earth.

Europe’s interest, Congo’s choice

The strongest European connection is not a speculative cable from the Congo River to European homes. It is the prospect of a different industrial relationship. Europe seeks secure supplies of critical minerals and lower-carbon industrial inputs. Congo needs energy, jobs and greater value addition.

If renewable power can be combined with copper, cobalt and other minerals, Congo could produce more of the intermediate goods required by the energy transition. That would allow trading partners to buy higher-value Congolese output rather than raw material alone.

But the arrangement will be developmental only if industrial capacity takes root inside Congo. Supply security for foreign buyers is not the same as prosperity for Congolese citizens. The terms of contracts, the distribution of rents, local skills, environmental safeguards and the strength of domestic suppliers will decide whether a new mineral boom merely modernises extraction or changes the structure of the economy.

A young country needs work

The urgency is demographic. A World Bank assessment cited in the manuscript estimates that almost 65 per cent of the population is under 25. About 22 million people were aged 15 to 24 in 2025; that figure is projected to reach roughly 26 million by 2030. About a third of young people are neither in education, employment nor training, while roughly 40 per cent struggle to find work.

A young population is neither automatically a dividend nor inevitably a danger. It becomes an economic advantage when education, electricity, investment and functioning markets allow people to be productive. Without those conditions, demographic scale can intensify exclusion and instability.

This is why Congo’s industrial debate must be about jobs as much as exports. Capital-intensive mining can generate revenue without employing people on the scale the country requires. Processing, construction, energy, logistics, agriculture, services and regional manufacturing offer a broader employment base—but only if skills policy and industrial policy are designed together.

Peace as economic infrastructure

No such strategy can succeed while conflict continues in the east. Violence is first a human catastrophe. It is also a destruction of economic possibility: roads go unbuilt, schools are disrupted, responsible investment becomes harder and informal or illicit systems gain ground.

The IMF has identified governance weaknesses, mineral dependence, youth exclusion, conflict and the regional dimensions of insecurity among the DRC’s drivers of fragility. The implication is that peace cannot be treated as a security file isolated from economic policy.

The DRC and its neighbours have a material interest in replacing the economics of conflict with the economics of connection. Electricity links, roads, railways, ports, digital networks, agricultural value chains and lawful cross-border trade can raise the opportunity cost of destabilisation. Integration is no guarantee of peace. But an economy organised around shared production and exchange offers a stronger foundation than one organised around contested extraction.

Finance, and the test of delivery

Development institutions have begun to finance parts of this agenda. As of September 2023, the African Development Bank’s active DRC portfolio consisted of 27 operations worth about $1.45bn across transport, information and communications technology, energy, water and sanitation, and agriculture. Its 2023–2028 country strategy focuses on industrialisation, employment, infrastructure, agricultural value chains, human capital and the business environment.

The energy commitments cited in the manuscript include $22.4mn in parallel AfDB financing alongside $73.1mn of World Bank support approved in 2014 for Inga-related technical assistance. In December 2024, the AfDB was appointed mandated lead arranger for the $340mn Moyi Power Metro-Grids project, intended to bring cleaner, more reliable electricity to more than one million people in three cities.

These commitments show that Congo’s needs are recognised. They do not, by themselves, prove transformation. Portfolios, strategies and mandates are inputs. The meaningful outputs are functioning grids, reliable transport, competitive firms, transparent institutions and work that pays.

The missing chain

Congo’s agenda is often presented as a list: better mining contracts, more roads and rail, stronger security, technical education, regional power links, a better business climate. Each item is necessary. The more difficult insight is that they are interdependent.

Electricity without transmission cannot power a factory. A railway without predictable freight may not be financeable. Mineral processing without skills and reliable energy will not compete. Investment without accountable institutions can reproduce the very extractive bargain Congo needs to escape. Peace without legal economic opportunities may remain fragile.

The country therefore needs more than projects. It needs a sequence: secure productive regions; improve public institutions and contract transparency; expand electricity access and transmission; connect mines, farms and cities to markets; build technical capabilities; and use mineral and energy policy to support industries that can compete.

None of this is quick. Nor is it guaranteed. The same resources that make Congo strategically valuable also intensify struggles over rents and influence. Large infrastructure can create debt, displacement and governance risks if projects are badly designed. Regional interconnection creates opportunity, but it also requires patient diplomacy and institutions able to enforce agreements.

Yet the alternative is not stasis. Global demand for strategic minerals is placing Congo closer to the centre of the world economy. The country can remain indispensable as a source of raw materials while its citizens remain excluded from the value those materials create. Or it can use this moment to negotiate a more productive bargain.

The real test will not be whether the Democratic Republic of Congo finally “wakes”. Countries are not giants in fairy tales. They are political economies, built through choices and constrained by institutions.

Congo already has the assets. What it has not yet secured is the chain that joins them: peace to investment, power to production, minerals to industry, and national wealth to household prosperity. Building that chain would not merely alter Congo’s fortunes. It could change the economic geography of Africa.

World.title: Kenya: Gachagua Rules Out Ruto Alliance Deal, Says 'I Cannot Be Bought'
World.content:
Nairobi — DCP leader Rigathi Gachagua says he was ready to carry the opposition ticket if fellow leaders chose him, insisting that he would remain firm despite political pressure.

Speaking at his Wamunyoro residence when he had a consultative meeting with delegates from Isiolo, Gachagua ruled out working with Ruto, saying he could neither be bribed nor intimidated into joining the President's political camp.

"I saw yesterday that he said something very good during an interview. He said, "I am ready to work with any leaders except Riggy G. It is not that he does not want to work with me; it is because he knows it is impossible."

"I cannot take his money. He cannot bribe me. He cannot intimidate me. He cannot overthrow me. He has raised his hand against me and attacked me politically; it is impossible," Gachagua stated.

He said he was willing to work with other opposition leaders and urged them to unite around a common candidate.

"Kasongo, you have done well by telling Kenyans that you cannot work with Riggy G. So, for all those Kenyans who do not want Kasongo, there is now someone to rely on, because I am committed to making sure William Ruto serves only one term, and he knows this, because he knows me very well," the former DP stressed.

Gachagua warned politicians who accept Ruto's overtures that they would have to proceed without expecting their supporters to follow.

He maintained that his commitment was to remove Ruto from power through the ballot.

"I want to tell my colleagues in the opposition, that should you accept his invitation to work with him. be aware that you will go alone, Kenyans will not follow you, If you go to William Ruto, go alone," he added.

World.title: Somalia: Supreme Court Annuls Galmudug Election Results
World.content:
Galmudug, officially Galmudug State, is an autonomous region in central Somalia.

Somalia's Federal Supreme Court has annulled the Galmudug election results. The court made the ruling on Monday. Judges found that the July 30 vote broke the constitution and the electoral law. Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed announced the decision in Mogadishu. He also ordered a new election.

This ruling matters for Somalia. Galmudug held its first direct election on July 30. The Galmudug election results are now void. That raises new doubts about Somalia's shift to one-person, one-vote elections. It also adds strain between Mogadishu and Galmudug's leaders.

What the Court Decided

Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed announced the ruling after judges heard the case. They reviewed the evidence closely. Baashe said the vote broke Somalia's constitution.



"The elections were not administered in line with the constitution and the electoral law," Baashe said, according to the court's statement.

Judges said the errors could not be fixed. They said the errors damaged the vote's integrity. That damage reached the final results, the court said.

Why the Galmudug Election Results Were Voided

The July 30 election was a big moment for Galmudug. It was the state's first direct vote. Citizens picked local council members and state lawmakers.

Voting took place in 11 districts. Those districts sit in the Mudug and Galgaduud regions.

However, tension built for months before the vote. Federal officials and Galmudug's government disagreed on how to run the process. Critics also questioned the election body's independence.

As a result, judges found the flaws too serious. They chose to void the whole result instead of a partial fix.

What Happens Next in Galmudug

The court gave clear orders. It told Somalia's electoral commission, the NIEBC, to hold a new vote. It said the commission must act soon.

The new vote must follow the constitution and the electoral law. It must also follow related rules. Until then, the Galmudug election results remain void.

Meanwhile, current Galmudug officials will stay in their posts. This avoids a gap in local government. New, lawfully elected officials will replace them later.





Political Stakes for Somalia's Federal System

Galmudug is no stranger to political disputes. Its leaders and Mogadishu have clashed before over power and elections. This ruling reopens old tensions at a fragile time.

This is the first time Galmudug election results have been annulled since direct voting began. Somalia's federal government wants direct voting nationwide. Galmudug was only the second state to try it, after Southwest State. So a failed vote here matters beyond Galmudug's borders.

Close 

Meanwhile, Somalia is also preparing for national elections. Tensions between federal and state leaders remain high. As a result, many will watch closely to see if the rerun goes smoothly.

Learn more from the National Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission and the UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia.

World.title: Somalia: Six Million Somalis Face Acute Hunger As Drought and Conflict Worsen
World.content:
Six million people in Somalia are facing acute hunger, with nearly two million children at emergency levels, as severe drought, conflict and falling humanitarian funding deepen what the UN describes as one of the world's worst malnutrition crises. Medical charity MSF tells RFI it's sounding the alarm "before it's too late".

The World Food Programme (WFP), the UN agency providing food assistance, said around one third of Somalia's population is now facing acute hunger, with nearly two million children expected to suffer from acute malnutrition this year.

"Those are not abstract figures: they are families exhausting every option they have left to survive," the WFP said.

More than 200,000 people were displaced during the second quarter of 2026 as the country faced severe drought. Poor rainfall over several seasons has led to water shortages, crop failures and livestock losses.



Higher fuel and food prices, made worse by the conflict in the Middle East, have added to the pressure.

Somalia is also facing an insurgency by the Islamist al-Shabaab group and localised armed clashes.

Fears mount over resurgence of Al-Shabaab jihadists in Somalia

'Extreme' food shortages

The situation is particularly difficult in camps for displaced people in Baidoa, in the south-west of the country, where medical charity Doctors Without Borders (MSF) is working.

MSF said one in two children in the camps was suffering from acute malnutrition, while one in four had severe acute malnutrition. One third of families are surviving on just one meal a day, MSF said.

The charity is also concerned about a lack of funding to respond to the crisis.

More than 80 percent of the number of patients admitted to its nutrition programme last year had already been admitted by this point in 2026, said MSF health adviser Mitchell Sangma.

"What is worrying is not only the numbers, but also the severity of these cases. These are very sick children, suffering from many medical complications," he told RFI.

"They arrive at a very advanced stage after having gone hungry for many months, and we are now seeing the consequences of the extreme food shortage."

Many are also suffering from epidemic diseases such as measles and diphtheria, he said.

Under the same sky, climate change brings drought to Somalia and floods to Kenya

Long queues for food and water

Children treated in hospital are often readmitted after returning to camps where they have insufficient food and no access to safe drinking water, Sangma noted.

Close 

"Many are suffering from epidemic diseases, such as measles or diphtheria, which is very worrying. We receive these children, we treat them in our hospitals, we allow them to leave, but they end up being readmitted because they return to the same environment where they do not have access to enough food or safe drinking water," he said.

"It's very visible when you walk through the camps early in the morning. We see long lines of people with jerry cans waiting to receive water. Long lines of patients are waiting outside mobile clinics for their children to be treated. We are trying to sound the alarm about what we are seeing on the ground before it is too late."

Funding shortages

Humanitarian aid is struggling to meet the needs as international funding falls.

The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), the global system used to measure hunger, estimated in May that food assistance was reaching just 12 percent of the six million people facing acute food insecurity.

More than 200 health and nutrition centres have closed, the United Nations Children's Fund (Unicef) said, describing the budget cuts as "unprecedented".

At the same time, the El Nino climate pattern, which is expected to be strong, threatens to bring very heavy rainfall to Somalia towards the end of the year, increasing the risk of flooding.

This article was adapted from the original in French and has been lightly edited for clarity.

World.title: Zambia: Hichilema Wins a Stronger Mandate, but Zambia's Democratic Test Isn't Over
World.content:
analysis

Late reforms and weak checks on power expose democratic fault lines and raise the stakes for Hichilema's second term.

Zambia's 13 August election delivered a second five-year term for President Hakainde Hichilema. With last-minute changes to electoral law and a fragmented opposition, the result was not unexpected.

Hichilema secured 60.5% of the vote, against National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) candidate Brian Mundubile's 37.8%. The expanded National Assembly now has 226 directly elected members (up from 156) plus 40 proportional representation (PR) seats reserved for women, youth and people with disabilities. Constitutionally, the president can appoint up to 11 MPs, bringing the total to 277 seats.



So far, Hichilema's United Party for National Development (UPND) has won 138 seats, the NRPUP 60, with independents and smaller parties winning the rest. With the UPND's presidential seats and expected 24 of the 40 PR seats, the ruling party has 160 (62% of the house). Even so, the opposition retains a substantial bloc.

Roughly 57% of registered voters participated, down substantially from 70% in 2021 - likely reflecting living-cost frustrations and unequal campaign conditions.

Other issues also marred the polls, among them a 14 August raid by Zambian security forces on a Lusaka property, in which former transport minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was shot and killed. Eleven people, including senior opposition figures, were arrested for possessing military-grade weapons for an armed insurrection. Mundubile denied the claims, but he and senior opposition figures now face treason charges.

There is a striking coincidence between this situation and Hichilema's arrest after the 2016 election for allegedly endangering the president by obstructing his motorcade. Hichilema was held in a maximum-security facility for over 100 days until the Commonwealth intervened. The Commonwealth Secretariat has again expressed concern over the current post-election climate.

Several election observers noted that Zambia held a largely peaceful vote - but on an uneven playing field. The European Union (EU), Southern African Development Community and African Union-Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa missions all raised concerns about the implementation of last-minute electoral reforms.

The Constitutional Amendment Act No 13 (2025) created the new 226-seat parliamentary map. Allocations were done in April, with PR seats approved in May - three months before polling. Critics say adding most new constituencies in UPND-leaning rural areas benefitted the party.

Also, the PR system discouraged parties from nominating women for constituency seats, seeing seats reserved for women as a substitute for women's representation rather than being complementary. Female candidacy fell to 12.5% from 21.1% in 2021.

The change in electoral rules so close to the polls created uncertainty for parties, voters and election administrators (UPND was the only party to file a candidate for all available seats). The observer missions said electoral reform should strengthen competition, not leave the rules contested just before voting.

Hichilema's campaign also benefitted from his position as head of government. EU observers documented the use of state resources at campaign events and found that presidential and vice-presidential visits were exempt from the Electoral Commission of Zambia's (ECZ) five-day campaign timetable that applied to other candidates. Some unscheduled visits by Hichilema or his running mate resulted in opposition events being blocked or cancelled.

Transparency International Zambia's independent monitoring matched the ECZ's tallies within 1.1%, but flagged unsealed ballot boxes (which risk tampering) and delayed announcements in 32 of 221 constituencies checked. The Christian Churches Monitoring Group found turnout implausibly exceeding its estimates in 30 constituencies.

On 14 August, the ECZ suspended counting for around six hours over reports of violence against polling staff and theft of marked ballots. At the same time, Mundubile, citing his party's parallel count, pre-emptively claimed victory - a statement that ECZ warned candidates against making.

The NRPUP says it will challenge Hichilema's win in court, which could extend Zambia's transition period from seven to 15 days, as occurred after the closer 2016 polls. However, the 2026 winning margin is far larger - over a million votes (22.6%) compared to just over 100 000 (2.7%) in 2016. A recount probably wouldn't close that gap, and a costly court-ordered rerun would be disruptive.

The economic vote was likely decisive in giving Hichilema his second term. Although the president's macro-economic record on debt restructuring, lower inflation and improved relations with international lenders has not improved household welfare, more immediate and visible interventions gained traction among voters.

These include the Constituency Development Fund, which increased from K1.6 million ($84,160) per constituency in 2021 to K40 million (US$2.1 million) in 2026, higher student allowances at public universities, reduced power cuts and improved fertiliser payments in rural areas.

Mundubile's Tonse Alliance showed that anti-UPND sentiment could be consolidated into a real presidential challenge, inheriting strongholds of the former ruling Patriotic Front. The alliance's 60 parliamentary seats give it a base, but a coalition built mainly on opposing the incumbent doesn't constitute a governing alternative. Creating one requires a formal party structure with an agreed-upon line of succession, not centred on an individual.

Close 

A policy platform on jobs, energy and living costs that voters can organise around beyond opposing Hichilema is also vital. Finally, legal challenges to the election result must be based on evidence, not merely grievances, to prevent a court defeat that would cost the opposition what credibility it has left.

For the UPND, the stronger mandate gives the party the space to deliver on energy, jobs and living costs. It also creates a heavier duty to strengthen parliamentary scrutiny rather than rush legislation through with little debate, as occurred with the recent electoral reforms.

Zambia has shown democratic resilience, but the polls exposed real vulnerabilities. Hichilema enters his last term with a stronger mandate and fewer institutional checks on how he uses it. The test is no longer whether he can win elections, but whether he leaves behind a system that enables his successor to fairly compete in the democratic spirit the country is known for.

World.title: South Africa: World's Largest Research Funder Lifts Ban On South Africa
World.content:
The United States National Institutes of Health has lifted its ban nearly 18 months after an order to stop work with South Africa created a crisis for HIV and TB research.

Many clinical trials were halted, and many researchers were retrenched when the NIH stopped funding

The United States National Institutes of Health (NIH) has lifted its ban nearly 18 months after an order to stop work with South Africa.

The funding ban created a crisis for HIV and TB research, including NIH grants and US Agency for International Development aid.

Many of the world's major advances over the past two decades in understanding the science of HIV arose from South African scientists and from studies conducted here, the vast majority of them funded by the NIH.

The United States National Institutes of Health (NIH) has lifted its ban on South Africa, nearly 18 months after its February order to stop work with South Africa created a crisis for HIV and TB research.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

In January 2025, the United States began halting funding of South African projects, including NIH grants and US Agency for International Development (USAID) aid.

The scientific journal, Science, reported that an internal memo dated 17 August, signed by NIH director Jay Bhattacharya, had lifted the ban. We have since obtained the memo, which is marked "Not for distribution outside government". It states funding for "meritorious research projects" in South Africa may proceed.

The memo states that NIH grants are "distinct from the objectives traditionally associated with foreign aid or assistance".

A brief from May 2025 by Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders), US advocacy organisation Treatment Action Group, and the South African Medical Research Council (SAMRC) found that critical research initiatives and decades of investments in research infrastructure were affected by the NIH stop-work order.

The brief noted that research in South Africa, mostly led by South African scientists with NIH funding, has in the past two decades "shaped global health policies that have revolutionised TB and HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment and care, benefiting both the local population and communities worldwide, including people who live in the United States".

Ntobeko Ntusi, president and CEO of the South African Medical Research Council, confirmed that the decision comes after 12 months of negotiating with the NIH "to reverse their position on South Africa".

"Part of the mandate of the NIH to engage in international research collaborations should be viewed in light of the fact that South Africa is one of only few countries that co-funded biomedical research with the NIH, rather than merely being a recipient," said Ntusi.

"I welcome this apt decision of the NIH because no country can ever solve the challenges of global health alone ... We need scientific collaboration to drive scientific progress," he said.

Linda-Gail Bekker, director of the Desmond Tutu HIV Centre, said the centre had to retrench people when the funding stopped, since it was largely NIH funded. It had a partnership with NIH for decades.

Bekker said there has been a long hiatus from receiving research protocols from their networks in the US, such as the Advancing Clinical Therapeutics Globally (ACTG), HIV Vaccine Trials Network (HVTN), and others.

She said their networks are coming to the end of seven-year trials for their clinical trials units. "We haven't had confirmation that South Africa will be included. But we feel more optimistic than we did before," said Bekker.

She said they have received some funding from the SAMRC in reprieve of the lost NIH money but not anywhere close to the same volume.

In August 2025, the SAMRC announced that it had raised around R600-million in rescue funds to support research projects and groups affected by the cuts. This amount includes around R400-million from National Treasury, R100-million from the Gates Foundation, R100-million from the Wellcome Trust, and R14.4-million from the ELMA Foundation.

Bekker said the scientific advancements in South African HIV and TB research are also "good for the whole world" and the benefits have been "bidirectional".

Landon Myer, at UCT's School of Public Health, warned that South Africans should be "cautiously optimistic". He did not think things were going back to the way they were before NIH funding halted.

Close 

Myer said it was difficult to know what the memo means in practice. "Time will tell," he said.

Within the NIH there have been a large number of layoffs and resignations and budgets have been limited, possibly undermining their bureaucratic capacity, he said.

Myer confirmed Bekker's view that many of the world's major advances over the past two decades in understanding the science of HIV arose from South African scientists and from studies conducted here, the vast majority of them funded by NIH.

The memo also stated that the Fogarty International Center is "no longer supporting research training and career development applications from South Africa" due to SA being an upper-middle-income country. Myer said over decades the Fogarty training invested heavily in South African scientists which in turn led to so many "scientific accomplishments" here.

Co-published with Spotlight

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - August 24, 2026
World.content:
30 Killed as Rubbish Mound Collapses in Guinea

At least 30 people have been killed and 22 injured after a mound of rubbish collapsed onto homes at a major waste site in Conakry, Guinea, following heavy rain. Six of the injured are in serious condition. Fears remain that the death toll could rise. Rescue teams, including the military, have been searching through the debris with excavators for survivors. Prime Minister Mamadou Oury Bah visited the site to oversee the response. The government had recently ordered the expulsion of nearby residents in informal housing due to a fear of collapses . A similar landslide at the waste site killed 10 people in 2017.

DR Congo and M23 Rebels Agree on Peace Roadmap



The Democratic Republic of Congo government and the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group have agreed on a roadmap for peace talks after five days of negotiations in Switzerland. The deal includes a mechanism to monitor ceasefire violations and sets timelines for negotiations under a 2025 US-brokered peace framework. However, disagreements remain over sanctions, detainees and political reforms. The latest negotiations were attended by M23, the government of DR Congo, Qatar, the US, the Republic of Togo, the African Union Commission and host Switzerland. Fighting has continued in eastern DR Congo despite previous ceasefire commitments, with the conflict having killed thousands and displaced hundreds of thousands of people.

Mogadishu Home Demolitions Spark Clashes

The demolition of homes in Mogadishu's Tookiyo neighbourhood has sparked clashes between government forces and residents resisting the operation, with nearly 10 people reportedly injured. Authorities began demolishing homes as part of efforts to reclaim land considered government property. Residents have said that they have lived in the area for decades and are demanding clarity over land ownership and a proper legal process. Concerns are growing over further violence and displacement. The Somali government has yet to issue an official statement on the reported injuries.

Nigeria Police Rescue 75 Kidnap Victims

Nigerian police have rescued 75 people, including men, women and children, after they were kidnapped from commercial buses in Kaduna State. The victims, identified as Fulani travellers, were abducted by gunmen on August 19. They were held inside a cave in a mountainous forest near Birnin Gwari. Police, acting on intelligence from the local transport workers' union, raided the area and forced the kidnappers to flee, rescuing all 75 victims unharmed. Authorities urged residents to remain vigilant and share information with police while warning against vigilante action. They further warned members of the public against taking the law into their own hands, cautioning that vigilante actions or reprisals could escalate violence and result in the loss of innocent lives.

Close 

Mystery Elephant Deaths Alarm Kenya Conservationists

Since June, at least 20 elephants in Kenya's Amboseli ecosystem have died after developing symptoms of extreme weakness and paralysis, leaving conservationists and Maasai communities searching for answers. The Kenya Wildlife Service has said that toxicology tests found high levels of cyanide in some carcasses, raising suspicions of pesticide poisoning. However, local wildlife experts dispute the theory. They said that scavengers feeding on the carcasses have not shown signs of poisoning. Authorities have said that there is currently no evidence of an infectious disease. Investigations continue to determine what is killing the elephants.

World.title: South Africa: Cape Town Taxi Violence Sparks Talks - South African News Briefs - August 24, 2026
World.content:
Cape Town Taxi Violence Sparks Talks

The Western Cape Department of Mobility is engaging taxi industry stakeholders following a recent flare-up of taxi-related violence in Cape Town, reports EWN. Four men were killed and two wounded in two separate shootings. An informal trader was also shot dead at Dunoon Taxi Rank. The latest violence comes weeks after authorities mediated a deadly dispute between four taxi associations over routes in the southern suburbs. The department has said that it is working with stakeholders on measures to restore stability. The South African National Taxi Council (SANTACO) is attempting to facilitate peace talks between rival associations.

Three More Arrested Over Boxer Zolani Tete Murder



Eastern Cape police have arrested three more suspects in connection with the murder of former two-division boxing world champion Zolani Tete, reports SABC News. This brings the total number in custody to four. Tete, 38, was shot dead outside his home in Mdantsane. A 27-year-old woman travelling with him was wounded and remains in hospital. One of the suspects, a 22-year-old man, has been charged with murder and attempted murder and is due to appear in the Mdantsane Magistrate's Court. Police say further arrests are expected.

Steve Biko Death Inquest Set to Resume

The reopened inquest into the death of anti-apartheid activist Steve Biko is set to resume at the Gqeberha High Court, nearly five decades after he died in police custody, reports EWN. Biko was arrested in August 1977 and died weeks later from severe injuries sustained in custody. A 1977 inquest accepted the police account that he had been injured in a scuffle, and no one was prosecuted. The new inquest will examine whether any acts or omissions surrounding Biko's death amounted to criminal offences, potentially providing long-awaited answers to his family and the country.

MEXICAN NATIONAL FACES FEDERAL CHARGES AFTER CBP FINDS $238K IN FENTANYL INSIDE ELECTRIC MOPED

JEANINE PIRRO CALLS OUT 'DIRTBAGS' AFTER 14 CHARGED IN ALLEGED COCAINE RING OPERATING FEET FROM A SCHOOLYARD

World.title: Houston Uber driver caught in wild police chase as officers seen on dashcam video hitching a ride in his car

A Houston Uber driver was caught "off guard" but kept his cool when two police officers jumped into his vehicle and directed him to chase a suspect fleeing on foot, wild dashcam video shows.

Anthony Baines said he was driving for Uber at about 12:20 a.m. Aug. 8 in a Houston Heights neighborhood, when a shirtless man ran across the street in front of his vehicle with two Houston Police Department officers close behind, according to Storyful.

The video shows Baines getting waved down by an officer and stopping as she approaches and hops into the front passenger seat.

HANDCUFFED SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY SLIPS RESTRAINTS, STEALS DALLAS POLICE CRUISER WITH OFFICER TRAPPED IN BACK SEAT

"Hey, give me a ride over there please," the officer says in the video. "Go, go that way … go, go, go, go, go!"

Baines can be heard asking which way he should drive as officers point him in the direction of the suspect. After driving a short distance, the officer signals for her partner, who's carrying a flashlight, to get in the vehicle, too, and opens the car door and jumps into the backseat.

RIDESHARE PASSENGER HELD HOSTAGE FOR EIGHT HOURS DURING ARMED STANDOFF WITH POLICE IN SWANKY NEIGHBORHOOD

The officers rode with Baines for several minutes while searching the area before one of them appeared to spot the suspect. Both officers jump out of the Uber and resume their pursuit on foot.

"What the f---?!" Baines is heard saying as the officers dart from his car.

BODYCAM SHOWS POLICE K-9 LEAPING INTO ACTION AFTER SUSPECTED IMPAIRED DRIVER REFUSED TO SURRENDER

"It caught me completely off guard," Baines told Storyful. "I’ve never had anything like that happen driving. I was surprised but just did what the officer asked in the moment."

Houston police confirmed the authenticity of the video and the incident to KPRC 2, which reported officers had been responding to a terroristic threat call involving allegations that the suspect threatened to shoot a woman and her children after becoming upset over a belief that someone had stolen from him.

Police said officers tried to detain the man as he left an apartment, but he refused to cooperate and ran away. An officer asked the driver to take them around the block to the apartment complex, where the officers returned to their own vehicle, according to KPRC.

FLORIDA MAN ARRESTED IN IHOP RESTAURANT AFTER POLICE SAY HE STABBED A RIDESHARE DRIVER

Despite the unusual assistance, police did not locate the suspect. His identity has not been released, and the investigation remains ongoing.

Baines later appeared to confirm in a social media post that he was the Uber driver behind the dashcam footage.

"Yep, that was me," he wrote. "The Uber driver whose dashcam caught two HPD officers jumping in my car to chase a suspect."

World.title: Abdul El-Sayed grilled on past statements on Sharia law and White supremacy, taxing the rich
