World.title: Washington, D.C.'s first IndyCar race packed the National Mall
World.content:
Washington, D.C.'s first IndyCar race packed the National Mall

toggle caption Nathan Howard/Reuters

In the end, it was an American who took the crown.

The first-ever street race in the nation's capital ended with Florida native Kyle Kirkwood on the podium. He led 128 of the 147 laps, finishing with a commanding win.

toggle caption Chris Graythen/Getty Images

toggle caption Finn Gomez/Getty Images/Getty Images

toggle caption Aaron Schwartz/Reuters

Over the weekend, the Freedom 250 Grand Prix transformed some of the nation's most famous streets – Pennsylvania, Constitution, and Independence avenues – into a race track.

Tens of thousands of people packed into the National Mall to attend each day of the two-day event. There was no shortage of American flag paraphernalia: red, white and blue hats, shirts, earrings and dresses. Many in the crowds sported bald eagles splashed on bright shirts as well as "Freedom 250" merch. (And a real bald eagle flew over the racetrack during the singing of "God Bless America" before returning to its handler.)

toggle caption Tierney L. Cross/Reuters

toggle caption Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

toggle caption Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

toggle caption Allison Robbert/AP Photo/Allison Robbert/AP

toggle caption Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

toggle caption Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images

toggle caption Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

"Oh man — patriotic and electric," Cameron Graves said, describing the energy at the event. Graves wore American flag pants and a Freedom 250 shirt and hat. He already had a front row seat by 8:15am on Sunday.

Sponsor Message

Pre-race celebrations were filled with pomp and circumstance. There were multiple flyovers and military bands flooded the racetrack. Before waving the green start flag, President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump took a ceremonious lap in Trump's armored car, nicknamed "The Beast." Crowds cheered and chanted "U.S.A."

toggle caption Tierney L. Cross/Reuters

toggle caption Doug Mills/Pool/The New York Times/AP

toggle caption Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images

toggle caption Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

toggle caption Jacquelyn Martin/AP

toggle caption Mike Kropf/Getty Images

The Freedom 250 Grand Prix was pulled together in just seven months – a relatively short period of time to overcome security issues, satisfy permit requirements and address safety issues. Over 200 manhole covers had to be welded down because otherwise they could be road hazards.

The race brought people together from across the country. Devoted IndyCar fan Mick Bryant, a dealer of collectibles, including IndyCar cards, came from Greenfield, Ind. He was decked out in a full black-and-white checkered outfit down to his socks.

"I'll tell you what, I've been going to the [Indianapolis] 500 for decades... and I still get goosebumps," Bryant said. "There's nothing like it. I just love the sound. Love the smell."

Kathleen Lazorchack and her husband travelled from West Virginia for the race. Lazorchack is a director at Summit Point Motorsports Park. She said the best part about motorsports is the people.

"If you ever have an opportunity to walk through the paddock and talk to people, it'll make your hair stand up on your arms," Lazorchack said.

Sponsor Message

Along with the longtimers, there were also brand new fans.

toggle caption Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

toggle caption Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

toggle caption Allison Robbert/AP

toggle caption Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

toggle caption Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

toggle caption Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

In the front row of the stands, Omar Saenz and his 14-year-old step-son Damien Macwithey were carrying racing helmets signed by drivers. They had traveled from Dallas, Texas for their first IndyCar race.

"It's like a bum rush of people," Damien said, holding his helmet tight in his lap with the protective wrapping still on it. "It's going to be very loud."

And it definitely was.

Michael Milton, a D.C. resident wearing a bald eagle hat, was struck by the thundering sounds at his first IndyCar race.

"It does something to you, right? It gets inside of you," Milton said as the cars shot by. "It's almost a visceral feeling."

toggle caption Gabriella Demczuk for NPR

toggle caption Gabriella Demczuk for NPR

toggle caption Gabriella Demczuk for NPR

The Grand Prix also received plenty of pushback. Some D.C residents were wary of one more stamp President Trump was putting on their city. Others complained about the traffic jams and parking restrictions in the runup to the event.

Johnny Ring, who lives in D.C. and was there with his husband, said he had mixed feelings. (He might have been the only person reading a book at the track before the race began.)

toggle caption Gabriella Demczuk

toggle caption Gabriella Demczuk for NPR

He was excited to view a once in a lifetime event, but said he also does not support the Trump administration.

"It feels like it's kind of shoved down our throats," said Ring. "But, you know, I want to be able to be kind of a little bit a part of history."

World.title: In candid interviews, National Guard members speak out about D.C. deployment
World.content:
In candid interviews, National Guard members speak out about D.C. deployment

toggle caption Illustration by Mari Fouz​ for NPR

As the sight of armed, uniformed National Guard troops became ubiquitous in Washington, D.C., over the past year, one voice has been notably absent from the public discourse around the deployment: the guard members themselves.

"I will say very frankly that the bad taste that this mission left in my mouth, it actually embarrasses me to be involved in any way," one guard member who was part of the deployment for several months recently told NPR.

Thousands of National Guard members have been patrolling the streets of Washington, D.C., for more than a year now, in what has become President Trump's largest and longest domestic military deployment. Their presence has become a common, and controversial, topic of conversation among D.C. residents and constitutional experts alike, raising concerns about the normalization of armed troops in a city for an extended period of time.

Sponsor Message

Members of the military are not allowed to speak to the press without authorization. Under this administration, those rules and the ramifications for breaking them have gotten even stricter.

But some members who are no longer a part of the mission have become more open to sharing their thoughts as the deployment enters its second year — and has been extended to the end of President Trump's term.

"I don't want to think about the National Guard. I don't want to necessarily discuss my affiliation with the National Guard. I don't want to fulfill my normal National Guard duties just because of the abuses of the National Guard in this D.C. mission," the guard member said, noting that isn't how he's felt after previous domestic deployments.

That guard member was one of three who spoke to NPR on the condition of anonymity because they are still serving and are barred from speaking publicly. All of them were deployed as part of the D.C. Safe and Beautiful mission for many months, and each has more than a decade of service.

In candid interviews, the guard members described their feelings throughout their time on the deployment, and their worries about the new norms it's establishing. They discussed the cost, which is expected to run into the billions. And they say they worry that Trump's unprecedented use of the troops is damaging the National Guard's reputation with the American public.

Sponsor Message

All were skeptical about the administration's original reason for the deployment — to help with law enforcement after declaring a "crime emergency", despite a 30-year low in violent crime in the city.

"Now, with it being a year, it's hard to feel like that justification holds any water," said one guard member. "It feels like the guard is being exploited in a sense."

Another said it feels more like a political stunt, pointing out the way the guard has been inserted into certain narratives by the administration, like being ordered to patrol the perimeter of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool following its faulty renovation.

toggle caption Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

"I hope that there will be some accounting someday — probably after President Trump is gone — about why we were there, and was it worth it? But none of that is gonna happen right now," that member said.

NPR reached out to both the White House and the D.C. Joint Task Force regarding the concerns raised by the guard members.

The White House responded by reiterating how safe D.C. is now, without providing evidence that the guard is responsible for decreasing crime.

In a statement, Brig. Gen. Leland Blanchard II, the interim commanding general of the D.C. National Guard, called the deployment "unique" and pointed to "significant accomplishments" that guard members contributed in the past year, including assisting law enforcement with apprehensions, rendering medical aid and reuniting lost children with their families.

"Whatever individual perspectives they carry away from their experience, their service and sacrifice deserve our respect," Blanchard wrote.

"My initial reaction was just shock"

Trump first deployed the D.C. National Guard in August of 2025 — something he can do since the president controls the district's guard. Hundreds of guard members in the district were pulled from their civilian jobs and immediately called up.

"My very initial reaction was just, I guess, shock and feeling like this context and this situation just felt like a very authoritarian move that kind of felt uncharacteristic of something you would see in our country," said one member of the D.C. guard, adding that the reasoning behind the deployment contributed to the confusion.

Sponsor Message

In the days and weeks that followed, Republican governors began sending members of their guard to help with the mission.

"Walking into it, we had no real specifics," one guard member who was deployed from West Virginia remembered thinking. "The president is calling out the guard to make D.C. safe. Well, what the what the f*** does that mean?"

All remembered a scramble in the early days to figure out what everyone should be doing, as more and more troops — who were all deputized as special law enforcement and armed with a handgun — arrived. They said that despite the confusion, there was a collective effort to figure out how to be useful and effective. Military members are trained to be apolitical and follow orders.

"All of these people showed up, and then it was more of an after-the-fact figure out what we're going to do," one said, saying everyone was really trying to be as helpful as possible to the community with whatever resources they were given, like providing Naloxone to counter the effects of an opioid overdose or helping a bicyclist who had been hit by a car. "We can argue about why they were there and whether they should be there, but soldiers and airmen were trying to do the best with what they had."

In the early days, troops were largely assigned to help with beautification projects around the city: clearing trash along the road, bagging leaves in public parks or trimming trees at the National Mall. The guard member from West Virginia said that many of the members he had arrived with — most of whom had raised their hand for the deployment — became quickly disillusioned.

toggle caption Andrew Leyden/Getty Images

"I know there were a lot of people that showed up from West Virginia specifically that were just like, I want to help, and then later they found out that they were taking out trash and setting up (logistical equipment). I think they later fell off mission as soon as they could get off," he said.

Sponsor Message

Patrolling the streets

As the deployment continued, troops were assigned less to beautification projects and more to presence patrols around the city — which the task force says are an effort to deter crime — and settled into a routine that one guard member described as "mundane" and another as "monotonous."

"At some point, I found myself going, well, at least this isn't that bad. At least I'm not doing anything illegal, and that's always counterbalanced with, like, this is wasting everyone's time," one said, adding that it became clear that the "point of the mission is presence."

One member who served in Afghanistan likened the patrols to tactics commonly used by the U.S. military during the War on Terror in communities to instill goodwill and monitor the opposition.

toggle caption Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

Another said the lack of clear goals made the deployment feel never-ending, even as Trump falsely claimed there was "almost zero crime" in D.C. and touted its success.

"If it's safe now, then why are we here?" one guard member asked. "You don't really know when good is good enough, or when we can go home. It's just a continuing thing."

Two recent studies have found that the National Guard presence has had no effect on violent crime in the city, while it has minimally decreased more opportunistic crime, like petty theft and vehicle break-ins. Both also found that local policing could produce better outcomes for less money.

The deployment comes with perks

A majority of the nearly 4,700 guard members deployed to D.C. are from other states or U.S. territories, most of which are led by Republicans, and have volunteered for the assignment. All three guard members said that despite their concerns, they understood why people might raise their hand.

"It's a good paycheck, and I can't blame them for wanting to better their own financial situation when the economy is how it is right now," one said, noting that many of the troops are very young, come from more rural communities and might not have steady income back home.

Sponsor Message

There are a host of other incentives as well, from per diems to boosts to their retirement benefits.

The guard member from West Virginia said that normally, on domestic deployments, he was used to sleeping on the floor of an armory, maybe without electricity, and eating ready-to-eat military meals. But this D.C. deployment was much more comfortable.

"The food on the mission was very good. My hotel was very nice," he said, noting that was different even from other times he had come to D.C. on deployment for events like the inauguration.

The thousands of out-of-state guard members have been staying in hotels throughout the city for more than a year. Recently, the federal government awarded a nearly $300 million contract — the largest of its kind ever — to a local company for thousands of furnished, luxury apartments, saying the move would ultimately save money on extended lodging for the troops in D.C.

That guard member said that when elected officials or other leaders would come visit the troops, they would always ask how they could make it better.

"There was never a discussion of whether you should be here. It was always, 'What do you need?'" he said. "Which is nice as a military member, but once we see what all this is going to cost in the very end, it's probably not going to feel so great."

An estimate from the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office found that the D.C. deployment at its current level costs about $3 million per day. The Pentagon estimates extending the deployment until 2029 will cost an additional $1.4 billion. A total cost estimate by the nonpartisan watchdog Project on Government Oversight for the deployment is around $3.4 billion.

A personal cost

The deployment has also had a human cost, after a gunman shot two guard members from West Virginia patrolling near the White House last November. One of those members, 20-year-old Spc. Sarah Beckstrom, was killed. It was a pivotal moment in the deployment.

"I remember feeling just really sad," one guard member said, starting to tear up a bit. "And I kept thinking — did they have to be here?"

Another said the killing similarly made him question the necessity of the deployment in real terms.

toggle caption Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

"The thing that really stuck out to me was how absolutely futile that death felt, and that was hard to live with," he said, noting he still thinks about Beckstrom almost daily and sometimes visits the spot where she was shot, even though he didn't know her personally. "After her death, this mission became untenable for me emotionally."

Sponsor Message

Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, called the shooting a "direct challenge to law and order in our capital," and the White House responded by adding hundreds more troops to the city.

The guard member from West Virginia said he's been specifically angry about the shooting, saying he's had to work in therapy about guilt he's felt for not being there when it happened.

"We were made a target, and I don't know that anybody did a very good job of planning for the worst-case scenario," he said.

Blanchard refuted that, saying that "no mission is without risk" and the loss "remains deeply felt across the National Guard."

"Force protection and the safety of our Soldiers and Airmen remain paramount. We continually assess the operating environment and adapt to changing conditions to better protect the force while accomplishing the mission," he said in a statement.

A harm to the National Guard's reputation

The extended and growing deployment — and the administration's unprecedented use of the National Guard in other parts of the country — has led to a rising anti-guard sentiment, which all three members acknowledged.

Throughout D.C. in the areas most patrolled by the troops, signs are plastered on lampposts and chalked on sidewalks urging "National Guard Go Home" and "Troops out now." Residents regularly approach the patrols and speak their mind, sometimes with what one of the guard members called "misdirected anger."

toggle caption Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images

The guard member from West Virginia said it was the first time he'd ever not had the community in a domestic deployment welcome the help, since the guard usually shows up after floods or natural disasters.

All were concerned that there was damage being done to the reputation of the National Guard.

"If we continue down this path, where this kind of 'presence patrol' mission becomes the new definitive image of the National Guard, it's going to completely rebrand everything that was noble about the National Guard into being mundane at best and threatening at worst," one guard member said.

Sponsor Message

"I would like to think there would be enough mechanisms to have checks and balances that would be able to say overtly that's not what we want to see in our country," another one said.

The member paused before adding: "I don't know if that's the case right now."

World.title: Sean Grayson, former deputy convicted of killing Sonya Massey, dies in prison, lawyer says
World.content:
Sean Grayson, former deputy convicted of killing Sonya Massey, dies in prison, lawyer says

toggle caption Illinois State Police/via AP

CHICAGO — Sean Grayson, a former Illinois sheriff's deputy whose fatal shooting of Sonya Massey inside her home became a flashpoint over police use of force, died Sunday while serving a 20-year prison sentence.

Grayson's attorney, Daniel Fultz, confirmed that his client died earlier Sunday but declined to provide any further details.

Grayson, 32, was convicted of second-degree murder in October in the fatal shooting of Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman who had reported a possible prowler outside her Springfield-area home. Body camera video of the July 2024 encounter showed Massey crouching in her kitchen and apologizing moments before Grayson shot her in the face.

He was sentenced in January to the maximum 20 years in prison.

Grayson had been diagnosed with colon cancer before Massey's killing, and his attorneys said at his sentencing that the disease had spread to his liver and lungs. In May, only months into his sentence, he sought medical release under an Illinois law for prisoners with terminal illnesses or serious medical conditions. The Illinois Prisoner Review Board denied his request last month.

Sponsor Message

Massey called 911 early on July 6, 2024, to report someone prowling outside her home. Grayson and another Sangamon County sheriff's deputy responded.

Video showed Grayson directing Massey to remove a pot of hot water from the stove. As she held the pot, Massey told the deputies, "I rebuke you in the name of Jesus."

Grayson threatened to shoot her, drew his handgun and ordered her to drop the pot. Massey apologized and ducked behind a kitchen counter before Grayson fired three times.

The other deputy, Dawson Farley, later testified that he did not consider Massey a threat and drew his own weapon only after Grayson did.

Grayson was fired after the shooting and charged with first-degree murder. Jurors convicted him of the lesser charge of second-degree murder after Grayson argued that he feared Massey would throw the hot water at him.

Massey's killing drew national attention and protests and raised questions about how Grayson had moved through several law enforcement agencies before being hired by the Sangamon County Sheriff's Office.

Illinois lawmakers later passed the Sonya Massey Act, requiring law enforcement agencies to more closely review an applicant's previous employment records before hiring an officer.

The Justice Department also opened a civil rights investigation after Massey's death and later reached an agreement with Sangamon County, its sheriff's office and other agencies requiring changes to policing and emergency response. Those changes included additional training for interactions with people with behavioral health disabilities and development of a mobile crisis response program.

World.title: Ford calls Trump 'king of bankruptcies' and a 'loser' in response to latest 50% tariff threat on autos
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Premier Doug Ford called U.S. President Donald Trump a 'dictator' and said he can 'kiss my ass' while speaking at a news conference in Hamilton Monday as the fallout of the Canada-U.S. trade war continues. CBC’s Shawn Jeffords breaks down the latest.

Here's how Ontario is responding to U.S. tariffs

Ontario Premier Doug Ford doubled down on saying U.S. President Donald Trump could "kiss my ass" as the two leaders exchanged blows on Monday, with Trump referring to the premier as "Flunky Ford" and the "less charismatic, intelligent" version of his late brother Rob Ford.

The insults are the latest in the fallout of the Canada-U.S. trade war, which re-escalated after trade talks between the two countries collapsed over the weekend.

Fifty per cent U.S. tariffs on about $28 billion worth of Canadians goods came into effect early Saturday. Prime Minister Mark Carney said retaliatory, dollar-for-dollar tariffs will hit the U.S. Sept. 8.

Ford first made the comment on Toronto radio station Newstalk 1010, saying the U.S. president can "kiss my ass" in response to his tariff threats.

The premier later reiterated the comment at a news conference in Hamilton while vowing to protect the "jobs and paycheques" of Ontario workers. He was joined by Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli and Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy.

WATCH | Torontonians react as Canada-U.S. trade war escalates: As Canada-U.S. trade war escalates, some Toronto residents say they’ll 'buy Canadian' | Duration 3:19 Fifty per cent U.S. tariffs on a variety of Canadian goods came into effect early Saturday. As the Canada-U.S. trade war escalates, Toronto residents share how they’re feeling about the tariffs — with some saying they'll be buying Canadian.

Trump took aim at Ford in a Truth Social post during the premier's news conference Monday afternoon.

He described Ford's commentary as "bluster" and referred to both Ford and Carney as "clowns" and bad leaders.

When asked by a CBC reporter to react to the post, Ford said he won't respond to "a dictator like President Trump."

"He's the type of guy in school that would take your lunch money one day, take your toque off your head the next day and then steal your running shoes," Ford said.

"I'm not going to take any advice from a guy that's the king of bankruptcies."

During the news conference Ford also said that "everything is on the table" when it comes to retaliation measures

He told The Associated Press earlier Monday that he was willing to cut off electricity and critical minerals to the U.S. as the trade war drags on. Ontario sends power to about 1.5 million people in Michigan, New York and Minnesota.

Trump promises new tariffs

Before Trump's online attack on Ford, the U.S. president had escalated the trade war with a post to Truth Social Monday that slammed Canada for "ripping off the United States" and announced that starting Jan. 1, 2027, the U.S. will increase tariffs on Canadian automobiles, car parts and steel to 50 per cent.

Currently, the levy on Canadian steel is already 50 per cent, while the levy on car parts and automobiles is 25, according to the Canadian government's website .

Ford said Carney has his "full support" in his decision to walk away from Canada-U.S. trade negotiations. Other premiers have also largely backed Carney's decision to reject the trade deal.

Earlier Monday, Ford told Toronto radio station Newstalk 1010: "We need to throw everything in the kitchen sink at them. He's arrogant. He's cocky."

WATCH | Ford voices support for Carney's decision to walk away from trade deal: Premier Ford says suspended trade talks avoided a 'bad deal' for steel, auto sectors | Duration 1:49 Ontario Premier Doug Ford slammed the proposed trade agreement with the United States as a 'bad deal' for the province's steel and auto sectors. Ford said he supports Prime Minister Mark Carney's decision to suspend negotiations and that the province will help workers and businesses who now face a 50% tariff from the U.S.

Opposition parties demand Ford recall legislature

In the midst of the trade deal fallout and Ford's news conference, the Ontario NDP and Liberals called on the premier to immediately recall the legislature to take urgent action on U.S. tariff relief.

In a news release Monday, Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles said it is "our duty as elected officials to immediately get to work in the fight against Donald Trump's inexcusable and dangerous tariffs."

Stiles called on the Ford government to take on a number of retaliatory measures, including cancelling any government contracts with U.S. businesses and prohibiting any new AI data centre agreements that "benefit U.S. companies."

John Fraser, interim leader of the Ontario Liberals, said Ford's announcement in Hamilton "wasn't a plan."

"There were no new measures. Not even a mention of direct income or benefit support for workers who could lose their jobs or house," he said in a news release.

Fraser also said Ford's comments to Trump resembled a "WWE smackdown" and they aren't "what Ontario families need."

Green Party Leader Mike Schreiner also called for a return to the legislature "so that all parties can work together to protect Ontario jobs, workers and companies," in an emailed statement Monday.

During his new conference, Ford did announce that the province would "immediately" expand eligibility for its Protect Ontario Financing Program, which provides emergency funding to businesses facing "significant tariff-related disruptions," according to its website.

Ford said Carney has his 'full support' in his decision to walk away from Canada-U.S. trade negotiations. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

Ford calls on support from federal government

Ford did not sugarcoat Monday that the trade war would come with economic pain and said "all levels of government" will need to work together to "get through this fight."

In addition to calling on municipal leaders for co-operation, he called on the federal government to "step up" with "major support and regulatory change," including:

Eliminating federal greenhouse gas emissions standards for Canadian-made vehicles.

Exempting tariff-impacted sectors from federal emissions performance standards.

Investing significantly in auto, steel, and manufacturing industries.

Targeting "deep red states" in counter tariff response.

CBC News reached out to Global Affairs Canada for comment.

In an interview with CBC's Power and Politics Monday, Minister of Canada-U.S. Trade Dominic LeBlanc said "further measures" to protect Canadian workers and industries will be announced "this week."

WATCH | Former World Trade Organization ambassador on what's next in the trade war: Former Canadian ambassador to the WTO Stephen de Boer on what's next in the U.S.-Canada trade war | Duration 9:12 Get the latest on CBCNews.ca, the CBC News App, and CBC News Network for breaking news and analysis

Canada negotiated in good faith: expert

Daniel Tisch, CEO of the Ontario Chamber of Commerce, said tariff retaliation from Canada has to be "surgical," such as targeting American products that have a clear Canadian alternative readily available.

"The reality is the Canadian government negotiated with a good faith that was not returned," Tisch told CBC Radio's Metro Morning Monday.

"We're dealing with somebody in the White House who doesn't believe in win-win outcomes. But at the same time, that's the foundation, as we know, of every business relationship," he said.

Despite the failed trade deal, Tisch said he is optimistic Canada will "get through this dark time," noting that Canada, including Ontario, has led the U.S. in job growth and unlike some dire predictions, the country's economy didn't enter a recession.

"I still like our odds and I still believe that with the right collaboration between business and government we can actually make a positive difference."

World.title: WestJet flight attendants vote to ratify new collective agreement
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WestJet flight attendants have ratified a new collective agreement with the airline, with a 90.2 per cent vote in favour of the deal.

"This is a strong mandate from our members and recognition of the meaningful gains we made at the bargaining table," Alia Hussain, president of CUPE 8125, said in a news release.

"This is only our second contract, and we made important progress, including making sure our members are compensated for more of the work they already do."

The Canadian Union of Public Employees said the agreement includes a more than 18 per cent wage hike over three years as well as new compensation for work done on the ground.

The contract will give workers a 13 per cent wage increase this October, followed by a 2.75 per cent hike in January and a 2.5 per cent raise at the start of 2028.

The airline did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Contract talks had been ongoing since January, with WestJet and the CUPE WestJet Component at odds over wage increases and the cabin crews' claim of unpaid ground work.

The union had long complained that much of the work done when members are not in the air is unpaid. WestJet, however, had argued all duties are compensated through a "credit hour" system rather than an hourly rate.

The new three-year agreement is in effect from Jan. 1, 2026, until Dec. 31, 2028.

The deal followed tough negotiations, particularly around boarding pay, that culminated in a one-day strike by some 4,400 cabin crew earlier this month.

WestJet's flight schedule gradually ramped up after more than 900 flight cancellations at the peak of the summer travel period.

The aviation industry has been rattled by a series of labour actions over the past several years, with strikes by Air Canada flight attendants and WestJet mechanics briefly bringing operations at the country's two biggest airlines to a halt.

WestJet operates more than 600 flights a day, carrying more than 70,000 passengers on some days.

World.title: Victim of Prince George plane crash identified as devoted coach, volunteer and mother of 2
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Tributes are pouring in for a mother of two killed when a plane crashed into her vehicle along a Prince George road last week.

Alex Garneau has been identified as the victim in the incident, which saw a twin-engine Beech King Air 200 touch down on Foothills Boulevard, crashing through three lanes of traffic and hitting four vehicles.

Garneau was involved in many aspects of the community, particularly through sports where she was an athlete, coach and volunteer, particularly for the teams of her two school-aged children.

In an online fundraiser set up to support her family, Garneau is described as "a wife, a daughter, a sister, a friend and the hockey mom," who made everyone feel like they belong.

A small memorial set up alongside Foothills Boulevard in memory of Alex Garneau, who was killed Aug. 20 when a twin-engine plane making an emergency landing hit her vehicle. (Andrew Kurjata/CBC)

"She was the kind of person who was behind the scenes of almost every team and activity her kids were part of," the fundraiser reads. "She made the drive. She organized. She cheered. She made things happen. Her children are both incredible people and hockey players, and she had big dreams for them and the lives they will lead."

Similar sentiments have been expressed in posts across social media from organizations she was involved in.

"There are some people who become such a familiar part of the rink that it’s hard to imagine being there without them. Alex Garneau was one of those people," wrote the Cariboo Cougars minor hockey club, describing her as "infectiously positive and always, always smiling" and "insanely creative."

The Prince George Youth Volleyball Club shared a collage of photos showcasing Miller as a high school athlete and later a coach. (Prince George Youth Volleyball Club)

The Prince George Youth Volleyball Club described her as having a "lasting impact on the sport of volleyball in Prince George," starting as a high school player who joined Team B.C. before going on to play at a varsity level at North Vancouver's Capilano University. After moving back to Prince George, she became a coach for the club.

"She will be remembered for her smile, her laugh and how good she made those around her feel," the post says.

The fundraiser raised more than $100,000 within two days of going live, with organizers saying the money will go directly to Garneau's family.

Investigation ongoing

The twin-engine Beech King Air 200 that made an emergency landing on a Prince George road has been towed to a nearby gravel pit where it is being secured and prepared for removal under the supervision of the Transportation Safety Board. (Andrew Kurjata/CBC)

Meanwhile, the investigation into what caused her death is ongoing. According to the Transportation Safety Board (TSB), the plane made an emergency landing after losing power on one of its two engines.

The plane itself has been towed off the road and is currently in a nearby gravel pit under the supervision of the TSB, which has taken control of the investigation.

The TSB says the plane was destined for the Prince George Airport from the remote Sturdee Airstrip.

Skidmarks stretching about 200 metres can be seen on Foothills Boulevard in Prince George, B.C., ending where a plane making an emergency landing came to a stop after careening through four vehicles. (Andrew Kurjata/CBC)

Eight people were on board: two pilots and six passengers, some of whom have been identified as resource workers. No one on board was injured.

The plane was registered to Sekani Air Ltd., an industry charter flight company based in Prince George, which has declined to comment.

Former TSB investigator Bill Yearwood said one of his key questions is what caused the plane to come down, given it is supposed to be able to fly on a single engine.

He said he suspected other factors were at play, and emphasized that pilots are trained to react in split-seconds to emergency situations and that sometimes "there's no easy choice."

"You're going down, you can't waste time choosing a spot and if there are few spots, you're stuck with those," he said.

World.title: 'Unfortunate accident' at Montreal's Trudeau airport sends employee to hospital

An employee at Montreal's Trudeau International Airport was sent to hospital following an incident involving a plane on Monday evening.

"We can confirm that emergency measures were deployed at the YUL International Montreal-Trudeau Airport at around 7:30 p.m. following an unfortunate accident involving an aircraft and a member of the airport community," reads a statement from the airport.

According to the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM), the person's injuries are serious.

World.title: What is Dominion Society of Canada and why are people of different political backgrounds worried?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Dominion Society of Canada is planning on hosting a conference in Hamilton on Aug. 29. CBC Hamilton reporter Justin Chandler explains who they are, why their organizing tactics matter and how people across the political spectrum are responding.

Dominion Society of Canada says it's planning a conference featuring Canadian and international speakers at a venue in the Hamilton area on Aug. 29.

Elected officials and anti-hate groups have spoken out about the anti-immigration group, accusing it of spreading hate.

The self-proclaimed nationalist group — which advocates deporting millions of people from Canada — registered as a non-profit in 2025, according to a federal corporation database.

What is the group about?

According to Evan Balgord, who directs the Canadian Anti-Hate Network, Dominion Society likely has thousands of members — mostly young white men and boys.

The group was founded by Daniel Tyrie, former executive director of the People's Party of Canada, which is led by Maxime Bernier.

Balgord said to understand Dominion Society, you need to know "they speak out of both sides of their mouth."

On its website, Dominion Society describes itself as "promoting Canadian nationalism and immigration reform."

However, "when they're talking just to their supporters, they're talking about how they need to deport people from Canada who are not the right kind of white and European," Balgord said.

Balgord said the Canadian Anti-Hate Network found Dominion Society has "neo-Nazi members" and shares members with "more openly extreme" white nationalist groups, including Diagolon and Second Sons .

He said Dominion Society gave a special membership card to a co-leader of Second Sons with the number 88, which white supremacists use to mean "heil Hitler." That member posted an image of the card online last summer.

When asked, Tyrie didn't say whether or not his group includes neo-Nazis or members from other nationalist groups. He said its membership "includes Canadians from a wide variety of political backgrounds and associations."

"We have absolutely no interest in foreign political movements of the 1930s," he said in a followup email. "We are entirely focused on Canada's heritage and political solutions for the problems of the 2020s."

But Balgord said statements made to supporters "and to the white nationalism ecosystem are more truthful than the statements that they provide necessarily on their website and to journalists.... In other words: When they tell you who they are, believe them."

What does the group want?

Balgord describes Dominion Society as "the political arm of the white nationalist movement," seeking to make its ideas mainstream so that one day, white nationalists can seize political power.

The website also outlines a plan for "remigration," or the mass deportation of five million to nine million people, including temporary foreign workers, permanent residents and people born in Canada to non-Canadian citizens.

It also promotes the great replacement conspiracy theory, which suggests white people are being replaced by racialized people.

Barbara Perry, who directs the Centre on Hate, Bias and Extremism at Ontario Tech University, previously told the CBC that the group's arguments are "inherently racist and xenophobic" because it lays the country's problems at the feet of immigrants.

When it comes to who the group wants to see deported, "I think it's pretty clear from their language that what they mean is non-white, non-Christian," Perry said. "Their very presence is intimidating to the sorts of communities they would like to remove."

WATCH | CBC looks at concerns surrounding Dominion Society, other groups: Anti-immigration group could be looking to rent your venue | Duration 2:12 The Dominion Society of Canada, a group advocating for the deportation of millions of immigrants, says it’s hosting a conference in the Hamilton area Aug. 29. Local anti-racist organizations are asking businesses not to host them. They've also produced a guide on how to avoid accidentally renting to groups they say promote hate.

Ultimately, Balgord said, Dominion Society wants to make its ideas mainstream so white nationalists can take political power and enact their agenda.

Why are people speaking out?

People with different political ties have criticized Dominion Society. They include Jason Kenney, former Alberta premier and onetime Conservative MP.

"There are a bunch of totally legitimate concerns about what I would characterize as imprudent or irresponsible immigration policy," Kenney, federal immigration minister from 2008 to 2013, told CBC Hamilton in an interview this week.

"But I think that is categorically different than basing our immigration policy on race."

Dominion Society, he added, seems more interested in the colour of people's skin than the kind of contribution they're making to Canada.

"That is clearly un-Canadian, and it needs to be called out.

"People like me, who are on the right of centre of Canadian politics, have a special obligation to do that," Kenney said. "I think it's really problematic to have a group like that wrapping itself in Canadian patriotism and nationalism that is trying to exploit public concern about immigration and turn it into, frankly, a racist message."

LISTEN | Why people say Canada's immigration consensus broke: Front Burner 21:48 Canada's immigration 180: Part 1 It wasn't too long ago that much of Canada's political class was united in their embrace of immigration to help grow the population and with it, the economy. Now, many of those same politicians are singing a different tune as it's regularly stated as fact that Canada's immigration consensus is broken. Today, part one of a two-part documentary on the political 180 on immigration, how it happened so quickly, and what it means for Canada as the country shrinks its population for the first time in history. For transcripts of Front Burner, please visit: https://www.cbc.ca/radio/frontburner/transcripts [https://www.cbc.ca/radio/frontburner/transcripts]

What's the impact of this messaging?

Hamilton labour organizer Ritch Whyman said Dominion Society's rhetoric is "dangerous" because it divides working-class people.

"The cost of living has just gone insane," the Hamilton & District Labour Council executive member told CBC. "Groups like the Dominion Society try to use a racist message to explain why that's the case."

When push comes to shove, Whyman said, "people realize it's not someone that came here on foot or crossed a border on a boat that's the problem. It's their CEO who flies around on a Learjet that is the problem."

Blaming immigrants is "an attempt to deflect from the top and convince working-class people that they should be attacking the people with the least amount of power in society," Whyman said. "That actually emboldens employers and will lead to a race to the bottom for working-class people."

Caitlin Craven, who directs the Hamilton Centre for Civic Inclusion, said the Dominion Society is not really trying to have a policy discussion.

"They are trying to create a feeling of belonging and acceptance for a certain group of people and a feeling of fear and exclusion for other people," she said.

Tyrie denied trying to make anyone afraid.

Dominion Society's planned August event, called DomCon 2026, is "part of the growing movements that we're seeing of anti-immigrant, anti-Indigenous, anti-trans movements across the country," Craven maintains.

In an open letter, the Hamilton Centre for Civic Inclusion and other Hamilton organizations urged businesses and institutions not to rent conference space to Dominion Society.

In an Aug. 13 YouTube video, Tyrie said the group already has a venue. Earlier this month, a spokesperson said the group is keeping the conference's precise location secret so its members aren't targeted by people who disagree with them.

World.title: Denmark's PM blasts plastic surgeon for his unsolicited offer to 'fix' spot on her nose
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen is fed up with getting unsolicited beauty advice.

The 48-year-old wrote on Instagram Monday that she had just returned back home from a trip to Ukraine, where she was exposed to air raid sirens amid the ongoing war, only to find a message from a plastic surgeon offering to "fix that little spot on your nose."

"I've lost count of how many messages I've received over the years about my appearance," Frederiksen wrote. "Especially that I have ugly teeth and thin hair. That I have an ugly 'wart' on my nose and well-meaning advice to get some Botox."

She posted a screenshot of the plastic surgeon's offer without identifying him.

She also posted her response: "Oh no. I'm happy with my body — I really don't need a male plastic surgeon to have an opinion about it!"

Frederiksen, a Social Democrat and Denmark 's second female prime minister, is now in her third term, making her one of Europe's longest-serving and most experienced leaders. She has led the European Union and NATO member country since mid-2019.

She has pledged to maintain a firm stance against U.S. President Donald Trump's ambitions for Greenland, the kingdom's semiautonomous territory, and continue supporting Ukraine against Russia's war of aggression.

Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen walks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the Mariinskyi Palace in Kyiv on Sunday. (Mads Claus Rasmussen/Ritzau Scanpix/The Associated Press)

On Instagram, Frederiksen stressed that she does not interfere with other people's appearance and wrote: "I'm perfectly fine with my body — as it is when you're a woman approaching 50."

She added that "if you're going to write to me (and you're more than welcome to), I hope you'll use your time to talk about something more meaningful. Not my nose."

The prime minister also said that those unsolicited beauty tips and suggestions made her feel "indignant" and that "today, I'm sending an extra loving thought to all of you who have to put up with the 'perfect imperfections' we all walk around with every day."

World.title: At least 47 people killed in violent weekend attacks in Haiti, UN says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

At least 47 people were killed and 22 ‌more injured in an overnight gang raid on a neighbourhood overlooking Haiti's capital of Port-au-Prince, the UN said on Monday, prompting anger over the lack of protection from repeated deadly attacks.

The United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti said estimates could still change.

Jean Massillon, the mayor of Kenscoff, said armed men raided the community late on Sunday, setting fire to homes and killing residents.

The hillside community overlooking routes into the capital has ​suffered a dozen attacks by armed gangs since last year, forcing thousands ​to flee their homes.

Powerful gangs under a broad alliance have for years cemented their influence over Haiti's capital and expanded to nearby regions, despite attempts by foreign nations to reinforce the country's outgunned police.

Even as ‌Haiti's government decried a "heinous attack" and promised to reinforce security, residents demanded the local police chief step down, saying officers failed to protect people killed just minutes from the police station.

"Kenscoff will not be abandoned," the prime minister's office said on social media. "The government's authority will be restored, without weakness and without delay."

WATCH | CBC News got access in June as UN's secretary general toured Haiti: : UN chief visits Haiti as new Gang Suppression Force moves in | Duration 3:07 CBC's Paul Hunter joined UN Secretary-General António Guterres on a visit to Haiti's dangerous, gang-ridden capital, Port-au-Prince, where a new UN-backed Gang Suppression Force is attempting to quell violence and restore order. | CORRECTION (June 18, 2026): An earlier version of this video and description called this mission a UN force. In fact, it is a multinational effort backed by the United Nations.

'They sowed chaos'

Wails filled the air in Kenscoff as survivors found the bodies of friends and family strewn on the streets early Monday.

"They killed my son!" one woman kept yelling as people nearby tried to comfort her.

One man flung himself on the side of the road, head on his right arm as he cried on the ground. Nearby, people picked up the bodies of those killed, some wrapped in blood-spattered sheets.

Robert Jean recalled how he heard shooting before dawn and tried to rustle people from their sleep to escape being killed. He said he was frantically looking for his brother, who was killed: "I was calling to see if everyone was safe. I could not find my brother."

Another Kenscoff resident blamed the government for the killings. "If only we had a good police force that would have placed an armoured truck here, what happened here would been prevented," said Verti Enold-Saint as he lifted a sheet over the body of his brother-in-law.

Mathurin Pierre, 41, a farmer, told The Associated Press he lost 14 loved ones and that an unknown number remain missing.

Residents of Kenscoff try to flip over a car to block a street as they call for police intervention following the deadly attack. (Odelyn Joseph/The Associated Press)

Massillon blamed the attack on members of Viv Ansanm, which the U.S. government designated as a foreign terrorist organization last year.

"They sowed chaos," Massillon said.

He said gang members targeted a church and homes, including those owned by Dr. Jean (Bill) Pape. He is a renowned doctor who runs a non-governmental organization in Haiti that helps patients, including those with HIV and tuberculosis.

Gangs control an estimated 70 per cent of Port-au-Prince, the capital, with Viv Ansanm repeatedly targeting nearby Kenscoff.

Gang violence has displaced a record 1.5 million people across Haiti, where more than 3,100 people were reported killed from January to June and another 1,189 injured, according to UN statistics.

WATCH | Ottawa urged to protect Haitian refugees fearing deportation to U.S.:

Quebec advocates urge Canada to protect Haitian refugees fearing U.S. deportation | Duration 2:35 In June, the U.S. removed protections that prevented Haitians from being deported. Now, some advocates say Canada needs to rethink its Safe Third Country Agreement with the U.S. for Haitians seeking asylum.

The attack comes less than a week after the U.S. government deported more than 160 people to the troubled Caribbean country for the first time since the Trump administration won a legal battle to end temporary protected status (TPS) for some 350,000 Haitians.

Haiti's government has said some of the deportees included TPS holders working legally in the U.S. and even some who were Haitian in origin but not born in Haiti. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in a statement to the AP on Monday that those deported on Friday included several gang members with criminal records ranging from assault to drug trafficking.

Haiti is scheduled to hold general elections for the first time in more than a decade on Dec. 13, and it has been registering voters in Port-au-Prince and beyond. Experts have warned it's currently too dangerous to hold elections.

World.title: De la Espriella calls for “iron fist” against crime in Colombia
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the security forces to impose the law “like a giant with an iron fist, the iron fist of the State.”

During a meeting with commanders of the security forces, De la Espriella stressed that security “is the cornerstone of our government and the most forceful government policy.”

The president urged the security forces to confront crime with an iron fist and stressed that “our soldiers and police officers have the full and unconditional support of this government. Never again will they be mistreated or forced to bow down to crime.”

Here we must act like a giant with an iron fist—the iron fist of the state. And that ability to convey a sense of unity is what has a psychological impact on crime and sends a clear message to citizens: we are here to protect you, to look out for you, but also to enforce the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella called to erase the distinction between organized crime and illegal armed groups, and “treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups,” claiming they are interconnected.

We have to stop treating these criminals differently. We must treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups, because the criminal pyramid we have in Colombia—whose base is drug trafficking, followed by illegal mining, extortion, and smuggling—is all perfectly interconnected. The foundation of all crime and the primary source of all forms of violence is drug trafficking. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“When it comes to fighting crime, there are no differences—neither in the state’s actions nor in its response and certainly not in the categorization” that allowed peace talks with groups like the FARC and ELN, according to the president.

“That is over in this administration. They are all terrorists, and we are going to treat them as such, no matter what happens,” said De la Espriella.

World.title: De la Espriella claims 123,700 barrels stolen monthly from Colombia’s state oil company
World.content:
Oil thieves from north Colombia would be stealing at least 123,700 barrel of gasoline, diesel and naphtha, a month, claimed President Abelardo de la Espriella.

According to De la Espriella, the theft of the refined oil products that wee imported or produced by state-owned oil company Ecopetrol “is utterly alarming, and demands an immediate and forceful response from the State.”

Every month, approximately 123,700 barrels of refined products—gasoline, diesel, and naphtha—imported or produced by Ecopetrol would be stolen. This would occur solely on a 14-inch pipeline that connects Pozos Colorados, in Santa Marta, to the interior of the country, and the losses are concentrated mainly in Cesar and Magdalena. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“We would be talking about more than 1.5 million barrels a year, with losses exceeding $500,000 million for Ecopetrol and, therefore, for the nation,” the president said in a post on social media platform X.

De la Espriella added that “these fuels are used as raw materials in the illicit processing of cocaine” by illegal armed groups that operate in the country’s periphery.

If we confirm that a large portion of this fuel is being used to power cocaine production facilities, then we are not only dealing with a massive theft from Ecopetrol: we are dealing with a criminal network that may be linking the theft of hydrocarbons to drug trafficking and the financing of armed terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president ordered a “joint operation” of the military, police, prosecution and administrative authorities “to comprehensively combat this criminal economy” led by Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora.

“I want results and periodic report on progress,” said De la Espriella.

Organized crime and illegal armed groups have been involved in fuel theft for decades.

World.title: Colombia expands disaster region in 2nd emergency decree
World.content:
Colombia’s government drastically expanded the region affected by the August 10 earthquake in a second decree declaring an economic emergency.

According to the decree, President Abelardo de la Espriella declared the emergency in 15 of the country’s 32 provinces “for a period of thirty (30) calendar days, in order to conjure the crisis and prevent the spread of the disaster’s effects.”

“The territorial scope includes all municipalities listed in UNGRD Situational Report No. 36 and any additional municipalities where direct damage from the August 10, 2026 earthquake is specifically demonstrated,” said the decree.

The emergency decree declared a State of Exception, which allows the government to “adopt, through legislative decrees, all additional necessary measures and budgetary/credit operations to address the crisis” in the emergency region.

According to the decree, the government is considering the following extraordinary measures to respond to the disaster that left more than $9.5 billion in damages.

Tax, credit, and budgetary flexibility to direct new resources to disaster recovery.

Expedited public credit operations bypassing lengthy CONPES/DNP approvals.

Use of the Royalty Savings and Stabilization Fund (FAE) resources as repayable loans.

Expanding the “Works for Taxes” (Obras por Impuestos) mechanism to affected municipalities.

Direct management and monetization of seized assets administered by SAE/FRISCO to fund emergency shelters and humanitarian relief.

Authorizing financial cooperatives to temporarily extend credit and savings services to non-members affected by the disaster.

Streamlining judicial operations, education delivery (remote/alternative spaces), school feeding programs (PAE), housing subsidies, telecommunications repairs, and labor support transfers.

Previously, De la Espriella announced a “Miracle Fund,” which would be used to channel donations from the private sector and international partners.

Since then, Colombia’s elite donated COP1.6 trillion ($526 million) of the $30 billion the government believes it needs for reconstruction.

World.title: Colombia’s government publishes “white paper” on corruption by Petro
World.content:
The government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella gave Prosecutor General Luz Adriana Camargo a white paper with more than 80 complaints over alleged corruption by the previous government.

The 135-page “Book of Truth that was presented by De la Espriella, contained “the result of the work carried out under the coordination of Vice President José Manuel Restrepo during the transition weeks between the presidential election and August 7” when he took office.

De la Espriella suspended the transition process on July 7 after Petro said he refused to recognize the president as his legitimate successor.

Consequently, the book contains mainly political criticisms of the previous “regime” and no evidence of misdeeds that hadn’t been picked by the Comptroller General’s Office, which monitors public spending.

This white paper, my fellow Colombians, does not intend to replace, far less anticipate, judicial investigations or the outcome of actions taken by prosecutors, inspectors, and comptrollers. The book actually represents something simpler and, at the same time, more serious, monumental, and decisive: the fulfillment of my duty as Head of State. I am fulfilling the responsibility that falls upon me by gathering available information and not allowing the facts recorded here in the book I have just delivered to be buried by silence and impunity. The duty of a leader is to bring the truth to the doorstep of justice and stop there, scrupulously respecting the independence and majesty of the judicial system. That moment has arrived. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president blamed the budget deficit on the “sacking” of the Petro administration rather than Congress’s failure to approve the legislation that allowed the previous government to carry out its 2026 budget.

De la Espriella previously said he would extradite Petro if the US Government asked him to.

World.title: Colombia says 377 still missing three days after 7.4M earthquake
World.content:
The director of Colombia’s disaster management agency UNGRD said Thursday that at least 273 people died and that 377 were missing from the region that was struck by a 7.4M earthquake on Monday.

According to UNGRD director David Tamayo, the earthquake affected a total of 97,515 people.

So far, rescue workers and neighbors were able to rescue 348 people from the rubble alive and 3,826 people were injured.

The earthquake, which was the strongest in a decade, destroyed 12,563 homes and damaged another 75,654.

At least 172 apartment buildings collapsed, said Tamayo.

Damaged public infrastructure

217 health centers and hospitals

2,206 educational facilities

825 community centers

226 roads

71 aqueducts

24 vehicular bridges

8 pedestrian bridges

5 airports

The disaster triggered President Abelardo de la Espriella to declare an economic emergency in the disaster area, and in the southern Putumayo and the eastern Norte de Santander province where no damages were reported.

This State of Exception allows the president to govern by decree when it comes to matters related to disaster relief and reconstruction in the affected area.

The State of Exception will last three months and can be extended by another three with congressional approval.

World.title: Colombia declares economic emergency to rebuild after earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella said he would declare an economic emergency and create a reconstruction fund for homes and small businesses that were destroyed in Monday’s earthquake.

In a press statement, De la Espriella said that the government would initially support victims with temporary relief and will declare an economic emergency to find the funds for reconstruction.

Finance Minister Miguel Gomez said the government was not yet considering raising taxes to find the approximately COP20 trillion ($6.4 billion) that would at least be needed for reconstruction.

The president said his government would initially prioritize relief for the estimated 24,000 families from the west of the country who have lost their homes or businesses.

The temporary relief measures would include:

The payment of public services for affected families by the government.

Housing rent subsidies for those who lost their homes.

Tax and financial relief measures.

Economic support for the most vulnerable families.

Support mechanisms for merchants and small business owners who have been affected by the earthquake.

As part of the emergency, De la Espriella announced the creation of a “Miracle Fund, an entity that will channel national and international contributions destined for the reconstruction of hospitals, educational centers, properties, roads, and airports that suffered damage from the earthquake.”

“The state of emergency must encompass economic reactivation measures that stimulate investment, reduce obstacles to project development, and generate more jobs in the affected areas,” said the president.

An economic emergency gives the president three months to issue decrees related to the cause of the emergency without having to go through Congress.

The legal validity of the decree declaring an emergency and those that follow will only be tested by the Constitutional Court.

At the time of publication the President’s Office had yet to issue its first decree.

World.title: Colombia asked US to carry out joint military operations: Hegseth
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella asked the US Government for joint military operations “to destroy terrorists and terror networks,” said US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth Wednesday.

At an event of the so-called Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC) in Panama, Hegseth said that “Colombia will join the ACCC, becoming the 19th member.”

Through the newly inaugurated president, as our president likes to say “President El Tigre,” Colombia has already requested that our department of war join Colombia in its fight against narcoterrorism. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth

Hegseth’s announcement was rejected by leftist opposition party Historic Pact, whose Senate chief Ivan Cepeda said that “the US citizen Abelardo de la Espriella wants to surrender our government, our territory and our sovereignty to the strategic interests of the United States.

Cepeda stressed that Colombia’s constitution allows only the Senate to permit the entry of foreign troops to the country.

Colombia’s sovereignty is not up for negotiation, it is not to be surrendered, and it cannot be subordinated to the military interests of any foreign power. To defend it is to defend the dignity of the nation, the independence of the Republic, and the right of the Colombian people to freely decide on their territory and their destiny. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Ahead of taking office on Friday, De la Espriella said that he would join US-led alliances that allegedly seek to combat drug trafficking.

In his inaugural speech, the president said he intends to “defeat, without truce, narco-terrorism and all criminal organizations that threaten the freedom of Colombia.”

The State Department last week announced that it would seek to send a $1 billion military aid package to Colombia to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).

Meanwhile, President Gabriel Boric Font attended the wake of a firefighter in the town of Coronel. ”Chile is crying with you. I am here to tell you that you are not alone, that the family of Yesenia (Muñoz, the deceased firefighter) will not be alone,” he said.

According to Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred), the number of fires being fought went down from 87 to 51. “We are experiencing a small window of improving weather conditions during Sunday and Monday. That means that we are not with extremely high temperatures,” Monsalve said.

Undersecretary Monsalve also told reporters that 10 people have been arrested for their responsibility in starting some of the fires for which the red alert was still maintained. Of the total number of fires, 22 occurred Sunday for a total of 283 active fires, of which 151 were under control and 71 are being fought.

Given the magnitude of the fires in size and number, international help has been summoned. “We have just sent a plane to Chile with a contingent of the Military Emergency Unit to collaborate in extinguishing and controlling the fires that are raging in the country. All our support to the Chilean people,” tweeted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Chile’s Foreign Ministry also said assistance was being coordinated with Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, the United States, and Mexico, while Boric’s administration has declared a constitutional state of catastrophe in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío and La Araucanía, to speed up additional resources while restricting free transit and involving military forces to contain the disaster.

In 2017, another chain of fires destroyed some 460,000 hectares, left 11 people dead, nearly 6,000 injured, and more than 1,500 homes burned.

Monsalve also warned that this week high temperatures will continue, as well as the risk of low humidity and strong gusts of wind, which will make it difficult to extinguish the flames. – MercoPress

World.title: Parts of Chile under red alert for major forest fires in central region
World.content:
The Government of Chile has declared a “red alert” in the central part of the country due to the heat wave stemming from 39 major forest fires as the wave keeps spreading throughout the country, most of them in Araucania (17) but also in Bío Bío (7), Ñuble (7), Maule (4), Los Lagos (3), and one in the Santiago Metropolitan Region.

The National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response reported that in addition to the 39 fires currently being fought, there were four others under observation, while 141 were already under control, and 20 had already been extinguished.

Authorities ordered a series of preventive evacuations in several towns, as well as the interruption of highway traffic in the most affected areas where 181 hectares of scrubland and pastureland were burned out, threatening nearby homes.

The main cause for the fires is said to be the summer high temperatures which reached 41 degrees Celsius in the Chillán area.

Meteorologists forecast that the heat wave will last until Sunday. The last major fires to affect Chile were recorded in the summer of 2017 when the flames swept through entire villages, causing 11 deaths and more than 580 thousand hectares affected.

The state-owned National Forestry Corporation (Conaf) reported that in the Ñuble region, the fire has already affected some 550 hectares in the area of Chillán Viejo and another 200 hectares in another town near the regional capital, burning infrastructure and some houses.

Agriculture Minister Esteban Valenzuela told reporters that in addition to the heat wave, the dry and hot Puelche wind from the eastern cordillera was also expected in the central-southern zone. Valenzuela also announced the temporary closure of seven national parks from Santiago to the south in the Metropolitan, Ñuble, Biobío, La Araucanía, and Aysén regions to prevent new fires, and also ordered the evacuation of rural areas of Ñuble, where simultaneous forest fires were reported.

– MercoPress

World.title: Chilean airlines will reimburse cost of boarding taxes under certain conditions
World.content:
Chile’s national Consumer Service, Sernac is calling all consumers who purchased tickets directly from airlines between 2015 and 201l and did not make use of them, to claim from the companies the reimbursement of the boarding taxes paid.

Following on a Voluntary Collective Procedure reached at the beginning of 2020 with LATAM, and at the end of 2021 with Sky, Avianca, Jetsmart, Aerolineas Argentinas and COPA, the airlines agreed to reimburse the boarding taxes cost for flights not done between May first 2015 and 24 December 2021, with the exception of Jetsmart, which only started operations in Chile in July 2017.

Accordingly the universe of beneficiaries reached 1.108.416 passengers and involved some US$ 12 million for domestic flights and US$ 1,4 million for international flights. The amount to be reimbursed to each potential passenger depends on the distance to travel and if it was domestic of international travel.

In Chile the domestic boarding tax is equivalent to some US$ 14 and overseas US$ 50. Allegedly following the agreement the companies were to inform the beneficiaries of their reimbursements.

Reimbursements can also be checked by filling forms at the airlines’ offices. For further information on the agreement and the sums involved consumers are invited to check the web.

World.title: Remembering Steve Anderson
World.content:
BENJAMIN WITTE

I was neither the first nor the last of the many interns and editors who peopled the office of the Santiago Times during the quarter century founder Steve Anderson captained the ship. But for whatever reason, I stuck around longer than most, and it was with great sadness that I learned yesterday about the automobile accident that ended his life.

My first encounter with Steve came in late 2002, after he had offered me the editor’s job—sight unseen, via e-mail—and I accepted, knowing only that I’d earn about US$500 a month and should show up in Santiago with an AP style guide and a copy of Strunk and White’s The Elements of Style. That it all seemed a bit rushed and loosey-goosey gave me pause for concern, but I was eager for an excuse to return to Chile, so hopped on a plane and flew down from Costa Rica.

Still, after our first meeting, I wondered just how wise my decision really was. It was then that I realized the Santiago Times wasn’t, as I’d imagined, a print paper. It was Internet-based, with a rudimentary website that was only half functioning. “We got hacked,” Steve told me. He also explained that he was living at that moment in Puerto Montt—1,000 kilometers to the south—and that he was recovering still from a recent and quite serious car accident. It had been a very bad year, he said.

I gave the gig a chance, though, and things gradually improved. Some energetic new interns trickled in, as they always did at the Santiago Times. A talented British/Australian writer showed up too, and I asked Steve to hire him as a kind of co-editor. The business couldn’t really afford another paid staff member, but Steve honored my request, and for the next year or so we had a great run. Then the money ran out.

“I can’t afford to pay you both, so one of you has to go,” Steve told us one morning. “I’ll leave it up to you two to decide which one.” And so we did—over a liter of beer, even though it was like nine-something in the morning.
