The sequence of events early Monday

Two Costa Rica earthquakes jolted the Coronado area before dawn on 24 August 2026. The first tremor hit at 1:37 a.m. local time, followed by a second about two minutes later.

The Red Sismológica Nacional (RSN) reported the first quake as M5.4 at a depth of 7 kilometers. Its epicenter was located 11 kilometers north of Cascajal, Vázquez de Coronado.

The second quake measured M4.8 at a depth of 10 kilometers, according to RSN. Both tremors occurred in the same general area of central Costa Rica.

Seismologists recorded more than 30 aftershocks after the initial pair of quakes. Residents reported feeling several strong shakes throughout the early morning hours.

How different agencies measured the first quake

The three main monitoring institutions gave different magnitudes for the first tremor. The RSN revised its reading to M5.4, while the Volcanological and Seismological Observatory of Costa Rica (OVSICORI) initially reported M5.0.

The United States Geological Survey (USGS) listed the event as M4.9 near the town of Cot at a depth of 10 kilometers. OVSICORI placed its epicenter near San Isidro de Coronado at 11 kilometers depth.

These discrepancies are common because agencies process preliminary data differently. The RSN later revised its reading, which is considered the most consistent final local value.

All agencies agreed the quake was shallow, between 7 and 11 kilometers deep. Such shallow depth typically increases shaking intensity near the epicenter.

Damage reports from affected communities

Damage from these Costa Rica earthquakes was minor and localized, according to emergency officials. The National Emergency Commission (CNE) reported only isolated incidents across the affected region.

A damaged house wall was reported in Dulce Nombre de Jesús, a community near the epicenter. A fallen utility pole was confirmed in San Vicente de Moravia, disrupting local power briefly.

Debris on Route 32 near kilometre 30 caused traffic delays for early commuters. Road crews cleared the material quickly, restoring normal flow within hours.

No deaths or injuries were confirmed by any agency following the earthquake sequence. The relatively minor damage reflects the moderate size of these tremors.

Why no tsunami warning was issued

No tsunami warning was issued for these Costa Rica earthquakes, and none was expected. Both quakes struck inland, not beneath the ocean floor where tsunamis can form.

The United States Tsunami Warning System explicitly stated no tsunami statement was issued for the event. This is standard procedure for earthquakes that occur on land.

Tsunami alerts are reserved for undersea quakes capable of displacing large water volumes. The Coronado area sits inland in the central highlands of Costa Rica.

Residents along the Pacific and Caribbean coasts experienced no unusual sea activity. The lack of an ocean connection made any tsunami threat virtually impossible.

Aftershock activity and ongoing monitoring

Seismologists recorded more than 30 aftershocks following the main quakes on Monday morning. These smaller tremors continued for several hours after the initial pair.

Most aftershocks were too weak to be felt by residents, according to RSN. A few reached magnitudes that caused additional minor shaking in nearby communities.

The RSN and OVSICORI continue to monitor the seismic swarm closely. Both agencies are analyzing data from the sequence to understand the fault behavior.

Costa Rica sits in a seismically active region where such earthquake sequences are common. The country experiences hundreds of tremors each year, most too small to notice.

Public response and emergency coordination

The CNE activated its emergency protocols shortly after the first tremors were detected. Officials assessed damage across the Coronado area and surrounding districts.

Emergency crews inspected infrastructure including roads, bridges, and utility lines. They found only the fallen pole in Moravia and debris on Route 32.

Local authorities urged residents to remain calm and follow safety guidelines. Many people in San José and nearby cities felt the shaking and took precautions.

No evacuation orders were issued because damage levels did not warrant them. The response focused on quick damage assessment and restoring normal services.

Context of seismic activity in Costa Rica

Costa Rica Earthquakes are frequent because the country sits atop several active tectonic plate boundaries. The Cocos plate subducts beneath the Caribbean plate along the Pacific coast.

This collision zone generates frequent tremors of varying intensity across the country. The Coronado area has experienced earthquakes before due to local fault lines.

Scientists at OVSICORI and RSN continuously monitor these fault systems. Their early warning systems provide valuable seconds of notice before strong shaking arrives.

Monday’s pair of Costa Rica earthquakes was moderate compared to historic major events. The country’s building codes have improved significantly since destructive quakes in the past.

What residents should do after the quakes

Residents should check their homes for cracks in walls and damage to gas lines. The CNE recommends reporting any structural issues to local authorities promptly.

People should be prepared for possible continued aftershocks in coming days. Having an emergency kit with water, food, and flashlights is always advisable.

Those living near steep slopes should watch for landslides after heavy rain or shaking. Route 32 authorities will monitor the area for new debris falls.

Stay informed through official channels like CNE, RSN, and OVSICORI for updates. These Costa Rica earthquakes serve as a reminder to review personal emergency plans.

Frequently Asked Questions

What time did the two Costa Rica earthquakes occur on Monday? The first quake struck at 1:37 a.m. local time, followed by the second about two minutes later. Both tremors hit the Coronado area of central Costa Rica. How big were the earthquakes according to different agencies? The RSN measured the first quake at M5.4, while OVSICORI reported M5.0 and the USGS listed M4.9. The second quake was measured at M4.8 by RSN. Was there any damage from these earthquakes? Damage was minor: a damaged house wall in Dulce Nombre de Jesús and a fallen utility pole in San Vicente de Moravia. No injuries or deaths were confirmed. Was a tsunami warning issued after the quakes? No tsunami warning was issued because both earthquakes struck inland, not under the ocean. Such warnings are only necessary for undersea quakes that can displace water. How many aftershocks were recorded after the main quakes? Seismologists recorded more than 30 aftershocks following the initial pair of tremors. Most were weak but some caused additional minor shaking in nearby areas.

— The catch The 4.4% is a cumulative first-half figure, not a forecast for the full year.

— Who pays Private consumption, investment and exports are fueling the expansion, according to Banguat.

Central bank data shows steady expansion led by commerce, manufacturing and real estate.

Guatemala’s economic activity grew 4.4% in the first half of 2026, according to Banco de Guatemala (Banguat) data. The monthly activity index rose 4.2% year over year in June, up from 3.9% a year earlier.

Guatemala City’s National Palace; the economy grew 4.4% in the first half of 2026, the central bank says.

Central Bank Data Shows Solid Expansion

Guatemala growth reached 4.4% in the first six months of 2026, according to Banguat data reported on 21 and 22 August 2026. This accumulated figure measures economic activity through June, using the monthly IMAE indicator.

The IMAE, or monthly economic activity index, rose 4.2% year over year in June. This compares with a 3.9% increase in June 2025, showing slightly faster momentum.

Banguat, the central bank, compiles these statistics to track the country’s economic pulse. The June reading confirms a steady expansion in the first half of the year.

Economists watch the IMAE closely because it offers timely signals on economic health. The June data points to sustained growth across key sectors.

Commerce and Manufacturing Lead the Way

Commerce and vehicle repair activities were the main drivers of the IMAE growth in June. Manufacturing also contributed significantly to the monthly expansion.

Real estate activities added to the positive performance, according to the Banguat-based reporting. These three sectors together powered much of the 4.2% yearly rise.

Strong consumer demand helped fuel commerce, while manufacturing benefited from steady industrial output. Real estate activity reflected ongoing construction and property transactions.

The sector mix suggests broad-based growth rather than reliance on one area. This diversification supports the overall Guatemala growth narrative.

Banguat Raises Its GDP Forecast for 2026

Banguat raised its GDP forecast for 2026 in a separate outlook report, citing several supportive factors. The bank pointed to private consumption as a key engine of expansion.

Public and private investment are also expected to boost activity. Dynamic exports and remittances from abroad are helping support household spending, Banguat said.

Remittances, money sent home by Guatemalans working overseas, provide a steady income stream for many families. That supports consumption and overall demand.

The higher forecast reflects confidence in the economy’s momentum. This positive outlook aligns with the first-half growth data.

Private Consumption Drives Household Spending

Private consumption remains a critical pillar of the Guatemala growth story in 2026. Household spending is fueled by remittances and stable employment, according to Banguat.

Banguat’s analysis links the upswing directly to consumer demand. Public investment in infrastructure also plays a role in stimulating economic activity.

Private investment decisions by businesses add to the positive picture. Together, these factors create a supportive environment for sustained growth.

The central bank’s language suggests confidence in the durability of the current expansion. This stands out in a region with mixed economic performance.

Exports and Investment Bolster Economic Momentum

Dynamic exports are contributing to the economic upswing, Banguat reported on its 2026 outlook. External demand for Guatemalan goods adds to domestic strength.

Public and private investment together are helping build productive capacity. This investment supports job creation and long-term competitiveness.

The combination of exports and investment creates a balanced growth model. Banguat’s forecast revision reflects these positive trends.

Exports benefit from strong demand in key markets, particularly in North America. Investment responds to a stable policy environment.

Reported Figures and Their Context

The 4.4% first-half figure is an accumulated measure, not an annualized rate. It shows total growth from January through June 2026.

The IMAE’s June reading of 4.2% year over year indicates a slight acceleration. That is up from 3.9% in the same month last year.

These figures come from Banguat’s official statistics, reported widely on 21 and 22 August. No other growth figures were published in the reports.

Comparisons with past years show a steady recovery pattern. The data underscores the resilience of the Central American economy.

What This Means for the Region

Guatemala’s growth rate positions it as a standout performer in Central America. Many regional peers struggle with slower expansion or fiscal challenges.

The 4.4% pace suggests healthy domestic demand and external linkages. This could attract investor attention to the country’s market.

Regional analysts often highlight Guatemala’s macroeconomic stability as a plus. The current data reinforces that reputation with concrete numbers.

Sustained growth also supports government revenue collection. That revenue can fund public services and infrastructure projects.

Outlook and Monitoring Ahead

Banguat’s revised GDP forecast signals optimism for the rest of 2026. The central bank sees current trends continuing through the year.

Monitoring the IMAE monthly will show if momentum holds. A slowdown in any key sector could affect the full-year outcome.

Remittance flows and global demand for exports remain watch items. These external factors can shift quickly and impact economic performance.

For now, the first-half data points to a solid year ahead. Guatemala growth appears set to remain a positive regional story.

World.content:

Uruguay · BUSINESS

Key Facts — What happened Montevideo’s Casino Parque Hotel closes as a municipal casino on 28 August 2026 and transfers to national control.

— How big The casino has 46 workers, with 35 taking early retirement and 11 moving to other municipal jobs.

— The catch The building, inaugurated in 1909, has operated from Casa de Andalucía only since 2015, not its original site.

— Who pays The Intendencia de Montevideo ends its subsidised operation after the casino posted losses in 2024.

— What comes next The Ministry of Economy reopens the casino around 9-10 September 2026 with its own staff.

— Investment note IBF Negocios has invested over US$200 million in Uruguayan companies over 15 years.

Uruguay’s only municipal casino moves under national control from September, as investment firm IBF Negocios expands.

Montevideo’s Casino Parque Hotel, Uruguay’s only municipal casino, will close on Friday 28 August 2026 after years of losses. The national Ministry of Economy and Finance takes possession on 1 September 2026 and will reopen it days later.

Casino chips (illustrative); the Casino Parque Hotel concession passes to Uruguay’s finance ministry on 1 September.

Why the Casino Parque Hotel leaves municipal hands

The Casino Parque Hotel is Uruguay’s only municipal casino, housed in the Casa de Andalucía building in Parque Rodó. The Intendencia de Montevideo, the city government, has managed it for years, but the operation has run persistent deficits.

In 2024, the casino posted losses, described in Spanish as ‘números en rojo,’ meaning red numbers. That financial performance convinced city officials the casino was no longer sustainable as a municipal business.

A formal resolution ends municipal management, transferring the building and casino operation to the national Ministry of Economy and Finance. The ministry will take possession from 1 September 2026, according to reports from 21 August 2026.

El País reported on 21 August 2026 that the decision follows successive deficit balances. The transfer reclassifies Casino Parque Hotel from a municipal casino to a national one under existing state regulations.

The legal and administrative background of the transfer

The Intendencia de Montevideo issued a resolution to end its management and transfer the property to the Ministry of Economy and Finance. This starts a formal process called ‘toma de posesión,’ meaning taking possession, from September onward.

Historically, the Parque Hotel building opened in 1909, and the city government acquired it in 1915. In 2015, casino operations moved from the historic building into the Casa de Andalucía premises, where they currently function.

State casinos in Uruguay operate under the Dirección General de Casinos, an agency under the Ministry of Economy and Finance. This agency already manages casinos at Nogaró, Victoria Plaza, Piriápolis, Rivera, and 31 gaming halls nationwide.

Group R Multimedio reported on 21 August 2026 the historical details and the resolution’s content. The transfer brings Casino Parque Hotel under the same regulatory framework governing other national casinos.

What happens from 1 September 2026

Casino Parque Hotel closes as a municipal casino on Friday 28 August 2026. The Ministry of Economy and Finance takes possession of the building on 1 September 2026.

The casino is expected to reopen under national management around 9 or 10 September 2026. New staff, hired by the national casino authority, will operate the gaming floor.

Montevideo Portal reported on 21 August 2026 the planned reopening date and new staffing. The venue remains an emblematic casino point in Parque Rodó, now part of the national network.

Subrayado confirmed on 21 August 2026 the possession date and operational shift. The building itself is not being repurposed away from gaming, just changing management.

Workers face retirement or reallocation

Casino Parque Hotel currently employs 46 workers under the Montevideo municipality. A negotiated agreement between the city and the workers’ union settles their future.

Thirty-five workers will take early retirement, called ‘retiro anticipado,’ with economic incentives. Their years of service count as ‘insalubres,’ meaning unhealthy work, allowing retirement at a lower age.

The remaining 11 workers will move to other municipal jobs, the Adeom municipal workers’ union said.

Pablo Nisivoccia, vice-president of the Association of State Casino Workers, noted new staff will arrive with the Ministry. The casino reopens under state management in early September, as reported by Subrayado on 21 August 2026.

The hotel building and its future use

The Casino Parque Hotel building, an emblematic structure in Parque Rodó, ceases to be a municipal asset from 1 September 2026. The national Dirección General de Casinos assumes operational control of the gaming operation.

This agency will use its own personnel to run the casino, according to Grupo R Multimedio on 21 August 2026. The venue stays as a casino, integrated into the state-run network across Uruguay.

Available reports focus on the casino use and labor aspects, not on any separate hotel-lodging business. The current activity is described as a municipal casino in Casa de Andalucía, without mention of overnight guests.

The main change is institutional and operational, from municipal to national control. El País reported on 21 August 2026 that the building remains in gaming use, not repurposed away from it.

IBF Negocios and its US$200 million investment

IBF Negocios, an investment firm, marks 15 years of activity in Uruguay in 2026. Over this period, it has invested more than US$200 million in Uruguayan companies, according to Ámbito on 24 August 2026.

The firm began around 2011 with seven or eight founding partners. It has since grown to about 600 investors participating in its investment vehicles.

Since roughly 2021-2022, IBF accelerated its pace, investing between US$40 million and US$50 million per year. This marks a clear shift from its earlier, more gradual growth phase.

As of 2026, companies in IBF’s portfolio collectively generate over US$250 million in annual sales. The firm has built a diversified set of holdings across the Uruguayan economy.

Sectors targeted by IBF Negocios

IBF Negocios operates across several real-sector and consumer-oriented industries. These include food, agribusiness, veterinary products, technology, and mass-consumption goods.

The firm’s strategy involves diversifying its acquisitions across different economic segments. This approach spreads risk and captures growth in various Uruguayan markets.

Ámbito reported on 24 August 2026 the full list of sectors in IBF’s portfolio. The firms in these industries range from small enterprises to larger companies.

The acceleration since 2021-2022 allowed IBF to add broader and larger companies. This fits a pattern of aggressive expansion in the country’s investment landscape.

A concrete deal: IBF joins Edintor S.A.

IBF Negocios has taken an equity stake in Edintor S.A., an importer and distributor in Uruguay. This company distributes INGCO, a leading brand in the local tools market.

The association aims to ‘acelerar su expansión en Uruguay y la región,’ meaning accelerate its expansion. IBF adds Edintor as a new company to its portfolio, according to a business note from 20 August 2026.

Public summaries focus on strategy and aggregate numbers, not listing all portfolio companies. Edintor S.A. stands as one confirmed example of IBF’s concrete investments.

The deal supports Edintor’s growth plans within Uruguay and the wider region. This fits IBF’s pattern of backing firms in distribution and consumer-facing sectors.

World.title: Costa Rica Relies on One Machine for Key Cancer Treatment
World.content:
Costa Rica’s public health system depends on a single machine at Hospital México to provide an important form of cancer treatment, leaving patients vulnerable if the equipment stops working, according to the internal auditors of the Costa Rican Social Security Fund (CCSS).

The machine provides brachytherapy, a type of radiation treatment used particularly for cervical cancer. Instead of directing radiation at the tumor from outside the body, doctors place a small radioactive source inside or very close to the affected area. This allows doctors to deliver a strong dose directly to the tumor while limiting radiation exposure to nearby healthy tissue. Brachytherapy can also be used for prostate, breast and other cancers.

The CCSS Internal Audit raised the concern in an advisory issued on July 21. It warned that the institution’s entire ability to provide the treatment is concentrated in one unit at Hospital México. That means a mechanical failure, maintenance problem, shortage of specialized supplies or difficulty with the hospital’s infrastructure could interrupt brachytherapy across the public health system.

The risk is not theoretical. The previous machine failed beyond repair in December 2021, leaving Costa Rica without the equipment needed to continue the treatment. The CCSS responded by providing financial assistance for some patients to travel abroad for care. That arrangement increased costs, created additional paperwork and placed patients at risk of delays during treatment.

A replacement machine has since been installed, but Costa Rica still has no second public unit available as a backup. The concern is especially serious for patients with locally advanced cervical cancer. Brachytherapy is often used alongside chemotherapy and radiation delivered from outside the body. For some patients, ordinary external radiation is not considered an equal substitute.

Timing also matters. Cancer treatments are planned in a specific order and within a recommended period. An interruption can make it harder for doctors to complete the treatment as intended. The auditors said Costa Rica will continue to need brachytherapy for decades, even as vaccination against the human papillomavirus, commonly known as HPV, and improved screening help prevent more cervical cancer cases.

HPV causes most cervical cancers. Vaccination and early detection can greatly reduce the risk, but they do not remove the immediate need to treat people who already have the disease.

The audit urged CCSS authorities to examine ways to reduce the Costa Rica’s dependence on the Hospital México machine. Possible solutions would need to be considered as part of the institution’s plans for equipment purchases, hospital infrastructure, maintenance and emergency preparation.

The available information did not include a deadline for obtaining a backup machine or expanding the treatment to another public hospital. The warning comes as the CCSS is carrying out wider changes to Costa Rica’s radiotherapy services. Hospital México is replacing aging radiation equipment, while additional treatment capacity is planned for other hospitals.

However, those projects involve several types of radiation technology. A new external-radiation machine does not automatically provide the same treatment as a brachytherapy unit. For patients, the audit’s main point is that Costa Rica once lost access to this treatment because its only machine failed, and the public health system remains exposed to the same basic risk.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Mangroves Face Growing Threats From Pollution and Development
World.content:
Costa Rica’s mangrove forests protect coastal towns, support fishing communities and provide breeding grounds for marine life. Researchers warn that pollution, construction and changes to rivers are slowly weakening these important coastal ecosystems. Mangroves are forests that grow where rivers meet the sea. Their tangled roots create sheltered areas where young fish, crabs, shrimp and other marine animals can grow before moving into open water.

Those roots also hold soil in place and absorb some of the force from waves, flooding and storms. Without mangroves, coastal areas can become more vulnerable to erosion and rising water. Costa Rica’s 2021 mangrove ecosystem map estimated that Costa Rica has approximately 52,802 hectares, or 130,477 acres, of mangrove environments. Most are found along the Pacific coast, including the Gulf of Nicoya, the Térraba-Sierpe wetlands and the Osa Peninsula.

Despite legal protections, many of these forests remain under pressure. The main threats include garbage and polluted water flowing down rivers, construction near the coast, agricultural runoff, sediment buildup and the clearing or filling of wetland areas. Some of the waste begins far from the coast. Plastic, sewage, chemicals and other pollutants from communities in the Greater Metropolitan Area can travel through rivers before reaching mangroves and the ocean.

Research from the University of Costa Rica has found pesticides, detergents and pharmaceutical substances in mangrove environments. These pollutants can damage water quality and affect the animals living among the roots. Changes to rivers create another problem. When a river is straightened, diverted or surrounded by farms and construction, the natural movement of water and sediment can change. Too much sediment may bury mangrove roots or block the normal exchange between fresh water and seawater.

Researchers have raised concerns about the Aranjuez River in Puntarenas, where changes to the river and years of sediment buildup have affected the nearby mangrove. Environmental specialists warn that further deterioration could leave parts of Puntarenas more exposed to coastal erosion and flooding.

The effects are already visible in some locations. Monitoring around Punta Flor on Isla Chira has found fewer crabs and other small marine animals in degraded sections of the mangrove than in healthier areas. A 2025 study of the Morales mangrove in Puntarenas found that the forest lost approximately 24 hectares, or 59 acres, between 1944 and 2020. Researchers linked much of that decline to changes in how surrounding land was used.

The loss of mangroves can also hurt the local economy. Fish, shrimp, crabs and shellfish depend on these forests during part of their life cycle. When mangrove habitats decline, fishing communities may eventually find fewer animals available to catch and sell. This is especially important around the Gulf of Nicoya, where families have long depended on small-scale fishing and the collection of shellfish. Damage to the mangroves can therefore affect jobs, household income and local food supplies.

Mangroves also store large amounts of carbon in their soil and roots. When the forest is destroyed or the soil is disturbed, part of that carbon can be released into the atmosphere, adding to the problem of climate change. Costa Rica has promised to protect and restore thousands of hectares of coastal wetlands as part of its international climate commitments. Scientists say restoration can help, but preventing pollution and further damage is usually easier and less expensive than trying to rebuild a mangrove after it has collapsed.

The warning is not that every mangrove in Costa Rica is disappearing at the same rate. Conditions vary considerably from one location to another. The larger concern is that damage has continued for decades while many coastal communities depend on these forests for protection and income.

World.title: Fewer Humpback Whale Sightings Reported in Costa Rica’s Golfo Dulce
World.content:
Tour guides in Costa Rica’s Golfo Dulce say humpback whales have been more difficult to find this season, raising questions about whether warmer ocean water is changing their normal movements. Guides have said August usually brings regular whale sightings inside the gulf but this year, however, this year they have experienced days when dozens of tour boats searched the area but very few whales were seen.

On one recent morning, guides said that only one of approximately 30 to 40 boats reported seeing a whale. The observations do not prove that Costa Rica has fewer humpback whales this year but there has been no official population count showing a decline. The whales may simply be spending more time outside Golfo Dulce or moving between different parts of the southern Pacific coast.

Still, guides with years of experience say the change has been noticeable. Captains and guides, who has worked in the area for more than 12 years, said the whales previously remained inside the gulf for longer periods. This season, they appear to leave the protected waters more frequently and stay outside for longer.

The guides believe warmer ocean water could be influencing that behavior. They say they have personally noticed higher water temperatures while swimming and snorkeling. Some have also reported seeing coral with signs of partial or complete bleaching, which can occur when the ocean becomes unusually warm.

Golfo Dulce is one of Costa Rica’s most important whale-watching destinations and humpback whales from the Southern Hemisphere travel thousands of kilometers from waters near Antarctica to Costa Rica’s warm Pacific coast. The whales come north to mate, give birth and care for their calves before beginning the long journey back toward their feeding grounds. The southern whale season normally runs from July through October, with sightings often reaching their highest point during September.

Conditions inside Golfo Dulce are usually well suited for mothers and young calves. It’s warm, relatively calm water gives the animals a protected place during the first weeks of a calf’s life. Scientists have found evidence that water temperature and food availability can affect when humpback whales begin migrating.

A study published in 2025 followed 42 humpback whales traveling from breeding areas in Costa Rica, Panama and Ecuador toward feeding grounds near Antarctica. The researchers found that the whales used information from their surroundings, including water temperature and the amount of marine life in the water, to help decide when to leave.

Warmer water and El Niño conditions were connected with changes in the timing of their southward migration. The research suggests that humpbacks can adjust their movements when ocean conditions change. However, that study used tracking information collected between 2009 and 2016. It does not establish that warmer water is responsible for the sightings reported by Golfo Dulce guides in 2026.

Confirming such a connection would require current water-temperature measurements, whale counts and comparisons with previous seasons. For local tourism businesses, fewer sightings can create a difficult situation. Whale watching supports boat operators, guides, hotels, restaurants and other businesses across the Osa Peninsula and southern Puntarenas.

Guides sometimes remain at sea longer than usual while searching for whales because they know that visitors may have traveled a considerable distance for the experience. But sightings are never guaranteed, even during the busiest part of the season. Visitors can still encounter dolphins, sea turtles and other marine wildlife in Golfo Dulce. Tours in the area also commonly include snorkeling, mangrove visits and trips along the coast.

The guides’ reports offer an early warning worth examining, rather than proof of a permanent decline. Continued monitoring will be needed to determine whether this is an unusual season or part of a larger change in humpback whale migration.

World.title: Mother of five Nichole McDonald granted $800 bail after more than two months on remand; Says she took anger management classes in prison
World.content:
Mother of five Nichole McDonald granted $800 bail after more than two months on remand; Says she took anger management classes in prison

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Mother of five Nichole Gilda McDonald is out of the Belize Central Prison after a Magistrate granted her bail on Monday in connection with the alleged assault of a doctor at the Matron Roberts Polyclinic.

McDonald, 38, had been on remand since June 8, when bail was denied after she was charged with harm upon a doctorand aggravated assault upon a nurse stemming from an incident at the clinic two days earlier. At the time, the court found that the new charges allegedly breached conditions attached to bail she had received just days before in another case.

On Monday, McDonald was granted bail in the sum of $800 plus one surety of the same amount. As conditions of her release, she must report to a police station once weekly and must not be arrested and charged with another offence while on bail.

McDonald was also provided with 10 pages of disclosure in the harm case involving the doctor. Trial has been set for October 21, 2026.

The June 6 confrontation at Matron Roberts drew significant public attention after videos circulated on social media. The doctor later spoke publicly about the incident and called for stronger legal protection for healthcare workers.

McDonald has pleaded not guilty and maintains that she will contest the allegations at trial.

She told reporters following her release that her time in prison included a period under sanction and that she participated in the Ashcroft Rehabilitation Programme and an anger-management programme. While maintaining her innocence, McDonald said she was grateful for what she learned from the programme and was looking forward to returning home to her children.

McDonald also has other pending criminal matters. She faces six charges arising from separate alleged incidents in early June, including aggravated assault, common assault, damage to property, insulting words and wounding.

Separately, McDonald is accused of using a computer system to disseminate a false statement concerning former Commissioner of Police Chester Williams. That charge was previously dismissed but was reinstated in May 2026. In July, the Magistrate’s Court was informed that the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions had directed that the cybercrime matter proceed on indictment to the High Court rather than be tried summarily in the lower court.

McDonald remains unrepresented in the criminal matters and maintains her innocence.

World.title: Lloyd Parchue rejects 4-year sentence indication after gun allegedly found in SUV; remanded to prison
World.content:
Lloyd Parchue rejects 4-year sentence indication after gun allegedly found in SUV; remanded to prison

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A former security guard accused of being caught with an unlicensed 9mm pistol and eight live rounds of ammunition has been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after rejecting a sentencing indication of four years and one month behind bars.

Thirty-three-year-old Lloyd Parchue, a resident of southside Belize City, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday, where he was charged with keeping an unlicensed firearm and keeping ammunition without a gun licence.

Police allege that at around 3:40 a.m. on Sunday, August 23, members of the GI3 Unit were patrolling near Flamboyant Street and Croton Lane when they noticed a white SUV travelling at high speed.

Officers reportedly stopped the vehicle after it came to a halt in front of a residence on Croton Lane. Parchue, who was identified as the driver, was ordered out of the vehicle and informed that police would conduct a search for firearms, ammunition and drugs.

According to police, nothing illegal was initially found inside the glove compartment; however, officers allegedly discovered a silver 9mm pistol with a brown handle and eight live S&B 9mm rounds concealed behind the glove compartment.

Parchue was subsequently detained and taken to the Queen Street Police Station.

During his arraignment, Parchue requested a Maximum Sentence Indication (MSI) to determine the sentence he could face if he pleaded guilty.

The magistrate indicated that he would receive four years and one month imprisonment on each charge, with the sentences to run concurrently, meaning he would serve a total of four years and one month.

Parchue declined the indicated sentence and instead pleaded not guilty to both charges.

Due to the nature of the offences, bail was denied and Parchue was remanded to the Belize Central Prison until October 23, 2026.

World.title: Motorcyclist Jaime Catalan killed in Cayo collision; second rider detained
World.content:
Motorcyclist Jaime Catalan killed in Cayo collision; second rider detained

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have detained a man in connection with a motorcycle collision that claimed the life of 46-year-old Jaime Haroldo Catalan of San Marcos Village.

The crash occurred shortly before midnight on Friday, August 21, between Duck Run 1 and Billy White Village in the Cayo District.

Catalan was found unresponsive on the roadway with grave injuries. Police also found his damaged motorcycle and a second motorcycle with minor damage.

Investigators believe Catalan was travelling toward Billy White when 26-year-old Javier Pinelo of Bullet Tree Village overtook him. According to preliminary information, Pinelo encountered oncoming traffic and swerved back in front of Catalan, leading Catalan’s motorcycle to collide with the rear of Pinelo’s motorcycle.

Pinelo was also injured and taken to the San Ignacio Community Hospital. Police obtained a specimen from him, detained him under police guard and issued a Notice of Intended Prosecution.

Investigations continue.

World.title: Police review Crime Fusion footage after Christopher Smith found shot dead on Arlington Drive
World.content:
Police review Crime Fusion footage after Christopher Smith found shot dead on Arlington Drive

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating the murder of 23-year-old Christopher Smith, whose body was discovered in a yard on Arlington Drive in Belize City on Sunday morning.

According to police, the body was reported at around 7:00 a.m. on August 23. Investigators found Smith unresponsive with apparent gunshot injuries and recovered several expended shell casings from the scene.

Police believe Smith may have been shot at around 1:20 that morning, when reports were received of gunfire in the area. Officers who responded at that time, however, were unable to establish a crime scene.

Investigators have since retrieved surveillance footage through the Police Department’s Crime Fusion Center, and police say that footage has provided leads which are now being pursued.

No motive has been established.

Police also confirmed that Smith was known to them. He had previously been charged in connection with the 2024 double murder of Belmopan taxi drivers Marvin Cante and Juan Carlos Raymundo, whose bodies were found in a shallow grave near Hattieville. Importantly, however, the murder charge against Smith was withdrawn on November 28, 2025, on instructions from the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions.

World.title: Sherman Hemmans, Alberto Arreaza charged in armed home invasion and theft of 2026 Wingle pickup
World.content:
Sherman Hemmans, Alberto Arreaza charged in armed home invasion and theft of 2026 Wingle pickup

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have charged two men with aggravated burglary following an armed home invasion in which a resident was reportedly robbed of a 2026 Wingle pickup truck.

Twenty-nine-year-old Sheffan Hemmans, described by police as a post guard officer, and 26-year-old Alberto Arreaza, a Cayo District labourer, have been jointly charged.

Police say the complainant reported that at around 7:45 p.m. on Thursday, two masked men entered his home, one armed with a firearm, and demanded the keys to his black 2026 Wingle pickup.

Fearing for his safety, the victim complied and the men drove away with the vehicle.

Police activated operational procedures and, at around 9:45 p.m., officers in the Santa Rosa area of western Belize intercepted the stolen pickup.

Police also observed another vehicle in the area which sped away. Officers pursued that vehicle and eventually intercepted it. Hemmans was reportedly found aboard.

A search of Hemmans allegedly led to the discovery of 50 live rounds of .22 LR ammunition.

In addition to the aggravated burglary charge, Hemmans was charged with keeping ammunition without a gun licence.

World.title: Three charged after San Pedro raid turns up cannabis, cocaine and crack
World.content:
Three charged after San Pedro raid turns up cannabis, cocaine and crack

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Three San Pedro residents have been jointly charged with drug trafficking following a police raid in the Boca del Rio area.

Police say an operation was conducted at a residence on August 21 and resulted in the discovery of 1,312 grams of suspected cannabis, 21 grams of suspected cocaine and 28 grams of suspected crack cocaine.

Police subsequently arrested and jointly charged three people, including 26-year-old Horace Anthony Crawford and 24-year-old Bridget Alcer, along with another 26-year-old San Pedro resident.

The trio each face three counts of possession of controlled drugs with intent to supply to another.

World.title: High-speed SUV stop leads police to loaded 9mm; Lloyd Parchue charged
World.content:
High-speed SUV stop leads police to loaded 9mm; Lloyd Parchue charged

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man has been charged with firearm and ammunition offences after police say a high-speed SUV caught the attention of officers conducting an anti-crime operation.

Police say GI3 personnel were operating in the St. Martin’s area at around 3:40 a.m. when they observed an SUV travelling at high speed.

Officers pursued and intercepted the vehicle.

A subsequent search allegedly led to the discovery of a 9mm Smith & Wesson pistol containing a magazine loaded with eight live rounds of ammunition.

Police formally arrested and charged 33-year-old Lloyd Parchue of Croton Lane, Belize City, with keeping a firearm without a gun licence and keeping ammunition without a gun licence.

World.title: Three Belize City men charged after armed robbery caught on camera at Independence Village store
World.content:
Three Belize City men charged after armed robbery caught on camera at Independence Village store

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have charged three Belize City men following an armed robbery at a store in Independence Village over the weekend, which was caught on camera.

The robbery occurred at approximately 2:30 p.m. on Saturday, August 22.

Police say two men entered the establishment, one armed with a firearm, and made demands of the store owner. The robbers took several items belonging to the proprietor before fleeing.

Information on the suspected perpetrators was circulated to police formations, and officers later intercepted a vehicle reportedly connected to the robbery.

Three men were found aboard and subsequently detained.

Police identified two of the accused as Dorian Garnett, 36, and Krishna Flores, 35, and Anthony Smith.

All three have been jointly charged with robbery.

Police said the suspects are persons known to authorities in connection with activities in the Belize District, but investigators have not established that they regularly operated in southern Belize.

World.title: 11 years after decriminalisation, ganja use complicating mental health care
World.content:
AI image of a young man smoking marijuana. (Adobe stock)

Eleven years after Jamaica decriminalised ganja, the use of the substance features heavily among patients presenting with psychosis and schizophrenia. While there is currently no data establishing whether use of the herb is causing or contributing to the mental health problems, its prevalence is complicating treatment.

This is against the background of data from the National Council on Drug Abuse (NCDA) pointing to an increase in high-risk usage of cannabis and the potency of the substance in Jamaica, as well as an increase in admissions for psychosis and schizophrenia over the last decade.

“What we do know is that the majority of psychiatric admissions in our public hospitals are coming from psychosis or schizophrenia. And the majority of those persons do use cannabis. So, we can look at that relationship and see that it is strong,” said Director for Treatment Services at the NCDA, Dr Kristen Robinson Barrett.

Still, Robinson Barrett noted that there is little data specifically exploring cannabis-induced psychosis.

Psychiatrist at Bellevue Hospital, Dr Brian Kazaara concurred that cannabis use has a striking presence among patients presenting with mental issues, but suggested that the substance rarely causes psychotic disorders.

“We don’t have official studies performed at Bellevue Hospital regarding cannabis use among patients, but from a cursory observation I can safely say the vast majority of patients admitted to the hospital also use cannabis,” he said.

Kazaara, who previously worked at the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI), pointed to a survey carried out by UHWI that revealed that the majority of persons admitted to the institution’s psychiatric ward smoked cannabis.

“What studies show is that persons with common psychiatric conditions like major depressive disorder or anxiety disorders use cannabis far more frequently than persons who do not have mental illnesses,” he said.

Despite this, Kazaara explained, “Cannabis-induced psychosis is not the norm. It is rare. At Bellevue we very, very rarely see that diagnosis. I also worked at UHWI for seven years [and] rarely saw it, almost never.”

Cannabis is a psychoactive drug and can affect the way that people perceive the world, leading to relaxation, paranoia, or other effects.

“It binds to our cannabinoid receptors around our body, but particularly in our brain, and that’s how we get the effects. It tends to create effects as it relates to emotions and feelings,” Robinson Barrett said. “They might experience changes as it relates to their time perception, so things might feel slowed down… issues with their concentration, so their attention and their awareness, their reaction time will change.”

Kazaara cautions that cannabis use can muddle the treatment of mental health issues.

“Cannabis definitely complicates psychosis, because for persons who use cannabis, they are more likely to develop an earlier onset of psychosis. So it may happen earlier than if they didn’t use it. It makes symptoms worse. It makes it harder to treat,” he explained.

Jamaica has a strong culture of recreational cannabis use, and Research Analyst at the NCDA Uki Atkinson explained that while overall population use has not necessarily changed over the last decade following decriminalisation of the drug, the potential for high-risk use has.

She supported her assessment with results from the Cannabis Abuse Screening Test (CAST) which was used during surveys in 2016 and 2023.

“We were able to compare the levels of high-risk use from 2016 to 2023. In 2016, 50 per cent of the people who used cannabis in the past year were deemed to be at high risk for misusing it,” Atkinson said, noting “this has increased by 16 per cent in 2023. So, it shows not necessarily that more people are using ganja… But there’s a significant increase in high-risk patterns of use.”

In addition to high-risk usage, the potency of cannabis being consumed in Jamaica is also a concern.

According to a European study, using high-potency cannabis with a tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) concentration over 10 percent, significantly increases the risk of developing psychotic symptoms or disorders, especially with daily use.

Robinson Barrett expressed serious concern about current potency trends worldwide compared to a potency of around four per cent in the 1990s.

“As of 2024, we’re looking at potencies of 15 to 20 per cent,” Robinson Barrett indicated.

“The potency trends of cannabis in Jamaica measured between 2014 and 2020, were showing that over that decade, the cannabis potency would have moved from about one per cent to over 10 per cent across 12 parishes,” she continued. “So, we’re concerned… because we have a culture of heavy use in young age groups…it’s a very concerning picture as it relates to all young people and any other vulnerable group.”

Outside of general risks, Robinson Barrett noted that there are some who may be particularly susceptible to the effects of cannabis use, including youth.

“Generally speaking, the earlier the age of onset for any substance is going to increase your risk for addiction, and it’s going to increase your risk for its effects…for the cannabis, we’re looking at increased risk for development of psychosis, increased risk for cognitive impairment,” Robinson Barrett said.

She also highlighted people who are genetically vulnerable, or have a family history of mental illness as well as heavy users who smoke regularly.

While cannabis has many cannabinoids, Robinson Barrett explained that the main ones are Delta-9-THC, which most people know as a psychoactive component, and CBD, which can have a calming or relaxing effect.

Kazaara agreed that cannabis misuse can complicate mental health treatment.

“Yes, it does. Cannabis complicates the treatment of psychiatric conditions. For example, in the case of schizophrenia, it can worsen symptoms and also make the medication we use for it, less effective,” he explained.

In the meantime, Atkinson stressed that the NCDA was not demonising cannabis, highlighting the medicinal benefits and scope for a medicinal industry.

“We recognise the value, but we see the downside in our clients and in some of the young people who we have to treat,” she explained.

She urged that use must be balanced with ensuring that the population, especially youth and those with a predisposition to mental illness, understand the risk of use, particularly in a problematic manner.

World.title: Honorary consul to Atlanta Elaine Grant-Bryan ‘humbled’ by OD recognition
World.content:
Elaine Grant-Bryan

When Elaine Grant-Bryan settled in Atlanta in 1990, that city was long acknowledged as the mecca of black empowerment in the United States. She joined a growing Jamaican community which has made an impact in commerce and community politics.

Grant-Bryan has been Jamaica’s honorary consul to Atlanta since 2018. Currently in her third term, she has been awarded the Order of Distinction (Officer class) by the Jamaican government for service to the diaspora.

That award will be presented during the National Honours and Awards ceremony on October 19 at King’s House in Kingston.

In an interview with Observer Online, Grant-Bryan spoke of being “deeply humbled” by recognition of her work. Like New York City and South Florida, she said Jamaicans have made their mark in Atlanta and neighbouring areas such as Decatur and Stone Mountain.

“This region has grown significantly, especially after COVID-19 as Jamaicans moved from colder regions in the United States in great numbers. Our community has doubled, and many have successfully assimilated in the Georgia culture and made significant contributions to Jamaica and this region,” Grant-Bryan stated.

An educator and real estate broker, she points to initiatives started with her husband Gregory as major achievements of her tenure. These include the Elaine Bryan Foundation which drives the Jamaican Pioneer Programme and STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, Mathematics).

The pioneer programme allows Americans of Jamaican heritage to gain citizenship in their family’s homeland. Once that is secured, they increase their contribution to Jamaica’s education system by mentoring and assisting needy students.

STEAM is an enrichment curriculum she developed with her husband, a programmer and Information Technology expert. It teaches coding/programming and offers career assessments, internships, entrepreneurships, and scholarships to Jamaican students completing degrees in STEAM fields.

Empowerment was a buzz word in Elaine Bryan’s home in Kingston, where she was born to a father who was an engineer and her mother, a nurse. A past student of Excelsior and Kingston Technical high schools, she was head girl at the latter.

Staying true to her profession, education is the thrust of upcoming projects by the Elaine Bryan Foundation.

“We will continue to include additional students who are completing degrees in the STEAM fields in Jamaica. The projection for 2026-7 is to extend mentorship programmes in Jamaica, study abroad and exchange programmes,” she disclosed.

World.title: ‘Long overdue’
World.content:
Minister of National Security and Deputy Prime Minister Dr Horace Chang and Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Olivia Grange are all smiles as they receive the keys to the third Government-run shelter for women facing domestic abuse. (Photo: JIS)

LOCAL gender advocates have welcomed news that work has been completed on a third shelter for victims of domestic abuse.

Minister with responsibility for gender affairs Olivia Grange made the announcement last Friday as she toured the facility at an undisclosed location.

“We made a commitment that we would establish three centres, safe spaces for women, and we have achieved that,” said Grange as she pointed out that prior to the Dr Andrew Holness-led Administration there were no State-run shelters for women wishing to leave violent relationships.

In the last few years the Government completed, and is operating, two shelters for women. Grange said the addition of the third shelter will enable the ministry to offer up to 70 safe spaces for women and their children.

Grange said the completion of this third shelter, which is scheduled to begin providing a safe space for women after September 1, enables the Government to provide much-needed services to vulnerable females across the entire island.

“The completion of this space advances the gender agenda, because what we have been able to do now is to provide the spaces across the island, and we are now better equipped that when we get the call we are able to activate the kind of network that is necessary to move [women in abusive situations] into safe spaces,” said Grange.

On Sunday, gender and development practitioner Judith Wedderburn told the Jamaica Observer that the new shelter was long overdue.

“It is certainly very welcome because, not only from my experience but from the reports of women who do suffer, they have been beaten by a male partner and have experienced gender-based violence. The data does show us that it’s not getting better. More and more reports are coming out that it is happening,” said Wedderburn

According to Wedderburn, she became aware of plans to construct the new shelter through discussions with officials of the Bureau of Gender Affairs, however she was uncertain of the completion time.

“I am acknowledging that I have been in meetings in the last couple months where it was reported by somebody from the bureau that a third shelter was going to be built in a different part of the island, outside of Kingston. My understanding was it was going to serve the western part of the island,” said Wedderburn.

Pointing to a recent article published by the Jamaica Gleaner headlined, ‘The cop who finally listened’, Wedderburn said the presence of another shelter in the country serves as a call to action.

“Two women who recounted years of fear after ending abusive relationships are grateful to a corporal for standing with them. What it said was the woman who had been so badly abused was paying tribute to the only policeman who took her report seriously, the only policeman that supported her. And if you reflect on not just this article but other reports, on many occasions, unfortunately, a woman will not gather up the strength to go to a police station to report the incident,” Wedderburn argued.

Welcoming the initiative Joy Crawford, co-founder and executive director of female support group Eve for Life, told the Observer that the move strengthens the national response to gender-based violence (GBV) and expands access to safety for women and children leaving abusive situations.

“We recommend convening a robust, national GBV shelter working group comprising Government, NGOs, community-based organisations and other stakeholders to improve coordination, effectiveness, and accountability across the shelter system. This should include deliberate efforts to strengthen and expand non-government shelter models, recognising that Government cannot do this alone,” said Crawford.

She told the Observer that the country needs more diverse, accessible safe spaces across the island for survivors with different needs, including women with children, women with complex needs, adolescents, and other vulnerable groups.

“NGOs and community organisations play vital roles in victim identification, referral, psychosocial support, and sustained engagement. Formal referral pathways and partnerships can help survivors access appropriate services and safe accommodation earlier,” added Crawford.

For advocacy officer at Jamaica Coalition for a Healthy Society Philippa Davies, the provision of a third shelter by the Government is a commendable initiative but it is unfortunate that the problem of GBV exists.

“It is always better that society encourages, teaches, and supports healthy, safe relationships between men and women. As such, the family is the fundamental foundational institution of any society. The very real need for such places is evidence of family pathology, which is often passed on through generations,” said Davies.

She argued that the Government needs to establish a Ministry of the Family to address the critical role of the family and the need to prioritise its welfare.

“This would include strongly encouraging women and men to exercise discernment when choosing romantic and life partners, and to seek wise advice before and when challenges arise. It is scientifically established that the brain hormones released during sex bonds partners to the point of overshadowing danger signals such as the potential for or the occurrence of abuse,” added Davies who argued that the Government should also consider providing support for men who may be victims of abuse.

In announcing the completion of the new facility Grange said the Government-run shelters not only provide safety but also provide a therapeutic environment for women to rebuild their lives.

“We not only ensure that we protect them, but we help them to gain skills where they don’t have skills, we provide counselling, we have adequate space that we can facilitate a family — mother and children,” said Grange.

She revealed that during the last few years, one shelter hosted a mother and five of her children, while another mother gave birth while residing at another shelter.

Meanwhile, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Security and Peace Dr Horace Chang, acting in his capacity as chairman of the Citizens Business Group — a Government team that is mandated to manage social interventions across the country — said the establishment of Government-run shelters for women has been a big part of a programme to seek to impact, in a positive way, a number of vulnerable communities in Jamaica and, in particular in this case, women who have suffered abuse.

Chang noted that in the past few years the ministry has established domestic violence intervention centres at selected police stations as part of the strategy to eliminate domestic violence.

World.title: People and culture give Ja tourism edge, says Tortuga Resorts CEO
World.content:
Member of Parliament for St James East Central, Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett (front row, third right), members of his East Central Education Fund team, and chief executive officer of Tortuga Resorts Leonardo Schlesinger (front row, right), stand with recipients of the constituency’s 2026 tertiary awards at the Montego Bay Convention Centre last Thursday. Horace Hines

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Leo Schlesinger, chief executive officer of Tortuga Resorts which recently acquired Hyatt Hotels’ interest in Playa Hotels & Resorts brand, says Jamaica’s greatest competitive tourism advantage is its culture and people — which no other destination can reproduce.

“Many countries have beautiful beaches. Anyone can copy a beach [but] nobody can copy Jamaican culture — that is Jamaica’s true competitive advantage,” Schlesinger told the St James East Central Scholarship and Welfare Fund’s annual tertiary awards at Montego Bay Convention Centre last Thursday.

According to Schlesinger, the warmth, energy, music, food, humour and authenticity associated with Jamaica give the island a distinctive appeal in the global tourism marketplace.

“Guests may forget the room they stayed in [but] they never forget how Jamaicans make them feel,” declared Schlesinger.

He said the value of that cultural advantage extends well beyond tourism branding as culture has become an important economic asset for Jamaica.

“When tourism is 30 per cent of the economy, culture is, in a very real sense, one-third of the Jamaican economy.

“Culture is not just heritage; it is a tool for the future. We often talk about culture as something to preserve. In Jamaica’s case, we should also think of culture as something we use to create the future,” added Schlesinger.

Tortuga Resorts has expanded its footprint in Jamaica through the acquisition of the former Playa properties — including Secrets, Breathless, Hyatt Ziva, Hyatt Zilara and Dreams resorts — and Schlesinger said the company plans to maintain its focus on the Jamaican market.

“We are deeply invested in Jamaica, and we intend to keep investing in the country,” said Schlesinger.

He argued that tourism’s economic impact reaches far beyond hotels, with visitors generating opportunities for airport workers, taxi operators, hotel employees, farmers, fishermen, construction workers, retailers, musicians, and other service providers.

The Tortuga Resorts CEO warned, however, that Jamaica’s ability to sustain its competitive advantage would ultimately depend on the quality of its human capital.

“The countries that succeed will not necessarily be the ones with the most resources. They will be the ones with the best educated, most adaptable, and most innovative people,” he said.

Schlesinger said while Jamaica faces significant challenges — including climate change, hurricanes, labour constraints, immigration, and infrastructure gaps — its people remain its most valuable resource.

“If you invest in a person in their education, skill, confidence, and creativity, the person grows,” he said. “Knowledge grows when it’s shared. Skills grow when they’re practised. Ideas grow when people collaborate,”

He called on universities to move beyond simply preparing students for employment and underscored that tertiary institutions have an equally important responsibility to develop critical thinkers and responsible citizens who will question, analyse, distinguish fact from opinion, listen to ideas they disagree with, and think independently.

“A healthy democracy does not just need educated professionals, it needs educated citizens,” he added.

For his part, Member of Parliament for St James East Central, Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett said he wants his contribution to education and human capital development to be his enduring legacy.

Bartlett revealed that 60 tertiary students from the constituency received scholarships from his education programme, valued at just under $10 million this year.

He said the scholarship programme — which began 47 years ago at the start of his political life in St Andrew Eastern and has continued for the past 30 years in St James East Central — reflects his long-standing commitment to education as a vehicle for social mobility and national development.

“If I should be asked, ‘What is it that you would really like to be remembered by 100 years from now?’ — and somebody wants to remember this fat-faced fellow from Westmoreland — I would want to be remembered as the person who made a difference in the lives of the people in this country,” Bartlett said.

“And I would like to be remembered as the one who recognised that education was the surest way for social mobility and human advancement,” added Bartlett.

World.title: Burger Gully residents welcome MP’s relocation plan
World.content:
Residents who live closest to the banks of the gully in the community known as Burger Gully are the ones Member of Parliament Philip Paulwell wants to relocate.x

SEVERAL residents of the flood-prone east Kingston community of Burger Gully have welcomed the announcement from Member of Parliament for Kingston Eastern and Port Royal Phillip Paulwell that close to 150 of them will be relocated.

Paulwell made the disclosure during his address at his annual constituency conference at Vauxhall High School just over one week ago.

“I am willing to relocate; a lot of people are willing too. We really want to see it happen. We a feel it, man. As high as the windows them be, water goes through them. All the stoves and fridge you seeing here, a wash them wash out a people house,” said one female resident as she pointed to several flood-damaged appliances.

“This has been happening for more than 40 years. I have been living here for 38 years and it has been flooding since then,” added the woman who noted that many persons are forced to start over when their homes are flooded during heavy rain.

Her sentiments were echoed by Alton Giscombe, a shopkeeper in the area.

“When it floods, the water comes straight into the shop; I have to place my goods on top of crates. Two a me fridge them mash up,” said Giscombe.

“I am comfortable with relocating because I wouldn’t want for the gully to be flooded again and it flood out my things them,” Giscombe added.

For Frank Smith, another resident, while he appreciates the initiative, he would rather the gully walls be adjusted to prevent the frequent flooding.

“They could have raised the gully a little higher and everybody could be happy. If they carry the gully wall another four feet or five feet high I think we would be happy because the water would just go down,” said Smith, who added that he recently learnt about the relocation initiative.

According to Smith, when the gully overflows its banks the water enters his house and destroys everything.

“Over the years I have been flooded out like six times. You have a time water come here and it don’t trouble me but when the gully bursts, it floods my home.

“Even right now my car is there. When I came out of my house the last time [the gully] burst, it flooded the car. It destroyed my transmission, seat, and engine — everything full of water,” Smith said, pointing to an abandoned car along the side of the gully.

For Hyacinth — who has lived in Burger Gully for 54 years — even though she is not directly affected by the flood waters, the initiative is welcomed.

“The last time the gully come dung it barely came into my house, [and] it did not destroy my stuff. But if it is safer and the community that we will be living in is okay, I will go,” said Hyacinth even as she underscored that she will miss her current community if she relocates.

The flooding of Burger Gully, an informal settlement also called 17 1/2 Mountain View Avenue, has been an ongoing problem but worsened last year as sections of the gully which runs through the community were damaged by flood waters.

According to Paulwell, the Government has already allocated $30 million to repair the gully, with work expected to be completed by next month.

He told the Observer that lands have been identified in the communities of Mountain View and Rockfort for the relocation of Burger Gully residents, but he is awaiting a response from minister with responsibility for works Robert Morgan.

“I have identified three different parcels of land in and around the community. It is for the ministry now to come and do the proper surveying of the land,” Paulwell said.

World.title: Voice House expands
World.content:
Some of the 50 students selected from across the island for the free Singing Summer Intensive hosted by Tessanne Chin Foundation rehearse an item in preparation for the programme’s final showcase on August 23 at Louise Bennett Garden Theatre.

Singer and recording artiste Tessanne Chin, through her charitable foundation, just hosted over 50 talented children — her largest cohort to date — for a 4th annual Summer Singing Intensive training camp.

The programme’s signature end of camp showcase — this year titled Out of the Box — got underway on Sunday, August 23, at Louise Bennett Garden Theatre (Ranny Williams Centre).

The group was coached by Chin and a team of highly qualified performance instructors, among them Evad Campbell, Lori Burnett, Diana Sancho, Victoria Taffe, and Kelly Barrett.

This year’s edition also marks a major milestone for one of Jamaica’s most prominent singers who has plans to expand her year-round performing arts academy, called The Voice House, at a newly dedicated home now located in Liguanea, St Andrew.

She also pointed out that the dynamic performance ensemble associated with the programme will also now be known as The Voice House.

“It has always been my dream is to create a space where children can develop their voices and their confidence all year long. Through The Voice House we will offer comprehensive training in singing, voice acting, stagecraft, and performance development, giving young talent a structured pathway to grow their skills throughout the year,” shared Chin.

“Over the past three years we have been successfully hosting an after-school programme and our kids have been consistently engaged for several corporate and entertainment events, demonstrating the high-calibre output that we are delivering. We see so much potential to deliver so much more under our expanded programme,” she further highlighted.

Looking ahead, Chin and her team are laying the groundwork to establish a talent agency for children, creating a safe, structured avenue for young performers to access auditions, bookings, and industry opportunities both locally and internationally.

“Our new home has and will continue to allow us to give them the kind of consistent, world-class training that builds not just performers, but empowered young people,” she added.

Chin’s vision is being strengthened by the support of some of Jamaica’s most influential artistes, including Sean Paul, who this year has generously offered scholarships to help children access the year-round programme and pursue higher education in the performing arts.

She also noted the kind contributions of this year’s sponsors Tastee, Supreme Ventures, Sagicor, Sandals Foundation, CHASE Fund, Digicel Foundation, Lasco, GraceKennedy Group, Loshusan, and Wisynco.

She also expressed gratitude for her production partners and Jamaica Cultural Development Commission (JCDC) for their involvement in making the programme a success.

World.title: ‘JUST HAVING FUN’
World.content:
Oblique Seville (foreground) celebrates winning the men’s 100m event at the Silesia Diamond League athletics meeting in Katowice, Poland, on Sunday. Photo: AFP

World Champion Oblique Seville says his men’s 100m victory at the Wanda Diamond League meeting in Silesia, Poland, on Sunday, sets him up well for the remainder of the season.

The Jamaican ran a meet record 9.83 seconds (1.4m/s) during the Kamila Skolimowska Memorial, effectively securing his place in the Diamond League final set for Brussells, Belgium, in two weeks.

Kenny Bednarek ran a season’s best 9.87 for second and fellow American Christian Coleman was third in 9.93. Jamaican Ackeem Blake ran 10.26 in his first-round race and failed to advance.

Seville, 25, said he is also eyeing success at the first-ever Ultimate Championships set for Budapest, Hungary, in mid-September.

“I am in pretty good shape and I feel pretty good about the win. I am in great shape for the Ultimate Championships. The victory feels nice — especially as I ran close to my personal best — and I am just having fun,” he said.

After placing second at the London Diamond League last month, he qualified for Sunday’s final after running 9.90 (1.9m/s) in the preliminaries. He then broke the meet record of 9.87 that was held jointly by three men, including compatriot Kishane Thompson.

“There are great things ahead of me,” Seville said. “Many sprinters ran under 10s, that is really special. For the rest of the season I would like to keep winning, and the next win should be in Brussels.”

Brianna Lyston was the best-placed Jamaican in the women’s 100m, placing fourth in 10.96(0.6m/s). The race was won by American Melissa Jefferson-Wooden, who maintained her unbeaten run all year with a season’s best-equalling 10.78. Jefferson-Wooden defeated St Lucia’s Olympic Games champion Julien Alfred who ran a season’s best 10.83. Another American, Sha’Carri Richardson, placed third in 10.96.

Tina Clayton, who had a good start, faded to sixth place with 11.01, while her twin sister Tia was ninth with 11.24.

Megan Simmonds was second in the 100m hurdles, running 12.62 (0.2m/s) behind American Alaysha Johnson who won in 12.52. Poland’s Pia Skrzyszowska placed third with 12.64.

Ackera Nugent, who raced in Finland four days prior, was fourth with 12.64, while two-time world champion Danielle Williams was fifth in 12.70.

Nickisha Pryce ran a season’s best 49.49 for second in the women’s 400m as world champion Marileidy Paulino of the Dominican Republic clocked 48.87 to win for the fifth-straight time on the Diamond League circuit.

Salwa Eid Naser of Bahrain finished third with a season’s best 49.57 while Stacey Ann Williams was sixth with 49.81.

Three days after he competed at the Diamond League in Lausanne, Switzerland, Orlando Bennett was fifth in the 110m hurdles in 13.25 (-0.7m/s).

American Ja’Kobe Tharp, who had finished at the back of the race in Switzerland, rebounded to win with 13.05 in a clean sweep of the top three places for Americans. Trey Cunningham was second with 13.08, just ahead of Jamal Britt (13.09),

Rajindra Campbell was sixth in the men’s shot put with 21.61m as Italy’s world leader Leonardo Fabbri won in dramatic fashion, coming from fourth place with 22.08m in fourth round.

Early leader Jordan Geist of the United States was second with 21.96m while his country man Joe Kovacs was third with 21.86m.

Olympic Games champion Roje Stona was sixth in the men’s discus throw with 67.65m while national champion Ralford Mullings threw a season’s best 66.44m for seventh after starting with two fouled efforts.

Mykolas Alekna of Lithuania set a Diamond League and meet record 72.58m to beat Kristjan Ceh (68.93m) of Slovakia and Daniel Stahl (68.25m) of Sweden.

Alekna broke his own own Diamond League record of 71.70m set in London last year and the meet record 68.60m set by Germany’s Robert Harting in 2013.

Commonwealth Games medallist Ackelia Smith finished eighth in the women’s triple jump with 13.97m (-0.7m/s) as Saly Sarr won with a Senegalese national record 15.08m (0.2m/s). Sarr defeated the Cuban pair of Leyanis Perez Hernandez, who recorded 14.91m (-0.2m/s), and Davisleydi Velazco, who jumped 14.84m (1.2m/s).

Lamara Distin was ninth in the women’s high jump, clearing 1.89m. Yaroslava Mahuchikh of Ukraine equalled the meet record of 2.00m to win. Mahuchikh topped her compatriot Iryna Geraschenko (1.98m), with Australia’s Commonwealth Games champion Eleanor Patterson (1.98).

World.title: How Dis Mek: RIVER RAFTS
World.content:
Visitors to the island boarding a raft at the start of the Rafting on the Martha Brae tour. (Photos: Gavin Jones)

RIVER rafting is one of Jamaica’s popular vacation activities for locals and visitors alike but have you ever considered the mechanics behind the making of the rafts?

Claude Johnson, raft captain #102 at Rafting on the Martha Brae, explained to the Jamaica Observer’s How Dis Mek the process behind the making of rafts during an interview on the banks of the Martha Brae river in the hills of Trelawny, where dozens of his coworkers’ rafts were docked.

Bamboo, Johnson explained, is ideal for raft creation because each joint on a stalk is essentially an air-filled sealed vacuum, allowing the stalks to float extremely well.

“The reason why we choose bamboo is because it’s air-packed, so as the joints don’t burst, everything is okay. The bamboo can take [withstand] up to a thousand [pounds] on it. You see the more length you have, the more weight you can take on top of it. You can build it 28 feet, 29 feet — those lengths are the good lengths,” said Johnson.

He explained that even if some of the bamboo joints pop open, due to age or sun damage, as long as the others remain sealed the integrity of the raft is maintained.

The use of rafts in Trelawny is well documented. Initially, rafts were used to ferry goods from rural Trelawny to the parish capital of Falmouth. Recreational rafting began in the 1970s under the Jamaica Tourist Board and has been operated by River Raft Limited since 1985.

Raft captains must be fully trained and certified before they can operate, with lessons in controlling the raft and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) certification compulsory.

Once licensed, the captains are responsible for the creation of their own rafts. To create the raft, captains need what they refer to as a “dozen stalks of bamboo”.

“If you don’t have any and you can’t go into the field to cut it, you have some people cut it and sell it for $10,000 for a dozen, [but] when we say dozen we mean 14 bamboo to make a raft,” Johnson explained.

Then to move forward, captains need a partner, because raft building is a two-person job.

Working alongside Richardo Geinues, Captain #114, Johnson demonstrated that the stalks must first be cut to the same length, placed exactly next to each other, and bound tightly to create a flat surface.

Captains use ratcheting straps to tightly bind the stalks and prevent any chance of movement. Before the binding, the stalks are pierced at one end, at the same spot, to allow for a stick to be threaded through them and bound with metal wire and pliers.

The tension from the metal wire keeps the stalks together, forming the flat bed of the raft. Then another stalk is cut into five pieces and threaded in a similar manner on top of the raft.

Außerdem ordnet er die Rentenpläne und die Umfragewerte der AfD in Sachsen-Anhalt ein.
