World.title: 3 Bambiha members deported from Malaysia
World.content:
NEW DELHI: In a major operation against the Bambiha criminal network, Indian agencies have executed a coordinated crackdown on its key overseas operatives, deporting three of its members from Malaysia who were ordering hits and carrying out extortions in India on behalf of the group's kingpin Lucky Patial.

Announced by Union home minister Amit Shah on X Monday, the high-profile action targeted Jaspreet Singh (alias Jas Behbal) of Faridkot, alongside Ajay Singh (alias Ajay Malaysia) and Pawandeep Singh, both from Rajasthan's Sri Ganganagar district. Shah posted that Indian agencies had got the three absconding gangsters apprehended in Malaysia and deported to India.

"The fugitives....are linked to the Bambiha gang and are accused of multiple crimes, including extortion, cross-border arms and narco-trafficking, and a foiled grenade attack in Ludhiana...our agencies have facilitated the deportation of 51 hardened criminals in 2026 alone."

World.title: Abhishek Banerjee in SC for speedy order on rebel MPs
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Trinamool general secretary and Lok Sabha MP

has moved the Supreme Court seeking an expeditious decision by Speaker Om Birla on petitions seeking disqualification of the 20 rebel party MPs who have aligned themselves with Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI).

According to the SC website, a bench comprising CJI and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana has listed Banerjee's plea for hearing on Aug 25.

The petition challenges the delay in deciding on the disqualification proceedings against the rebel MPs. In the recently concluded Monsoon session, Banerjee had also met LS Speaker Om Birla on Aug 12 to reiterate his demand for a speedy decision.

World.title: Showcase India's strengths to woo tourists: PM Modi
World.content:
NEW DELHI: PM Narendra Modi on Monday asked young diplomats to showcase India's civilisational, cultural and geographical strengths to make it a more attractive global tourism destination.

Talking to officer trainees of the 2025 batch of Indian Foreign Service, he asked them to serve as catalytic agents for the country's economic engagement with the world.

Stressing the importance of strengthening the digital presence of missions, he said a website is often the first gateway through which people interact with an institution and suggested leveraging the "Bharat ko Janiye" Quiz to generate greater interest in India among young people across the world and encouraged the use of AI to make initiatives engaging.

World.title: In a first, Census 2027 will not record data on begging
World.content:
NEW DELHI: In a departure from previous exercises, Census 2027 will not record data on begging separately, with the questionnaire having omitted the category 'beggars and vagrants etc' from the list of 'non-economic activity'.

This, as per sources, is due to the very less return in this category in the last census; just around 3.8 lakh non-workers and marginal workers declared themselves as 'beggars and vagrants' in Census 2011.

Another key change in is the inclusion of 'natural calamities' as a 'reason for migration', in addition to work, business, education, marriage, moved after birth, moved with household and 'any other'.

While the 2011 census and earlier had listed 'beggars and vagrants etc' as marginal and non-workers engaged in 'non-economic activity' - in addition to students, household duties, dependents, pensioners, rentiers and others - they will now be counted among 'others'; as a result, the number of beggars in the country or their classification by age, religion, state/UT, educational status etc will no longer figure in census tables.

Sources said the count of 'beggars and vagrants' returned by previous census exercises was not considered reliable, as many respondents in this category were reluctant to return themselves as such due to associated social stigma. "Census rules require the enumerator to record the occupation/non-economic activity as declared by the respondent," an officer said. The count of non-worker beggars/vagrants was thus recorded at around 3.8 lakh in Census 2011, 6.3 lakh in Census 2001 and around 5.4 lakh in Census 1991.





As for the new census fields 'father's particulars' and 'mother's particulars' - which will capture date and place of their birth as well as religion - sources said they need to be filled only where the mother and father are not listed in the same household or are no longer alive. The enumeration form already records the religion and date and place of birth of each member of the census household, including parents.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Sources told TOI that some of the trends that may emerge from recording religion of both parents include generation-wise prevalence of inter-faith marriages and history of religious conversion.

Also, date and place of birth of parents will give the aggregate data on how many Indians fulfil citizenship criteria as per Citizenship Act.

While the latest questionnaire seeks details like mobile number, Aadhaar, voter ID and Indian passport number, where "available", technically requiring every individual having these documents to share their number, sources said the enumerators have been trained to only persuade the respondents to do so, by assuring them that all individual data will remain confidential. If the respondent is still reluctant, the enumerator shall leave these fields empty.

"Even blank fields will enable the census team to cull out data on which of the documents - Aadhaar, voter ID and passport number - respondents are most reluctant to share due to privacy concerns," an official told TOI.

World.title: Why has Delhi University allowed some colleges to admit students based on Class 12 marks? | Explained
World.content:
The story so far: Admissions to undergraduate courses in the University of Delhi have, for the second year in a row, entered a mop-up round, in which some colleges were permitted to admit students based on their Class 12 Board exam results instead of their Common University Entrance Test (CUET) scores.

The university said that over 13,300 of the approximately 71,600 undergraduate seats across its affiliated colleges remain vacant after multiple rounds of admissions. These admissions were conducted on the basis of candidates’ CUET scores and their course and college preferences.

While some of the vacant seats, especially those in reputable colleges on the North Campus, will be filled in a spot admission round on the university’s Common Seat Allocation System (CSAS) portal based on CUET scores, several other colleges, mostly those located off campus, have been given permission to admit students based on their Class 12 marks.

From board exams to CUET

Until 2022, the university’s undergraduate admissions were conducted almost entirely based on Class 12 exam results. Each college would publish its individual cut-offs for different courses, and candidates whose Class 12 marks were above these cut-offs would be eligible to take admission.

This system, however, led to ever-increasing cut-offs, with many colleges seeking well over 90% marks for their most-sought-after courses, and some even demanding 99% to 100%. This also led to criticism that different school Boards, such as the Central Board of Secondary Education, the Council for the Indian School Certificate Examinations, and the various State Boards, applied different standards for awarding marks in their exams and that this made the university’s cut-off system biased in favour of students whose Boards were more liberal in handing out marks.

In 2022, the University Grants Commission (UGC) made it mandatory for all Central universities to adopt CUET, a centralised entrance test, as the basis for admissions. The UGC said this would be a standardised method that eliminates the disparities between different school Boards and creates an equal field for all candidates.

Using 12th results for mop-up rounds

Those writing CUET can mark their choices for the course and college they want in order of preference. This creates thousands of unique course-college combinations, and there will be some combinations, such as ones that comprise little-known colleges and not-so-sought-after courses, which will have few takers. This means that among the CUET candidates registered under the CSAS portal, there may not be enough who have chosen particular college-course combinations to fill those seats.

To ensure that such seats do not remain vacant, the UGC in 2024 released a set of standard operating procedures (SOPs), including allowing universities to conduct their own entrance tests, to fill the vacant seats. It also permitted the use of Class 12 marks to admit students to such seats, if necessary.

What Delhi University has done?

On August 20, 2026, the university published a list of 11 colleges, mostly off-campus ones, which were allowed to conduct admissions on the basis of Class 12 marks. On August 21, it added four more colleges to the list, and on August 23, even more colleges, including some reputable ones such as Indraprastha College for Women and Gargi College, were added to the list.

Last year, too, after the university reported nearly 7,000 vacant seats following several rounds of admissions, colleges were allowed to conduct a mop-up round using Board exam results.

University officials have stressed, however, that CUET will remain the primary means by which students are admitted to undergraduate courses. Class 12 exam results will be used only to fill seats that remain vacant after multiple rounds, officials said.

World.title: Remembering Chennai’s Pilot Theatre, once Royapettah’s modern cinema
World.content:
For many in Royapettah and nearby neighbourhoods, an evening at the movies once meant a trip to Pilot Theatre.

Opened in November 1968, the 900-seat cinema was among Madras’s most modern, with a large screen, imported projection equipment, an elaborate sound system, and air-conditioning. Built by the founder of Pilot Pens in India, P.A. Sanjivi, with Cinerama in mind, it initially used 70 mm projection after technical delays, opening with The Ballad of Cable Hogue.

Pilot soon became part of the cinema circuit for residents of Royapettah, Triplicane, Mylapore, and T. Nagar.

Retired bank employee T.P Gopal, 72, who lived in Triplicane in the late 1970s and early 80s, recalls how the cluster of theatres nearby made catching a film an easy part of evenings with friends. “We were residents of Triplicane in those days, and it was considered a bachelor’s paradise, with affordable messes for food, the seashore nearby and several theatres within two to three km,” he recalls.

For Gopalan and his friends, Pilot was often a post-work, post-dinner destination. On one occasion, expecting a Tamil film, they sat through an English film thinking it was a trailer, only realising their mistake when “INTERMISSION” appeared.

Film historian and actor Mohan V. Raman, who lived eight houses away, recalled watching hundreds of films at the theatre, sometimes returning home during the interval and making it back for the second half, in a 2017 The Hindu article.

The theatre featured cushioned tilt-back seats, generous legroom, a 53 ft. by 24½ ft. screen and an RCA sound system. Its air-conditioned projection booth was described as the country’s first of its kind. The broad-fronted building also had extensive parking, a landscaped compound with an underwater-lit lily pond, four main entrances and two side gates. Opening s highlighted its Cinerama capability and 70 mm projection.

Pilot later hosted the Chennai International Film Festival in 2003 and 2008. Closed since mid-2014, it was demolished by February 2017 under court orders.

Pilot remains a reminder of a phase when the theatre itself was part of the attraction and of evenings that began with dinner, friends and an impulsive second show.

World.title: From celluloid to digital: the changing face of Chennai’s cinema industry
World.content:
Nothing gives a better idea of what Madras was like 80 years ago than scenes from the film En Manaivi, released in 1942. Indian medicine specialist Vembu Iyer, played by the late T.R. Sarangapani, tells his friend and patient that he moved from Pattanam (Mylapore) to the village of Kodambakkam to prevent his wife from visiting her relatives regularly.

The film begins with the arrival of a train at Kodambakkam railway station, surrounded by trees, waterbodies, and houses set amid paddy fields. In 84 years, Kodambakkam — or Kollywood, the heart of Tamil cinema — has changed beyond recognition. So has the Tamil film world.

The film was produced by A.V. Meiyappan, who established the AVM studio in Vadapalani on 10 acres of land that once housed a tannery. He bought the land for ₹37,500, a princely sum in those days.

He constantly experimented with filmmaking and was among the first to achieve post-synchronisation when the required technology was not available. In the film Sri Valli, when the heroine, Kumari Rukmini, could not match the pitch of the hero, T.R. Mahalingam, Meiyappan recorded the songs in the voice of playback singer Periyanayaki.

In his memoir, Enadhu Vaazhkai Anubhavangal, he writes that his experiment was a phenomenal success, and that the film — produced on a budget of ₹2 lakh in 1945 — earned a tenfold profit. He introduced the latest technology and imported the U.S.-made Mitchell 35 mm camera, which is preserved at the AVM Heritage Museum, offering a glimpse into the sweeping changes embraced by the film world.

Who would have thought that cinemas that once ran with a single projector — with four breaks as there was no second projector to keep the entire film ready for screening — would adapt to IMAX, even though they have fallen on hard times with the advent of exclusive film channels and OTT platforms?

Even filmmaking has undergone great changes — from shooting thousands of feet of film to embracing digital technology. Writer Ashokamitran, in My Years with Boss at Gemini Studios, recalls how thousands of feet of film shot for Avvaiyar were trimmed to create the final product. “Vasan (the boss) sat down to select from the miles of footage — only in films can the footage be in miles. He sat for hours viewing the projection of all that had already been shot, while his editors stood by with scissors and splicers. Every time he closed his eyes, a thousand feet were cut. He streamlined the multi-styled rendering, freshly shot, and inserted connecting links from scene to scene, gave a truly poetic beginning to the film, and ended it with a spectacular ‘ascent to the heavens’ finale,” he writes.

But Meiyappan dispensed with the practice of shooting 20,000 feet of film and inserting over 50 songs, and began making shorter films. When he released Naam Iruvar, S.S. Vasan congratulated him on making a good film in a small town without sophisticated equipment.

Cinematographer-turned-actor M. Ilavarasu said the primitive Mitchell camera, due to its pull-down claw and pin registration, could shoot only up to 24 frames per second (fps), both forward and reverse. It gave way to the German Arriflex 2C and 2BV, which, designed with pressure pad registration, could shoot up to 48 fps. But this was not suitable for masking double action shots. Later came Mitchell high-speed cameras with 144 fps, but they were not popular in India, he said.

“In the early days, the Mitchell camera was the non-reflex type, with a rack-over viewfinder; camerapersons could start shooting only after plenty of rehearsals as they could not see through the viewfinder while filming. The Arriflex 2C and 2C BV are high-speed cameras capable of shooting 48 fps, but with a fixed viewfinder,” he, who worked with Stills Ravi and cinematographer Kannan, the cinematographer of Bharathiraja, before working as a cinematographer for 11 films between 1991 and 2005, said. Subsequently, filmmakers imported Arriflex 3C and Arri 3 with rotating viewfinders, and much later, the Arri 435, whose viewfinder could be shifted to the other side for left-eyed camerapersons, he added.

The film reels, stored in boxes (petti), were transported across the State to cinema halls for release/screening in the past. “Potti vanthuruchu, potti vanthuruchu,” the chorus in the film Aan Paavam after the arrival of the reels in a box, recalls the years when films were made on the expensive celluloid.

Writer Perumal Murugan, in his memoir Nizhal Mutrathu Ninaivugal, recorded how multiple theatres would screen the same film by quickly dispatching the reels to another after a screening. Any delay would anger the audience, who would be eagerly waiting to watch the next part of the film.

“My Vaathiyar (mentor) Balu Mahendra used to tell me how careful he had to be while using film for shooting. He recalled the days when he worked as a cinematographer on the film Chattakari (1974), directed by K.S. Sethumadhavan, who would touch his shoulder while saying ‘cut’,” recalled writer and director Suka.

But today, digital technology has revolutionised filmmaking, and cinematographers and directors can experiment with any number of takes until they are completely satisfied.

“Digital cameras allow 120 fps and come with an additional monitor that lets a third person supervise the production while the cameraperson focuses on the viewfinder,” Mr. Ilavarasu said. Nowadays, films are sent in the file format for screening, with amazing sound effects.

Theatres have survived all odds to become one-stop destinations — they sell everything and allow online ticket booking, making the rush to buy tickets and the beeline to the canteen for a cup of tea, goli soda, a thattu murukku or a bun, things of the past.

World.title: From protest streets to the stage, Mumbai’s Gen Z voices speak out
World.content:
On Monday (August 24, 2026), Mumbai saw students, political representatives, performers and social media personalities gather to discuss youth participation in the recent protests and the role of young people in Indian politics.

The event titled “Dil Se Bol: Mumbai with Gen Z Rising” was organised by DIL Se Bol at the Y.B. Chavan Centre and hosted by stand-up comedian Varun Grover.

The event featured performances by poet Puneet Sharma and comedian Abish Mathew, followed by a panel discussion involving NCP (SP) spokesperson Anish Gawande, social media influencer Riya Ahir and Raghuram. Other poets and artists performed meaningful pieces with the theme of freedom and the protests.

Much of the discussion centred on the Cockroach Janta Party-led student protests . Ms. Ahir recalled her experience on July 20, when a photograph of her holding out her hand in front of a police van went viral.

She said the incident angered her and prompted her to take action.

“The incident on July 20 burned my blood. So I decided to step out and do something,” Ms. Ahir said. She also said that she photographed the vehicle’s number plate at the site and found that it did not bear the mandatory High-Security Registration Plate (HSRP). She also found nine other vehicles without the HSRP licenses.

Mr. Gawande spoke about the solidarity he witnessed during the protests, recalling people staying overnight at Jantar Mantar and volunteers distributing food and other essentials.

“No one expected that the resignation would happen. The most hopeful and powerful thing is that everyone who was there said they won’t go home until we get the resignation. There were times when 50 people were sleeping on the street throughout the night. One grandmother had come to bring food. One woman came from West Bengal and was distributing biscuits. This just shows that the Government can try, but they can’t break the spirit of India,” he said.

Actor Shabana Azmi, who also addressed the gathering, said the protests had challenged the perception that young people were politically disengaged. “The idea that India doesn’t care has been removed. We made the wrong accusations against the youth saying they don’t do anything, but we never set a good example for them. The sight I saw when I was at the protest on July 19, 20, was surreal. We matter, and the youth has shown us that we matter,” she said.

AISA national president Neha Bora, in her closing remarks, also spoke about the July 20 protests and questioned the use of tear gas against people gathered at Jantar Mantar. She said the demonstrations reflected an anger among young people that is rooted in a history of injustice that has been going on in the country, and even criticised mainstream television news coverage.

“There is pent-up anger in the youth of our nation. Godi media has earned the disrespect of Gen Z by falsifying the realities of what happened during the protests,” she said. She also added that, more than the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, people were calling for the resignation of Narendra Modi and Amit Shah.

Ms. Bora said young people would continue to challenge attempts to erase or distort the history of India’s freedom struggle. She also called for greater political engagement among the youth and said Gen Z would determine how political parties are received both in Parliament and on social media.

World.title: Romance, longing, life, and cinema on Chennai’s beach
World.content:
Filmmakers have always used certain symbols, motifs, and signifiers to represent ideas, concepts, and places. Over the many years, popular city landmarks, including the hotel Taj Mahal Palace in Mumbai and the Cubbon Park in Bengaluru, have been used as establishing shots to depict the city in which a film is set. For Chennai, it has always been a toss-up between Marina/Elliot’s Beach, Central Station, Anna Flyover, Spencer Plaza, and LIC Building.

While one could argue that the LIC Building established the “big city” vibe and that Spencer Plaza represented Chennai’s “modern and capitalist” aspects, the beach has always been used to represent love and life.

Remember the song, Enna Paarvai, Undhan Paarvai, from Kadhalikka Neramillai, a popular 60s film that many, swear to be the unmatched “evergreen romantic” comedy. The song showcases a young couple — Muthuraman and Kanchana — shaking a leg to a melodious song at the beach, unrecognisable with manicured lawns and the absence of cars. Similarly, in Mani Ratnam’s Alaipayudhey, staying true to the perception of the beach as a sanctuary for those in love, the lead-in to the song, Snehithane, shows the hero waiting for the heroine at the beach.

The iconic Ilaiyaraaja song Idhu Oru Pon Malai Pozhudhu from the film Nizhalgal showcases the beach as a place where college students go to smoke weed after bunking classes and build grandiose dreams about their future.

Filmmaker Venkat Prabhu’s debut film, Chennai 600028, captured another aspect of the beach — its popularity as a space for playing sports, until the police began imposing restrictions. While the Gen Z crowd may not be aware, the black tar road on the beach used to be where hundreds of tennis ball cricket matches took place in the evenings, while the fiercely contested football and volleyball games happened on the beach sands. The final “match” with the school kids at the beach reflected its popularity as a space for playing sports, until the police began imposing restrictions.

Filmmaker Vetrimaaran’s Vada Chennai portrayed the lives of those who live near the coast and depend on the Kasimedu Fishing Harbour for their livelihood. While the film itself is about Chennai’s underworld, it focuses on the trials and tribulations of those living near the beach through various points in recent history. Not just the beach, but its people, their politics and economic conditions were the focus of the critically-acclaimed film.

In actor Sivakarthikeyan’s Marina, the beach becomes a place of refuge for those running away from home.

In a way, the Marina, the Elliots Beach, and the sandy beaches along the East Coast Road evoke different perceptions. While the Marina has maintained its position as the city’s major landmark for tourists, the Elliots’ Beach and those further down the East Coast Road have slowly transformed themselves to attract the hip and fashionable youngsters of Chennai.

With the city growing at a rapid pace, there may be more “landmarks” or cultural markers that the filmmakers will be interested in, but one thing is for sure, the beaches in Chennai will continue to fascinate the storytellers for many years to come.

World.title: Children being treated worse than animals: CJP writes to state governments, seeks data on school infrastructure
World.content:
The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which has put state government schools at the centre of its ongoing campaign, wrote to all state governments on Monday (August 24, 2026), seeking data on school infrastructure, teacher vacancies, and funding over the last five years.

In identical letters addressed to Education Ministers, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke said visuals from government schools circulating on social media showed that many children still lacked basic facilities such as safe drinking water, functional toilets, proper classrooms, and even benches.

"It has been 80 years since India gained Independence...No child in this country should be forced to study in such conditions. They are being treated worse than animals," Mr. Dipke wrote.

The letters are the latest step in CJP's campaign regarding the condition of government schools. The youth-led outfit has been highlighting dilapidated school buildings and inadequate facilities on social media while demanding greater public spending on education.

The campaign has also seen confrontations on the ground. A CJP team, including co-convenor Ashutosh Ranka, was allegedly assaulted during a recent visit to a government school in Rajasthan.

The CJP accused BJP workers of carrying out the attack, a charge the party disputed, and cross FIRs were subsequently filed over the incident.

In its letters to the states, the CJP has now sought details of the number of government schools renovated over the past five years and those still requiring repairs or complete renovation.

It has also asked state governments to disclose the number of sanctioned, filled and vacant teaching posts and provide figures on funds allocated to government schools over the past five years against the amount actually spent.

The party also sought estimates of how many additional government schools are needed to ensure reasonable access to quality education and details of non-teaching duties assigned to government school teachers.

It has also sought data on how many schools have adequate computers and digital-learning facilities, clean and functional toilets, and proper sports facilities and equipment.

"This is not about politics or any one government. This is about the future of our children," Mr. Dipke said.

"Every child, irrespective of where they are born or how much their parents earn, deserves a safe classroom, clean drinking water, a functional washroom, a bench to sit on, and a teacher to teach them," he added.

The party has urged the Education Ministries to make the information public and take "urgent steps" to address deficiencies in government schools, calling for improvements to public education infrastructure on a "war footing".

World.title: Family issues, stress account for nearly one-third of child missing cases in first five months of this year in Keralam
World.content:
As many as 932 children were reported missing between January and May 2026 in Keralam, according to the State’s Women and Child Development department (WCD).

Family issues/stress accounted for 343 of these cases, a submission made by the department at a zonal consultation for southern States convened by a committee constituted by the Supreme Court for preparation of a standard operating procedure (SOP) on missing children/child or human trafficking said.

Elopement with romantic partners or friends accounted for 161 cases, while kidnapping cases came to nine. Significantly, most of these missing children were traced within a week, according to officials.

In the year 2023, 2,401 children went missing. Of them, 2,397 were traced. In 2024, 2,665 of the 2,681 children reported missing were traced. In 2025, of the 2,600 children reported missing, all but 26 were traced.

When fertility falls

The WCD submission also pointed out that fertility had fallen to below replacement in Kerala. International experience has shown that where fertility fell while demand for children and cheap labour persisted, markets in human beings — infants at birth, children and women for sexual exploitation, domestic servitude, forced labour, organ removal and begging — expanded and established themselves unless systems were built in advance to check these.

According to the WCD, a total of 716 drives were conducted during 2025–26 for prevention of child trafficking and child labour. Of these, 168 were conducted jointly with the police.

Trafficking cases

The rescued children were either released to family or sent for institutional care or repatriated through child welfare committees (CWCs). Where trafficking with the involvement or connivance of the family was found, the children were not restored, and care and protection vested with the State authorities and the child welfare committees.

As many as 44 meetings of task forces for missing children that function in all districts through inter-departmental coordination (Labour, WCD, Kerala Police, Health, and local self-government institutions) had been held. The task forced had identified 150 hotspots relating to child trafficking and children in street situations, according to the WCD.

APL households

Interestingly, 61% of the children reported missing in the first five months of 2026 were from APL (above-the-poverty-line) households. “The emotional, social and economic vacuum around the child — not the stranger at the gate — drives most disappearances,” according to the WCD.

The State plans to implement ward-wise vulnerability mapping of families by the DCPUs; panchayat-level support committees to address underlying economic, social and mental-health problems of mapped families; a supervised cadre of trained social-work students and practitioners assigned to the children identified as vulnerable and provide them sustained emotional support.

Other measures that are planned include regular awareness classes for children, families and communities through schools and anganwadis — covering grooming, enticement, online risks, safe migration, and the lawful complaint channels; counselling-led repatriation that is institutionalised through DCPU counsellors; and continued interventions in the hotspots and continuation of Saranabalyam drives.

World.title: Amid Sri Lanka’s green energy push, communities in Mannar fear environmental fallout
World.content:
Mannar

For about a decade now, successive governments in Sri Lanka have sought to tap Mannar’s strong winds to power the island’s transition to green energy. But renewable energy projects — existing and proposed — have left local communities increasingly fearful about the possible impact on their environment and livelihoods.

Residents in villages across Mannar district, on Sri Lanka’s north-western coast, report recurring flash floods in recent years, growing demand for land from both the government and private companies, the constant noise from wind turbines near their homes, and a shrinking fish catch. They fear that the growing number of renewable energy projects could be contributing to these changes and impacting the environment. If decades of war meant contending with deaths, disappearances, and displacement, the post-war years have forced another struggle upon the people of Mannar — for development that meets their needs. The renewable energy projects are yet to speak to them.

“We are often asked if there is scientific proof linking these changes to the renewable energy projects. Sometimes, everyday lived realities of people reveal more than science does,” said Fr. G. A. Arulraj Croos, Director, Caritas Valvuthayam, the social arm of the Catholic Diocese of Mannar. “It is a survival issue, not merely an environmental concern.”

Residents have no scientific evidence to substantiate their claims so far. But they contend that the authorities, too, have not shown them research that rules out any impact on their environment. “We can only tell you what we see and experience. The course of waterways in our village has changed. We can see the coastline eroding,” said a resident of Arippu village who leads a local fishermen’s association. “Following land acquisitions in the district to accommodate wind turbines, rainwater does not drain out like before. We are frequently experiencing floods,” he said, requesting not to be named. “They [the authorities] think we oppose everything”.

Mannar district spans the country’s north-western mainland and a small, dolphin-shaped island connected to it by a causeway. It is on this island that Talaimannar, Sri Lanka’s closest point to India, is located – once connected to Rameswaram by a short ferry ride across the Palk Strait. It is also here that some of the strongest winds on the island blow.

Harnessing the winds

Thirty towering turbines bearing the name of their Danish manufacturer, Vestas, line the southern coast at the Ceylon Electricity Board [CEB]’s Thambapavani wind farm — Sri Lanka’s first large-scale wind project. Conceived in 2018 to add 104 MW to the national grid, the nearly $200-million project was financed through an Asian Development Bank loan and officially inaugurated in late 2020 by then Prime Minister Mahinda Rajapaksa, when his brother Gotabaya Rajapaksa was President.

Less than a year later in October 2021, Adani Group chairman Gautam Adani flew to Colombo and met Mr. Gotabaya to discuss the Colombo port terminal project that Adani Ports was executing. He also discussed potential renewable energy projects and visited Mannar with his team in a Sri Lanka Air Force chopper to see one of the island’s most resource-rich regions.

Five months later, the CEB signed an agreement with Adani Green for a $500 million, 500 MW wind power project. The Rajapaksa administration approved the investment without a competitive bid, triggering many questions and a prolonged controversy. The succeeding Ranil Wickremesinghe administration, too, through the Board of Investment, cleared the wind power project in Mannar and nearby Pooneryn in February 2023. One of the biggest FDIs to come into the island after a devastating economic crisis, the wind farm project soon faced legal challenges from environmental groups and local communities. It was in the spotlight until Adani Green pulled out in February 2025, even as President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s government resisted the company’s “excessive” power purchasing tariff. Adani Green left, but locals’ apprehensions remain.

Green energy ambitions

Sri Lanka aims to meet 70% of its total energy requirement through renewable sources. The Indian government is executing a hybrid renewable project across Delft, Analathivu, and Nainathivu islands, off the Jaffna peninsula, with an $11-million grant.

Colombo has identified Mannar as a key source of wind energy, given its potential. In the wake of persistent protests from locals voicing fears about the apparent environmental impact of the projects, including their impact on a key bird corridor that draws seasonal flamingos, the Cabinet decided late last year to halt all new wind power projects on Mannar Island.

President Dissanayake instructed authorities not to proceed with future projects “without the consent of the people living on Mannar Island”. Meanwhile, the government is pressing ahead with projects already decided upon, with local energy firms Hayleys Fentons, WindForce, and Vidullanka winning bids to execute wind farm projects in Mannar.

Residents are reassured that new projects are on hold, but they do not know what to make of ongoing projects. They voice concerns about the possible tremors from turbines and worry that these might affect pregnant women and children. When information is scarce, the line between verified reports and vague rumours blurs.

“If authorities are not transparent, you cannot prevent speculation and scaremongering,” said M.A. Ameerun Nisha, a member of the local council or Pradeshiya Sabha. “The government needs to tell the local communities what these projects are about, how much land they need, what benefits they will bring to the local community and what the environmental risks are.”

Those active in local campaigns against wind power projects say they were not consulted. “This government opposed the Adani project not because of the environmental risks that we locals raised, but because they found the tariff high,” said A. Robert V. Peries, an engineer in Mannar. Activists like him understand the importance of switching to renewable energy, especially in the wake of the global energy crisis. But the irony of a country’s push towards green energy possibly threatening local environments is hardly lost on them. “When we flag unusual flooding, a fall in our harvest or a drop in fish catch, authorities must take note,” Mr. Peries said.

Sri Lanka’s total installed energy capacity is 6,345 MW, with a peak demand of about 3,000 MW, and most of the country’s demand is met by hydropower. The government aims to add 300 MW from renewable energy sources to the national grid by the end of next year, according to Deputy Minister of Energy Arkam Ilyas. Pointing to the “economic strain” from energy imports, Mr. Ilyas told The Hindu: “Some months we are spending nearly 30% of our foreign reserves to import fuel. Our aim is to reduce it to 10%.”

On the apprehensions of locals and environmental activists, he said: “We are aware of their concerns and are taking them on board. I have been visiting the villages to better understand their issues, so we can raise awareness and respond constructively. We are working to ensure that the projects benefit locals by generating employment and enhancing development prospects.”

Senior human rights activist and chairman of the Mannar-based NGO Organization of People for Engagement and Enterprise Raga Alphonsus pointed to rapid changes in the district amid a growing push for aquaculture, sand mining and wind power projects. “There are many questions regarding how consent from communities is obtained. Also, while there are individual environmental impact assessments, we do not know the cumulative impact that all these projects could have on our environment,” he said, calling for a comprehensive study of risks.

World.title: Amid distrust, Tehran wants US to initiate de-escalation
World.content:
Pakistan’s Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir exchanges views with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian during their meeting in Tehran.—Reuters

• CDF Munir holds meetings with Pezeshkian, Ghalibaf and Rezaei

• Iranian leaders stress commitment to Islamabad MoU; say Washington’s approach hindering regional stability, eroding trust in US

• Discussions focused on preventing further escalation, reopening of Hormuz, swift end to conflict, ISPR says

• Oman FM due in Tehran today for next round of talks on Hormuz

ISLAMABAD: The United States must take the first steps towards de-escalation by fulfilling its commitments under the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), Iran conveyed to Pakistan on Monday, as the latter sought to revive the diplomatic process for ending the US-Iran conflict.

The message was conveyed during Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir’s meetings in Tehran; with Iranian President Dr Masoud Pezeshkian, chief negotiator and Parliament Speaker Bagher Ghalibaf, and Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Gen Mohsen Rezaei, as he sounded out Tehran on the possibility of reviving the June understanding.

“We are committed to implementing the terms of the Memorandum of Understanding. It is the United States that must adhere to its commitments based on the agreement,” Ghalibaf told Field Marshal Munir, according to an Iranian account of their meeting.

This sentiment was echoed by Gen Rezaei in his meeting with Field Marshal Munir, who was quoted by IRNA as saying: “We distrust America and it must change its behaviour”.

Field Marshal Munir said Pakistan would continue its efforts to help restore stability in the region, Press TV reported.

According to Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi accompanied the army chief during the one-day visit, which also included meetings with Iranian Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

“Comprehensive discussions focused on measures to prevent further escalation, reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and expedited termination of the conflict. The two sides also exchanged views on regional peace and the ways to arrive at a negotiated settlement to the disputes,” ISPR said.

The Iranian leadership appreciated Pakistan’s constructive role and sincere efforts towards facilitating dialogue, de-escalation and a peaceful resolution of the conflict, the statement noted.

The field marshal’s visit comes as the two warring sides have returned to hostilities following the expiry of the 60-day armistice brokered under the Islamabad MoU.

Pakistan has, however, continued to regard the agreement as the available framework for a return to dialogue, while Iran has insisted that Washington must first address what Tehran considers breaches of the understanding.

The visit assumes added significance because Field Marshal Munir spoke by telephone with US President Donald Trump last week, before travelling to Tehran. The contents of that conversation have not been made public, but the contact provided Islamabad with a direct channel to carry the US position to Tehran, while seeking to assess whether Iran was prepared to re-engage.

The army chief’s trip began just before Washington announced a fresh economic pressure campaign against Iran, with sanctions and restrictions on Iranian oil exports likely to form a major part of the new measures.

Tehran has warned that further US pressure would deepen the confrontation rather than create conditions for negotiations.

Ghalibaf described Washington’s approach as “hinder[ing] regional stability and further erod[ing] trust in Washington”.

“Americans know that no one buys their bombast, the United States is not in an economic position to further restrict its relations with other countries,” he said in a post on X after meeting Field Marshal Munir.

The Strait of Hormuz remains central to the impasse. Iran has been insisting that US first fulfil its commitments relating to the waterway, before it considers a wider reopening and a return to the next phase of negotiations.

Field Marshal Munir’s meeting with Gen Rezaei was particularly significant because the Iranian general has recently taken over as secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, placing him at the centre of Tehran’s national security decision making at this critical stage in its confrontation with Washington.

During their conversation, Rezaei particularly emphasised Iran’s security interests in the Strait of Hormuz and the need for any settlement to address the military and economic pressures imposed on Tehran.

The issue of Strait of Hormuz is meanwhile being discussed in a separate diplomatic track in the shape of Iran-Oman talks on arrangements for navigation in the strait.

Omani Foreign Minister Badr Al Busaidi is due in Tehran on Tuesday, adding to the diplomatic activity surrounding the strait at a time when Pakistan is seeking to regain its role in the wider US-Iran process.

Published in Dawn, August 25th, 2026

World.title: Govt fails to maintain quorum as PPP stays away from National Assembly
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: The ruling PML-N on Monday suffered an embarrassing setback in the National Assembly as the lower house was adjourned within minutes for lack of quorum after its estranged ally, the PPP, stayed away from the proceedings over the alleged rigging in the recently-held Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) elections.

The government failed to muster the required number of 84 lawmakers in the 336-member house, forcing the chair to adjourn the session without taking up any agenda item when quorum was pointed out by an opposition member from the PTI.

“No PPP, no quorum, simple,” posted PPP’s Sharmila Farooqui on her official social media account on X soon after the adjournment of the sitting.

Later, Ms Farooqui told Dawn PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari had already declared the party would “no more cooperate with PML-N on quorum and legislation” in the parliament till their grievances over the alleged rigging and mismanagement in the AJK polls were addressed.

Sharmila says ‘no PPP, no quorum, simple’

Even those party MNAs who were present at the start of the Question Hour left the chamber immediately seeing only 20 to 25 PML-N members on the treasury benches, she said, adding that the PPP had been completing the quorum in the assembly previously.

Ms Farooqui made it clear that the strategy would not change until their concerns over the AJK polls issue were addressed. She, however, did not elaborate any specific demand when asked as to what steps the party wanted the PML-N to take in order to allay their concerns when the election process had already been completed.

When Speaker Ayaz Sadiq earlier announced the opening of the Question Hour, PTI’s Iqbal Afridi pointed out lack of quorum. His action came when the speaker refused him the floor to speak on a point of order.

The speaker ordered a headcount and suspended the proceedings till the completion of the quorum. Some 35 minutes later, Deputy Speaker Ghulam Mustafa Shah was seen in the chair when the house resumed its proceedings. He adjourned the sitting till Tuesday after finding the house still not in order due to lack of quorum.

While the PPP had supported the government in the passage of the two security-related bills last week, Mr Bhutto-Zardari, in the presence of PM Shehbaz Sharif, had objected to the manner with which the government had been doing legislation.

After developing differences with the PML-N over the issue of AJK elections, a PPP delegation headed by Mr Bhutto-Zardari called on opposition leaders and sought their cooperation on the legislation in the parliament and its committees.

Hina Javed’s murder

At the outset of the sitting, the NA speaker expressed his concerns over the brutal murder of Hina Javed in Rawalpindi and referred the matter to the relevant house committee.

Mr Sadiq disclosed that Hina Javed had been posted in the National Assembly by the National IT Board on attachment from December 2019 till June this year after which she returned to her parent department. He said though such matters generally fell under provincial jurisdiction, the case was of particular concern since she had served at the NA.

He said the manner in which Hina Javed was murdered, and the violence against women, were matters of serious concern for everyone.

He appreciated the Women Parliamentary Caucus for taking up the matter and said the NA would provide full support in monitoring the case and extending whatever assistance was required.

Minister for Law and Human Rights Azam Nazeer Tarar said the ministry was in constant contact with the Rawalpindi police regarding the murder investigations. Two suspects were on three-day physical remand, he said, expressing the confidence that the culprits would be brought to justice.

World.title: 3 more Adiala inmates seek private care
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: At least three inma­tes of Adiala jail have approached the Isla­mabad High Court seeking treatment at private hospitals and greater access to their families, following the Supreme Court’s recent order directing authorities to shift former prime minister Imran Khan to a private hospital for medical examination and treatment.

The petitions before the IHC vindicate the government’s concern that the SC order in Imran Khan’s case could set a precedent for other prisoners to seek similar relief.

The federal government, in its review petition before the Supreme Court, had argued that allowing a convict to receive treatment at a private hospital could disturb the existing prison system and trigger a “floodgate” of similar applications from other prisoners.

The issue is now before the IHC, where Justice Muhammad Asif sought comments from the jail superintendent on petitions filed by prisoners Ilyas Khan, Muhammad Ismail Khan and Owais Altaf. The court also issued noti­ces to prison authorities, and adjourned proceedings until Aug 27.

During the hearing, Barrister Akhtar Chheena, representing Ismail Khan, said his client was suffering from haemophilia and had developed internal bleeding. He submitted that the prisoner had been taken to hospital around 10 times in the last two months, but his condition had not improved.

According to the counsel, treatment for the particular condition was presently possible only at Shifa Interna­tio­nal Hospital. He relied upon the SC’s recent ruling and argued that where a disease could not be treated at a government hospital, a prisoner could be shifted to a private facility, with the family bearing the cost of treatment.

The counsel requested the court to constitute a medical board to determine whether the required treatment was available at a government hospital. He questioned whether a prisoner should be denied access to a private facility if a necessary procedure, including a liver transplant, was not available at a government hospital.

The petition filed by Owais Altaf was also pressed before Justice Muh­am­­mad Asif. His lawyer, Syed Jafar, ap­­p­eared through video link and submitted that the prisoner was suffering from fever and a heart ailment.

He argued that receiving proper medical treatment was a fundamental right of a prisoner and maintained that the required treatment was not available at a government facility. The counsel consequently sought an order for Owais Altaf’s transfer to Shifa International Hospital for treatment.

In another plea, Ismail Khan sought permission to communicate with his brother, who has been living in Dubai. The counsel requested that the jail authorities be directed to facilitate communication between the prisoner and his brother.

World.title: Govt increases petrol price by Rs0.39, high-speed diesel by Rs2.40
World.content:
The government on Monday raised the price of petrol by Rs0.39 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs2.40 per litre.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs341.98 per litre while HSD will cost Rs370.69 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices will be applicable on August 25 (Tuesday).

The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28.

The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.

Earlier, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

The government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

World.title: Rawalpindi police chief rules out suicide in Hina Javaid’s death
World.content:
RAWALPINDI: Regional Police Officer (RPO) Babar Sarfraz Alpa has disputed the impression that Hina Javaid’s death was a suicide.

He categorically said “it was a murder”, adding her husband and a domestic servant are in police remand custody, while the father-in-law of the victim is under investigation.

The RPO was speaking at a hurriedly-called joint press conference with City Police Officer Hassan Mushtaq Sukhera, the SSP investigations and the SP Potohar at the Police Lines auditorium on Monday night.

A special team has been formed to investigate the murder of digital media executive, Hina Javaid, 45.

Says husband and servant in remand custody, father-in-law under probe

Initially, it was portrayed as a suicide; however, after examining the body, the impression of suicide was ruled out. The victim’s father-in-law has been included in the investigation but has not been arrested.

“The investigation into the case is at an early stage, so it is not appropriate to reveal certain things at this stage. However, as the investigation progresses, those who have played a role will be identified. As soon as concrete evidence is found against the victim’s father-in-law, action will be taken against him according to the law,” the RPO said.

He said that on August 20, at 6am, Asghar Ali Fayyaz came to the police station and gave the initial information that thieves had broken into his house located on Faisal Alvi Road.

He said on receiving the information, the police reached the spot where the body of Ms Javed was found in the bathroom of the apartment. “The body was tied to the shower and her hands were tied behind her back.”

On the request of the deceased’s brother Fahad Javed, a case was registered under murder charges.

The deceased’s husband Faisal Asghar Imam, father-in-law Asghar Fayyaz and domestic servant Zeeshan and an unknown person were named in the FIR.

The RPO said that the investigation was being conducted from all angles and a special team had been formed under the leadership of the SSP investigations.

He said the suspects, Zeeshan and Faisal, are in police custody. The RPO said all means, including technical and human intelligence, are being used in the investigation.

The servant revealed to the investigating team that Faisal and Hina had a quarrel on the night of the incident over some issue during which she was reportedly tortured. As she tried to escape, she was strangled, he added. Later, she was taken to the bathroom to give an impression that she had committed suicide.

The suspect had initially given a different statement but during the remand custody he made the disclosures.

World.title: 5 women from GB successfully summit Spantik
World.content:
GILGIT: Four women mountaineers from Gilgit-Baltistan, joined by a Romanian climber and a male mountaineer from Punjab, successfully summited 7,027-metre Spantik Peak without the assistance of high-altitude porters, marking an inspiring achievement amid challenging conditions in the region.

The Alpine Club of Pakistan confirmed that the four-member local women’s team reached the summit and safely returned to Skardu on Monday.

The successful climbers were Shama Baqir and Samana Rahim of Shimshal Valley, Zooni Aslam of Gulmit Valley in Gojal, Upper Hunza, and Zaiba Batool Shigri of Shigar district.

Bismah Hassan of Lahore was also part of the expedition but returned around 250 metres below the summit after experiencing a health issue.

Bad weather hampers efforts to bring to Skardu bodies of Dr Asma Mushtaq and American climber Sarah Mallory Geis

Alpine Club of Pakistan General Secretary Ayaz Shigri told Dawn that the women reached the summit either a day before or on the same day that climber Dr Asma Mushtaq died while descending from the mountain.

He said weather conditions had been favourable at the peak before Friday, but subsequent deterioration created difficulties for rescue and recovery operations.

The expedition also featured Alexandra Visan of Romania, who, despite battling cancer, successfully climbed Spantik and descended safely. Her expedition was organised by Broad Boy Adventures, owned by Pakistani mountaineer Shehroze Kashif.

Zaiba Batool from Shigar waves the Pakistani flag. —Dawn

In a social media post, Mr Kashif said Ms Visan was accompanied by local high-altitude porter Ali Ameen of Shigar. He described her achievement as a story of perseverance, saying some climbs are about finding the strength to continue when life itself becomes the mountain.

Punjab climber Ayyan Adeel also summited Spantik. According to Mr Kashif, the attempt was notable because Ayyan became the youngest climber to summit the peak without high-altitude porter support, carrying his own equipment with assistance from fellow expedition members Awais Choudary and Talha Khalid.

While the successful summits brought encouragement to the mountaineering community, deteriorating weather has continued to hamper efforts to bring to Skardu the body of Dr Asma Mushtaq, who died at an altitude of around 6,250 metres on Thursday while descending from the Spantik summit. Her body remains at Camp 3.

Mr Shigri said a six-member team of high-altitude porters reached Camp 2 on Sunday and attempted to proceed towards Camp 3. However, heavy rain and snowfall forced the team to turn back to Camp 2.

Weather conditions are expected to improve on Tuesday, after which rescuers will make another attempt to bring Dr Mushtaq’s body down to base camp. Pakistan Army helicopters are then expected to airlift the body to Skardu.

Bad weather has also prevented helicopter operations at 8,047-metre Broad Peak, where the body of American climber Sarah Mallory Geis remains at the base camp awaiting airlift.

World.title: FBR eases sales tax registration for businesses
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has announced new measures to streamline sales tax registration for businesses, particularly those considered low risk.

Under the new system, applications filed through the IRIS portal will be screened using risk-based checks. The measures were notified through Sales Tax General Order No. 20 of 2026, issued on Monday.

Under the new procedures, applicants falling in the low-risk category will be processed within three working days under a risk-based framework, provided all required documents are complete. Applications will be submitted through the computerised IRIS system.

The FBR has directed all field formations not to demand additional documents unless they are legally required or flagged by the risk-based system.

Bars field offices from seeking unnecessary documents

To further facilitate manufacturers, the FBR has asked sectoral associations under the Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry to issue pre-registration certificates to their members.

These certificates will confirm that the applicant is engaged in manufacturing, that the business premises are identifiable, that the activity corresponds with the relevant sector and that the details provided match the association’s records. The certificates will be sent electronically to the local registration office (LRO) along with other required documents.

The FBR clarified that these certificates are intended only to expedite verification and do not replace legal requirements or grant any exemptions. It also pointed out that associations will be held responsible if false information is discovered during physical checks. Local registration offices must also conduct on-site verification of manufacturers within three working days.

At the same time, the FBR stressed that applications flagged as high-risk will continue to face stricter scrutiny, including pre- and post-verification. Even low-risk registrations may be rechecked later if irregularities are detected.

To make the registration process quicker and more transparent, the FBR has laid out a step-by-step procedure. All applications filed through the IRIS portal will be screened using a risk-based system. Those identified as low-risk will be given priority and, if complete, processed within three working days.

Field formations have been instructed not to ask for additional documents unless they are legally required, needed to verify information or flagged by the computerised risk system. If an application is incomplete, the applicant must be informed within seven days, with clear details of what is missing, what needs to be corrected and how much time is allowed to rectify the deficiencies. The order also directs that no vague or general objections be raised — every objection must be specific and linked to a clear requirement. Once the missing information is provided, the application should proceed without requiring the applicant to restart the process.
