World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Groundwork is set for BOJ rate hike next month, ex-official says
World.content:
The Bank of Japan will probably raise its benchmark interest rate next month, validating widespread market speculation, and follow up with another increase as early as January, according to a former BOJ board member.

As of Monday afternoon in Tokyo, traders were assigning a roughly 80% probability of a rate hike when the board delivers its next policy decision on Sept. 18.

With the yen still weak even after U.S.-Japan coordinated intervention, a decision to hold settings steady could reignite a selloff of the currency, raising the risk of faster inflation due to costly imports, Seiji Adachi, who served on the board until March 2025, said Monday in an interview.

World.title: New cars sold in Japan from September 2031 must have driver monitoring systems
World.content:
Automakers will soon be obligated to install a system in new cars sold in Japan that monitors drivers for signs of distraction or drowsiness, as the number of accidents caused by mobile phone use while driving increases in the country.

The Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism Ministry will revise its ministerial ordinance in September to make it mandatory for carmakers to install driver monitoring systems (DMS) for new car models from September 2031. For existing models, it will be mandatory from 2033.

“We decided to revise domestic regulations since new international regulations adopted in March, which makes DMS installation mandatory, will take effect in September,” said Shinji Morokawa, a transport ministry official in charge.

A DMS uses cameras and sensors installed in front of the driver to monitor attention. It alerts drivers if it suspects they are looking at their smartphones, for instance.

The transport ministry regulation will be revised to have the DMS sound the alarm if the driver looks down at their hands for 3.5 seconds while driving at 50 kilometers per hour or more, and for six seconds if they are driving between 20 kph and 50 kph.

The DMS will monitor the driver’s eyelids and movement of the steering wheel when a vehicle is driven between 70 kph and 130 kph. It will alert the driver if signs of drowsy driving are detected.

Carmakers such as Toyota, Subaru and Mazda have already installed such systems on some of their luxury car models. A DMS add-on for vehicles without it typically costs around ¥100,000 ($630).

According to the National Police Agency, the number of deaths and severe injuries attributed to mobile phone usage while driving has risen every year since 2020. The number reached a total of 148 cases in 2025.

The agency noted that the fatality rate for automobile accidents between 2021 and 2025 was 3.4 times higher when mobile phone use was involved compared to instances in which it wasn’t.

The Japanese mandate comes on the heels of the approval of additional regulations by the U.N.’s World Forum for Harmonization of Vehicle Regulations (WP.29) earlier this year, which addressed warning systems for driver drowsiness and distraction.

DMS mandates have been put into place elsewhere in the world, most notably in the European Union.

Under the bloc’s General Safety Regulation (GSR), driver drowsiness and attention warning systems have been required for all new road vehicles since July 2024.

Advanced driver distraction warning systems have also been mandated since July this year for all new vehicles hitting the EU market. The EU estimates that the GSR will prevent over 25,000 deaths and 140,000 serious injuries by 2038.

Staff writer Spencer Landers contributed to this report.

World.title: Bessent’s ‘D-Day’ sanctions against Iran would deepen tensions with China
World.content:
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s threat to unleash an “economic D-Day” against Iran risks setting the U.S. on a collision course with China, its main trading partner.

But that’s only if Bessent actually follows through on a threat the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump has made before. And many are skeptical about whether he will, especially when it comes to China — which buys around 90% of Iran’s oil — as Washington tries to maintain a fragile trade truce with Beijing and avoid a global economic shock.

On Monday, Bessent promised an “economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe” as Trump tries to wind down his unpopular war in the Middle East.

World.title: Silencing TaiwanPlus would weaken the island democracy
World.content:
In an era when authoritarian states pour vast resources into global media empires to shape perceptions, Taiwan’s sole international English-language news channel, TaiwanPlus, faces an existential threat from within.

The Kuomintang (KMT)-led opposition is pushing to slash nearly its entire budget subsidy. This is not mere fiscal scrutiny. It is a politically biased, shortsighted move that risks silencing Taiwan’s primary platform for speaking directly to the world — precisely at the moment when Beijing is intensifying its cognitive warfare and disinformation campaigns against the island democracy.

TaiwanPlus, on which this writer has appeared, stands as the only dedicated English-language news service produced by Taiwan for international audiences. While state-backed outlets such as China’s CGTN, Turkey’s TRT, Russia’s RT, Pakistan Television and Qatar’s Al Jazeera aggressively expand their reach and influence operations, TaiwanPlus has quietly built a meaningful presence in key democracies, including India, the United States, the Philippines, Canada and Singapore. Its achievement is all the more remarkable given the constraints under which it operates. Yet instead of recognition, it has drawn fire from opposition legislators, who often side, ironically, with Beijing.

World.title: How geoeconomics is redefining global power
World.content:
The age when governments could pretend that trade was about commerce and geopolitics was about power is ending. Tariffs, export controls, sanctions, critical minerals and supply chains have become instruments of statecraft, wielded by the world’s two largest economies in an intensifying struggle over the international order.

There is a name for this: geoeconomics.

At the recent Helsinki Geoeconomics Society Week, private-sector executives, legal experts, policymakers and scholars wrestled with what the term means and why it matters. Stripped of academic jargon, the answer is straightforward: Geoeconomics is the use of economic tools to achieve political and strategic objectives.

World.title: Takaichi pledges to continue sanctions on Russia over its war on Ukraine
World.content:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has pledged to steadily continue Japan’s sanctions on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine.

Attending an online meeting for leaders of the Coalition of the Willing on Ukraine on Monday, Takaichi said, “We will continue steadily imposing sanctions on Russia and supporting Ukraine” with four and a half years having passed since the start of the invasion.

“We always stand with Ukraine, and this stance is unwavering,” she said. The meeting took place in Kyiv.

Referring to Russia’s increasing military cooperation with North Korea and its deepening collaboration with China, Takaichi said, “The security of the Euro-Atlantic region and that of the Indo-Pacific region are inseparable, and cooperation among allied and like-minded countries is becoming more and more important.”

“It is essential for the international community to unite and support Ukraine in order to bring peace to the country,” she added.

World.title: Japan to set up expert panel on CBRNE terrorism
World.content:
The government on Monday compiled an action plan to address terrorism involving chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear and explosive, or CBRNE, materials.

Under the plan, the government will establish an expert panel to improve initial responses to CBRNE attacks, strengthen intelligence functions, improve medical care systems and secure medical supplies.

At a related meeting at the Prime Minister’s Office in Tokyo, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said, “We can’t rule out the possibility that our country will be a target of terrorism in the future.” He ordered the prompt implementation of the action plan to “protect the people from disasters.”

The panel will include doctors, academic experts, former Self-Defense Forces and police officers who were previously in charge of antiterrorism measures. It will advise the government’s antiterrorism headquarters, which will be established in the event of a terrorist attack and headed by the prime minister.

A panel of related ministries and agencies will also be set up to collect and analyze information, including on drones and artificial intelligence that could be used for terrorism.

Additionally, the government will develop a system to stockpile medical supplies to treat victims and distribute them promptly in the event of a terror attack. The government will also expand training for medical institutions that are expected to accept injured and sick people.

The action plan also calls for strengthening cooperation with other countries to prevent the proliferation of nuclear and other weapons of mass destruction, particularly with North Korea in mind.

World.title: Hong Kong needs clearer framework for handling high heat on work sites
World.content:
Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at [email protected] or filling in this Google form . Submissions should not exceed 400 words.

Public debate over Hong Kong’s recent heatwave has rightly focused on protecting frontline workers. However, one group remains largely absent from the discussion: site managers and project supervisors who carry responsibility for worker safety, project delivery and contractual compliance. Increasingly, they are being asked to balance those obligations without a clear framework.

Recent criticism of Hong Kong’s Heat Stress at Work Warning system has focused on whether the Hong Kong Heat Index adequately reflects conditions faced by outdoor workers exposed to direct sunlight. Three former directors of the Hong Kong Observatory have argued that the internationally recognised Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) might be more suitable for assessing heat risks at open-air worksites.

Regardless of which methodology ultimately prevails, the debate has exposed a gap between contractual requirements and operational reality. What should site managers do when local conditions appear unsafe but the official warning framework does not respond accordingly?

The latest generation of construction contracts increasingly recognises extreme heat as a potential ground for extension of time claims. However, such relief is linked to the Labour Department’s Heat Stress at Work Warning system.

That helps explain why the heat on August 9 raised concern. Despite temperatures reaching 39.8 degrees Celsius (103.6 Fahrenheit) in Sheung Shui, the Heat Stress at Work Warning remained at amber, the lowest level. Site managers who believed stronger precautions were warranted could have found themselves without the higher-level official trigger on which contractual protections depend.

The core issue the Labour Department needs to address is what happens when a site manager believes conditions on the ground warrant stronger precautions, but the official trigger on which contractual protections depend is absent.

World.title: Landslide kills 18 people in Hong Kong’s Sau Mau Ping – SCMP archive
World.content:
This article was first published on August 26, 1976.

Tragedy hits Sau Mau Ping

At least seven people, including four children, were killed by the landslide that hit Sau Mau Ping Estate yesterday (August 25, 1976).

Yesterday’s disaster was only a few blocks away from a slope which slipped on June 18, 1972, killing 67 people.

Fire Services teams, assisted by the Army, spent the night under search lights trying to locate people still not accounted for and thought to be buried under tons of mud which engulfed half the ground floor of Block 9 — housing about 1,200 people.

The Governor, Sir Murray MacLehose, has ordered an urgent survey of slopes in the area.

Sir Murray arrived at the estate a few hours after the disaster occurred to inspect the extent of the damage and to talk to rescue workers.

He also talked to some of the affected families in the Estate Office, where about 200 people were temporarily accommodated.

World.title: Hong Kong to revamp senior secondary science and maths curriculum from 2029-30
World.content:
Hong Kong’s education authorities will revamp the senior secondary school science and extended maths curriculum by providing additional syllabus options from the 2029-30 academic year in a bid to attract more students and nurture talent in the field.

The Education Bureau also said it had asked schools to actively encourage students interested in science and mathematics to take two or more science subjects to create a synergistic effect.

The bureau said in a circular to schools on Monday that the revamp was aligned with the strategy in the nation’s 15th five-year plan to “invigorate the country through science and education” and supported Hong Kong’s development as an international innovation and technology centre.

Edith Tse Yuen-ching, principal assistant secretary for innovation technology education at the bureau, said in a blog post that the city was “strengthening the cultivation of innovation and technology talents to respond to the development needs of the country and Hong Kong”.

The circular said a draft of the updated curriculum and assessment for the science subjects – physics, chemistry and biology – had been released for consultation. It said the bureau would brief educators early next month before finalising the draft in the next academic year.

Schools have been invited to give their views on the revamp by the end of next month.

World.title: Reflections of a reformed grammar Nazi
World.content:
“Nothing bad can happen. It can only good happen.” Donald J. Trump

It would be easy to write off the regular word salads of America’s 47th president as the increasingly incoherent ramblings of an elderly man in obvious mental and physical decline.

However, one can also argue that Trump’s seemingly dyslexic struggles with the English language reflect a deliberate disregard for grammar rules that resonates with his support base. It’s the level of language that up to half of Americans happily use and identify with, if you think about it.

Laugh if you will at his limited vocabulary, disrespect for formal syntax and contempt for punctuation, but they have never been detrimental to getting his message across as an effective public speaker and communicator.

His very lack of linguistic sophistication – simple words, short sentences, constant repetition, blunt delivery – makes maximum impact with minimum polish, grammar rules and hoity-toity talk be damned.

Trump’s dumbing down of the language is but a microcosm of a global shift towards hyper-simplified English usage, stripped bare of formalities and tuned to resonate on digital platforms. All without the encumbrance of archaic or arbitrary rules and the rigid structure that we are expected to adhere to without even remembering why we have to in the first place.

World.title: Want to keep a big dog in Hong Kong? Experts share what you should know
World.content:
Heat, humidity and crowded living spaces could pose challenges for Hongkongers hoping to keep large or aggressive dogs as pets, experts have said, urging potential owners to consider the needs of such animals before deciding to house them.

They issued the warning after a woman and two small canines were mauled in two separate attacks last week.

The woman was found collapsed in Ping Yeung Tsuen, hours after she was attacked at a dog training centre by a canine suspected of being a mixed-breed fighting dog. She was certified dead at the scene.

The smaller dogs were mauled to death in Yuen Long by an unleashed 60kg (132lbs) mastiff-type canine earlier that week.

Discussing the importance of correctly caring for big dogs, Lau Yun-yu, chairman of the Hong Kong Society for Pet Nutrition, said large canines, particularly those with thick coats, could face greater challenges in Hong Kong’s hot and humid climate.

“Dogs rely primarily on evaporative cooling through panting rather than sweating,” he said, adding that sustained high humidity could significantly reduce their ability to cool themselves.

World.title: Hong Kong woman arrested for allegedly wearing seditious T-shirt outside court
World.content:
Hong Kong police have arrested a woman for allegedly wearing a T‑shirt with a seditious message outside West Kowloon Court.

The force said on Monday night that the woman was detained last week on suspicion of disorder in a public place, obstructing police and acting with seditious intention.

“The purpose of the security operation was to ensure public safety and order, though details of the operation cannot be disclosed,” a police spokesman said.

The arrest came hours before judges delivered a verdict against two former leaders of the now‑disbanded alliance behind Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil.

Shortly after 5am on Friday, more than 50 people had queued outside the courthouse to cover or hear the judgment against former chairman Lee Cheuk‑yan and former vice‑chairwoman Chow Hang‑tung of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China.

The pair and the alliance were accused of inciting subversion under the national security law by calling for an end to “one‑party dictatorship” in mainland China.

World.title: Chinese tech, pharma firms eye Hong Kong as springboard for global expansion
World.content:
Mainland Chinese technology and pharmaceutical companies are using Hong Kong as a launching pad for global expansion, industry leaders have said, as a major state-owned drugmaker weighs whether to invest in the city’s Northern Metropolis megaproject.

The comments highlighting the city’s international background and professional expertise were made during a six-day trip to the rest of the Greater Bay Area , which was arranged by the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office and started on Sunday.

“Hong Kong is stepping up efforts to develop its innovation and technology sector. Its unique blend of Chinese and Western cultures, along with its high degree of internationalisation, gives the city a clear advantage in developing the traditional Chinese medicine industry,” Chen Jiehui, vice-chairman of Guangzhou Pharmaceutical Holdings, said on Monday.

“Through Hong Kong’s international platform, global languages and standards can be leveraged to help traditional Chinese medicine go global … such as Southeast Asian countries which could serve as a prime example of markets expanding internationally via Hong Kong.”

Chen Jiehui, vice-chairman of Guangzhou Pharmaceutical Holdings, has said his company is considering investing in the Northern Metropolis. Photo: Vivian Au

Chen added that his company, a major state-owned pharmaceutical enterprise, was considering investing in the Northern Metropolis and had previously held alignment discussions with relevant parties. He did not reveal details of the possible investment.

The Northern Metropolis megaproject aims to turn 30,000 hectares (74,132 acres) of land near the border with the mainland into a technological and economic hub.

World.title: Beijing slams West for criticising Hong Kong court verdict in Tiananmen vigil case
World.content:
Beijing has slammed Western nations for interfering in China’s internal affairs over their criticism of the conviction of the now-disbanded alliance that organised Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigils and its former leaders for inciting subversion.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian used a regular press briefing on Monday to hit out at “certain countries and organisations” for using the case to smear Hong Kong and denigrate its rule of law.

He made the comments in response to questions about expressions of concern from the US and other countries over a Hong Kong court ruling last week, which found the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, ex-chairman Lee Cheuk-yan and former vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung guilty of attempting to undermine the fundamental system of the People’s Republic of China under the national security law

Albert Ho Chun-yan, another former alliance chairman, previously pleaded guilty.

The ruling triggered criticism from the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Australia, which characterised it as an example of eroding freedoms in Hong Kong.

US Assistant Secretary of State Riley Barnes called for the defendants’ immediate release, while UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said residents should be allowed to speak without fear of arrest or prosecution.

World.title: Education, health fees among key concerns
World.content:
China to legislate on preschool education

China will push for legislation on preschool education to provide a legal guarantee for the operation and management of such institutions, Vice-minister of Education Tian Xuejun said on Nov 30.

Tian made the remarks at a news conference organized by the State Council Information Office regarding a child abuse case at RYB Education New World Kindergarten in Beijing that received widespread attention in November. He said the Ministry of Education was already doing research on the legislation.

"The ministry will also complete the requirements on qualifications of teachers engaged in preschool education and is considering formulating a code of ethics for them," Tian said.

He also said a plan is on the way to step up supervision of kindergartens and solve the problem of insufficient resources for preschool education. Tian said the case exposed the conflict between public demand for preschool enrollment and insufficient development of preschool education.

"It also showed that some local authorities and kindergartens still have problems of unsound management and failure to implement or fully implement regulations," he said.

Rural health fee increase explained in detail

The National Health and Family Planning Commission recently responded to public concern of newly increased fees for a new rural cooperative medical system.

Fees charged in the new rural cooperative medical system have recently been raised from 30 yuan ($5.5) to 180 yuan.

The NHFPC explained that while fees for individuals have been raised, government financial subsidies to individuals have also been raised accordingly in recent years from the previous 20 yuan per person to 450 per person. At the same time, the government has a comprehensive medical assistance system for those unable to afford such fees. Also, the reimbursement proportion for hospitalization costs for those in the new rural cooperative medical system has also been raised from 35 percent to 75 percent.

Anti-espionage law will help national security

The State Council issued a circular on China's anti-espionage law on Wednesday with detailed rules for implementing the law.

The circular explains several terms in the law, including overseas institutions and organizations, individuals, spy organizations, spy organization agents and hostile organizations. It was made clear that national security departments under the State Council will identify unacceptable behavior.

According to the circular, providing funds, venues and materials to spy organizations and individuals will be identified as helping them.

Conducting espionage activities in the territory, accepting overseas funds to endanger national security or connect them for spying activities will also be deemed as collusion.

Staff members at national safety departments are authorized to arrest and hunt criminal suspects, and their anti-espionage activities will not be interrupted by any other illegal actions.

It said that Chinese people and organizations retain the right and privilege to secure national safety, and their contributions such as providing clues about spying activities, collaborating with national security departments and fighting espionage activities will also be rewarded.

World.title: International group praises green revival
World.content:
High-level advisory panel pitches 15-year pollution fight, but holds China up as model

A high-level international advisory body applauded China's efforts to improve the environment and suggested a 15-year strategy against pollution in a draft recommendation report on Monday.

China has made building an ecological civilization an important goal and has taken comprehensive measures to improve the environment. This has resulted in positive results, including improved air quality, Vice-Premier Zhang Gaoli said when chairing the annual meeting of the China Council for International Cooperation on Environment and Development, a high-level international advisory body.

Like Zhang, Erik Solheim, executive director of the United Nations Environment Programme, said he was impressed by China's tremendous achievements regarding its environment in recent years, in particular curbing much of the smog problem.

"China is capable of solving the environment problems themselves," said Solheim, the council's vice-chairman, adding the best practices taken by China could provide guidance to other areas facing similar issues.

His praise of China's approaches to move toward being an ecological civilization won wide support from other members of the environmental council, which includes senior officials and experts from home and abroad.

The council's draft recommendation presents highlights of the war against pollution in air, water and soil, and suggests the creation of a 15-year strategy that will be "focused on cost-effectiveness, synergies and ways to build public confidence about eventual results".

Ideally, the integrated rollout should be ready before 2020, to be in line with the 2035 pivot point, when China expects to be a "basic modern country", the draft said.

Solheim said he is confident that China can reach the 2035 goal to build a "beautiful China", considering the determined and effective efforts adopted in recent years.

Along with the longer-term strategy to curb pollution, council members suggested creating conditions for fair competition and incentives for green industries.

Based on the input from Monday's meeting, the advisers and their support teams will modify their proposal and provide a final version to the State Council through the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

zhengjinran@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Beijing, Moscow drill for potential missile warfare
World.content:
China and Russia kicked off their second joint computer-assisted anti-missile drill on Monday, a move experts said could deter potential missile threats amid rising tensions on the Korean Peninsula.

The drill began on Monday in Beijing and is expected to conclude on Saturday, China's Defense Ministry said on its website on Monday. "This is a practical measure in fulfilling the important consensus reached by both countries' leaders on deepening Sino-Russian antimissile cooperation," it said.

"It will strengthen Sino-Russian mutual strategic trust, improve anti-missile cooperation between the two militaries and has great significance in jointly dealing with regional ballistic and cruise missile threats," the ministry said.

The exercise does not target any third party, it said. "China and Russia oppose the development of global anti-missile systems. The two militaries will increase practical cooperation in anti-missile defense, and jointly safeguard Chinese and Russian security interests and regional strategic balance."

The goal of the exercise is to "jointly train for anti-missile combat planning and preparation, launch command and firing coordination," Senior Colonel Wu Qian, the Defense Ministry spokesman, said in a news briefing in November.

Tension on the Korean Peninsula has been mounting since the Democratic People's Republic of Korea launched its Hwasong-15 intercontinental ballistic missile in November. DPRK media reported the missile could carry nuclear warheads and reach the continental United States.

Su Hao, a professor at the China Foreign Affairs Academy, said that it is crucial for China and Russia to bolster strategic trust and cooperate in anti-missile defense to protect their nations from potential threats.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Memorial Day a time to 'remember', 'inspire'
World.content:
A memorial service to mark the 80th anniversary of the Nanjing Massacre committed during the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-45) brought together hundreds of activists and members of the Chinese and other Asian communities on Sunday in San Francisco.

The memorial, organized by the Rape of Nanking Redress Coalition, the Committee to Promote Reunification of China, the Alliance for Preserving the Truth of Sino-Japanese War and Comfort Women Justice Coalition, has been held annually for the past 20 years with the aim of exposing the Japanese Imperial Army's war crimes and encouraging people to understand and never forget the dark chapter of history.

"The Japanese army blatantly violated international conventions and committed the extremely cruel atrocity in Nanjing, where 300,000 Chinese were murdered and one-third of the buildings were destroyed," Zha Liyou, acting Chinese consul general in San Francisco, said at the service.

Japanese troops captured Nanjing, which was China's capital at the time, on Dec 13, 1937. It then began a slaughter that lasted more than 40 days. Tens of thousands of women were raped.

"Our stories are linked. The fate of over 400,000 women sexually enslaved by the Japanese Imperial Army during World War II is part and parcel of what happened during the Nanjing Massacre," said Judith Mirkinson, president of the Comfort Women Justice Coalition.

She said the 20th century has been called the most violent century in the history of the world, and that one way to ensure peace in the 21st century is through truth and reconciliation.

"Reconciliation does not come without truth. So the Japanese government must acknowledge their crimes," she said.

"They must give justice to those few people who still survive from the Nanjing Massacre and to the memory of what happened there," she said.

From the time that Japan invaded Northeast China in September 1931, followed by a full-scale invasion that started on July 7, 1937, around 35 million Chinese soldiers and civilians were killed or injured during the occupation, which continued until 1945.

To honor the victims and the survivors and to pursue justice and an enduring peace, the Chinese community worldwide joined hands this year to commemorate this historic event, which was designated by the Chinese government as National Memorial Day for Nanjing Massacre Victims.

"To remember the atrocities committed by the Japanese army during World War II does not mean to pass on the enmity but rather to remind people not to forget the history and inspire them to love peace," said Zha Liyou.

In 2015, the Nanjing Massacre was entered onto the UNESCO Memory of the World Register, a compendium aimed at preserving documented heritage of universal value.

liazhu@chinadailyusa.com

World.title: More military technologies targeted for civilian sector to boost economy
World.content:
Greater integration will spur innovation and cultivate new engines of growth

China will strengthen innovation by developing high-tech industries with military technologies to boost military-civil integration, a move that aims to cultivate new growth drivers and boost the economy, said a recent State Council guideline.

This was one of the seven key tasks set by the guideline on deepening the military-civil integration in the defense technology industry, which was released by the State Council, China's Cabinet, on Monday last week.

The guideline targets sharing technological innovation bases and facilities between military and civilian sectors while more efforts will be made to apply military technologies to non-military areas.

The military integration will also focus on key areas such as space, cyberspace and maritime sciences, while private capital is encouraged to enter military industries, the document said.

The guideline was the latest move by the central government to promote the military-civil integration to widen military contract orders to civilian sectors and apply high-end military technologies for civilian purposes as part of the supply-side structural reform.

In June, the General Office of the State Council released a guideline on civil aviation development to open airspace less than 3,000 meters in altitude and other industries such as cybersecurity and satellite navigation.

Shi Haiming, an associate professor at the National University of Defense Technology, said the guideline brings benefits for both private and military enterprises while pre-entry approvals will be changed into post-entry reviews to streamline administration, except those linking strategic weapons.

Meanwhile, Shi said the guideline lowers the access threshold for enterprises to enter the field of weaponry equipment and will make the process more transparent.

The document also will further reduce institutional costs for private enterprise by building better platforms to promote military-civil integration, he said.

In fact, many developed economies are highly reliant on military-civil integration.

For example, the United States' airplane maker Boeing sells China civil aviation aircraft worth billions of dollars each year and is known for its high-end military aircraft. Many Japanese multinational companies such as Toshiba and Mitsubishi have a department to take military orders.

The integration is a worldwide trend to fully improve the national defense capability, said Jiang Luming, a professor at the National Defense University of the People's Liberation Army.

In countries such as the US, the United Kingdom and Germany, less than 15 percent of military technologies are solely for military purposes and more than 80 percent are used for civilian purposes, Jiang said.

Jiang said in October last year that China has about 290,000 national defense intellectual property rights not being used due to the previously separated military and civil industries.

For example, breakthrough technologies such as engines and aluminum alloy materials can help ease production overcapacity and transform China's economy, he said. These new technologies can essentially boost economic growth and national defense, Jiang said.

The military industry has the priority to apply cutting-edge technologies and also make breakthrough innovations, Lu Guangshan, chairman of the Avionics System Co under the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, was quoted by Shanghai Securities News as saying.

"For example, virtual reality headsets were first used in helmets for fighter jets and my company has developed six civilian industries such as virtual reality, drones, robotics and smart wearing," Lu said.

Military companies are encouraged to work with local governments to promote their advantageous expertise and develop a large number of new high-tech industries, Long Hongshan, chief engineer at the State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense, told a news conference last week.

These new industries will play a vital role in promoting local economic growth and creating new employment opportunities, Long said.

Currently, 30 percent of products made by China's military companies are for military purposes and the other 70 percent for civilian purposes, he said.

In the future, high-tech industries will cover half of the military-related economy, Long added.

World.title: Dangerous stunts get thumbs-down from video platforms
World.content:
Multiple social media and video streaming platforms will limit who can view videos that depict dangerous stunts - and may even prohibit such material - in an effort to discourage imitators.

In November, daredevil stunt climber Wu Yongning fell to his death while scaling a skyscraper in Changsha, Hunan province. Wu, 26, had more than 1.3 million followers on social media who regularly devoured his breathtaking videos and photos. He climbed with no protective gear.

Last month, Wu's account on Sina Weibo stopped updating, leading followers to worry about his well-being.

On Friday, Wu's girlfriend confirmed on social media that the "rooftop daredevil" had fallen and died.

"Today is Dec 8. It makes me think of Nov 8, the day that you left us, left this world," she wrote.

Wu's family also confirmed his death to Jiefang Daily, a newspaper in Shanghai.

Meipai, Kuaishou, Xiaohuoshan and other video platforms on which Wu posted content, expressed their condolences, according to ThePaper.cn. Platform representatives told the news outlet that China currently has no law regulating extreme stunt videos, but each platform will update its content policy to discourage imitators.

Kuaishou said Wu's account had been restricted - meaning that only the uploader can see it - in September because of its depictions of dangerous acts.

Xiaohuoshan said it will ban video livestreams of dangerous stunts because live interactions between the performer and the audience could be a distraction and lead to catastrophic results.

The platform also said it will respect the desires of Wu's family in dealing with the videos.

All of Wu's stunt videos on the three platforms had been restricted or taken down as of Monday. A cellphone video of Wu performing his last stunt and falling to his death on Nov 8, has also been taken down.

Wu was part of an informal community of young thrill-seekers around the world who engage in "roof-topping" - climbing to the top or to high ledges of buildings, often without a permit or protective gear, to take stomach-churning pictures and videos. The activity is generally illegal.

In January, an 18-year-old identified as Alexander Sh, fell to his death from Europe's second-tallest building - the 350-meter OKO Tower in Moscow. He was trying to take a selfie when he slipped and fell, Russian media reported.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Taiwan's New Party vows to help improve relations
World.content:
Delegation to Beijing reaffirms support for one-China, rejection of agitators

Top political adviser Yu Zhengsheng met with a Taiwan delegation representing the island's New Party in Beijing on Monday to discuss the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations and how to achieve the "great rejuvenation" of the Chinese nation.

Yu praised the New Party's unbroken stance upholding the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, since the party's establishment, as well as its peaceful approach to relations.

The 19th National Congress of the Communist Party of China, which was held in October, further clarified the guidelines and policies addressing Taiwan, Yu said.

In his opening address to delegates during the congress, Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Central Committee of the CPC, called the one-China principle the political foundation of cross-Straits relations, and said that attempts to move toward "Taiwan independence" in any form will be defeated.

Taiwan will share development opportunities on the Chinese mainland, and its residents will enjoy the same treatment as mainland people as they pursue studies, start businesses, seek jobs or come to live on the mainland, Xi said in the address.

Yok Mu-ming, chairman of the New Party and head of the Taiwan delegation, said the party has firmly upheld the one-China principle and promoted peace.

The delegation also met on Monday with Zhang Zhijun, head of the State Council's Taiwan Affairs Office.

Zhang and Yok agreed that the one-China principle must be upheld going forward, expressed firm opposition to separatist activities and vowed to make efforts toward peaceful relations.

Both sides agreed to establish and improve mechanisms of communication, share opinions on major issues in the relationship and promote exchanges and communication in all fields - especially between youth. They further agreed to create a constructive and convenient environment for the development of Taiwan youth on the mainland.

Zhang said cross-Straits relations have faced challenges because the island's Democratic Progressive Party has refused to clearly express support for the one-China principle, which led to the mainland suspending official communications with the island.

He said that a "Taiwan independence" force had recently stirred up the island, proposing the removal of Chinese mainland elements in a variety of fields.

"Its aim is to cut the historical ties between Taiwan and the mainland, reduce public awareness that Taiwan people are part of the Chinese nation and limit many cultural influences on the island," he said.

Some people advocating "Taiwan independence" have pushed for amending the law, and have proposed changing the island's constitution. "This shows that separatist activities and the group supporting 'independence' pose the most serious threat to the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations," Zhang said.

He warned that people from both sides should be vigilant and firmly oppose such activities.

luowangshu@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Former Chongqing political official facing corruption investigation
World.content:
Sun Zhengcai, the former secretary of Chongqing Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China, has been placed under investigation on suspicion of accepting bribes, according to the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Monday.

According to the procuratorate, Sun has been placed under "coercive measures", which may include summons by force, bail, residential surveillance, detention and arrest.

The investigation is underway, the procuratorate said in a statement released on Monday.

In July, the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection launched an investigation into Sun for "serious violations of Party discipline".

The CCDI said in a news release that Sun betrayed Party principles and ignored the Party code of conduct and rules.

He was found to have seriously violated the CPC's eight-point code on frugality and maintaining close ties with the masses, seeking pomp, ostentation and privileges, according to the CCDI.

The CCDI said he was guilty of nepotism and seeking benefits in selection of officials. He was found by the CCDI to have leaked confidential Party information and seriously breached Party rules on integrity.

Moreover, he abused power and used his job to gain benefits for others, then accepted their huge bribes in return, either paid in cash or properties, the CCDI said. He was found to seek substantial benefits for his relatives' businesses and accepted valuable gifts, the CCDI said.

The anti-graft inspectors also accused Sun of bureaucracy and sloth in work and degradation and power-for-sex trades, according to the CCDI.

Sun totally deviated from the Party spirit and political requirements of senior officials, the CCDI said in the statement, adding that his misconduct betrayed the trust of the CPC Central Committee and the public, inflicting huge harm to the Party and the country with "extremely bad" social influences.

The CCDI transferred the criminal evidence involving his case to judicial authorities for further investigation.

In September, the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee expelled Sun from the Party and dismissed him from public office.

China Daily - Xinhua

World.title: From Film Sets to Prompts: The AI Short-Drama Revolution
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018927/From Film Sets to Prompts: The AI Short-Drama Revolution
World.content:
China’s booming ultra-short drama industry is being reshaped by the rapid rise of AI-generated video. In Zhengzhou, one of the country’s major production hubs, directors, actors, crews, and film bases that once fueled the industry’s explosive growth are now facing shrinking budgets, fewer shoots, and an uncertain future. Meanwhile, in other cities like Wuxi, AI studios are embracing the same technology to produce dramas faster and at a fraction of the traditional cost. As the two worlds increasingly converge, the question is no longer whether AI will change filmmaking, but what role humans will have in it.

Additional reporting: He Qitong; story editors: Apurva and Qi Ya; video editor: Lü Xiao

World.title: Chinese Mother Buys Daughters Extra Train Seat, Sparking Debate
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018928/Chinese Mother Buys Daughters Extra Train Seat, Sparking Debate
World.content:
“We bought three tickets,” a teenager says to a woman asking to use the empty seat beside her — occupied by snacks — her sister sitting on the other side.

“We’re all in the same carriage,” the standing woman says. “Shouldn’t we help each other out?” She calls a train attendant for help.

“Places 5, 6, and 7 — those seats are theirs,” the attendant says after checking the teens’ tickets. “You need to talk to them about it. Telling me won’t help.”

This scene, which took place Aug. 18 on a slow train traveling from Shanghai to the southwestern city of Chengdu — a 27-hour journey — was captured in a video that went viral in China this past week.

Online, people heatedly discussed whether the girls should have shared the seat or whether they were entitled to keep it for themselves. The topic rose to the second-highest place on Chinese microblogging platform Weibo’s trending list, receiving over 37 million views and 12,000 discussions as of Monday.

Many were in support of the girls’ decision, arguing that giving up their seats would be a favor, not an obligation, as the teens themselves had paid for the three tickets. Others said that they were “wasting public resources.”

Still others contended that the train attendants should have been more proactive, pointing to railway ticketing rules that say customers can only buy one ticket for themselves per train and that if the ticket holder does not board, their seat should be reassigned by train attendants.

Despite these stipulations, passengers can buy tickets for others using their identification information on train ticket purchasing platforms.

The girls’ mother did just that, buying their tickets as well as entering her own information for the third seat, according to a now-deleted post she made on Aug. 20 on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok.

“My original intention was to keep them from taking up other people’s space because they had too much luggage, so I bought an extra ticket,” she wrote. “Since they’re both girls and didn’t want to sit with others, I bought three tickets together.”

In response to the issue, 12306 — China’s official train ticketing and service platform — told Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper that in the event that a passenger does not board the train, their ticket remains classified as “sold” in the train’s online system. In addition, if a ticket is purchased for a passenger but they do not board, the person whose ID was used to buy the ticket retains the right to decide how the seat is used.

On Aug. 21, the Chengdu Bureau of China’s National Railway responded to the controversy, seemingly contradicting 12306: “If a passenger fails to board after purchasing a ticket due to personal reasons, the passenger is considered to have forfeited their right to use the seat … according to the rules, the seat cannot be occupied by a third party.” The bureau noted that such instances should be reported to the train staff.

But a day later, the case shifted from a dispute over passengers’ rights and entitlements to discussions on the lack of support for children traveling alone, as well as the difficulties faced by migrant families. The girls’ mother, speaking to domestic media on Aug. 22, explained that she works in Shanghai and was sending her two daughters back to their hometown. She added that she did not have enough time to escort them and wanted them to “develop their independence.” The extra seat, she said, could also serve as a place to lie down for the two, as she worried about male strangers sleeping beside them in sleeper cars.

She also noted that, under ticketing rules, minors cannot buy tickets themselves and their tickets must instead be purchased alongside an adult ticket.

In a commentary, The Paper wrote that “behind the purchase of the three tickets lies a harsh reality faced by millions of working families, leaving migrant families with no alternative.” It recommended that the railway system follow airlines — which allow parents to apply for service for unaccompanied minors in advance — as an example.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A video screenshot shows the empty seat that gave rise to a national debate. From Weibo)

World.title: China’s Short-Drama Boom Was Built on Speed. Then AI Got Faster.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018902/China’s Short-Drama Boom Was Built on Speed. Then AI Got Faster.
World.content:
Editor’s note: This is the first of a two-part series on how AI is reshaping China’s ultrashort-drama industry.

HENAN, Central China — When a tow truck stopped beside three luxury cars at Zhoutu Culture’s compound in the central Chinese city of Zhengzhou in July, crew members assumed they were headed to another shoot.

Zhoutu was shooting so many ultrashort dramas that the company calculated owning the cars would eventually cost less than renting them as props, and bring some tax savings. Founder Wang Huan and his business partners had each chosen a model they had long wanted.

But the Mercedes-Benz G63, Aston Martin DB11, and Bentley Continental GT were leaving for good. Zhoutu sold all three for a combined 4.5 million yuan ($650,000).

Wang photographed the three cars before they left and posted the images on social media with the caption: “Selling cars and all in short dramas.”

“Of course it stirred up some emotions,” he later told Sixth Tone. “But it wasn’t anything like what people might imagine — like feeling we’d gone bankrupt or something.”

Within months of adding the cars to its fleet, Zhoutu’s output had plunged from as many as 200 ultrashort dramas a month to around 30. Its full-time workforce had fallen from more than 500 employees at its 2025 peak to around 200. More than 20,000 costumes had been moved to a nearby building as an AI studio took over their former space. Even the canteen was closed.

Beyond Zhoutu’s gates, shoots were disappearing across Zhengzhou, one of China’s largest ultrashort-drama production hubs, often dubbed the country’s “Vertical Hollywood.”

The smartphone-first dramas, typically told in episodes lasting only a minute or two, reached 851 million users across China by May, in an industry now worth more than 100 billion yuan. Major platforms fueled the boom with scripts, guaranteed funding, and incentives for producers that could deliver at scale.

But the production model underpinning the industry’s rise began to unravel in February. AI was rapidly reducing the cost of work that had previously required live-action crews, while major platforms began cutting the guaranteed funding that had helped sustain breakneck expansion.

Across the live-action industry, people began calling it a “winter.”

Shot clock

“Master Comes Down the Mountain, Tasks Me With Wooing His Daughter” is one of the few Zhoutu productions still shooting in July.

In one scene, four armed guards sent by two sisters from a powerful family rush the protagonist, played by Cai Zhongyuan. He waves one hand and sends them sprawling. One draws a gun and fires; Cai catches the bullet between two fingers.

Director Li Jun adds both flourishes on set, giving the hero two more moments of triumph typical of male-oriented ultrashort dramas.

Cai then turns his attention back to the sisters, whom he had earlier encountered while they were bathing, and continues flirting with them. When the elder sister finally loses her temper and slaps him, the two collide — and kiss.

Li steps away from the monitor before the kiss. “Don’t pull away too quickly. Three seconds. Separate only after I say so,” she tells the leads. She adjusts a side light, tells the camera operator to shoot in slow motion, then calls action.

“Perfect.” In just three takes, the drama’s most important romantic scene is finished.

“Master Comes Down the Mountain” will eventually run for around 100 minutes. Li has three days to shoot it, on a budget of roughly 200,000 yuan.

Barely 160 centimeters tall, with cropped hair and a voice that carries across the set, she keeps the production moving almost without pause.

When crew chatter continues as the cameras are about to roll, Li cuts across it: “Why don’t you chat in front of the camera instead?” A stalled fog machine, missing prop, or crew member drifting into frame brings another rebuke.

“For simple shots like this, don’t come back to me asking what to do,” she tells the assistant director, pushing the crew to keep routine shots moving without waiting for her.

A comparable production last year would have cost around 300,000 yuan and taken seven or eight days, Li says. The roughly 30-person core filming crew has remained largely intact, but around 10 jobs tied to stunt work and special effects have been cut after related scenes were removed or shifted to AI.

At her busiest, Li directed roughly four dramas a month. From preparation to release, she says, an ultrashort production could take less than a month, with crews routinely working 14 to 16 hours a day.

Wang Ruoyan, 24, who plays the elder sister in “Master Comes Down the Mountain,” remembers getting only around 10 hours of sleep during one five-day shoot as lunch breaks disappeared into costume and makeup changes.

“I even fell asleep in the shower once,” she says. “When I woke up, 30 minutes had passed.”

Wang also saw actors carrying quick-acting heart medication on set. Li says she did the same during especially intense periods, urging actors on her crews to keep some with them to “save their lives.”

Last summer, Li recalled ambulances arriving three times in a single afternoon.

“Some people had acute myocarditis, some suffered heatstroke, and some were simply exhausted from working too hard and staying up too late,” she says. “People would become mentally disoriented, and if they weren’t careful, they could easily fall and get injured.”

On more demanding productions, Li says, actors might finish at 3 or 4 a.m. and be back on set four hours later.

“No one has the energy or passion to create,” Li says. “They’re just thinking about finishing, getting off work, and going to sleep.”

Luo Haoyu, an actor who frequently worked with Li, was on set as many as 28 days a month at the height of the boom. Some nights, he filmed until 5 a.m., then rushed straight to another shoot without even removing his makeup.

“Deep down, everyone knew those crazy days wouldn’t last forever,” Luo says. “We were burning ourselves out because everyone understood that last year was an exceptional period for short dramas.”

Hard landing

Those “crazy days” lasted until February.

That month, TikTok owner ByteDance released Seedance 2.0, an AI video model capable of generating increasingly polished footage for around 1 yuan per second.

Soon after, Hongguo — ByteDance’s ultrashort-drama platform and a major source of scripts and financing — began withdrawing guaranteed funding from many small and midsize live-action projects.

The shift hit companies like Zhoutu particularly hard: three years earlier, a Hongguo-backed rebirth melodrama, “My Daughter Pulled the Plug on My Oxygen Tank,” had given the company its breakout hit, generating more than 10 million yuan in user spending on its first day.

“The landing was extremely hard,” says Zhoutu founder Wang Huan.

Zhoutu has since opened a 50-person AI studio, while about 20 live-action directors also work on AI productions. It makes six to eight AI dramas a month, largely, Wang says, to “maintain a presence” in the market.

At the same time, the company is using cheaper live-action projects to keep its remaining workforce employed. “With so much investment and so many employees, our strategy is still to operate on a model that keeps more people working,” Wang says. If that fails, he says, Zhoutu may shrink further.

The company had already spent nearly two months after the Spring Festival, in mid-February, with little work coming in. “When you don’t know what to do, the safest option is to stop,” Wang says. “At least you won’t lose more money.”

Productions booked before the downturn kept Li on set for a few weeks. Then new scripts dwindled to roughly one a month, and by April her team had nothing to shoot. Directors around her began moving into AI production, while actors suddenly found themselves waiting for work.

Luo says his monthly income fell from around 20,000 yuan during the boom to roughly 5,000 yuan. In the first three months after the Spring Festival, he worked just 20 days in total.

“I felt confused and lost,” he recalls. “What am I supposed to do in the future?”

He began binge eating, sometimes until he felt he might vomit. For an actor normally careful about his weight, the behavior unsettled him.

“At the time, I thought, things were already this bad. Eating at least made me feel a little better,” he says.

He considered leaving the industry altogether, but could not bring himself to do it. “I still want to see whether audiences can once again have higher expectations for live-action productions,” he says.

Yet producers kept pouring into AI. More than 95% of the 128,000 ultrashort dramas released in the first quarter of 2026 were AI-generated, according to the China Netcasting Services Association (CNSA).

By May, Bytedance pledged 1.5 billion yuan to support live-action short dramas, while six major platforms announced at least 6 billion yuan in planned investment. Regulators also allocated funding for higher-quality productions across 11 provinces.

Live-action output rebounded in the second quarter, partly due to shelved projects returning, though CNSA data shows AI still accounted for 64% of releases.

But Wang is reluctant to bet Zhoutu’s future on another round of platform money. “If Hongguo stopped giving you money tomorrow, what would you do?” he says.

For Shi, a 22-year-old background actor, the slowdown meant days spent waiting for work. During the boom, small speaking roles and regular extra work could bring him close to 10,000 yuan a month. By the time Sixth Tone met him, he had landed just one job in 10 days.

For 110 yuan, Shi spent the morning waiting to appear for a few seconds as a guard: charge at the hero, pretend to be hit, fall to the ground.

He was also still owed 800 yuan from a production the previous December. The company had disappeared, as had the person who recruited him. All Shi had left was their nickname on messaging app WeChat.

“We don’t even know who to ask for our money,” says Shi, who asked to be identified only by his surname. “Construction workers can at least find someone to demand their wages from. With film crews, they’re long gone.”

Shi barely watches live-action ultrashort dramas anymore. He prefers AI-generated comic dramas.

“AI is especially good at stories that rely heavily on visual effects,” he says. “It does those really well.”

Still rolling

For the opening scene of “Master Comes Down the Mountain,” the male lead falls from the sky. Last year, Li says, the crew would have used wire work and spent at least half a day filming it. This time, the actor simply lay face down on a round stone table in front of a small green screen.

“AI can generate all the surrounding scenery,” Li says. “It can make the male lead descend through the clouds, and even create a sweeping aerial shot following him all the way to the ground.”

The whole shot took less than 30 minutes, and Li estimates it saves around 10,000 yuan.

Months earlier, Zhoutu had offered many of its directors the option of switching to AI production. For Li, that meant planning shots and guiding a team through the video-generation process.

After a day or two learning the job, Li says she could already do the work. The pay was about 30% lower. Of roughly 10 directors around her who faced the same choice, eight switched to AI. Li refused.

“Live-action short dramas need a director more,” Li says. “With the right prompt, anyone can make AI videos. But with real filming, you have to work with the actors, camera, and lighting. The sense of achievement is different.”

Zhoutu now rarely makes premium live-action dramas with big budgets. Instead, it focuses on cheaper remakes of proven hits, particularly modern-day rural stories that can be filmed quickly.

“AI’s advantage is making two immortals arguing in the sky, not people arguing outside a village house,” Wang says. A family-conflict drama can cost less than 50,000 yuan to shoot with real actors. Internally, Zhoutu calls these “emotion-driven dramas for lower-tier markets.”

Many of Zhoutu’s remaining live-action productions are male-oriented stories and remakes of plots that have already yielded success. Wang says they can be shot faster than female-oriented dramas, which typically require more time for atmosphere and emotional development.

In one scene from “Master Comes Down the Mountain,” Wang Ruoyan and the second female lead enter the hero’s bedroom in lace and bunny-style nightdresses. Before filming, Li adjusts two strings of hanging round plastic discs. Placed close to the lens, the pieces blur into soft circles of light; she moves them farther apart until the effect sits where she wants it in the frame.

“This is the craftsmanship I only use in female-oriented dramas,” she jokes.

The extra effort does not always pay off. Some of her carefully polished dramas have performed poorly; others that she rushed through became hits.

“Those times make me wonder whether I really understand the market,” she says. “I started doubting myself.”

The final scene of “Master Comes Down the Mountain” has Cai seated at a dinner table as three women, including the two sisters, confess their love. The elder sister tells him to choose one.

“Can’t I have all three?” he replies.

The women rush him, pulling his ears and grabbing his arms as the camera pushes in. Freeze frame.

Although it’s the ending of the drama, it’s filmed on the first day of the three-day shoot. Li still has two days of scenes to get through.

At lunch, she makes the cast a promise: “I’ll do my best to get you back to the hotel by 7 p.m., so you can order takeout from bed.”

“That would be heaven,” Wang Ruoyan says.

Additional reporting: Lü Xiao; editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Monitors show a scene being filmed by director Li Jun in Zhengzhou, Henan province, June 2026. Reedited by Ding Yining; photo by Lü Xiao/Sixth Tone)

World.title: China Before the Infinite Camera Roll
World.content:
Of the many consumer goods that entered China in the 1980s, one small item transformed how millions of families recorded their lives: 35mm color negative film.

In 1984, Fujifilm established its Beijing office, as Chinese photographers were beginning to embrace the company’s color film, known for its green packaging and the distinctive greenish cast of its prints. Kodak, Fujifilm’s main rival at the time, soon followed, expanding its presence and introducing a network of express color photo stores across China in the 1990s.

These developments, together with the arrival of point-and-shoot cameras that required little skill to achieve proper exposure and sharp focus, enabled ordinary Chinese people to record their lives in color. The film was developed to produce negatives, which were then printed as photographs for family albums.

Not everyone kept the negatives. Many ended up at recycling plants, which is where French artist Thomas Sauvin’s work began. In 2009, Sauvin met Xiaoma, a Beijinger who recovered silver nitrate from X-rays, CDs, and negatives. The two struck a deal, and Sauvin received his first batch of negatives to digitize. Their partnership would eventually help create one of China’s largest private archives of photographic negatives: the Beijing Silvermine.

The project gives broader significance in banal, amateur images. As patterns emerge across dozens, sometimes hundreds, of photographs, personal moments become part of a collective record. One example is a series of portraits taken beside refrigerators, an appliance many Chinese households were acquiring for the first time in the 1990s. Together, such images document the transformation of everyday life as a rapidly changing China became wealthier and more urban.

Much has changed since then. Film gave way to digital cameras, and then to smartphones. People can now easily take thousands of photos a year, a number unthinkable to most families in the 1990s, when a roll of film contained just 36 exposures.

More recently, however, analog photography has enjoyed a revival on social media, where users are drawn to its vintage tones and textures. In 2025, Lucky Film, a Chinese manufacturer that once competed with Kodak and Fujifilm, announced the return of its color negative film amid growing demand from nostalgic millennials and curious Gen Z consumers. Yet a roll of film and lab processing now cost more than 100 yuan (US$14.80) for just 36 photos, leaving analog photography a niche hobby.

The intention behind analog photography has also changed, according to Sauvin. “Now, when people take analog photos, what’s in their mind is that they will scan the negative, and they will post it on Xiaohongshu or Instagram,” said Sauvin, who does not shoot film himself.

What has been lost? Humor, perhaps. Looking through the Beijing Silvermine images, it is hard not to be struck by the ease with which people posed and smiled, gazing into the camera with little of the self-consciousness or affectation common in photography today. Before social media, people seemed simply to be enjoying the moments they were living.

In June, Sixth Tone sat down with Sauvin to discuss what analog photography reveals about the lives of ordinary Chinese people in the 1990s and today, his own relationship with the archive, and the challenges posed by artificial intelligence. The interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Sixth Tone: What was your first impression of the earliest batches of recycled negatives, and how did you begin to interpret their meaning?

Sauvin: They were very banal. Quite boring, sometimes very repetitive. It took maybe two or three years before I started to understand what I could do with them. At some point, because of the quantity, you leave the universe of personal stories and enter the universe of collective memory.

A simple example is that, at the beginning of the project, I came across a photo of a woman posing next to a fridge. And I thought, “Oh, having your portrait taken with a fridge is an unusual thing to do.” Then I saw another one, then another one, and now I probably have a series of 25 pictures like this. In the early 1990s, households in Beijing began acquiring refrigerators. They would decorate them and take photos with them. And that’s something no one else would really record. A photojournalist would never make a series about this, nor would a historian or an artist. It’s too close to daily life. It’s too simple. Yet ordinary people, accidentally and unconsciously, capture the bigger picture in these negatives.

Sixth Tone: Is there a single frame or series that interests you most?

Sauvin: So many. I like the photos taken at Beijing World Park. It opened in 1993, and people went there to get a sense of travel, to experience the outside world and its monuments. In the archive, I have thousands of photos taken there in 1993, 1994, and 1995. It was the perfect playground for taking photos. You could have your picture taken with the Twin Towers, the Statue of Liberty, the Eiffel Tower, and so on.

Then, when I went through photos taken in the early 2000s, these Chinese tourists weren’t at the World Park anymore. They were in the actual countries. And when I look at these negatives, as a French person, I always wonder: Is it the real one or the World Park one?

Sixth Tone: Besides the Eiffel Tower series, were there any photos that connected the collection to your own life?

Sauvin: A lot. I was born and raised in Paris, so I’m attentive to photos taken there. I found photos taken on Rue Fabert in the 7th arrondissement, where I learned to walk when I was 1 year old. It’s my home. Seeing someone posing right where I learned to walk was a strange feeling.

I also remember going to the Louvre Museum as a kid and seeing tourists taking photos: flash, flash, flash! Two or three decades later, I started the Silvermine project and found those kinds of photos. Because they were photographing oil paintings with a flash, you always get this big white dot in the image. I made a series about them called “Dazzling Old Masters.”

But the entire archive also has a very strong connection with me. The first time I went to Beijing was in 1999, on a family exchange. In 2009, exactly 10 years later, I started this project, which allowed me to discover the Beijing that existed before I arrived. I wouldn’t have done that with any other city in the world.

Sixth Tone: Have you been able to contact the people in these images?

Sauvin: There’s a photo I found in 2010 that I absolutely love: a young girl posing on a red motorcycle on a street in Dashilar, Beijing. One day, she got in touch with me on Weibo and said, “That girl on the bike, it’s me.” She sent me the printed photo from her family album.

I immediately sent her the other 35 photos from the same roll, and she discovered many that she’d probably never seen because people didn’t always print every photo. Looking through them, she realized that the roll contained four consecutive birthdays, meaning the film had been in the family camera for more than four years. They had to wait that long to finish the roll, have it developed, and finally see the images.

That says a lot about how our relationship with photography has changed and how analog photography captures who we are as human beings in a very pure way. Because it costs money and takes time, you make sure to record the moments that matter. I really like the idea of these latent images sitting in a film canister for four years, then one day being put into chemicals and revealing all these moments. And I find it crazy that, after waiting four years, the negatives could be thrown away the very next day.

Sixth Tone: There is a fine line between the privacy of these images and the public nature of your collection and exhibitions. How do you navigate that tension?

Sauvin: Of course, I’m dealing with very private, intimate photos that were never meant to be used in a book or shown in an exhibition. People are vulnerable because they are themselves. That’s something I always try to keep in mind.

I always make sure not to make fun of people. That’s not easy, because a very important part of the Beijing Silvermine’s visual universe is its sense of humor. There’s something very light, funny, and fresh about it. So you need to preserve that sense of humor because it’s the soul of the project, while never crossing the line into making fun of people.

Another rule I’ve given myself almost since the beginning is that I generally avoid using two images of the same person. That way, I make sure never to delve too deeply into one person’s life. What brings the photos together are more anthropological themes. The photos come together and contribute to a theme. But I would not be comfortable showing many photos taken by the same person.

In 2015, a very good friend of mine in Beijing came to me with a big cardboard box containing all the negatives and photos of her late father. He took a lot of photos and organized everything very neatly, with handwritten information everywhere: Here are the 120 films; there are the 35mm films. It was absolutely beautiful.

She gave it to me and said, “I think you’re doing great things with negatives, so this is yours, and just do what you want with it.” I was never able to open the box a second time because it was not my place to deal with this material. It all comes from one person. I know who this person is, so I can do absolutely nothing with it.

Sixth Tone: How do your curatorial decisions reflect the way you view analog photographs within their historical context?

Sauvin: In this exhibition, curated by Holly Russell at Fotografiska Shanghai, we present one room with 1,300 prints. That’s the selection I’ve been working on for 16 years. The selection was organized around themes, topics, and angles that emerged organically from the archive.

But when we brought the archive to Shanghai, we decided not to present each series together. Everything is mixed, so it’s up to the viewer to look at the photos and, just like I did, start seeing connections between them. I also didn’t decide which photo would go where. They were hung quite randomly by the workers who installed the show, and some amazing connections happened simply because of that.

We also decided to present everything as 10-by-15-centimeter prints, which is probably the size of the prints that would have been made from these negatives for family albums. No photo is bigger than another, so we’re not claiming that one is more important. What makes them powerful is their coming together.

There’s something about found photography, about vernacular photography, that is completely crazy: Quantity is more important than quality. You need quantity to make the switch from personal memory to collective memory. That’s how you end up with a gigantic photo album. It’s not the album of a family. It’s the album of a city, a generation, a place, and a time.

Sixth Tone: We have seen a resurgence of analog photography recently, globally but especially in China. Lucky Film is producing color negative film again. What do you make of this renewed interest? Why do you think it appeals to young Chinese people?

Sauvin: I suppose it’s about our relationship with the medium. We’re always drawn to technologies from the past. We’ve seen this with music. We had vinyl records, then CDs, MiniDiscs, and MP3s, and now we are going back to vinyl. There is a worldwide trend of people going back to analog photography. I’m not sure I’m very interested in that. Now we’re at a stage where we’re mass-producing images, and I’d rather live in my time and do that than go back to an earlier, previous tool.

And there’s something very different. People 30 years ago were shooting analog, but there was no artistic intention or intention to share these photos online. There wasn’t this element of staging or representation.

Now, when people take analog photos, what’s in their mind is that they will scan the negative and post it on Xiaohongshu or Instagram. So the intention is not pure. In the end, what does it mean? It means it’s a filter, like a vintage filter of some kind. That’s why I’m not very interested in the trend. I love analog photography, but it died about 20 years ago.

Sixth Tone: Artificial intelligence is being used to restore and recreate faded or damaged negatives. Do you see it primarily as a boon or a bane?

Sauvin: I find it completely fascinating, and I’m sure that, combined with the right idea, it could be an amazing tool. I’m really open to it.

That being said, I need to be very careful because I have this Silvermine archive of 1 million photos, all made of flesh and blood, that come from ordinary people. They are physical objects, and for so many years, when I scanned a photo and shared it, people trusted that the photo existed. There was no question about that.

Then suddenly, about a year ago, we had this explosion of AI-generated images, and it changed people’s minds, mine as well. Now when you see a photo, the first question you ask yourself is: Is it real, or is it AI?

I really don’t want that confusion to happen with the Silvermine. I want to make it very clear: I deal only with analog photography, and I do not modify the photos in any way.
