World.title: China’s First Booster Landing Marks Leap Toward Reusable Rockets
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018923/China’s First Booster Landing Marks Leap Toward Reusable Rockets
World.content:
China has landed an orbital rocket’s booster, rather than discarding it, for the first time, paving the way for sustainable rocket launches and potentially cutting future launches’ costs by tens of millions of yuan.

The Aug. 19 milestone by Chinese aerospace startup LandSpace also makes China the second country after the U.S. to successfully recover rocket boosters on both solid ground and at sea — the latter feat accomplished last month.

U.S.-based aerospace companies SpaceX and Blue Origin were previously the only enterprises to have successfully landed rocket boosters on solid ground. SpaceX has also recovered boosters at sea — by landing them vertically on drone ships — compared with China’s net-capture method.

On Wednesday at 7:35 am, the 66.1-meter-tall Zhuque-3 lifted off from the Dongfeng Commercial Space Innovation Pilot Zone in the northern Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, and delivered an internet satellite into its designated orbit.

The rocket’s stainless-steel booster, carrying nine liquid oxygen-methane engines, later landed 390 kilometers away in neighboring Gansu province.

A similar attempt by the same company on Dec. 3 last year failed following combustion. On the latest model, the team improved the landing propulsion system and added protective structures, domestic media reported.

China’s push to build extensive low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks — “megaconstellations” of coordinated satellites operating 2,000 kilometers or less above Earth — is driving growing demand for cheaper, more frequent rocket launches.

Such networks aim to provide services such as high-speed internet access in remote areas. The country currently has a few hundred satellites in orbit, and tens of thousands are ultimately planned.

A rocket’s booster, located at the bottom of the ship and used in the initial stage of launch, is commonly the most expensive component, accounting for 70% or more of a rocket’s hardware costs, LandSpace told domestic media. Traditionally, however, they are discarded after launch, leaving the upper part of the rocket to continue toward orbit.

Reuse of a common nine-engine booster could save at least 20 million to 50 million yuan ($2.9 million to $7.4 million), Zhang Liang, technical lead of a reusable rocket research team at Sun Yat-sen University’s School of Aeronautics and Astronautics, told domestic media.

However, Zhang added that China still faces a shortage of launch facilities. The cost advantage of reusable rockets will only become significant if there are enough launches for rockets to be reused multiple times a year.

According to LandSpace, the cost per launch could fall by about 45% after five uses. The Zhuque-3’s first stage is designed to be reused at least 20 times, with the company ultimately aiming to bring launch costs below 20,000 yuan per kilogram of payload.

LandSpace told domestic media that it plans to relaunch the recovered booster as soon as possible.

Over the past decade, supportive policies from the central government have led more private companies to enter China’s space sector, which state-owned enterprises previously dominated.

Last November, the China National Space Administration released a two-year action plan pledging to expand access to rocket testing facilities and strengthen international cooperation. The space sector is also listed as a strategic priority in China’s 15th Five-Year Plan, which began this year.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: LandSpace’s Zhuque-3 rocket booster lands in Minqin, Gansu province, Aug. 19, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018922/Chinese Supermarket Chain Recruits Ex-Cons for 2nd Consecutive Year
World.title: Chinese Supermarket Chain Recruits Ex-Cons for 2nd Consecutive Year
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018922/Chinese Supermarket Chain Recruits Ex-Cons for 2nd Consecutive Year
World.content:
Chinese supermarket chain Pangdonglai has announced the recruitment of former convicts for the second year in a row, expanding its hiring scope to employees who have spent at least five years in prison. The move has sparked renewed debate over the line between reducing employment discrimination against former inmates and upholding public safety.

The plan, announced Aug. 14 by the company’s branch in Zhengzhou, capital of the central Henan province, involves recruiting 20 people who have served sentences of at least five years. The store is set to open in October.

Pangdonglai was founded by Yu Donglai in 1995. Based in Henan’s Xuchang City, it has gained a reputation for offering relatively high pay, shorter working hours, and generous time off — emphasizing employee well-being over profit.

Employees work no more than 36 hours per week — in China, the legal limit is 40 hours — and receive 40 days of paid leave annually, including 10 “mental health” days. In the first quarter of 2026, employees’ average monthly salary was 9,600 yuan ($1,400), compared with roughly 5,800 yuan at China’s private wholesale and retail businesses.

Last year, the company recruited former convicts for the first time. Applicants were required to have served no more than 10 years in prison, be under the age of 35, and have a middle school education or higher.

Yu said in a Saturday post on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, that all 30 former convicts hired last year remain employed by the company.

This year, the company looks to recruit former inmates who have served sentences of at least five years.

The move quickly divided opinion online. Supporters praised the company for giving convicts a second chance. Lin Minming, founder of Red Apple Public Welfare, an organization that supports the children of prisoners, told domestic media that the company’s decision to continue hiring ex-convicts, particularly those who “may be facing even more difficult employment challenges,” is “worth paying attention to.”

“In the past, people would make baseless assumptions when talking about this issue — worrying that former inmates would be difficult to manage, unstable, or likely to cause problems,” Lin said. “Now that there’s at least a group of real (ex-convicts) working in a real company, we can see what happens.”

Former inmates in China face significant barriers to finding jobs. Fewer than 40% secure employment because of their criminal records, according to local media.

But others raised concerns. “Many people serving more than five years (in prison) were convicted of serious crimes,” one user wrote online. “Supermarkets are crowded places frequented by ordinary people, including children and the elderly. People who have turned their lives around deserve a second chance, but customer safety should not be overlooked.”

Others argued that giving special opportunities to former inmates is unfair to those who have always obeyed the law.

Responding to the concerns, the company told domestic media that people convicted of sexual or violent offenses are ineligible, and that applicants with nonviolent offenses will be prioritized. It added that those hired will initially be assigned to back-office positions such as warehousing and logistics, rather than customer-facing jobs, and undergo a six-month trial period.

China has been strengthening support for former inmates returning to society. A revised Prison Law, passed in April and set to take effect this November, states that discriminating against former convicts in employment, education, or social security matters is illegal.

Former inmates will also be required to undergo “pre-release education” — including legal and psychological counseling, vocational training, and daily-life skills — encouraging them to pursue employment and entrepreneurship.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Customers crowd a Pangdonglai supermarket in Xuchang, Henan province, May 1, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018916/Cold Comfort: What Europe’s Heat Wave Means for Chinese Factories
World.title: Cold Comfort: What Europe’s Heat Wave Means for Chinese Factories
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018916/Cold Comfort: What Europe’s Heat Wave Means for Chinese Factories
World.content:
Two gray-green production lines glow beneath harsh white lights, their conveyor belts moving ceaselessly like mechanical rivers. Clanging metal, the rip of packing tape, and the dull thud of cardboard boxes mingle with the hurried footsteps of workers shuttling goods back and forth.



It’s July 10, and the Pinotec electric fan factory in Suzhou, in the eastern Jiangsu province, is running at full capacity to meet several rush orders that have come from Europe in the wake of a record-breaking heat wave.

As temperatures soared in June, exports of Chinese air conditioners to the European Union jumped nearly 73% year on year, according to China’s General Administration of Customs. Sales of fans and evaporative air coolers also surged on global e-commerce platforms.

For the managers and employees at Pinotec, which manufactures fans under the Booster brand, the extreme weather represented a lifeline. After taking a major hit from the China-U.S. trade war and the ongoing Middle East conflict, the sudden spike in orders gave the company an opportunity to expand into European markets and turn its finances around.

But as demand has risen, so have the costs of metals and electrical components, while the market competition has rapidly intensified. Add a weakening euro against the yuan — which erodes the value of European revenue when converted back home — and the factory’s profits remain razor-thin.

Despite the hot market, Pinotec and other small- and medium-sized businesses in China are facing the cold, hard reality that this summer boom could leave them weaker, not stronger.

Final countdown

Every hour, factory manager Zhu Guangshuai anxiously paces through the workshop to gauge his workers’ progress. For the past two weeks, Pinotec has been rushing to complete an order for 500 large fans from a customer in Germany — and shipment is scheduled for 8 p.m. tonight.

Zhu had been confident that just two hours would be enough time for final assembly, but the first hour is already gone and only 223 units are finished. To speed things up, he opens a second, smaller production line, initially assigning two additional workers to help with wiring and soldering, before eventually asking the floor supervisor and materials handler to also step in.

In the end, 15 workers drop what they are doing to help their colleagues reach the finish line — attaching screens, installing handle grips, snapping on base plates, tightening screws. Then, they all proceed to packaging.

Multi-skilled workers who can easily switch between roles have become essential for the factory’s survival in recent times. When the Chinese fan market contracted last year, the company merged two assembly lines and laid off any inexperienced or temporary workers, halving its workforce to just 60.

Away from the factory floor, Pinotec also shut down its 40-person domestic e-commerce operation, dispensed with its content creation team for Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, and dismantled its livestreaming studio.

The company initially made massage guns but switched to manufacturing electric fans in late 2023, focusing on high-powered turbo blowers before introducing a range that includes a palm-sized, handheld model. Profits rose early on, but sales dropped sharply once domestic competitors started to flood the market with cheaper alternatives.

Pinotec’s main markets are North America and Europe, where many people commonly use turbo blowers to clean debris from their cars or backyards. Domestic demand is extremely limited. When trade tensions between China and the United States escalated last year, disrupting global markets, 90% of the factory’s orders came from overseas.

Shortly after the U.S. introduced increased tariffs on Chinese exports in February 2025, an American supermarket chain canceled an order for tens of thousands of units. Then, European customers began asking to delay shipments until the economic outlook became clearer.

The company began losing more than 100,000 yuan ($14,835) a month — and that’s before the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East in February this year. Pinotec lost contact with its customers in Iran for almost six months; finished goods piled up in its warehouse, unable to be shipped or paid for.

Things only began to pick up in late May when Europe was hit by an extreme heat wave, with temperatures soaring as high as 45 degrees Celsius in some parts of Spain.

Inquiries flooded in through Pinotec’s international e-commerce platform: A customer in the United Kingdom ordered 2,500 turbo blowers, along with several handheld models; a Belgian distributor placed five orders over two months, totaling more than 2,000 fans, most bound for France; and other units were also shipped to Switzerland and the Netherlands.

To handle the additional workload, the factory reconfigured its production line. Normally, the assembled fans would undergo two days of charge-and-discharge testing, yet Zhu arranged for assembly and testing to be carried out simultaneously, allowing packaging to begin much earlier.

At 8 p.m. on July 10, the fans bound for Germany are shipped on time.

But Zhu barely has time to catch his breath before a new crisis arises. The electric control boards needed for tomorrow’s production order still haven’t arrived after three weeks of waiting. Pinotec has no option but to absorb the pressure. “We’re already right up against the delivery deadline,” Zhu says. “There’s no room to push it back.”

He decides to adjust the production schedule and bring forward another order. The company can’t afford to leave the assembly line idle for even a day.

And the problems keep coming. Whether it’s the time crunch or reduced staffing, defective products keep appearing on the line and need replacing, while a consignment of plastic casings from an upstream supplier is discovered to have color discrepancies between the upper and lower halves.

All Zhu can do is think on his feet to find solutions.

Changing market

According to Pinotec’s founder, Shen Guangping, the combined effects of rising material costs — prices for copper, iron, zinc, tin, lithium batteries, chips, resistors, and capacitors have all increased in 2026 — and fluctuations in the euro-yuan exchange rate have slashed profits by up to 20%.

Deliveries from component suppliers have also become unpredictable. Suppliers used to stockpile some materials, he says, but now no one is willing to hold inventory; materials are procured only after a customer places an order, affecting lead time.

Sometimes, electronic components suddenly increase in price on the same day an order is placed — but once a quote has been given, the factory often has no choice but to absorb the difference.

Pinotec has taken on nearly 200,000 yuan worth of business without passing on the additional material costs, Shen says. “Our sales volume has grown by more than 50% compared with last year, but there’s almost no profit. We’re mainly producing these orders to win new customers and maintain production volume.”

To drum up new business, Shen has been attending as many overseas trade shows as possible. Last year, he attended nearly 20 across the U.S., Germany, Brazil, and Japan. This year his target is 26, at least two a month.

At recent events, he noticed more customers asking about handheld fans. Sensing an opportunity, he began taking small Booster fans to trade shows and had his technical team develop a mini fan and other new products.

However, the market competition is now fierce. Fan manufacturers in Foshan and Zhongshan, two major manufacturing bases in the southern Guangdong province, have orders through September. Domestic factories are also adapting to international requirements, releasing new product colors and developing low-power, variable-frequency models tailored to European voltage standards and electricity costs.

The EU has imposed strict compliance controls on imported cooling products, and incomplete product certification can expose companies to multiple penalties.

Production cycle

It’s been exactly a week since the Pinotec workers rushed to complete the German order, and now they are halfway through assembling a batch of small handheld fans bound for Japan, which has also experienced extreme heat this year.

Suddenly, the production line is halted. An ultrasonic welding mold that fuses the plastic casing is malfunctioning, leaving scorch marks and gaps in the seams.

Zhu assigns a worker to adjust the mold while coordinating others to assemble the remaining components. Fortunately, the problem has come toward the end of the process — any earlier and the day’s production plan would need to be canceled. Just 24 hours earlier, the factory manager was forced to send workers home early due to a battery shortage.

However, when two representatives from the Japanese client later arrive to inspect the goods, they find the mold still hasn’t been repaired, and delivery is postponed.

As an on-site inspector, Du Kai’s task is to report and handle challenges like these. Before joining Pinotec in early 2024, the 28-year-old worked in sales in Beijing and the neighboring city of Tianjin, and as a property agent in the central Henan province. Rather than relying on commission, he had hoped factory work would provide him and his wife more stability.

After proving his versatility, Du was among those who kept his job when the company swung the axe in 2025. Another group that the company was reluctant to let go was its three qualified solderers, as the role requires delicate skill.

Feng Juan is the factory’s most recent hire. Once a temporary worker employed to apply glue, she was recruited as a solderer after someone else quit. In addition to the salary, the job comes with a 1,000 yuan monthly supplement, yet Feng was hesitant at first — she’d heard that the fumes from soldering were toxic and could affect fertility.

She thought it over, and as she already had two sons and wasn’t planning on having more children, she accepted. Her husband runs a lifting equipment installation business, earning 30,000 yuan a month, but Feng says the family still feels financial pressure. In the past year, the couple has renovated a condominium in their native Henan for their eldest son, and is now planning to buy one for their youngest.

Feng’s eldest son, in his late teens, also works at a factory in Suzhou — a temporary arrangement after he began acting out in school — yet she hopes he won’t end up toiling in a high-stress manual job like her.

Packaging line supervisor Wang Chao is also working to save money for his child. A 38-year-old single father, his parents care for his son back in Henan. He no longer has lofty career aspirations, nor is he interested in job-hopping in search of a better position. His only wish is to put away 5,000 yuan a month and have social insurance coverage.

Even as orders have surged, Wang’s packaging team has dwindled to only 12 workers. He hopes to hire five more, but finding them is proving hard. His two recent hires lasted just six days before quitting because the job was “too tiring.”

Zhu and the factory workers are trying to make the most of this summer boom and, in turn, bring more stability to their lives. They hope that, by evening, their finished fans are loaded onto the trucks and shipped overseas on time. Then, the next day, they can do it all again.

(Due to privacy concerns, Du Kai is a pseudonym.)

Reported by Wei Ronghuan.

A version of this article originally appeared in White Night Workshop. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Carrie Davies; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Workers pack items at the factory in Suzhou, Jiangsu province, July 2026. Lü Meng/White Night Workshop )

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018914/What Happens When Chinese Dreamcore Meets the Real World?
World.title: What Happens When Chinese Dreamcore Meets the Real World?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018914/What Happens When Chinese Dreamcore Meets the Real World?
World.content:
What if the zombie apocalypse was already here?

In the late 2010s, Chinese indie band Hardcore Raver in Tears imagined just such a world in “Take Her to Wanda Plaza,” a jagged, synth-heavy sendup of the country’s mindless consumer culture. Over pounding beats, singer Lu Yan sang of zombified shoppers and took aim at Wang Sicong, the scion of the Wanda real estate empire and one of the most infamous of China’s “second-generation rich.”

The joke landed because Wanda Plaza is more than a shopping mall; by the 2010s, it had become shorthand for a particular vision of urban life. In the 2000s, local governments across the country saw real estate and urbanization as key engines of economic growth as well as fiscal revenue. Teaming with developers like Wanda, they built vast new tracts of standardized residential districts across the country. These new neighborhoods needed new stores and restaurants, a niche that Wanda also filled by building over 500 Wanda Plaza malls in more than 200 cities nationwide.

At the time, this was all taken for granted as modernization in action. China was urbanizing at a staggering speed, and clean, convenient, and air-conditioned shopping malls like Wanda Plaza were welcomed by both the country’s rising middle class and brands hungry to tap an emerging market.

But for the generation that came of age during this transformation, the convenience and prosperity of the new urban landscape is increasingly tinged with a sense of sameness. Rapid urban expansion did not just change how Chinese cities looked, they argue; it also displaced what anthropologist Xiang Biao calls the “nearby”: the small-scale places and relationships immediately around us through which everyday life acquires meaning.

That longing has since found an outlet online. From obsessively documenting faded Y2K architecture to creating virtual cities and nostalgic video games, young Chinese are attempting to recreate an idealized virtual version of the turn-of-the-millennium city: chaotic but colorful, and full of corner shops, wet markets, arcades, street stalls, and other places to hang out.

The most obvious example of this trend is Chinese dreamcore, which blends aspects of the global dreamcore subculture with elements drawn from China’s own millennial moment. The walking simulator “There Exists Nobody,” for example, invites players to revisit China’s bustling millennium-era towns, where neighborhoods were filled with unpolished mom-and-pop shops rather than sleek shopping malls.

A more sophisticated case is artist Huang Heshan’s digital metropolis “Too Rich City,” which he dubbed a work of “socialist cyberpunk.” Drawing on Huang’s experiences growing up in the southern province of Guangdong, the virtual city mixes modern LED screens with nostalgic elephant slides and swan-shaped boats — both recurring motifs in Chinese dreamcore.

Similarly, Liu Yujia, a photographer better known by his social media handle, “Tiehe West Street,” has built a large following for his dreamcore-style documentation of China’s long-maligned Y2K architecture.

When asked why his work resonates with so many, Huang commented that China’s millennial buildings — many of which have been allowed to fall into disrepair — nevertheless remain vibrant in ways the newer, more uniform apartment blocks aren’t. They’re “a little chaotic, but also more human,” he explained.

Indeed, a key motive of Chinese dreamcore is a desire for more human-scale spaces. Cookie-cutter blocks of shopping malls, chain stores, and gated residential communities have smoothed the rough edges of many Chinese cities, yet their lack of texture — places with which people can establish organic connections — has also led to widespread disorientation and disillusionment.

It is in this context that the “nearby,” the academic term popularized by Xiang, has entered public discourse in recent years. Rather than accepting the numbing comfort offered by places like Wanda Plaza, China’s younger generation is searching for informal spaces and trying to rebuild tight-knit communities.

Standardized urban planning, alongside an increasingly digital economy, has also reshaped people’s sense of time. In 2000, an ordinary Chinese person might experience time through walking to a grocery store, a school, or a park. Nowadays, such embodied experience has been replaced by the “estimated time of arrival” displayed in food delivery and car-hailing apps. This abstraction has rendered interpersonal relationships likewise abstract and fragile, contributing to the desire to return to a slower, less hectic era.

It’s worth noting that Chinese dreamcore is not the only space where the younger generation is seeking shelter and trying to build a digital “nearby.” The anime and fandom subcultures, for example, offer a similar sense of belonging.

Much of this can be traced back to worldwide trends like the loss of “third places” where young people can hang out away from parents and teachers, forcing them into online spaces increasingly divorced from their physical surroundings and leading to what the scholar Keith Hayward calls a culture of “self-infantilization” — such as the global social media craze for kitsch toys like Labubu.

It’s not hard to see why dreamcore-tinged nostalgia would find such fertile ground in both the West and China, even if one romanticizes malls while the other rejects them. These online trends have limits, however. Loosely organized, they lack the capability to make an impact offline. Meanwhile, some of the very offline spaces dreamcore fans like to criticize have effectively incorporated the subculture, positioning themselves as a new kind of “nearby.” Shopping hubs such as Shanghai’s Bailian mall and Beijing’s Wangfujing street now host regular events for anime fans, while Changsha’s Wenheyou has redecorated its commercial complexes to look like vintage markets and evoke feelings of “old Changsha.”

Ultimately, Y2K nostalgia is not immune to the consumerism it seeks to reject. With mounting financial pressure for commercial real estate developers, the Wanda Plaza model may have passed its heyday. Yet the urban landscape it has imposed upon us seems likely to last. They may complain about monotonous “new districts” and their lack of organic street life, but young Chinese continue to find the convenience that modern cities offer irresistible. Chinese dreamcore provides a temporary relief — sooner or later, though, we’re snapped awake by the buzz of our phones.

(Header image: 500px/VCG)

World.title: [Vantage Point] Why I’m not panicking over Ayala Land
World.content:
I still see an important distinction between a falling share price and a collapsing business

I have been watching Ayala Land’s market decline with more than academic interest.

The stock is down a third this year and more than 40% over the past 12 months. Now comes another indignity: MSCI Inc. is deleting Ayala Land Inc. (ALI) from its Philippines Standard Index at the close of August 31.

MSCI Inc. (formerly Morgan Stanley Capital International) produces global stock indexes used by investors and fund managers as market benchmarks and guides for investment allocation.

There are reasons to worry. But I still see an important distinction between a falling share price and a collapsing business. The numbers tell me Ayala Land is having a difficult year; they do not yet tell me its underlying economic value has deteriorated by anything approaching the market’s punishment.

Start with the damage. First-half revenues fell 10% to P75 billion, while net income dropped 19% to P11.5 billion. Property-development revenues fell 22% to P41 billion and residential revenues declined 15% to P35.3 billion.

But look at the numbers quarter by quarter. ALI earned P5.4 billion in the first quarter (Q1) and P6.1 billion in the second quarter (Q2), a sequential improvement of 13%. That does not amount to a recovery, but earnings are no longer deteriorating quarter after quarter.

Weak spots

Residential demand is still the weak spot.

First-half reservation sales this year fell 19% to P53.5 billion, while Q2 reservations slipped to P25.6 billion from ₱27.9 billion in Q1. The weakness is hardly ALI’s alone: Philippine Statistics Administration (PSA) data show the value of residential construction nationwide fell 25.8% in June and residential floor area shrank 32.2%, even as non-residential construction value surged 56.4%. I am not declaring that the housing slowdown has bottomed; ALI still has to prove that.

Then there is debt, the intimidating number in the story.

Total borrowings rose to P337.6 billion at end-June from P318 billion at end-2025, while cash and equivalents stood at P17.4 billion, net gearing at 0.80 times and interest coverage at 4.4 times. The debt mix also became less defensive: 83% was long-term and 60% was fixed-rate, versus 90% and 71% at year-end.

Those numbers deserve attention. But one number changes the debt story: ALI says it had already completed 96% of its 2026 refinancing requirements by June 30, leaving only about P1 billion still to refinance this year.

That is why I refuse to look at P337.6 billion of debt in isolation. ALI does not owe P337.6 billion tomorrow. What matters is when obligations mature: whether the company generates enough cash to service them and whether capital markets remain willing to refinance what comes due. For now, Ayala Land has leverage to manage, not a solvency crisis to survive.

My greater concern is cash generation. ALI raised its 2026 capital expenditure (CAPEX) guidance to P60 billion from P50 billion after spending P39.5 billion in the first half. With reservation sales down 19%, every peso deployed now has to earn its keep. If operating cash flow weakens while investment remains heavy, ALI becomes more dependent on external financing.

There is, however, another piece of the capital story.

AREIT disclosed a P17.33-billion property-for-share swap involving four malls and two hotels from ALI and subsidiaries. Sponsored by ALI, AREIT is the first and largest Real Estate Investment Trust in the country, managing a diversified, income-generating portfolio of commercial offices, retail malls, hotels, and industrial land. The transaction would move mature income-producing assets into AREIT in exchange for 462.48 million new shares priced at P37.48 each. It brings no immediate cash, so I would not count it as a solution to ALI’s liquidity problem, but it gives ALI a funding option

Then comes MSCI. Many analysts warned in June that ALI faced a high probability of deletion. On that call, they were right. But predicting index eligibility and determining intrinsic value are different exercises. MSCI tells us ALI’s market capitalization has fallen enough to lose its place; it does not tell us its estates, malls, offices, and hotels have lost a similar proportion of earning power.

What interests me more is what ALI’s parent company, Ayala Corporation, has been doing while the market sells.

Earning power

On August 14, two days after MSCI announced the deletion, the parent bought another 5.45 million ALI shares at an average P15.411 each, or about P84 million. Reuters subsequently reported another 600,000-share purchase at P15.18. The MSCI battle was already lost, yet Ayala kept buying.

That does not prove the parent is right about valuation. But whatever role index defense may initially have played, purchases after deletion stopped being a mechanical tracking rule and now increasingly looks like a capital-allocation decision.

ALI generated P190.2 billion in revenues and P30.6 billion in core earnings in 2025. Simply annualizing first-half 2026 earnings gives about P23 billion, 25% below last year’s core profit. Yet the stock has fallen more than 40% over 12 months.

That comparison does not prove undervaluation. Markets discount the future, not the past. But it frames the question correctly: has ALI’s long-term earning power deteriorated as much as its market value suggests?

So far, I don’t think so. But ALI must earn my patience quarter by quarter. I want reservation sales to stabilize, operating cash flow to strengthen, leverage contained, and Q2’s sequential earnings improvement sustained. I also want to see whether capital recycling through AREIT reduces funding pressure. History earns credibility; future cash flow earns valuation.

That is why I am not panicking over Ayala Land. The debt is larger, reservations are weaker, and MSCI has delivered its verdict. But refinancing is largely done for the year, Q2 earnings improved sequentially, and the parent is still buying after deletion became inevitable.

The forensic question remains whether the business has permanently lost as much value as the market says it has — or whether fear has simply fallen faster than value.

This analysis is based primarily on Ayala Land and Ayala Corp.’s financial statements, investor presentations and PSE disclosures, supplemented by MSCI index announcements and methodology, AREIT disclosures, and PhilRatings reports. Calculations and interpretations are my own. This column is for informational purposes only and is not intended to influence the market or constitute investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any security.

I welcome your views on these and other issues where decisions made in power shape the country’s economic future.

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

World.title: Alex Eala’s #myMILOStory: From small wins to big breakthroughs
World.content:
Fueled by grit and hard work, Alex continues to reach new heights while staying grounded in her MILO Sports Clinic roots.

Editor’s note: This content is sponsored by MILO Philippines and was produced by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the production of this piece.

After a few intense exchanges, an errant return by Alex Eala’s opponent ended their opening-round clash in the 2025 US Open. It was decided — the 20-year-old had just become the first Filipino tennis player to win a Grand Slam main draw match in the Open era.

Did Alex know she’d win that round? Perhaps not, but what’s certain is that in that moment, she carried with her a lifetime of training–a journey that began at age four. And just like many Filipinos, Alex’s grit and discipline as a young athlete were also honed on the grounds of MILO Sports Clinic, sharing the dreams of those who had the same roots.



Even non-athletes can relate to Eala’s remarkable feat. For the MILO generation – those who grew up lining up for a free cup of MILO in grade school, to those who gushed over Taekwondo idol Japoy Lizardo – MILO was just more than a chocolate drink. In a way, it brought out the Champion in all of us. No doubt, we all might have #myMILOstory.

Play Video

Alex Eala now headlines MILO’s #myMILOstory campaign, where her breakthrough proves that grit, discipline, and teamwork have shaped her journey.

Coming from a family of athletes, Alex was no stranger to sports. Her mother, Rizza Maniego-Eala, is a former member of the national swimming team and won a medal in the Southeast Asian Games. Her older brother, Miko, also played tennis and attended the Rafa Nadal Academy in Spain together with Alex — the two introduced to the sport by their late grandfather Bobby. What was once only a family pastime grew into an unwavering passion.

From a four-year-old who showed promise on local courts to a rising star who has shone on the world stage, Alex was fueled by a dream and a cup of MILO. Here’s a visual look back at how Alex energized her path to becoming a national tennis icon.

As of writing, Alex is set to compete in the last Grand Slam of the year, the US Open, where she looks to surpass her second-round appearance in 2025.



Alex recently exited the Cincinnati Open, yielding to American world No. 10 Amanda Anisimova in the round of 32 in a loss that snapped her five-game winning streak against top-10 players.

After crossing milestone after milestone and pushing past her own limits, Alex Eala has already laid the groundwork for new generations of Tennis players in the country. From leaving home at an early age to train in Spain–trading comfort for discipline, to pouring her blood, sweat, and tears into every match, Alex’s victories are a collection of fragments of lessons, sacrifices, and values that trace back to her roots in the Philippines.

In an interview with Rappler, Alex shared her hopes that her unprecedented wins will ignite the fighting spirits of budding tennis players across the country. “The only thing I can do to give back to my country is to help inspire change, positive change, and to inspire people to pick up a racket, to watch more tennis, watch more women’s tennis,” said Eala.

This is Alex’s #myMILOstory. What’s yours? Find out how you can share and follow MILO Philippines’ Facebook page for more updates. – Rappler.com

World.title: Benguet under state of calamity as damage reaches over P1B
World.content:
SCARRED. A landslide scars a slope above the Amburayan-Boneng Provincial Road in Kapangan, Benguet, after days of heavy rain destabilized parts of the mountainside.

The declaration enables the provincial government to access P38 million for emergency response and recovery efforts

BENGUET, Philippines – The Benguet provincial government placed the entire province under a state of calamity on Monday, August 24, after weeks of heavy rain, landslides and damaged roads pushed losses past P1 billion.

The provincial board approved the declaration during its 52nd regular session in Basil, Tublay, following a recommendation from the Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council.

Based on a partial assessment by the Benguet Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office, damage has reached some P1.068 billion.

Of the initial report on the damage and losses, about P749.89 million was attributed to infrastructure and P318.64 million to agriculture, according to the Benguet PDRRMO.

Roads and bridges accounted for the biggest share of infrastructure losses at P708.70 million, followed by public infrastructure and assets at nearly P30 million and private properties at P11.19 million.

Agricultural losses included P317.53 million in crops and agricultural facilities, plus about P1.11 million in livestock, poultry, fisheries and farm structures.

The assessment showed that about 40,121 people or some 13,031 families were affected, while 211 houses were damaged.

It also counted 6,362 affected farmers, with damage to crops and agricultural facilities spanning about 1,315.86 hectares.

Benguet officials said the declaration was warranted after over 15% of Benguet’s population was found to require immediate emergency assistance and more than 30% of local livelihoods had been affected.

The prolonged severe weather triggered landslides and soil collapses, damaged roads and other public infrastructure, and caused substantial agricultural losses across the province.

Benguet Vice Governor Marie Rose Fongwan-Kepes said the declaration followed deliberations on the extent and severity of the damage.

The declaration allows the capitol to access about P38 million from its quick response fund for relief, emergency response, rehabilitation and recovery based on the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010.

Benguet’s declaration comes less than a week after La Trinidad, the provincial capital, was separately placed under a state of calamity on August 18.

La Trinidad had earlier reported millions of pesos in infrastructure and agricultural losses after prolonged rain triggered flooding, landslides and road damage.

The province-wide declaration expands the response beyond individual municipalities, allowing Benguet to mobilize resources for communities, farmers and infrastructure affected across the highland province. – Rappler.com

World.title: ASEAN Summer Festival Brings Southeast Asia Closer to Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – The ASEAN Summer Festival brought Southeast Asia closer to Kazakhstan on Aug. 22, turning the Kazakh capital into a showcase of the region’s cultures, traditions, food and tourism while underscoring growing people-to-people ties.

Organized by the Astana ASEAN Committee (AAC), comprising the Embassies of Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam, with the support of the Honorary Consul of Singapore in Kazakhstan, the festival featured traditional music and dance performances, a food bazaar and cultural presentations showcasing the diversity of Southeast Asia.

Held under the theme Navigating Our Future, Together and focused on ASEAN culture, the festival was part of broader efforts to strengthen engagement between Kazakhstan and the ASEAN.

Speaking at the event, Ambassador of Indonesia to Kazakhstan and Tajikistan Mochamad Fadjroel Rachman noted that ASEAN Day is an opportunity to strengthen relations between Kazakhstan and Southeast Asian countries.

“This is the second year we are celebrating ASEAN Day, and hopefully it could be yearly here in Kazakhstan, so we could strengthen the relation between Kazakhstan and ASEAN countries,” he said.

Representatives of Indonesia, Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand and Singapore participated in the celebration, reflecting the growing presence of ASEAN countries in Kazakhstan and the expanding scope of cooperation between the two regions.

Visa-free travel to boost tourism

Tourism and connectivity were among the key themes highlighted during the event. Rachman noted that Indonesia introduced a visa-free travel for Kazakh citizens on July 9, allowing them to travel to Indonesia without obtaining a visa in advance.

“Indonesia granted visa-free to Kazakhstan to go to Bali, just buying a ticket and then flying to Indonesia,” he said, noting the popularity of Bali among Kazakh travellers.

The ambassador expressed hope that the new arrangement would contribute to a significant increase in tourist flows, estimating that around 50,000 Kazakh people could visit Indonesia in 2026.

He also pointed to the wider opportunities for travel within Southeast Asia.

“If you buy a ticket, you could go not only to Indonesia, but also to Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore and other ASEAN countries,” he said.

According to Rachman, improved connectivity can help deepen relations between Kazakhstan and ASEAN not only through tourism but also through broader cultural and economic exchanges.

Connecting people through travel, education and business

Talgat Chinikeyev, honorary consul of Singapore in Kazakhstan, said relations between Kazakhstan and Southeast Asia have become increasingly people-oriented in recent years.

“Over the past several years, I have personally seen a significant change in the way Kazakhstan and Southeast Asia engage with each other. Our relations are no longer limited to official diplomacy or government-to-government contacts. They are becoming much more people-oriented,” he told The Astana Times.

He noted that improved connectivity has made Southeast Asia more familiar and accessible to Kazakh citizens, with growing numbers travelling to Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia and Singapore for tourism, education, business and healthcare.

At the same time, interest in Kazakhstan and Central Asia is growing in Southeast Asia, with more business delegations, investors, professionals and visitors exploring opportunities in the region.

Chinikeyev said he has observed these trends particularly in Kazakhstan-Singapore relations, with Singapore increasingly recognized in Kazakhstan not only as an Asian economic success story, but also as a center for education, finance, technology, innovation and healthcare.

Business exchanges between the two countries have also become more active, with potential for cooperation in investment, logistics, digitalisation, education and technology.

He highlighted President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s state visit to Singapore in 2024 as an important push for bilateral relations and stronger people-to-people ties.

“I believe we are now moving into a very interesting stage where Kazakhstan can become a natural gateway for Southeast Asia into Central Asia, while Singapore can serve as an important gateway for Kazakhstan into ASEAN,” said Chinikeyev.

Celebrating ASEAN’s diversity

The festival also provided an opportunity for the public to learn more about the cultural diversity of ASEAN, a region of more than 680 million people comprising 11 member states. The region is also home to hundreds of ethnic groups, more than 1,000 languages and diverse religious traditions.

According to the festival organizers, ASEAN’s ability to maintain unity amid such diversity is one of the region’s defining characteristics. For Chinikeyev, cultural events can help make Southeast Asia feel closer to people in Kazakhstan.

“My hope is that people who come to the ASEAN summer festival will not simply enjoy the food, music, performances and atmosphere, but will leave with a genuine curiosity about Southeast Asia and a desire to learn more about the region,” he said.

He added that culture has a unique ability to bring people together naturally, particularly when regions remain geographically distant from one another.

Culture as a foundation for long-term partnership

The festival was presented not only as a cultural showcase but also as an instrument of public diplomacy and engagement. Held in Astana, a city with a diverse population and an increasingly active international profile, the event sought to create direct connections between the public and ASEAN through food, music, traditional performances and cultural exchange.

The ASEAN summer festival builds on a broader increase in engagement between Kazakhstan and Southeast Asia, supported by direct air connectivity, growing tourism, business exchanges and high-level diplomatic contacts.

“This is how long-term partnerships are built – not only through agreements and official visits, but through friendship, understanding and genuine human connections,” Chinikeyev said.

World.title: Central Asia Sees FinTech As Next Frontier of Regional Integration
World.content:
TASHKENT – Digital and financial connectivity could become the next frontier of regional integration in Central Asia, as Uzbekistan seeks to accelerate its fintech development and advance greater connectivity within the region’s markets.

Central Bank of Uzbekistan Governor Timur Ishmetov called on global investors and innovators to work on infrastructure and standards that can connect markets across Central Asia and beyond.

“Regional financial connectivity cannot be built by one country alone. Build here. Test new solutions here. Invest here. Develop talent here. With the right partnerships, Central Asia can become a more connected, competitive and internationally integrated financial region,” said Ishmetov at the opening of the Silk Road Finance and Technology Forum 2026 on Aug. 24.

The initiative comes as Central Asia, a region of more than 80 million people, has been pursuing stronger economic cooperation while accelerating digital adoption and developing new channels for financial services.

Despite its demographic and economic potential, Central Asia’s share of global fintech investment remains “modest.” According to Ishmetov, in 2025, total venture capital funding across Central Asia amounted to approximately $320 million.

“This demonstrates the scale of the opportunity to convert the region’s young population, growing digital adoption, and developing financial infrastructure into sustainable investment and innovation,” he said.

For Ishmetov, the challenge is not simply to expand fintech within national markets but to create conditions for markets to connect with one another. Regional connectivity is seen as a key element of a sustainable fintech ecosystem along with regulation, infrastructure and investment.

“Efficient regional corridors are of utmost economic importance. There remains potential to strengthen payment connectivity between countries of our region and to expand the range of financial services available across borders. Digital finance changes the economic geography. Physical distance becomes substantially less restrictive and that is a strategic opportunity for our region,” he explained.

The economic foundation for connectivity has also been expanding. The report prepared by the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), in collaboration with the Institute for Advanced International Studies (IAIS) of Uzbekistan, highlighted the shift of the region from a peripheral destination into one of Eurasia’s more dynamic economic nodes over the past two decades.

Between 2000 and 2024, the countries of Central Asia significantly increased their accumulated stock of foreign direct investment. The UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) World Investment Report 2025 indicated that the region’s total inward FDI stock reached $220.5 billion as of 2024.

The growing scale of investment and cross border activity brings a broader question for the region whether financial infrastructure can keep pace with the movement of goods, capital and businesses across connected markets.

Otabek Nasirov, chairman of Central Asian Fintech Association, said the region can and should move toward common standards for digital identity, payments and open banking.

“We do not necessarily need identical regulations in all five countries. What we need is interoperability: compatible digital identity frameworks, common principles for secure data exchange and consent, interoperable payment infrastructure, and APIs that allow financial institutions and fintech companies to work across borders,” Nasirov told The Astana Times.

Central Asian countries are developing their digital financial ecosystems at different speeds. The next challenge is to connect these national ecosystems.

“If we can make digital identity, payments and financial data work across borders, a fintech company should eventually be able to scale across Central Asia much more easily – reaching a regional market of more than 80 million people rather than treating each country as a completely separate market,” Nasirov said.

This will require close cooperation between central banks, governments, financial institutions, fintech companies and industry associations.

“I believe we should start with practical areas where interoperability can deliver immediate value cross-border payments and QR interoperability, digital KYC [Know Your Customer] and identity verification, and common approaches to Open Banking and consent-based data sharing,” he said.

“The goal should not be to create one regulator or one system for Central Asia, but to build a connected regional digital financial infrastructure based on mutually recognised standards. That could become one of the strongest drivers of fintech growth, investment and regional economic integration in Central Asia,” he said.

Tashkent is hosting the Silk Road Finance and Technology Forum 2026. The event is supported by the Central Bank of Uzbekistan and Singapore-headquartered Global Finance and Technology Network (GFTN), and co-hosted by Ant International on Aug. 24-26.

The event connects more than 6,000 participants from 74 countries in Tashkent. The forum focused on five key themes including digital payments and infrastructure, Islamic finance and new economic corridors, AI and emerging technologies, tokenization and digital assets and cross-border finance and regulation.

World.title: Why Kazakhstan Is Creating Domestic Credit Rating Agency and What Will Determine Its Success
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is preparing to establish a national credit rating agency as part of a broader effort to develop its domestic capital market, but the institution’s success will ultimately depend on more than the creation of a new regulator-approved rating system. Its ratings will have to earn the confidence of investors and become a meaningful part of how companies are financed and risks are priced.

The new Law On Credit Rating Activities, signed by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on July 23, introduces common rules for credit rating agencies operating in Kazakhstan and provides for the establishment of a Kazakh rating agency, with the National Bank among its founders. The law sets requirements for capital, corporate governance, internal controls, conflict-of-interest management and disclosure.

It also expands the potential scope of rating activities beyond conventional credit ratings to include corporate governance, Islamic finance, sustainable development and other types of ratings, while the legislation is set to take effect on Oct. 21, with some provisions coming into force on July 1, 2027.

But the central question is not simply what the new agency will do. It is why Kazakhstan needs one in the first place, and whether it can change the way capital is allocated in the domestic economy.

The gap in Kazakhstan’s capital market

Kazakhstan already has access to the world’s major rating agencies. The new institution is therefore not intended to replace international players or create a domestic version of S&P, Moody’s or Fitch.

“Creating a national credit rating agency is not an attempt to make a Kazakh equivalent of S&P, Moody’s or Fitch, and certainly not a task of replacing international agencies. International ratings will retain their importance,” a leading Kazakh economist Ruslan Sultanov, who served as Chairman of the Board of the highly respected Economic Research Institute from 2019 to 2024, told the Astana Times.

The rationale is instead connected to the structure of the domestic financial market. Kazakhstan has been seeking to develop non-bank financing, corporate bonds and institutional investment. Yet a functioning capital market requires investors to be able to distinguish between borrowers according to their level of risk.

According to Sultanov, this is particularly relevant for medium-sized companies. An international rating may make economic sense for a large corporate borrower seeking substantial financing or access to international capital markets. For a smaller issuer, however, the cost and requirements associated with obtaining such a rating can become disproportionate to the size of the planned issue.

“As a result, a gap arises: there is a potential issuer, institutional investors have money, but there is often no independent and understandable market assessment of credit risk between them. The national rating scale makes it possible to solve another problem – to compare the credit quality of borrowers within a single jurisdiction in much greater detail than the global scale allows,” he said.

The distinction is important. A domestic rating system does not necessarily need to compete with international ratings. Its value could instead lie in providing more granular information about relative credit quality within the Kazakh market.

Ratings do not create liquidity on their own

A rating is an information tool. It can tell an investor how an independent analyst assesses a borrower’s ability to meet its obligations. But it cannot, by itself, create investors, issuers or demand for bonds.

“The creation of the agency itself will not create a capital market. An agency can be registered, methodologies approved and the first ratings assigned. Liquidity will not appear from that alone,” Sultanov said.

According to him, for the reform to have a broader economic effect, national ratings would need to become integrated into the infrastructure of the financial market: the investment decisions of institutional investors, risk-management systems, corporate disclosure and bond pricing. This means the agency’s real contribution could be measured by what happens after a rating is issued.

The potential benefit for companies and investors

For companies, the most immediate potential benefit is access.

“The main potential effect is a reduction in the barrier to entering the public debt market. This is especially relevant for issuers that do not need an international rating but still need to demonstrate their creditworthiness to investors,” Sultanov said.

For investors, the benefit is potentially greater transparency in comparing domestic issuers. The effect could also extend to banks, which occupy several positions within Kazakhstan’s financial system: they are borrowers, investors and major professional market participants. Over time, national ratings could be incorporated into their investment policies and risk-management systems.

According to Sultanov, they could also potentially be used in elements of prudential regulation if regulators determine that the quality and reliability of the ratings justify such treatment.

The National Bank’s role as one of the founders brings both advantages and potential questions. For investors, the key issue is not simply who owns the agency, but who controls the rating decision.

“The presence of the state or regulator among the founders in itself does not indicate the quality of a rating. For an investor, what matters more is whether the owner can influence the methodology, a specific rating decision or personnel decisions concerning analysts,” the economist said.

Sultanov points to several mechanisms that could help preserve independence: an independent board of directors, an autonomous rating committee, transparent methodologies, conflict-of-interest controls, rotation of analysts, internal oversight and disclosure of the reasons behind rating changes.

The real test will come later

The agency’s credibility cannot be established on the day it receives its registration. It will have to be built through a track record. An important part of that track record will be whether ratings actually correspond to the behaviour of the companies being assessed. Over time, investors should be able to see how frequently ratings are upgraded or downgraded and how often companies in different rating categories default.

“After several years, the market should be able to see rating migration matrices, the frequency of defaults in each rating category and compare the actual behaviour of borrowers with the risk that the agency previously indicated. In other words, measurable quality of the rating,” Sultanov said.

For large Kazakh companies seeking international financing, global ratings are likely to remain important. A national agency, meanwhile, could focus on the domestic market and provide a more detailed assessment of companies whose financing needs do not justify the cost or requirements of an international rating. The two levels of the rating system could therefore become complementary rather than competing.

“A rating agency has a rather unusual asset – trust. It cannot be contributed to the charter capital. It emerges gradually and step by step, when investors see that the same risk receives the same assessment regardless of the owner’s name, the size of the company or its relationship with the state,” Sultanov said.

For Kazakhstan, this may be the defining test of the new system.

World.title: Tokayev Makes Senior Appointments Amid Kazakhstan’s Constitutional Transition
World.content:
ALMATY – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has made a number of senior state appointments, reappointing the heads of the National Bank, National Security Committee and Supreme Judicial Council, as well as the Commissioner for Human Rights on Aug. 24.

Timur Suleimenov was reappointed the Governor of National Bank of Kazakhstan. He first became Governor in September 2023, having previously served as Deputy Chairman of the National Bank.

Yermek Sagimbayev was reappointed Chairman of the National Security Committee, a position he has held since January 2022.

Dmitry Malakhov was reappointed Chairman of the Supreme Judicial Council, a position he has held since September 2024. Prior to that, he headed the Agency for Financial Monitoring.

Artur Lastayev was reappointed Commissioner for Human Rights in Kazakhstan. He has held the position since January 2023.

The appointments come after Kazakhstan’s new Constitution took effect on July 1, establishing a new constitutional framework and introducing changes to the country’s political institutions.

The latest appointments also come as Kazakhstan begins implementing a series of institutional changes following the first elections to the new unicameral Kurultai on Aug. 23.

Further changes expected

Earlier, Tokayev said the government’s composition would undergo changes, while stressing that there are currently no grounds for concern about its work. He said personnel changes were a normal part of government work and should be aimed at giving the Cabinet new momentum rather than being made simply for the sake of dismissals.

Tokayev also said the name of the person who will take the newly established post of Vice President is expected to become known within the next seven to 10 days.

The appointments and planned institutional changes form part of the broader political transition following the adoption of Kazakhstan’s new Constitution and the establishment of the unicameral Kurultai.

World.title: Kazakhstan Gains US Recognition as Safe Tourism Destination
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan has received the least restrictive travel advisory level from the United States, adding to a series of developments leading to strengthening the country’s position as an international tourism destination.

On Aug. 18, the U.S. Department of State placed Kazakhstan at Level 1, the lowest (safest) of its four travel advisory levels. The advisory says Kazakhstan is generally a safe destination for travelers, while noting that flooding can occur in the country.

The assessment comes as Kazakhstan continues to expand its tourism infrastructure, international connectivity and number of tourists.

According to the Bureau of National Statistics, Kazakhstan received 15.7 million foreign visitors in 2025, 3.1% more than in 2024. Of these, 11.1 million were classified as foreign tourists. Tourism investment reached 1.26 trillion tenge (US$2.4 billion), increasing by 32.6% year on year.

The positive trend continued in the first quarter of 2026, when Kazakhstan welcomed three million foreign travelers. More than two million guests stayed at accommodation facilities, including more than 802,000 visitors to resort areas.

The Almaty Mountain Cluster was the most visited resort destination during the period, followed by the Shchuchinsk-Burabai resort area in the Akmola Region and the Mangystau resort area.

Kazakhstan also improved its position in the World Economic Forum’s Travel & Tourism Development Index, ranking 52nd among 119 economies in the 2024 edition, compared with 66th among 117 economies in the previous edition.

The country is also investing in transport infrastructure to make major tourist destinations more accessible. Kazakhstan plans to open or resume 15 international air routes in 2026, including services connecting the country with Vienna, Rome, Shanghai, Tokyo and Riyadh. Domestic connectivity is also being expanded.

The government is working to complete tourist airports in Katon-Karagai and Zaysan in eastern Kazakhstan and Kenderli in the Mangystau Region in 2026. Road improvements include routes leading to major tourist destinations, while new roadside service facilities are also planned. The Astana Times previously reported on measures to improve safety, transport and resort infrastructure ahead of the 2026 summer season.

Nature-based tourism is becoming one of the country’s key areas for development.

The Almaty Superski project is being implemented as part of the broader Almaty Mountain Cluster. The project is expected to expand access to mountain tourism and create infrastructure for skiing, hiking and other outdoor activities.

Visits to specially protected natural areas increased from 2.8 million in 2024 to 3.7 million in 2025, according to the Ministry of Tourism and Sports. National parks currently offer 179 tourist routes and 42 ecological trails.

Officials have emphasized that tourism development should be balanced with environmental protection, including ecological monitoring and visitor management.

Another indicator of Kazakhstan’s growing integration into international travel is the Henley Passport Index.

In the 2026 Henley Passport Index, Kazakhstan ranked 64th, with its passport providing access to 77 destinations without a prior visa. The Henley Passport Index measures international mobility, the number of destinations that passport holders can access without obtaining a visa in advance. It is separate from travel safety assessments.

Kazakhstan is also expanding opportunities for foreign travelers to enter the country.

Citizens of 105 countries can obtain electronic visas, while Kazakhstan has introduced additional visa mechanisms for certain categories of visitors, including the Digital Nomad Visa for IT specialists and the Neo Nomad Visa.

International arrivals are only part of Kazakhstan’s tourism market. Domestic travel continues to account for the majority of tourism trips by citizens.

According to the Bureau of National Statistics, Kazakhstan recorded 11.77 million tourist trips by citizens in 2025. Of these, 10.27 million, or 87.2%, were domestic trips.

Astana, the Turkistan Region and Almaty were among the most visited destinations, highlighting the importance of both major cities and regional tourism centers.

The new U.S. travel advisory is one of several developments strengthening Kazakhstan’s international tourism profile. Growing visitor numbers, rising investment, new air routes, improved access to regional destinations, simplified visa procedures and expanding mountain and nature tourism are collectively making the country more accessible to international travelers.

For Kazakhstan, the next challenge will be to ensure that tourism growth is accompanied by reliable services, safety measures and environmental protection.

The combination of a favorable safety assessment and expanding tourism infrastructure could further strengthen Kazakhstan’s position as a destination for travelers interested in nature, adventure, cultural heritage and the wider Central Asian region.

World.title: Kazakhstan Judo Team Wins Historic Mixed Team Gold at World Championships
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s national judo team secured its first-ever gold medal in the mixed team event at the World Judo Championships among cadets in Guayaquil, Ecuador, marking a historic achievement for the country’s judo programme.

The team title capped a record-breaking individual campaign, with Kazakh judokas winning 11 medals – four gold, three silver and four bronze – at the championships. The result was described as the best in the history of Kazakhstan’s judo at the youth world level, reported the Ministry of Tourism and Sports’ press service on Aug. 24.

Kazakhstan’s boys finished first in the team standings, while the girls placed second. Fatima Supygalieva also made history as the first Kazakh female cadet to win a world championship title.

The results come as part of broader changes to Kazakhstan’s national sports training system led by the Ministry of Tourism and Sports in cooperation with the Judo Federation of Kazakhstan and Zhenis (Victory) club.

Following the Paris Olympics, the federation began updating its approach to the preparation of national teams, with Kazakh coaches working closely with leading international specialists, including Ezio Gamba’s team. Cadet, junior and senior national teams are being integrated into a unified training system.

“We are building a single pathway: cadets – juniors – national team – Olympic Games. When an athlete moves from one age category to another, they should not have to start their preparation from scratch. They continue working within a unified model, with common requirements, scientific support and a clear development trajectory,” Minister of Tourism and Sports Yerbol Myrzabosynov said.

He described the team gold and record medal haul as concrete evidence that the new system is producing results.

“The team gold and record ten medals in the individual competitions are concrete confirmation that the new system works. Our task now is to consistently scale this experience to other sports,” he said.

The unified training model includes scientific analysis of the training process, functional diagnostics, individualized workloads, sports medicine, recovery programmes and continuous monitoring of each athlete’s progress. The National Sports University is expected to play an important role by providing national teams with scientific and analytical support.

Similar approaches are being introduced in fencing, boxing, wrestling and other sports, with the involvement of leading Kazakh and international specialists.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev congratulated the Kazakh judo team on its performance in Guayaquil, praising its victory in the mixed team competition and congratulating Gabit Rasulhan, Supygalieva and Adilzhan Zhaudinov on their individual gold medals.

Tokayev also held a conversation with International Judo Federation President Marius Vizer, who congratulated the Kazakh leader on the team’s unprecedented success at the world youth championships.

Tokayev expressed appreciation to Vizer for constructive cooperation with Kazakhstan’s national federation and the Ministry of Tourism and Sports, which contributes to the promotion and development of judo in the country.

World.title: Adilet Party Leads Preliminary Results in Kazakhstan’s First Kurultai Election With 71.17%
World.content:
ASTANA – The Adilet party secured 71.17% of the vote in Kazakhstan’s first elections to the Kurultai, according to preliminary results announced by the Central Election Commission (CEC) on Aug. 24.

A total of 9,351,539 citizens participated in the election out of 12,623,289 registered voters, bringing preliminary voter turnout to 74.08%. The Adilet party received 6,528,948 votes, or 71.17%, according to the preliminary results. The Auyl People’s Democratic Patriotic Party received 574,621 votes, or 6.26%, followed by Respublica with 509,631 votes, or 5.56%, the Aq Zhol Democratic Party with 478,083 votes, or 5.21%, and the Nationwide Social Democratic Party with 469,058 votes, or 5.11%.

The People’s Party of Kazakhstan received 285,395 votes, or 3.11%, while the Baytaq Green Party received 97,751 votes, or 1.07%. The Against All option received 2.51% of the vote.

Under Kazakhstan’s election legislation, political parties must secure at least 5% of the vote to qualify for seats in the Kurultai. Based on the preliminary figures, five parties crossed the threshold.

Voting concludes abroad

According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, all 79 overseas polling stations established at Kazakhstan’s diplomatic missions and consular offices in 61 countries have completed their work as of 8 a.m. Astana time.

A total of 9,623 Kazakh citizens cast their ballots abroad, representing a voter turnout of 84.4% among registered overseas voters. The protocols of overseas precinct election commissions will be transmitted to the CEC for inclusion in the overall election results.

What comes next

The figures announced by the CEC are preliminary. The commission is expected to establish the official election results by Aug. 30. The formation of the new Kurultai will trigger a series of political and institutional changes under Kazakhstan’s new constitutional framework.

Following the formation of the Kurultai, the government is expected to resign. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said on election day that changes would be made to the composition of the cabinet, while stressing that personnel changes should be aimed at giving the Government new momentum rather than being made for the sake of dismissals.

Another expected institutional change is the appointment of a Vice President. Tokayev said the name of the person who will take the newly established position is expected to become known within a week or 10 days.

First election under new constitutional system

The Aug. 23 election was the first parliamentary election held under Kazakhstan’s new constitutional system. The 145-member Kurultai replaced the country’s former bicameral Parliament under the Constitution that took effect July 1.

All seats are allocated proportionally through party lists in a single nationwide constituency. Seven political parties fielded a total of 545 candidates. A total of 10,423 polling stations were established in Kazakhstan and abroad, with more than 12.6 million citizens registered to vote.

Overall, 777 foreign observers from 42 countries and 13 international organizations were accredited to monitor the election.

World.title: Experts Say Tokayev’s G20 Invitation Will Test Kazakhstan’s Balancing Act
World.content:
ASTANA — President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s participation in the G20 summit in Miami this December is set to put Kazakhstan’s carefully balanced foreign policy to a new test, as growing United States (US) interest in the country creates opportunities for deeper economic and strategic cooperation while intensifying competition among the major powers with which Astana has sought to maintain close ties.

Kazakhstan is not a G20 member and has participated in the summit only twice before, in St. Petersburg in 2013 and Hangzhou in 2016, each time at the invitation of the host country. This time, however, the invitation comes from the US, amid a rapidly expanding Kazakhstan-U.S. relationship and a sharp rise in Washington’s interest in the wider Trans-Caspian region.

The invitation can therefore be read in two ways. It may signal that Kazakhstan has become a more important strategic and economic partner for Washington. But it may also reflect the Trump administration’s broader effort to strengthen ties across a region increasingly important for energy, critical minerals, trade routes and technology. The difference matters because Kazakhstan’s traditional strength — its ability to work with competing powers without aligning exclusively with any of them — may also become harder to sustain as geopolitical competition deepens.

Iskander Akylbayev, CEO of Xander Group and chairman of CFive, sees the summit as a practical opportunity for Kazakhstan.

“My expectation is that the Miami G20 will be highly pragmatic and transaction-driven,” he said, pointing to economic growth, secure energy supply chains and technological innovation as central priorities of the U.S. G20 presidency.

He added that Tokayev’s participation “should therefore be seen as more than a diplomatic gesture,” noting that the invitation reflects a wider change in Washington’s view of Central Asia, which he believes is moving “from the geopolitical periphery to the global economic agenda.”

For Akylbayev, Kazakhstan’s economic weight helps explain the shift. He noted that Kazakhstan generates more than 60% of Central Asia’s GDP and accounts for approximately 75% of the region’s trade with the US, while bilateral goods trade reached $5 billion in 2025.

The broader relationship has indeed acquired a markedly commercial dimension over the past year. During President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s November 2025 visit to Washington, Kazakhstan and the United States signed 29 agreements worth $17 billion across industry, digitalization, education, healthcare, transport and other sectors. The Astana Times reported at the time that the visit represented a new phase in the strategic partnership, with experts describing a shift from symbolic diplomacy toward a more results-oriented model of cooperation.

Akylbayev said Miami should therefore be seen not as the culmination of this process but as an opportunity to move it into a more advanced stage.

“For Kazakhstan, however, the invitation itself is not the result. The real task is to convert political access into investment, technology and market access,” he said.

He pointed to critical minerals, AI, advanced manufacturing and the Middle Corridor, as well as Kazakhstan’s accession in June to the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative, which focuses on trusted supply chains linking semiconductors, critical minerals, data centers, energy infrastructure and high-tech manufacturing. Akylbayev’s broader argument is that Kazakhstan should move beyond its traditional role as a resource supplier.

“Our ambition should not be to export minerals and later import the technologies made from them,” he said, highlighting that Kazakhstan should process more resources domestically, expand computing infrastructure, develop engineering talent and produce higher-value components.

The logic is attractive, particularly as the US seeks to diversify strategic supply chains. Kazakhstan has become an important supplier of uranium and has substantial deposits of tungsten, copper, lithium and other critical minerals, while its geographic position gives it a central role in the Trans-Caspian transport route linking China and Europe.

Akylbayev believes this lets Kazakhstan present itself in Miami as a “connector state”—linking East and West, natural resources and technology, and major powers without becoming dependent on any one of them.

But that proposition rests on an important assumption: that the same balanced foreign policy that makes Kazakhstan attractive to multiple powers will continue to be accepted as competition among those powers intensifies. Darren Spink, managing director of Janus Forum and a non-resident fellow with the Danube Institute, believes that assumption may face its greatest test in technology.

“Kazakhstan has built its foreign and commercial policy around a balanced approach, but artificial intelligence (AI) may be emerging as the sector where Washington is least willing to accept that balance,” Spink said.

He pointed to the Middle Corridor as an example of an area where competing powers can still pursue overlapping interests. AI, however, is different, he said, because Washington increasingly sees technology, data infrastructure, semiconductors and supply chains through a strategic rather than purely commercial lens.
