World.title: Convicted murderer Sue Neill-Fraser can now talk to media, law centre says
World.content:
Convicted murderer Sue Neill-Fraser will be allowed to speak to the media after a gag order that was part of her parole conditions was removed, the Human Rights Law Centre says.

Neill-Fraser was found guilty of murdering her partner Bob Chappell aboard his yacht in Hobart in 2009.

She served 13 years in prison and was released on parole in 2022.

Sue Neill-Fraser was convicted of murdering her partner, Bob Chappell. (AAP/Supplied)

In December 2024, the Tasmanian Parole Board added a condition that she not speak "directly or indirectly with any media outlet to claim [her] alleged innocence and/or wrongful conviction".

This was replaced by a new parole condition in May 2025, which the Human Rights Law Centre said was more restrictive.

The new condition prevented her from communicating "directly or indirectly — including through third parties, written statements, electronic communications, social media platforms, television, radio, podcasts, streaming services, online video-sharing platforms, or any other public or broadcast media — to assert claims regarding your alleged innocence, wrongful conviction, or dispute the legitimacy of your conviction or sentencing".

On her behalf, the Human Rights Law Centre challenged this new condition in the Supreme Court of Tasmania last year, arguing it was unreasonable and breached her freedom of political communication.

In a statement, the law centre said the parole board agreed to remove that condition on Tuesday.

Sue Neill-Fraser, with Bob Chappell, and Sue's daughters. (Supplied)

The Parole Board refused to confirm the condition's removal, telling the ABC it was unable to comment on individual matters or matters currently before the court.

Attorney-General Guy Barnett has been contacted for comment.

Neill-Fraser maintains innocence

Sarah Schwartz, legal director at the Human Rights Law Centre, said the removal of the condition was an important vindication of Neill-Fraser's rights.

"Freedom of expression is a fundamental right, and we are pleased that Susan is no longer subject to a restriction that prevented her from being able to participate in public debate," Ms Schwartz said.

"People who have experienced incarceration are often among the most important voices in discussions about the criminal legal system, and protecting their ability to speak out and advocate for change is an important safeguard against injustice."

Sue Neill-Fraser greeting supporters at rally in 2024 calling for an inquiry into her conviction. ( ABC News: Liz Gwynn )

Neill-Fraser was arrested in August 2009, about seven months after Mr Chappell disappeared, and was convicted of murder by a jury.

She has always maintained her innocence and has gained a loyal following of supporters over the years.

The parole conditions case returns to court on Monday.

World.title: Gym safety auditor calls for improvements after man crushed while weightlifting
World.content:
An incident that left a man crushed by weightlifting equipment on the Gold Coast has sparked calls to mandate safety equipment in Australian gyms.

Paramedics were called to a Broadbeach gym at about 8am on Friday and took a man in his 50s to Gold Coast University Hospital with life-threatening neck injuries.

He is now in a stable condition, according to Queensland Health.

Queensland Work Health and Safety said it was not investigating the incident. The gym has been contacted for comment.

Phil Bellinger says safety can be improved at gyms. (ABC News: Steve Keen)

Griffith University sports scientist Phil Bellinger said such incidents could be prevented by making safety racks mandatory for lifting equipment, particularly as many gyms moved to a 24/7 model with unstaffed hours.

The racks allow adjustable bars to be set at different heights to catch a barbell if gym-goers fail a lift.

Dr Bellinger said the "relatively simple precaution" of using a buddy or a spotter would also improve safety.

"Where problems tend to occur is when people may progress too quickly or push loads that are maybe a little bit too heavy for them," he said.

Experts say there needs to be better screening at gyms. (Pexels: Victor Freitas)

He said gyms also needed to properly screen and educate clients.

"In a lot of gyms, there's not a huge barrier in terms of someone walking in off the street that doesn't have a lot of experience and then being able to access that gym out of staffed hours," he said.

Concern about 24/7 gym model

The Gold Coast incident comes almost a decade after a 15-year-old boy died in hospital after he was crushed at a Brisbane gym while trying to bench press about 100 kilograms.

Ben Shaw was found by a staff member at the Pine Rivers PCYC gym pinned to a bench after the weightlifting accident occurred.

It was not clear how long he was trapped.

Selwyn Becker is concerned about the move towards a 24/7 model at gyms. (ABC News: John Gunn)

FitSafe Australia founder Selwyn Becker has more than 30 years of experience in auditing gyms across the country.

He said while safety measures such as CCTV and panic buttons could help during unstaffed hours, they were not enough.

"When I first started in the industry, there was gym instructors on the gym floor all the time," he said.

" I feel like that should come back. "

Experts say gyms need to be proactive with safety precautions. (Pexels: William Choquette)

Mr Becker, who has previously worked as a trainer, said he would discourage people bench pressing on their own.

"There's always that risk of it falling on your chest or even higher up onto your neck and that's not good," he said.

He said gyms needed to be proactive with safety precautions, including regular equipment maintenance and independent safety reviews.

"Prevention is always better than investigating what went wrong after the fact," he said.

World.title: More than $60m in Tasmanian labour hire contracts awarded without tender
World.content:
Tasmanian Independent MLC Bec Thomas has slammed the health department over $61 million worth of contracts awarded without a tender process, calling for an explanation.

Documents tabled in the Legislative Council show that as part of the Bluegum Digital Transformation Project 742 labour hire contracts were awarded at a value of $99,999 or lower.

Tasmanian government contracts worth $99,999 or less can be awarded directly without a tender process.

The 742 contracts were awarded to just 65 companies, with 22 companies receiving 10 or more contracts.

One company, Ignite Project Services Pty Ltd, received 86 contracts worth a total of $6.96 million.

Of the $61 million in contracts, $50.6 million has been spent thus far.

The Bluegum Digital Health Transformation is a collection of IT projects in health, overhauling record keeping and systems management in the state's health department.

Bec Thomas has called for an explanation regarding the tender awarding process. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Ms Thomas said the figures demanded explanation.

"My questions to the state government are simple. How was this allowed to occur, and who is responsible?" she said.

"The issue isn't simply whether each individual contract fell below the relevant procurement threshold. The issue is whether anyone was looking at the cumulative picture and ensuring this approach represented good procurement practice and value for taxpayers."

Auditor-general Martin Thompson has also raised concerns about the practice, finding 80 occasions where the department was in breach of the treasurer's instructions.

He also found several cases where the contract was awarded after the successful company had begun work.

'Complex' projects demand labour hire

In response to questions from Ms Thomas in the Legislative Council, the government said that "revised procurement arrangements" had been agreed to by the Department of Health and Department of Treasury and Finance for labour hire on this project.

A "structured quotation process" was being used for projects under $250,000, while open tenders were used above that amount.

A procurement review committee is also in place for oversight.

The government said the Bluegum Digital Health Transformation Program was a "uniquely large and complex undertaking" in Tasmania, which had a greater reliance on labour hire.

"The scale, specialist skill requirements and pace of delivery associated with implementing a statewide digital health transformation necessitate access to highly specialised ICT resources that are not readily available through the local labour market," the response read.

The government says the program was a "uniquely large and complex undertaking" which had a greater reliance on labour hire. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Health digital programs questioned before

The Bluegum Digital Health Transformation is not the first ICT project to be questioned by auditor-general Martin Thompson.

In May this year he wrote that the Human Resource Information System (HRIS) program had not been effective or economical.

The program, which began in 2020, had spent $47 million without delivering any intended human resource modules.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff pushed back on the findings, calling them "incomplete" and "potentially misleading".

Responsibility for the project was transitioned away from the Department of Health to the Department of Premier and Cabinet.

There has also been criticism of the Tasmanian government's direct contract rules.

In May this year the state opposition questioned a $95,000 contract given to JackJumpers head coach Scott Roth to become an ambassador.

Labor's Ella Haddad claimed the contract had been kept under the $100,000 threshold "so it could be hand-picked without open tender".

Former minister Jane Howlett said the contract had been awarded in line with appropriate procedures.

World.title: Concerns AFP drugs team may implicate Australia in US boat strikes
World.content:
Unanswered questions about the Australian Federal Police's (AFP's) new anti-drugs taskforce in Colombia have sparked concerns the initiative could contribute to the Trump administration's air strikes against alleged trafficking vessels.

In May, commissioner Krissy Barrett announced the AFP and New Zealand Police would fund an international joint investigations team (IJIT) "to gather evidence about illicit drug shipments to help stop it coming to our region".

"The magnitude and endless maritime trafficking of illicit drugs to, and through the Pacific, has become a serious national security threat for the Pacific and Australia," Commissioner Barrett said in a statement. "Our AFP members in Bogota, with Colombian law enforcement, have deployed to remote parts of the Colombian jungle to deliberately destroy cocaine production laboratories."

The commissioner said despite more than 20 tonnes of cocaine being seized in Colombia in recent years, and the AFP's presence there since 2000, the IJIT was needed because "it is time for us to be bolder and do more".

IJIT officers would work with Colombia's attorney-general's office, national police and navy, as well as "US law enforcement", INTERPOL, Mexican, New Zealand and Pacific authorities, she said.

Since September last year, the Trump administration has declared the US is in an armed conflict with Latin American drug gangs and launched lethal strikes against alleged "narco-trafficking" vessels in the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea.

The strikes have killed at least 221 people and not reduced the flow of cocaine into the US, The Washington Post reported.

Some academics and legal experts call the strikes "extrajudicial executions" that violate US and international law.

Loading...

Greens senator David Shoebridge has called for more transparency about the IJIT's work, and said any Australian complicity in aiding the strikes would raise "warning signs".

"Australia should have no part in providing information to the US, and its military and policing authorities, for extrajudicial murder," he told the ABC.

Phil Kowalick, president of the Australian Institute of Professional Intelligence Officers and a former AFP senior executive, said "tactical and technical intelligence" sharing in joint taskforces was common.

He said it "would be a concern" if Australian IJIT intelligence aided a lethal US strike, but acknowledged it would be impossible to control how partner countries used information shared with them by Australian authorities.

Questions about IJIT's budget and expectations shut down

The ABC questioned the AFP in June about the IJIT's allocated budget, operational commitments and measure of how it would be deemed successful, as part of a Freedom of Information request.

In its response, the AFP said it had 60 documents that would answer those questions.

The documents included budget summaries, executive briefs, internal emails, statements of intent written in English and Spanish, and a memorandum of agreement.

AFP officers will be based in Colombia as part of the IJIT. (ABC News: Nick Haggarty)

The AFP declined to release the detail of the documents to the ABC, citing national security and international relations concerns.

It said the information's publication would be harmful to relations between Australia and Colombia or divulge confidential detail regarding how AFP officers operate.

"The International Joint Investigations Team (IJIT) operates as a multinational investigation team that is still in the negotiation phase between countries," the AFP's response said.

"Releasing the operational roles, resource commitments and strategic priorities of the IJIT would significantly adversely affect trust with our international law enforcement partners, intelligence sharing arrangements and ongoing joint operations."

Krissy Barrett says the IJIT is needed because of the magnitude of the drugs threat that Colombia poses to Australia and the Pacific. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

The AFP did not respond to further questions from the ABC about whether Australian intelligence would be shared with the US as part of the IJIT.

Senator Shoebridge said while some sensitive policing information should be kept private to avoid tipping off criminals, he described the AFP's refusal to answer as "overarching secrecy".

"It's hard to believe … every single element of every single document needs to be kept secret and, if any of it is released, it will somehow empower Colombian drug lords and imperil our bilateral relationship with Colombia," he said.

"If the public is paying for police operations in a third country, there should be a well-articulated goal available to the public to work out whether it's value for money or it's a program that Australia should be a party to."

A Colombian police officer with sacks of charcoal mixed with cocaine seized in the city of Barranquilla. (Reuters: Luisa Gonzalez)

Shadow Home Affairs Minister Jonno Duniam supported the AFP's efforts to crack down on illicit drugs being moved towards Australia, but echoed Senator Shoebridge's concerns.

"Australians are entitled to know whether taxpayer-funded initiatives are actually delivering results," he told the ABC.

"Operational sensitivities should not prevent appropriate transparency and disclosure around expenditure, objectives and outcomes."

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke did not respond to the ABC's request for comment.

In this year's federal budget, more than $1.16 million was allocated to the AFP for "ordinary annual services" in policing assistance efforts abroad and on Australian external territories in 2026-27.

That figure is expected to rise to $1.4m next year, before dropping to $1.01m and $1.03m in the following two years, but the budget did not detail how much was set aside specifically for the IJIT.

Commissioner Barrett says 17 tonnes of illicit drugs, mostly cocaine, has been seized by "local and international" police since January this year and stopped from reaching Australia through the Pacific.

The ABC understands, to July this year, most of the offshore seizures were made in French Polynesia, AFP officers were not physically involved in any interceptions and none were in Australian territorial waters.

The Australian Border Force also told the ABC it detected almost 13 tonnes of "major" illicit drugs at the country's ports of entry by May 31.

A narco-sub washed up near their village. Inside was a troubling clue to its origins At least seven narco subs have been discovered in Pacific waters in recent years, signalling a troubling new reality.

The AFP takes part in intelligence sharing and police development training programs in Pacific countries.

Mr Kowalick said while he had not seen the detail of the AFP's IJIT postings, he expected them to include a small team of officers liaising with Colombian police and said the cost to Australian taxpayers could be "quite significant".

AFP officers would also likely not be among Colombian police teams sent to the front lines of anti-drug raids in the jungle, Mr Kowalick said.

He told the ABC he expected immersive cultural and language training prior to being deployed in order to forge worthwhile relationships with Colombian authorities.

Those measures have been tested in the past.

A hack of the Colombian attorney-general's department in 2022, reported by The Sydney Morning Herald, revealed the efforts of two AFP officers stationed there were hampered by persistent IT problems and an inability to communicate and assess evidence in Spanish without local translators, who were often overworked or unavailable.

Colombia's National Police, on behalf of the Ministry of National Defence, rejected the ABC's request for further comment about the IJIT.

Australians consuming 'more drugs than ever'

Australians' annual drug use continues to increase, the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission's (ACIC's) latest wastewater data from 14.5 million people shows.

ACIC chief executive Heather Cook said in April a record 26.8 tonnes of methylamphetamine, cocaine, heroin and MDMA was consumed between August 2024 and 2025, marking a 21 per cent annual increase and street value of $14.3 billion.

The 2026 UN World Drug Report showed most globally trafficked cocaine flowing into Australia originated in the Americas and Europe, while methamphetamine mostly comes from South-East Asia.

Between 2007 and 2023, 10.60 to 12.20 per cent of Australians used drugs, while 4.2 per cent of people in Australia and New Zealand aged 15 to 64 used cocaine in 2024, the UN says.

The magnitude of the drugs challenge in Colombia is immense.

Colombia has coca plantations, used in the creation of cocaine, spanning an area greater than the Australian Capital Territory. (Reuters: Daniel Becerril)

Colombia accounted for 966 tonnes of cocaine made in 2024, representing 40 per cent of the world's total supply, from coca bushes spanning at least 261,000 hectares of land, or more than the entire area of the Australian Capital Territory.

Colombian authorities also detected gangs using unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) as early as 2017 to fly as much as 130 kilograms of cocaine up to 100 kilometres.

Between 1993 and 2023, at least 228 drug-laden semi-submersible vessels were seized by Colombian authorities, the UN says.

In 2024, Colombia accounted for at least 40 per cent of the world's total supply of cocaine. (Reuters: Luisa Gonzalez)

Abelardo de la Espriella was this month sworn in as Colombia's president after an election campaign that promised a harsh crackdown on crime and drug trafficking, with the vocal backing of US President Donald Trump.

UNSW Latin America expert Anthea McCarthy-Jones said the threat posed to Australia by cocaine from Colombia was "a long-standing issue" that has grown "exponentially".

"We have quite an affluent population who pays some of the highest prices in the world for illicit drugs," she told the ABC.

"That's a problem that can't easily be fixed … it's also a problem we can't arrest our way out of."

Abelardo de la Espriella came to power promising to crack down on drug crime and with a strong endorsement from Donald Trump. (Reuters: Sergio Acero)

Dr McCarthy-Jones said the magnitude of the threat justified the AFP seeking to do more, but making a difference could be difficult because of the sophistication of Latin American narco-gangs.

"There's so much brokerage between different networks that make this complex mosaic as difficult to disrupt as it currently is," she said.

"The fact that there seems to be an increased interest and activity around developing [and] strengthening existing relationships with key stakeholders in this whole issue is a really good step," she said.

"It's something that will set Australia up to be in a better position to confront these types of challenges."

World.title: Driver, passenger trapped as bus crashes into train bridge
World.content:
Emergency crews have worked for more than an hour to free a bus driver who became trapped after the Adelaide Metro passenger service struck a concrete rail bridge support pylon at Port Adelaide.

The crash occurred shortly before 9am on Commercial Road, near Baynes Place.

The driver, a 37-year-old Kensington Park man, was taken to hospital in a serious but stable condition, while a 28-year-old female passenger was taken to hospital with non-life threatening injuries. Three other passengers were treated at the scene, SA Police said.

Clinton Daniels, from the SA Ambulance Service Special Operation Team, said the driver required "extensive treatment" at the scene, including blood transfusions, before he was taken to the Royal Adelaide Hospital.

"Both have significant injuries from the impact of the bus and the crumpling of the bus onto the patient themselves," he said.

"The driver was extensively trapped through being compressed through his lower limbs."

Clinton Daniels says the driver was trapped by his lower limbs. (ABC News)

He praised the efforts of the Metropolitan Fire Service (MFS) firefighters and the "technically difficult job" they undertook to free the driver and passenger.

MFS commander Simon Kirkmoe said the driver and passenger had been trapped on board by their lower limbs, while about four other passengers were able to get off the bus unassisted.

He said the MFS worked for about half an hour to remove the passenger from the bus, while the driver took "over an hour" to free.

“The driver presented more of a complex removal," Mr Kirkmoe said.

"We had to use some techniques to drag the bus backwards off the pylon to then use some hand tools and hydraulic tools to actually remove the steering column in the front off the bus off of those lower limbs to enable them to be removed."

Simon Kirkmoe says removing the driver was a "complex" task. (ABC News)

He said 19 firefighters were involved in the rescue, including a specialist technical rescue team.

“There is a lot of damage to the front of the bus and it would be one of the more significant accidents we’ve been to with busses in recent times," Mr Kirkmoe said.

In a statement, a Department for Infrastructure and Transport spokesperson said train services between Alberton and Outer Harbor were temporarily suspended and replaced with substitute buses, pending a safety inspection which had now been completed.

The train service has since resumed.

The crash occurred shortly before 9am today. (ABC News: Isabella Carbone)

SA Police said investigations into the crash were continuing, while road closures around the scene would remain in place until the scene was cleared.

World.title: Hastie warns Zempilas against waving 'white flag' in by-election
World.content:
Prominent WA federal Liberal MP Andrew Hastie has intensified his criticism of state opposition leader Basil Zempilas's strategy for Saturday's Secret Harbour by-election, suggesting he is putting up the white flag in the same way the Liberals disastrously admitted defeat before the 2021 state election.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who is in Perth but did not campaign in Secret Harbour, seized on the deepening rift between the Liberals, saying they were "running dead" in Secret Harbour and had basically folded into One Nation.

Speaking on the ABC's 7.30, Mr Hastie said it was clear, from what Labor and the Liberals told him, that One Nation candidate Luke Herdegen was ahead in the by-election, and the major parties needed to do much better in responding to the concerns of people in outer-metropolitan areas.

Luke Herdegen pictured with One Nation leader Pauline Hanson. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Mr Hastie said he disagreed with the premise, put forward repeatedly by Mr Zempilas, that a Labor loss in Secret Harbour would be a victory for the Liberals, even if they did not win.

"This is a state election contested on state issues, and I don't accept this idea that a win for One Nation is a win for the Liberal Party," Mr Hastie said.

"We're fighting for our lives, and we should be fighting for every single vote in Secret Harbour.

"Basil Zempilas said that a win for One Nation would be an opportunity. I don't see that at all."

'Voters sense weakness'

Mr Hastie then referenced the comments by former state Liberal leader Zak Kirkup three weeks before the 2021 state election, where the opposition was decimated, that he did not expect to win.

Loading TikTok content

"The lesson from the 2021 state election is you don't wave the white flag," Mr Hastie said.

"Voters sense weakness and they'll go to the strong horse if you signal weakness."

He said he did not agree with the state Liberals' political strategy in Secret Harbour and the message should be that they were fighting for every vote.

"I think we could have signalled to voters that we're fighting for them, we're fighting for a better deal for outer-metropolitan Western Australians," he said.

PM says Zempilas 'promoting' One Nation

The prime minister was interviewed on 102.5 ABC Perth this morning, when he continued the line of attack used by Premier Roger Cook to accuse the Liberals of giving up.

Anthony Albanese shares a laugh with WA Premier Roger Cook in Perth this morning. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"The Libs are running dead in Secret Harbour. Let's get real here," Mr Albanese said.

Mr Zempilas yesterday mocked Mr Albanese for not going to Secret Harbour, with a Where's Wally-type sign which said: "Where's Albo?"

"Who is the state Liberal leader?" the prime minister asked in response.

"He's not even trying to run the by-election. He's out there promoting another political party.

"I want my party to win. Does Basil? I don't think so."

The prime minister defended his decision not to campaign in Secret Harbour for Labor candidate Georgia Tree, saying he never campaigned in by-elections.

Zempilas hits back

Mr Zempilas denied he was running dead in the by-election and took a shot at Mr Hastie.

"What I know is what we've done, and that is not the case," Mr Zempilas said.

"It seems odd that a talking point of Labor's would be re-used by somebody else.

" And that's really what this is because those lines don't match the reality. We have worked our backsides off down here. "

Asked if he and Mr Hastie were on the same team, Mr Zempilas said disagreements were part of politics and he was not bothered by it.

Basil Zempilas says the Liberal Party has not given up in Secret Harbour. (ABC News: Keane Bourke )

He also denounced as a "ridiculous claim" any suggestion he was running soft in the by-election because he did not want to offend Australia's richest person and One Nation backer Gina Rinehart.

"It is simply fanciful to suggest anything like that," he said.

World.title: Ralph Carr sentenced to six years in jail for rape
World.content:
Disgraced celebrity agent Ralph Carr has cried as a judge sentenced him to six years in prison after he was found guilty of raping a woman in an "appalling" attack.

Carr's last-ditch legal bid to halt his case was today denied by Judge Frank Gucciardo, ending his hopes to be released on bail ahead of an appeal.

The one-time manager of top Australian singers and Richmond AFL great Dustin Martin will have to serve a minimum of four years before becoming eligible for parole.

Carr faced the County Court via video link, sobbing, shaking his head and muttering to himself throughout the hearing.

"Your conduct was appalling," Judge Gucciardo said.

" Rape is a crime of violence. This was committed by you in an egregious breach of trust. "

Carr was found guilty by a jury of two counts of rape and one count of sexual assault, dating back to March 23, 2023.

Celebrity agent Ralph Carr was found guilty in July of raping a woman in 2023. (ABC News)

The woman had visited Carr's house to discuss a job opportunity, before the pair headed to the celebrity agent's friend's place to watch football.

A night of drinking and drug-taking followed, the trial heard, before Carr raped the woman when the pair returned to his West Melbourne home.

The attack lasted a matter of seconds, the woman testified, before she punched Carr in the face and called him "a f***ing rapist".

The woman said Carr later asked her to perform a sexual act on him. She contacted her mother, who then called the police.

In describing the offending, Judge Gucciardo said Carr had taken advantage of an intoxicated, vulnerable young woman who had repeatedly told Carr she did not want a sexual relationship.

Carr denied the allegations of sexual assault and rape and pleaded not guilty at his trial.

"You maintain your innocence of these offences and consequently there is no evidence of your remorse or contrition," Judge Gucciardo said.

Judge Frank Gucciardo said Ralph Carr took advantage of a vulnerable woman, and has shown no remorse. (ABC News)

Judge Gucciardo said he took into account the public nature of Carr's downfall since the verdict, his age, prior lack of criminal history and his mental health when setting the sentence.

'Jerry Maguire of football' in 23-hour lockdown

Carr, who is currently being held at the Melbourne Assessment Prison, will be relocated to the Hopkins Correctional Centre in Ararat.

He is currently classified as a "high-profile" prisoner and subjected to 23-hour lockdowns but those conditions were expected to ease upon relocation, a Corrections Victoria manager testified.

At the height of his career, Carr was an influential figure in the entertainment industry and was once married to singer Tina Arena before a bitter falling out.

AFL footballer Dustin Martin, who has ended their professional relationship, was among Ralph Carr's clients. (Supplied)

His company Ralph Carr Management worked with artists including Vanessa Amorosi, Kate Ceberano, Jon Stevens, Pseudo Echo and Deborah Conway.

On his website, which has since been stripped of all detail, Carr touted himself as the "Jerry Maguire of footy".

His sports management clients included ex-AFL star Dustin Martin, who has since severed ties with Carr.

In court last week, Carr's barrister Dermot Dann spoke of his client's "good character" and that he was responsible for launching many careers in the entertainment business.

However, prosecutors noted that only one person from the industry had written a character reference for him.

Other women have publicly spoken out about being bullied and sexually harassed by Carr at work, allegations he has denied and not been charged over.

After Carr was charged with raping the woman in 2023, a suppression order was granted on mental health grounds, barring the media from reporting his name in connection with the case.

The secrecy ended nearly three years later, when Carr was found guilty and abandoned an application to extend the order.

Carr described prison as "a living hell", Mr Dann said, while his psychiatrist said she feared he would not receive adequate treatment for his mental health problems in custody.

The rape case put the issue of suppression orders back under scrutiny in Victoria following a similar scenario that played out in the rape case of Tom Silvagni, the son of AFL great Stephen Silvagni.

Ralph Carr and secrecy in Victoria's courts are on the front page Much like the high-profile case of Tom Silvagni last year, Carr's legal quest to protect his name has put issues of open justice and suppression orders in Victoria back on the agenda.

The Labor state government and Liberal opposition have pledged to amend the Open Courts Act to limit suppression orders, but are yet to specify exactly how the legislation will change.

Carr's lawyers are expected to lodge legal documents with the Court of Appeal within the next two months.

It could take months before an appeal is heard.

They made a rare application to stay — or delay — the judge's sentence today on the grounds that the jury's verdict was wrong and because of Carr's mental health.

Judge Gucciardo rejected the application, saying the jury was capable of deciding whether the complainant in the case was a credible witness.

"The jury were entitled to accept her responses as truthful," he said.

World.title: Major NSW property developer enters administration
World.content:
Major Sydney residential developer Bathla Group has fallen into administration after months of mounting financial pressure.

Administrators from Teneo were appointed on Tuesday to its main corporate entity, Universal Property Group, as well as Raj & Jai Construction, a company linked to the Bathla Group, documents lodged with ASIC show.

Voluntary administration is when an independent administrator takes control of a company in financial trouble and assesses its future.

Creditors then generally decide whether the company can be restructured or should be wound up.

Do you know more? If you have more information about this article or any other tips, you can securely contact reporter Lin Lin at lin.lin@abc.net.au or linreporting@proton.me.

Bathla Group is a major developer of lower-cost homes, townhouses and apartments, particularly in Western Sydney suburbs such as Schofields, Marsden Park and Tallawong.

In an Instagram post, managing director Bhart Bhushan said the developer was dealing with a "perfect storm" of softening sales, tax change impacts and higher construction costs.

As at June 30 last year, Universal Property Group had $3.2 billion in liabilities, the majority of which was reportedly owed to private credit funds.

The collapse is likely to intensify scrutiny of Bathla's extensive use of private credit to finance its property developments as administrators begin assessing the financial position of the affected companies.

Loading Instagram content

Universal Property Group has a highly complex corporate structure. ASIC records showing it sits at the top of a network of hundreds of separate companies.

Many are numbered UPG entities that extend as high as UPG 460. Others operate under different company names.

ASIC records UPG as the ultimate holding company for many of these entities.

Buyers in limbo

Kate, who does not wish to use her real name, bought an off-the-plan freestanding house in Lochinvar, in regional New South Wales, for $709,990 in the middle of last year.

Documents seen by ABC News confirm the purchase.

Kate told ABC News that, as a renter, she had been relying on the property becoming her family home.

"I am very worried and just scared this could jeopardise the completion of the house," the single mother said.

Kate said Bathla employees had previously told her the house would be ready by June, then August, but that the expected completion had since been pushed back to the end of this year.

"I have been nervous for some time, to be honest, as there seems to be no-one there working on the property on many days," she said.

"It seems like a ghost town."

Kate said she had hoped the house would help provide security for her two young daughters.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Porepunkah victims Neal Thompson, Vadim de Waart-Hottart honoured in ceremony; US issues deadlines to countries to stop all financial dealings with Iran
World.content:
Corporate Travel Management said it has concluded negotiations with the UK government potentially concluding an overcharging scandal that has so far resulted in the firing of its chief executive and resignation of its founder.

In April, the company said it planned to reverse revenues of up to £118 million ($224.8 million) in respect to fiscal year 2025 and prior years “as result of certain issues identified in the UK business”.

On Friday, it said it had received binding offers from key impacted UK customers that collectively account for £102 million (or 86 per cent) of a total estimated liability of £118 million.

Those offers will require Corporate Travel Management to refund a total of £87 million to the relevant customers, £11 million of which has already been paid.

“Reaching agreements with impacted UK customers representing 86 per cent of the total estimated liability is a major milestone for CTM and reflects our commitment to doing the right thing by customers,” said Ana Pedersen managing director and group CEO.

“These outcomes are the result of months of constructive engagement between CTM, its advisers and affected customers, whose cooperation and support throughout this process has been greatly appreciated.”

Shares in the Australian company have been in a trading halt for a year after it revealed overcharging of the UK government in 2025. The company fired its European and UK chief executive in December. Founder and managing director Jamie Pherous resigned in February.

World.title: ‘Beggars belief’: The proposed industrial port within WA’s newest marine park
World.content:
NationalWANingaloo Reef ‘Beggars belief’: The proposed industrial port within WA’s newest marine park Holly Thompson August 25, 2026 — 1:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A proposal for a major industrial port just 10 kilometres south of Exmouth goes against government plans to transform the region into Western Australia’s newest marine park, conservationists argue. As public comment opens in the state environment watchdog’s assessment of the Gascoyne Gateway Marine Complex proposal, which has been afoot since 2020, a campaign against the project is in full swing over concerns the plans would require extensive dredging and see shipping lanes cut through a critical humpback whale resting and nursing ground. A map of the Exmouth Gulf. Two other proposals within the Exmouth Gulf – the Subsea 7 oil and gas pipeline and a proposed industrial salt project – have both been withdrawn. Ningaloo was designated as a World Heritage area in 2011, however the boundaries of that designation do not include the Exmouth Gulf.



The proposed port would also be located next to Qualing Pool, a rare freshwater oasis that the state government has earmarked as a class A nature reserve, and which the Environmental Protection Authority has previously urged a higher level of protection for. The port would be used by large vessels including fuel tankers, cargo ships, cruise liners and other heavy shipping into the region. The proposal opened for public comment through the EPA on Monday. Protect Ningaloo and the Australian Marine Conservation Society have argued the port would be entirely incompatible with a marine park in the area. The region is home to threatened and listed species, including dugongs, turtles, manta rays, sea snakes and dolphins, as well as corals, seagrass meadows, and sponge gardens.



Since plans were first announced in 2020, Protect Ningaloo said that more than 20,000 emails had been sent to current and past WA environment ministers urging them to reject the proposal. AMCS-Protect Ningaloo is campaigning to stop the port that would attract shipping through a critical humpback whale resting and nursing ground. Brooke Pyke Australian Marine Conservation Society chief executive and Protect Ningaloo director Paul Gamblin said the industrial port and dredging proposal was “completely incompatible with the environmentally fragile Exmouth Gulf, and would change this marine wonder forever”. “An industrial port proposal, jutting nearly a kilometre into Exmouth Gulf and dredging of more than a million cubic metres of the seafloor in one of the world’s most important whale nursing grounds beggars belief,” he said. “People know that Exmouth Gulf obviously is no place for a port – its future is one of conservation and sustainable, light-touch economic activity, not industrialisation.



“Both the WA and federal governments have signalled that they are committed to protecting Exmouth Gulf so it’s time they made it clear that the future of this natural wonder is economic activity that treads lightly.” Cape Conservation Group chair Denise Fitch said Ningaloo was already under pressure from climate change. “We’ve recently experienced unprecedented coral bleaching and seagrass damage from marine heatwaves, and further destruction from Cyclone Narelle,” she said. “Now is not the moment to be adding industrial stressors to this fragile ecosystem and this is no place for an industrial port.” EPA Chair Darren Walsh said the public review marked a significant step in the assessment of the proposal.



“It has been some time since the last opportunity for public feedback on this project,” he said. Another perspective Marine life ‘Globally significant’ Exmouth Gulf to be transformed into marine park “The proponent has amended the proposal under assessment twice since the scoping stage, so this review provides specific details and the anticipated environmental outcomes related to all environmental factors under consideration by the EPA.” Walsh advised submitters to focus on the areas of key concern rather than trying to digest and scrutinise every aspect of the proposal. “The environmental review document and appendices that we have published today total more than 6000 pages,” he said.



“This is a complex proposal with multiple environmental factors and diverse values. Related Article Ningaloo Reef ‘You realise your children are probably never going to see Ningaloo the way you saw it’ “It is also important to note that this public review is not about the number of submissions, rather it seeks facts and information to genuinely inform the EPA’s environmental impact assessment. “Targeted community and stakeholder consultation will form an important part of EPA assessment considerations.” After the consultation closes on November 16, the EPA will consider submissions and the proponent’s responses to those submissions.



It will then complete its assessment and publish its recommendations. The environment minister will make the final decision on the proposal.

World.title: From Pokemon cards to cat videos: How to turn side hustles into six figures
World.content:
MoneyInvestingSide hustle From Pokemon cards to cat videos: How to turn side hustles into six figures Bernadette Schwerdt August 25, 2026 — 1:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

With the cost of living mounting and household budgets under pressure, it’s no surprise that more Australians are looking for ways to generate extra income. The good news? You don’t need a huge amount of capital, a business degree or a fancy office to get started. In fact, many of the most successful online businesses began as off-the-cuff experiments, one-off endeavours or personal passion projects. Having interviewed more than 40 of Australia’s top online entrepreneurs, I’ve discovered that there are a few secrets to turning side hustles into successful online businesses. MasterChef guest judge Kirsten Tibballs left school at 15 to complete a baking apprenticeship. Channel 10 Test before you invest If you’ve watched MasterChef, you’ll know Kirsten Tibballs. She’s a regular guest judge, has over a million followers and her own TV show dedicated to all things chocolate. What most people don’t know is how she got started.



She left school at 15 to complete a baking apprenticeship. The hours were brutal – 2am to 5pm – but she loved it. Years later, after competing internationally, she was invited to run a chocolate-making workshop in a supplier’s warehouse. Editor's pick Analysis

Side hustle Starting a side hustle? Here’s how to do the job right This was a weekend side hustle alongside her day job writing recipes for a leading chocolate brand. She took class bookings via fax, set up a trestle table and got started. The course sold out, as did the next and the one after that. Demand grew so quickly, she launched her own cooking school. To scale, she filmed her classes and put the videos online. Her students wanted to buy the equipment she used, so she uploaded her kitchen utensils to the website and hyperlinked them to her recipes. Today, she has more than 20,000 members in her online community, plus a global speaking career, brand partnerships, cookbooks and a retail distribution business.



Play the long game Social media was the perfect place for actor Adele Samus to launch her side hustle. By day, she worked in a fashion store. By night, she created comedic social media content based on the conversations she overheard from customers. Her goal was to land acting work. To achieve that, she first needed to build an audience, so she wrote her own scripts, acted out all the parts, and edited everything herself. After several years of consistent effort, she built a loyal following, found an agent, secured a host of brand deals and appeared as a stunt woman in Ryan Gosling’s film The Fall Guy. Her success was made possible because she committed to posting even when no one was watching, and to playing the long game. Acting is still a side hustle, but it’s attracting deals that help pay the rent and support her while she builds her personal brand.



Find your passion When it comes to building a side hustle, it helps to genuinely care about what you’re promoting. If you’re only showing up to sell something, people can spot the insincerity. Jenny Fisher (@FosterJen2072) is a perfect example. Jenny Fisher has rescued seven cats that she believes might not have survived in Hornsby. Edwina Pickles With 11 cats and four dogs, it’s fair to say she loves animals. What started as a personal Instagram account for sharing cat videos with family and friends soon evolved into something much bigger. Driven by her passion for rescuing cats and finding them loving homes, Jenny began showcasing the foster cat sanctuary she had built in her backyard. Complete with climbing towers, rope bridges, hammocks, tunnels and outdoor runs, it was the Taj Mahal for cats.



When she started sharing her videos with fellow cat lovers, her audience exploded, and within six months, had attracted 44,000 followers. Since then, she’s received collaboration opportunities from cat food, litter and pet accessory brands, along with an invitation to appear on the cover of a cat magazine. Jenny’s success came from building a community around a genuine passion. The audience came first, and the commercial opportunities followed soon after. Sell what you love You don’t have to go big to be successful. Dylan Schwerdt works in a bank by day but trades Pokemon cards by night. He buys the cards in the US, sells them in Australia and pockets the price difference. Some people call this arbitrage. He calls it “cardbitrage”. He spotted the opportunity on a trip to New Orleans, where he saw the cards in a gaming shop selling for 50 per cent less than in Australia. Months later, stuck at home with a broken arm, he set up a test.



He bought a few cards and listed them on eBay. He didn’t have a website, a brand or any proof of demand, but people could see what a good deal they were getting and piled in. That early success gave Dylan the motivation to keep going. Graded Pokemon cards can fetch up to tens of thousands of dollars in online markets. Joe Armao He dug out the thousands of cards he had lying around the house from childhood, catalogued them and listed them on eBay and Instagram, including running live online auctions and awarding the cards to the highest bidders. He works about 10 hours a week on his side hustle, makes over $100,000 a year, and now spends his annual leave travelling to Pokemon conferences around the world sourcing new stock. He loved Pokemon as a kid and still does. The difference is he’s now getting paid for it. “I mostly do it while I’m watching TV,” he says.



If you’re thinking about launching a side hustle, don’t overthink it. Start small, see what happens and pay attention to what people respond to. The market will tell you what to do next. Bernadette Schwerdt, author of Secrets of the New Online Entrepreneurs, is the founder of the Australian School of Copywriting, a TEDx speaker, and an award-winning author and ghostwriter for Australia’s leading CEOs and entrepreneurs. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: The Broncos ruled Adam Reynolds out of his own farewell. It hasn’t gone down well
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 The Broncos ruled Adam Reynolds out of his own farewell. It hasn’t gone down well Christian Nicolussi August 25, 2026 — 1:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Broncos teammates and rival players have criticised Brisbane coach Michael Maguire’s decision to deny skipper Adam Reynolds a Suncorp Stadium farewell. Reynolds confirmed on Monday he had played his last NRL game. The 36-year-old had been battling a calf injury, but completed a vital training session on Monday and was keen to play in Thursday night’s match against Melbourne. Loading However, Maguire and Broncos medical staff were concerned at the prospect of him breaking down again and ruled him out. “I got through training, I felt pretty good, but after talking with ‘Madge’ and the medical staff, they weren’t keen to see me go out there and finish with another potential injury, then go out like that,” Reynolds told this masthead late on Monday.



“They’ve worked with me behind the scenes for years. They know me better than myself. They didn’t want me being injured to be last image fans remembered me by.” The decision to deny Reynolds a final appearance in front of the fans who watched him lift the premiership trophy last October has not gone down well with supporters or teammates. It has thrust the spotlight back on Maguire and his relationship with the playing group. Adam Reynolds led Brisbane to a premiership in 2025. Getty Images Maguire’s future has been under the microscope since Payne Haas announced he was quitting the club at the start of the year to join South Sydney. Missing the finals has heaped more pressure on Maguire, while the decision to keep Reynolds on ice for a game that has no bearings on the finals is set to ensure the club remains in the headlines for the wrong reasons.



Reynolds’ comments on Monday did not sit well with the club, and the halfback is expected to clarify his position when he fronts the media on Tuesday afternoon. Friend and former teammate Cody Walker, who was one of several South Sydney players who offered to take a pay cut to keep Reynolds at his junior club in 2021, said on Tuesday: “I’m really disappointed for him. I just thought he deserved the opportunity to go out on his own terms, a put the jersey on one last time in his last home game. Cody Walker and Adam Reynolds both playing for the Rabbitohs in 2019. NRL Photos “He’s been a great servant of our game, in particular our club and the Brisbane Broncos. He’s had success at both clubs. Given what he’s achieved … he thoroughly deserves to go out on his terms. “It was tough watching him do a TV interview on Monday night. You could see he was choking up at the end of it. I feel for my little mate who isn’t able to get the send-off he thoroughly deserves.”



Related Article NRL 2026 NRL alters rules to allow Jai Arrow to return for South Sydney Broncos playmaker Ben Hunt told 4BC Radio on Tuesday morning: “We were excited to have one of the best players to play our game come back and our captain and play his final game at Suncorp. “He’s the little competitor he is. He wanted to get out there and from what I’m gauging most of the players are pretty disappointed, too. We thought he deserved that send-off.” Gorden Tallis, who has been critical of Reynolds in the past, said on NRL 360: “If it was my decision, Adam Reynolds would wear that jersey and go out there and say goodbye to the Brisbane fans. You think you would give him a farewell.” Reynolds finishes with 323 NRL games, including premierships at Souths and the Broncos in 2014 and 2025, as well as grand final defeats in 2021 with the Rabbitohs, and 2023 with Brisbane. Updated SportAFLAFL off-field behaviour Pictures emerge of Richmond’s Mad Monday after footage causes fresh headache for AFL Sam McClure Updated August 25, 2026 — 1:34pm ,first published August 25, 2026 — 9:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Richmond are investigating the conduct of their players after vision emerged from the club’s Mad Monday celebrations potentially appearing to mock the scandal engulfing the Sydney Swans. Competition sources have confirmed to this masthead that the Tigers are examining footage taken at the Garfield Hotel in Gippsland on Monday, which shows several Richmond players drinking and striking one another with belts. The hotel issued a staunch defence of the players and said the matter had been “blown out of proportion”. Photos taken on Monday appear to show pints of beer lined up on a ledge, a player climbing on a teammate’s shoulders and reaching onto a roof covering, and two players outside the venue appearing to urinate against a fence.



Richmond players celebrate Mad Monday. MEDIA-MODE.COM Five Sydney players – Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon – have been suspended for breaching club standards, and a separate police investigation into an allegation of sexual assault at the hotel continues. A scene from Richmond’s Mad Monday celebrations at the Garfield Hotel. MEDIA-MODE.COM No charges have been laid and this masthead is not suggesting any wrongdoing on the part of the five suspended players. In one piece of vision of the Tigers, young midfielder Josh Smillie appears to pull down his pants and feign shock as he is repeatedly struck on the backside by a teammate.



He appears to be spanked three times in the video and then after a fourth slap, reacts differently – which is possibly a recreation of allegations published by the Herald Sun, that one woman had claimed she was slapped on the buttocks four times instead of the three slaps that had been agreed. Richmond players outside the venue in Garfield. MEDIA-MODE.COM Another clip shows midfielder Tim Taranto using a belt to strike a shirtless teammate. The footage emerged just a week after five Sydney players were suspended for the remainder of the season for breaches of club standards following an incident at the team’s Melbourne hotel. Victoria Police continues to investigate an allegation of sexual assault arising from that night. No charges have been laid and there is no suggestion of wrongdoing by the five suspended Sydney players.



Richmond and the AFL have been contacted for comment. The footage of the Tigers’ Mad Monday celebration prompted Labor MP Dan Repacholi to criticise the behaviour. “Right now we need good blokes out there having the conversations around this and calling this out for what it is because this is unacceptable, and we need to make sure we do better,” he said. The Tigers’ season finished on Saturday after their loss to Geelong.



A statement was released on the hotel’s social media accounts on Monday, defending the players. “We hosted the Richmond Football Club at our venue today, and we could not speak more highly of the way they conducted themselves. For such a young group, they were extremely respectful and a fun group of boys to deal with,” the statement read. “They enjoyed a few quiet beers to unwind after a long season, and we see nothing wrong with that. They had booked out the venue for the afternoon, so they were the only patrons on site. They enjoyed their afternoon and moved on. “In our view, this has been blown out of proportion. Two members of the media were waiting on their arrival this morning and remained on site filming in the hope of capturing a misstep, which we consider disappointing.”

World.title: ‘I didn’t earn this’: The silent shame of inheriting family wealth
World.content:
MoneySavingInheritance Opinion ‘I didn’t earn this’: The silent shame of inheriting family wealth Paridhi Jain Money contributor August 25, 2026 — 1:16pm

August 25, 2026 — 1:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There’s a conversation I have with people privately that rarely reaches mainstream discourse – the challenges that come with receiving significant financial advantages. Your parents did well, and you reaped some of the rewards. Maybe you grew up with an awareness that your family was considerably wealthier than others. Maybe you have received – or know you’re due to receive – significant financial support (e.g. help buying a home, a significant inheritance, large cash gifts and so on). We have assumptions about what it means to have wealth, and we judge others (and ourselves) by them. Simon Letch You’re aware of your privilege and, as nice as it is, it also feels uncomfortable. You may feel a bit guilty, or embarrassed. You may feel judged – like people think you had it easy, you didn’t work for your successes, or didn’t earn it. But it’s difficult to talk about, for obvious reasons. It’s not the kind of problem that garners much sympathy. For most, it would be a nice problem to have. Nevertheless, it does come with its own set of unique challenges. Today, I’m sharing some of those challenges, and some of what I’ve found helpful in working through them with clients.



Proving or over-compensating How this shows up: You work extra hard to “become something” – not because it brings you joy, meaning, or fulfillment, but because you feel the need to prove yourself. As counter-intuitive as it might be, accepting your privilege might be the real road to freedom. Maybe you want to show – to yourself or others – that you’re more than just your privilege. Perhaps you think this is how you’ll earn respect. Maybe you feel a pressure to “not waste” your good fortune. Why this can be a problem: Proving and over-compensating can be exhausting. You aren’t really living life for you – you’re living the life you think you need to live, to prove something.



This can also rob you of a lot of enjoyment. Instead of enjoying the journey, you’re attached to a specific outcome because of what you think that outcome will prove. “Once I hit $X net-worth or Y milestone, then I will finally feel Z” (worthy, successful, admired, respected, etc). Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert Is being frugal really such a bad thing? Paridhi Jain Money contributor However, you can’t control what people think. No matter what you achieve, or how hard you try to prove something – “they” (whoever you’re trying to prove to) may never change what they think of you. You could spend your whole life attempting to prove something, to someone who may not need, want or accept your proof in the end. How to start shifting this: As counter-intuitive as it might be, accepting your privilege might be the real road to freedom. The freedom to fully own your own life – without guilt or shame. The freedom to cultivate and pursue your own unique individual path – not just live in the shadow of expectation. The freedom to pursue success – not because you have something to prove, but because it’s what makes you feel the most alive.



Holding back out of fear How this shows up: You hold yourself back from little luxuries you could easily afford – not because it’s an intentional choice in alignment with your values, but because on some level you’re scared of how you might be judged or perceived for making those choices. You’re worried about standing out, attracting attention, looking fancy or extravagant. It feels safer to stay under the radar – to stay in sync with those around you. Why this can be a problem: The point here isn’t to spend money just because you have it, or to start being loud and proud about your financial position. The question is – what is the real underlying driver behind your choices? Do you already feel like you’re living your life fully – or are you restricting your experience of life out of fear? Fear of what others might say or think, fear of being judged, fear of breaking out of your comfort zone? If it’s the latter, then you are limiting your ability to enjoy and experience your own life more fully.



How to start shifting this: Start by looking at your fears – the fear of what other people might say, think or do; your fear of judgment, criticism, or being ostracised. Then, start getting clear on what this is costing you. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I’m 64 and I just inherited $700,000. What should I do with it? Paul Benson Money contributor How much are you holding yourself back because of these fears? What opportunities, choices, or goals have you talked yourself out of? What would your life look like if your decisions weren’t being quietly shaped by your fears of what others might think? Many of the challenges that come with receiving significant financial advantages don’t really arise from having money, but from the meaning we (and others) attach to it. We have assumptions about what it means to have wealth, and we judge others (and ourselves) by them. So, what are the underlying beliefs you have about what it means to have wealth? And are those beliefs serving you – or holding you back from enjoying a fuller, freer experience of life?

Mark McVeigh has left his job as Sydney assistant coach to take the senior job at Essendon, the club he played for. Corporate Travel Management said it has concluded negotiations with the UK government potentially concluding an overcharging scandal that has so far resulted in the firing of its chief executive and resignation of its founder.

In April, the company said it planned to reverse revenues of up to £118 million ($224.8 million) in respect to fiscal year 2025 and prior years “as result of certain issues identified in the UK business”.

On Friday, it said it had received binding offers from key impacted UK customers that collectively account for £102 million (or 86 per cent) of a total estimated liability of £118 million.

Those offers will require Corporate Travel Management to refund a total of £87 million to the relevant customers, £11 million of which has already been paid.

“Reaching agreements with impacted UK customers representing 86 per cent of the total estimated liability is a major milestone for CTM and reflects our commitment to doing the right thing by customers,” said Ana Pedersen managing director and group CEO.

“These outcomes are the result of months of constructive engagement between CTM, its advisers and affected customers, whose cooperation and support throughout this process has been greatly appreciated.”

Shares in the Australian company have been in a trading halt for a year after it revealed overcharging of the UK government in 2025. The company fired its European and UK chief executive in December. Founder and managing director Jamie Pherous resigned in February.

World.title: ‘Beggars belief’: The proposed industrial port within WA’s newest marine park
World.content:
NationalWANingaloo Reef ‘Beggars belief’: The proposed industrial port within WA’s newest marine park Holly Thompson August 25, 2026 — 1:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A proposal for a major industrial port just 10 kilometres south of Exmouth goes against government plans to transform the region into Western Australia’s newest marine park, conservationists argue. As public comment opens in the state environment watchdog’s assessment of the Gascoyne Gateway Marine Complex proposal, which has been afoot since 2020, a campaign against the project is in full swing over concerns the plans would require extensive dredging and see shipping lanes cut through a critical humpback whale resting and nursing ground. A map of the Exmouth Gulf. Two other proposals within the Exmouth Gulf – the Subsea 7 oil and gas pipeline and a proposed industrial salt project – have both been withdrawn. Ningaloo was designated as a World Heritage area in 2011, however the boundaries of that designation do not include the Exmouth Gulf.



The proposed port would also be located next to Qualing Pool, a rare freshwater oasis that the state government has earmarked as a class A nature reserve, and which the Environmental Protection Authority has previously urged a higher level of protection for. The port would be used by large vessels including fuel tankers, cargo ships, cruise liners and other heavy shipping into the region. The proposal opened for public comment through the EPA on Monday. Protect Ningaloo and the Australian Marine Conservation Society have argued the port would be entirely incompatible with a marine park in the area. The region is home to threatened and listed species, including dugongs, turtles, manta rays, sea snakes and dolphins, as well as corals, seagrass meadows, and sponge gardens.



Since plans were first announced in 2020, Protect Ningaloo said that more than 20,000 emails had been sent to current and past WA environment ministers urging them to reject the proposal. AMCS-Protect Ningaloo is campaigning to stop the port that would attract shipping through a critical humpback whale resting and nursing ground. Brooke Pyke Australian Marine Conservation Society chief executive and Protect Ningaloo director Paul Gamblin said the industrial port and dredging proposal was “completely incompatible with the environmentally fragile Exmouth Gulf, and would change this marine wonder forever”. “An industrial port proposal, jutting nearly a kilometre into Exmouth Gulf and dredging of more than a million cubic metres of the seafloor in one of the world’s most important whale nursing grounds beggars belief,” he said. “People know that Exmouth Gulf obviously is no place for a port – its future is one of conservation and sustainable, light-touch economic activity, not industrialisation.



“Both the WA and federal governments have signalled that they are committed to protecting Exmouth Gulf so it’s time they made it clear that the future of this natural wonder is economic activity that treads lightly.” Cape Conservation Group chair Denise Fitch said Ningaloo was already under pressure from climate change. “We’ve recently experienced unprecedented coral bleaching and seagrass damage from marine heatwaves, and further destruction from Cyclone Narelle,” she said. “Now is not the moment to be adding industrial stressors to this fragile ecosystem and this is no place for an industrial port.” EPA Chair Darren Walsh said the public review marked a significant step in the assessment of the proposal.



“It has been some time since the last opportunity for public feedback on this project,” he said. Another perspective Marine life ‘Globally significant’ Exmouth Gulf to be transformed into marine park “The proponent has amended the proposal under assessment twice since the scoping stage, so this review provides specific details and the anticipated environmental outcomes related to all environmental factors under consideration by the EPA.” Walsh advised submitters to focus on the areas of key concern rather than trying to digest and scrutinise every aspect of the proposal. “The environmental review document and appendices that we have published today total more than 6000 pages,” he said.



“This is a complex proposal with multiple environmental factors and diverse values. Related Article Ningaloo Reef ‘You realise your children are probably never going to see Ningaloo the way you saw it’ “It is also important to note that this public review is not about the number of submissions, rather it seeks facts and information to genuinely inform the EPA’s environmental impact assessment. “Targeted community and stakeholder consultation will form an important part of EPA assessment considerations.” After the consultation closes on November 16, the EPA will consider submissions and the proponent’s responses to those submissions.



It will then complete its assessment and publish its recommendations. The environment minister will make the final decision on the proposal.

World.title: From Pokemon cards to cat videos: How to turn side hustles into six figures
World.content:
MoneyInvestingSide hustle From Pokemon cards to cat videos: How to turn side hustles into six figures Bernadette Schwerdt August 25, 2026 — 1:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

With the cost of living mounting and household budgets under pressure, it’s no surprise that more Australians are looking for ways to generate extra income. The good news? You don’t need a huge amount of capital, a business degree or a fancy office to get started. In fact, many of the most successful online businesses began as off-the-cuff experiments, one-off endeavours or personal passion projects. Having interviewed more than 40 of Australia’s top online entrepreneurs, I’ve discovered that there are a few secrets to turning side hustles into successful online businesses. MasterChef guest judge Kirsten Tibballs left school at 15 to complete a baking apprenticeship. Channel 10 Test before you invest If you’ve watched MasterChef, you’ll know Kirsten Tibballs. She’s a regular guest judge, has over a million followers and her own TV show dedicated to all things chocolate. What most people don’t know is how she got started.



She left school at 15 to complete a baking apprenticeship. The hours were brutal – 2am to 5pm – but she loved it. Years later, after competing internationally, she was invited to run a chocolate-making workshop in a supplier’s warehouse. Editor's pick Analysis

Side hustle Starting a side hustle? Here’s how to do the job right This was a weekend side hustle alongside her day job writing recipes for a leading chocolate brand. She took class bookings via fax, set up a trestle table and got started. The course sold out, as did the next and the one after that. Demand grew so quickly, she launched her own cooking school. To scale, she filmed her classes and put the videos online. Her students wanted to buy the equipment she used, so she uploaded her kitchen utensils to the website and hyperlinked them to her recipes. Today, she has more than 20,000 members in her online community, plus a global speaking career, brand partnerships, cookbooks and a retail distribution business.



Play the long game Social media was the perfect place for actor Adele Samus to launch her side hustle. By day, she worked in a fashion store. By night, she created comedic social media content based on the conversations she overheard from customers. Her goal was to land acting work. To achieve that, she first needed to build an audience, so she wrote her own scripts, acted out all the parts, and edited everything herself. After several years of consistent effort, she built a loyal following, found an agent, secured a host of brand deals and appeared as a stunt woman in Ryan Gosling’s film The Fall Guy. Her success was made possible because she committed to posting even when no one was watching, and to playing the long game. Acting is still a side hustle, but it’s attracting deals that help pay the rent and support her while she builds her personal brand.



Find your passion When it comes to building a side hustle, it helps to genuinely care about what you’re promoting. If you’re only showing up to sell something, people can spot the insincerity. Jenny Fisher (@FosterJen2072) is a perfect example. Jenny Fisher has rescued seven cats that she believes might not have survived in Hornsby. Edwina Pickles With 11 cats and four dogs, it’s fair to say she loves animals. What started as a personal Instagram account for sharing cat videos with family and friends soon evolved into something much bigger. Driven by her passion for rescuing cats and finding them loving homes, Jenny began showcasing the foster cat sanctuary she had built in her backyard. Complete with climbing towers, rope bridges, hammocks, tunnels and outdoor runs, it was the Taj Mahal for cats.



When she started sharing her videos with fellow cat lovers, her audience exploded, and within six months, had attracted 44,000 followers. Since then, she’s received collaboration opportunities from cat food, litter and pet accessory brands, along with an invitation to appear on the cover of a cat magazine. Jenny’s success came from building a community around a genuine passion. The audience came first, and the commercial opportunities followed soon after. Sell what you love You don’t have to go big to be successful. Dylan Schwerdt works in a bank by day but trades Pokemon cards by night. He buys the cards in the US, sells them in Australia and pockets the price difference. Some people call this arbitrage. He calls it “cardbitrage”. He spotted the opportunity on a trip to New Orleans, where he saw the cards in a gaming shop selling for 50 per cent less than in Australia. Months later, stuck at home with a broken arm, he set up a test.



He bought a few cards and listed them on eBay. He didn’t have a website, a brand or any proof of demand, but people could see what a good deal they were getting and piled in. That early success gave Dylan the motivation to keep going. Graded Pokemon cards can fetch up to tens of thousands of dollars in online markets. Joe Armao He dug out the thousands of cards he had lying around the house from childhood, catalogued them and listed them on eBay and Instagram, including running live online auctions and awarding the cards to the highest bidders. He works about 10 hours a week on his side hustle, makes over $100,000 a year, and now spends his annual leave travelling to Pokemon conferences around the world sourcing new stock. He loved Pokemon as a kid and still does. The difference is he’s now getting paid for it. “I mostly do it while I’m watching TV,” he says.



If you’re thinking about launching a side hustle, don’t overthink it. Start small, see what happens and pay attention to what people respond to. The market will tell you what to do next. The footage emerged just a week after five Sydney players were suspended for the remainder of the season for breaches of club standards following an incident at the team’s Melbourne hotel. Victoria Police continues to investigate an allegation of sexual assault arising from that night. No charges have been laid and there is no suggestion of wrongdoing by the five suspended Sydney players.



Richmond and the AFL have been contacted for comment. The footage of the Tigers’ Mad Monday celebration prompted Labor MP Dan Repacholi to criticise the behaviour. “Right now we need good blokes out there having the conversations around this and calling this out for what it is because this is unacceptable, and we need to make sure we do better,” he said. The Tigers’ season finished on Saturday after their loss to Geelong.



A statement was released on the hotel’s social media accounts on Monday, defending the players. “We hosted the Richmond Football Club at our venue today, and we could not speak more highly of the way they conducted themselves. For such a young group, they were extremely respectful and a fun group of boys to deal with,” the statement read. “They enjoyed a few quiet beers to unwind after a long season, and we see nothing wrong with that. They had booked out the venue for the afternoon, so they were the only patrons on site. They enjoyed their afternoon and moved on. “In our view, this has been blown out of proportion. Two members of the media were waiting on their arrival this morning and remained on site filming in the hope of capturing a misstep, which we consider disappointing.”
