World.title: ‘I didn’t earn this’: The silent shame of inheriting family wealth
World.content:
MoneySavingInheritance Opinion ‘I didn’t earn this’: The silent shame of inheriting family wealth Paridhi Jain Money contributor August 25, 2026 — 1:16pm

August 25, 2026 — 1:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There’s a conversation I have with people privately that rarely reaches mainstream discourse – the challenges that come with receiving significant financial advantages. Your parents did well, and you reaped some of the rewards. Maybe you grew up with an awareness that your family was considerably wealthier than others. Maybe you have received – or know you’re due to receive – significant financial support (e.g. help buying a home, a significant inheritance, large cash gifts and so on). We have assumptions about what it means to have wealth, and we judge others (and ourselves) by them. Simon Letch You’re aware of your privilege and, as nice as it is, it also feels uncomfortable. You may feel a bit guilty, or embarrassed. You may feel judged – like people think you had it easy, you didn’t work for your successes, or didn’t earn it. But it’s difficult to talk about, for obvious reasons. It’s not the kind of problem that garners much sympathy. For most, it would be a nice problem to have. Nevertheless, it does come with its own set of unique challenges. Today, I’m sharing some of those challenges, and some of what I’ve found helpful in working through them with clients.



Proving or over-compensating How this shows up: You work extra hard to “become something” – not because it brings you joy, meaning, or fulfillment, but because you feel the need to prove yourself. As counter-intuitive as it might be, accepting your privilege might be the real road to freedom. Maybe you want to show – to yourself or others – that you’re more than just your privilege. Perhaps you think this is how you’ll earn respect. Maybe you feel a pressure to “not waste” your good fortune. Why this can be a problem: Proving and over-compensating can be exhausting. You aren’t really living life for you – you’re living the life you think you need to live, to prove something.



This can also rob you of a lot of enjoyment. Instead of enjoying the journey, you’re attached to a specific outcome because of what you think that outcome will prove. “Once I hit $X net-worth or Y milestone, then I will finally feel Z” (worthy, successful, admired, respected, etc). Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert Is being frugal really such a bad thing? Paridhi Jain Money contributor However, you can’t control what people think. No matter what you achieve, or how hard you try to prove something – “they” (whoever you’re trying to prove to) may never change what they think of you. You could spend your whole life attempting to prove something, to someone who may not need, want or accept your proof in the end. How to start shifting this: As counter-intuitive as it might be, accepting your privilege might be the real road to freedom. The freedom to fully own your own life – without guilt or shame. The freedom to cultivate and pursue your own unique individual path – not just live in the shadow of expectation. The freedom to pursue success – not because you have something to prove, but because it’s what makes you feel the most alive.



Holding back out of fear How this shows up: You hold yourself back from little luxuries you could easily afford – not because it’s an intentional choice in alignment with your values, but because on some level you’re scared of how you might be judged or perceived for making those choices. You’re worried about standing out, attracting attention, looking fancy or extravagant. It feels safer to stay under the radar – to stay in sync with those around you. Why this can be a problem: The point here isn’t to spend money just because you have it, or to start being loud and proud about your financial position. The question is – what is the real underlying driver behind your choices? Do you already feel like you’re living your life fully – or are you restricting your experience of life out of fear? Fear of what others might say or think, fear of being judged, fear of breaking out of your comfort zone? If it’s the latter, then you are limiting your ability to enjoy and experience your own life more fully.



How to start shifting this: Start by looking at your fears – the fear of what other people might say, think or do; your fear of judgment, criticism, or being ostracised. Then, start getting clear on what this is costing you. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I’m 64 and I just inherited $700,000. What should I do with it? Paul Benson Money contributor How much are you holding yourself back because of these fears? What opportunities, choices, or goals have you talked yourself out of? What would your life look like if your decisions weren’t being quietly shaped by your fears of what others might think? Many of the challenges that come with receiving significant financial advantages don’t really arise from having money, but from the meaning we (and others) attach to it. We have assumptions about what it means to have wealth, and we judge others (and ourselves) by them. So, what are the underlying beliefs you have about what it means to have wealth? And are those beliefs serving you – or holding you back from enjoying a fuller, freer experience of life?



Paridhi Jain is a money and mindset coach who combines practical strategies with mindset transformation to help clients create more freedom and fulfilment in wealth, work and life. Find Paridhi at: skilledsmart.com.au Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. Expert tips on how to save, invest and make the most of your money delivered to your inbox every Sunday.

World.title: Bombers checked in with Swans over hotel scandal before McVeigh appointment
World.content:
Sydney reassured Essendon the Bombers’ incoming coach Mark McVeigh was not embroiled in the scandal surrounding the Swans and the events that unfolded at the Pullman East Melbourne a week ago. McVeigh said he was stunned when he learnt about the wild party at the Swans’ team hotel, which led to Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon being suspended for the rest of the season by their club for breaching behavioural standards. Mark McVeigh has left his job as Sydney assistant coach to take the senior job at Essendon, the club he played for. Getty Images “Just shocked, absolutely shocked,” McVeigh said. “Really disappointed and shocked.” McVeigh said he did not expect to be questioned by police as part of their investigation. Four Swans officials – senior coach Dean Cox, football boss Leon Cameron, head of player wellbeing and development Brett Kirk and head of media and communications Tom Chadwick – have given statements to police over a separate investigation an alleged sexual assault at the same hotel.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 The tough questions Hird fielded during his Essendon coaching interview The chaos took place as McVeigh was in the final steps of the Essendon coach search process. McVeigh was formally announced as coach on Monday and officially unveiled at the Hangar on Tuesday morning. “I think the Swans got on the front foot and delivered the news to the appropriate people about, ‘Look, they’re not directly involved at all’,” McVeigh said. “I felt comfortable. I didn’t feel moved to ring the footy club at all. I was OK, and you know I’m not here to speak to the Sydney Swans culture. I’m here for the Essendon footy club.”



There was speculation early in the week that staff members may have been with the five players. But the Swans released a statement emphasising that the players suspended were the only members of Sydney staff in the room and condemned some of what they described as misinformation being reported. The Bombers were liaising with several Sydney officials as part of the due diligence relating to McVeigh’s candidacy given his time at the club. World.title: Housing an 'enormous challenge' in this country, housing minister Chris Bishop admits
World.content:
Housing minister Chris Bishop says it doesn't sit comfortably with him that there is no guarantee of shelter for people on any given night.

"We have an enormous challenge around housing in this country" he added.

But he pointed out, that would have been the case under the last government too.

Last week, RNZ reported an admission from officials there was no guarantee shelter could be provided for anyone on any given day.

The admission was put to Bishop on Tuesday, and asked if it sat comfortably with him, to which he replied "no."

Bishop said he wasn't going to pretend "for a moment" there's not a challenge in terms of housing and homelessness.

"I've spent much of the last three years doing my best to try and fix it," he said, referencing the fast track legislation and "building more social homes".

"Last week, we announced 820 new social houses around the country, including areas that are really in severe housing need, like the east coast and the far north, for example, where we're now directing quite a lot of new social housing funding."

He also referenced expanding homelessness outreach services in Auckland, and maintained that emergency housing was available to those with a genuine need.

"I'm proud of our track record on it, but I don't pretend for a moment that we have solved the problem."

Asked if he'd like to see it guaranteed in New Zealand that people could access shelter if they needed it, he said a "legal guarantee would not be effective."

"What's important is that government services are effective, and that's what we're focused on."

Associtate housing minister Tama Potaka wouldn't be drawn on the issue of guaranteed shelter, saying instead what sat comfortably with him was that officials, agencies and community housing providers were "doing their very best to help those people who are rough sleeping and with a genuine need".

Associate housing minister Tama Potaka. (File photo) Alyse Wright

He said his role was to support those agencies to do that.

Asked if he was shocked shelter could not be guaranteed, Potaka said the context in which the question was asked had to be "very very carefully considered".

Someone might turn up at 2am, for example, Potaka said, and to access emergency housing you usually have to go at a certain time of day for people to process that request.

"So if you're saying every single second, every single minute, every single hour of every day and night, there may not be the appropriate mechanisms to enable emergency housing, which often goes through a grant and a bureaucratic process."

Potaka maintained he'd "regularly and consistently" said emergency housing was a "last resort" for those with a genuine need for a short term stay and temporary accommodation.

World.title: Labour promises to reinstate Smokefree Generation policy
World.content:
The Labour Party has announced plans to reinstate its Smokefree Generation policy.

The party's health spokesperson Ayesha Verrall announced the policy at a panel discussion on health and harm prevention in Parliament this afternoon.

Labour had already signalled an intent to bring back the policy in speech from Labour leader Chris Hipkins in 2024.

It would reverse the government's heated tobacco policy - which introduced a 50 percent reduction in the excise duty for heated tobacco products, Verrall said.

She also said the party would introduce a common licensing regime for tobacco and vape products.

The Smokefree Generation policy, when it was announced under the previous Labour government, would have meant that people born on, or after 1 January 2009 would never be able to purchase tobacco products again.

It also heavily restricted the number of stores selling tobacco products, and dramatically reduced nicotine levels.

The Health Coalition Aotearoa panel, held at the Legislative Council Chamber in Parliament. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

It was repealed in 2024 by the current government.

Verrall said Labour would reinstate the policy, but the birthdate after which people could purchase products would now change if the law passed. She did not say what that date was.

She said future generations needed to be protected "against the harms of tobacco", and gains in reducing smoking addiction had been wound back under the current government.

She said the policy would no longer seek to reduce the amount of nicotine in tobacco products to very low-levels.

That could drive people into a black market, Verrall said.

"It is a very stringent control on tobacco products.

"I'm very aware that expert views on this matters have changed, as we have watched very stringent tobacco controls in Australia, coincide with growth in an illicit market," she said.

Hūhana Lyndon RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Greens Party health spokesperson Hūhana Lyndon and Te Pāti Māori co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer, who were both at the panel event, said they supported re-instating the policy.

Lyndon said, "We're absolutely supportive of having that more stringent licensing approach. We know that vaping is also an issue, and it's an entry point for young people."

Debbie Ngarewa-Packer RNZ / Baz Macdonald

But associate health minister Casey Costello said she would not support a change to the heated tobacco excise policy.

"We are trying to get people to stop smoking and reduced-harm pathways are the best way to do it."

She said stringent policies in Australia had failed to deliver, resulting in a "massive" black market problem.

Costello said she was supportive of a common licensing policy for tobacco products.

It was also something which ACT's Todd Stephenson, who was also at the panel event, said the party was open to considering.

He said ACT was against prohibition-type policies, referring to black market concerns.

"I'd be open to considering it, but again it's not an ACT policy."

Finance minister and National deputy leader Nicola Willis said the government stood by its smokefree policies.

World.title: John Hart elected to represent Wairarapa on Greater Wellington Regional Council
World.content:
A new Wairarapa councillor has been elected to the Greater Wellington Regional Council in a by-election held after the sudden death of long-standing local leader and former mayor Adrienne Staples.

John Hart was the successful candidate, and will represent the Wairarapa General constituency for the remainder of the 2025-28 triennium.

Council chair Daran Ponter said Hart brought "extensive experience working with communities, catchment groups, landowners and local government agencies across the region".

His knowledge and commitment to the Wairarapa would be a valuable addition to the council table.

"I would also like to thank all candidates who stood for election and every voter who took part in the democratic process. Strong participation helps ensure local government reflects the communities it serves."

Hart had spent the past two years working with communities, catchment groups, landowners, and councils through his role with the Wairarapa Catchment Collective.

World.title: 'A deal is a deal': Bed tax still government policy, according to Winston Peters
World.content:
New Zealand First leader Winston Peters says bed levies in Auckland and Queenstown are still on the table, and if other parties want to renege on a deal to even consider a levy, that's up to them.

As part of its 'no new taxes' commitment, National has ruled out a bed tax if re-elected.

The move disappointed the mayors of Queenstown and Auckland in particular, with Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown aggrieved given a commitment to explore a bed tax was part of the Auckland Regional Deal.

"The deal is meaningless if the government cannot honour even a relatively modest commitment to explore an agreed proposal," Brown said.

Peters said the deal was made with the coalition government and those cities, not National and those cities.

"The signed deal with Auckland states that these levies will be considered by the government in 2027 - nothing has changed," he said in a social media post.

"The GOVERNMENT has NOT considered it yet. If other parties want to campaign on reneging on the deal to even consider the levy that's up to them. But in NZ First we believe a deal is a deal."

He accused the prime minister of going back on his word.

"When he made that statement, he was talking on behalf of the government, and we're going to make sure the government keeps its word. The National Party may not keep theirs, but we're keeping ours."

Peters said New Zealand First's view was that international tourists should be open to a bed levy that helps pay for key tourism infrastructure.

He believed it would be possible to make the levy only apply to international visitors.

"It'd be easy to do, just like Te Papa. If you walk in there and you're a New Zealander, you don't get charged."

National's concern has been that New Zealanders may end up being caught up having to pay the levy.

Finance spokesperson Nicola Willis said while the government's policy was to explore a bed tax, National's view was that in exploring it, there were problems and alternatives.

Willis indicated National would propose policies at the election to provide more support to local government in areas with significant tourism.

"We don't think it's viable to make every Kiwi pay more for their holiday. Winston Peters clearly does think that's a winner of a proposition. Up to him to go and argue it on the campaign trail."

The Department of Conservation also trialled differential pricing for Great Walks from 2018-2020, and conservation minister Tama Potaka has been looking at work to charge foreign visitors to access high-volume sites like Cathedral Cove, Tongariro Crossing, Milford Sound, and Aoraki Mount Cook, while keeping them free for domestic visitors.

But when asked whether that mechanism could be applied to the bed levy, Potaka deflected.

"My understanding is Labour is an absolute expert on tax. So maybe you should ask the Labour Party and their leadership how they want those taxes to be to be laid out on those beds."

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said the prime minister's signature was the one on the page, not the National Party leader's.

"Last I knew, he was still prime minister. It may not feel like that all of the time, but actually he is the prime minister in this government," he said.

"If the mayors across the country can't trust Christopher Luxon's signature, why should any New Zealanders?"

ACT leader David Seymour said it was "theoretically true" that the government was still considering a bed tax, but he was clear it should not be introducing new taxes.

Seymour said National had not been unfaithful, but had been inconsistent.

"We were never going to agree to it, but, you know, the National Party was going to support it. Now they're not, and I think that's great."

World.title: Gulf Harbour body trial: Religious group leader, wife jailed over manslaughter, kidnapping
World.content:
The leader of a fringe religious group Kaixiao Liu has been sentenced to 10 years and five months imprisonment for the manslaughter and kidnapping of one of his followers - 70-year-old Shulai Wang.

His wife, Lanyue Xiao, received a sentence of seven years and 11 months for her role.

Wang, from Hainan, China, was found wrapped in layers of black rubbish bags in Auckland's Gulf Harbour in March 2024, eight months after she arrived in the country to follow the religious instructions of Liu.

Kaixiao Liu at sentencing on Tuesday. RNZ/Nick Monro

Liu's mother, Xiuyun Li, and father, Jingui Liu, were also convicted in June - Li of kidnapping and Jingui Liu of misconduct to human remains.

They will be sentenced later this year, due to more material they plan to place before the court.

Wang and five other women from China stayed with Liu and his family in Ōrewa, where the Crown said Wang was punished for not complying with the strict rules of the household, and later put in a suitcase, denied food and water, following a failed escape just days before her death.

On Tuesday morning, Justice Mathew Downs handed Liu the prison sentence at Auckland's High Court.

Justice Mathew Downs. RNZ / Nick Monro

Liu's sentence, with a minimum non-parole period of 50 percent of his sentence, also covered Liu's convictions for interfering with human remains, perverting the course of justice and failing to give device passwords to police during a search warrant.

Xiao received a sentence of seven years and 11 months for kidnapping, manslaughter, perverting the course of justice and interfering with human remains.

Justice Downs didn't impose a minimum non-parole period for Xiao, acknowledging her lesser culpability compared to Liu, who made all the key decisions relating to Wang's detention and punishment.

He said Liu and Xiao's offending had several aggravating factors, including detaining Wang for 38 hours and restraining her for much of the period, taping her mouth to stop her from screaming, denying food and water - all whilst knowing that she was a 70-year-old overstayer who was entirely dependent on them.

Justice Downs emphasised Liu's position as the ring leader and his "callous indifference" to Wang and the other women in the house, referring to the evidence heard in trial that Liu had kept the black pushchair used to dispose of Wang's body and the black bed she was detained in as warnings to the other women in the house, telling them that the colour black represented death.

He said Liu's recordings of meetings at the house after Wang's death provided some of the best evidence of his offending - where Liu directed others to restrain Wang with wire, chain or other restraints, and directed that Wang be denied food or water.

Justice Downs noted that Xiao was party to those directions.

Lanyue Xiao and Kaixiao Liu. RNZ/Nick Monro

Turning to Xiao, Justice Downs said while she was not as culpable as he is, she was the next most culpable given her status in the household.

Justice Downs said he had observed Xiao during the trial and seen her disagree with her husband, and seen that at times her husband deferred to her.

"If you had sought to dissuade Mr Liu from the offending, there is a very real prospect he might have been so dissuaded," he said.

The sentences for Liu and Xiao included a 5 percent discount for the consideration that neither of them had previous convictions.

The sentences also included a 10 month reduction, in recognition of the time the pair spent on electronically monitored bail in the lead up to the trial.

Justice Downs said he was not persuaded by submissions for either defendants' good work or character references.

The judge also decided on no discounts on compassionate grounds for Liu's separation from his five children - four of whom were uplifted by Oranga Tamariki in September 2024 - and the youngest who was uplifted following the conclusion of the trial in June.

Justice Down said there was no grounds for him to grant the 10 percent discount based sought by Liu and Xiao, based on their background.

"Mr Liu, that it may be part of your culture to act as the head of the housheold, and to be seen to be so, does not in any way explain why you commited the offending,

"You could have for example, demonstrated compassion to Ms Wang and offered that response to your family as the relevant one for a role model, you did claim after all to be following Jesus".

Justice Downs said both Liu and Xiao are permanent residents in New Zealand, and are likely to be deported after serving their sentence.

He noted the couple met when the were in the United States, and moved to New Zealand in 2017.

Kaixiao Liu's lawyer, Ron Mansfield KC. RNZ/Nick Monro

Liu's lawyer Ron Mansfield KC, who did not represent him in the trial but is now representing him on appeal matters, had asked Justice Downs for leniency and compassion on several factors.

Mansfield said while Liu still doesn't accept the Crown's version of events, he does have remorse for the loss of life in his home.

"He is not a cult leader, nor require people to follow his cult," Mansfield said, adding that Liu had people who followed him as a result of his music, not his preaching.

Mansfield said life in custody for any foreign national is more difficult, and that there are positives in Liu's life such as being a parent and wanting to return to his children and family life.

Mansfield said the removal of the children had played a significant part in the proceeding in leading Liu to mistrust authority and the criminal process, and that the mistrust had led to Liu's inability to trust counsel appointed during the trial, which drove the way in which the trial was conducted.

He had asked the judge to consider a sentence of home detention for Liu.

"He won't in the future, have anyone other than his family living in his home, this event will never occur again, and it can be accepted in my submission that he's at low risk for further offending," said Mansfield.

Julie-Anne Kincade KC, who did not represent Xiao in the trial, represented Xiao at the sentencing.

She said Xiao did not accept the Crown's portrayal of events, but aknowledged that the sentencing hearing was not the place to raise those issues.

Kincade asked the judge to consider Xiao's background - that she went to a biblically centred university and has known faith all her life.

World.title: Luxury real estate firm hit by cyber security attack
World.content:
Luxury real estate firm Sotheby's International says it is investigating a cyber security incident that involved unauthorised access to data it was holding in a third-party software platform.

The platform is a system designed to hold contact information for marketing purposes.

Sotheby's said data that might have been accessed included names, addresses, emails and phone numbers.

"No email exchanges, documentation or other substantive material relating to properties have been accessed. The platform is not used to store information used for customer financial transactions," it said in a statement.

It said it took steps to contain the incident when it became aware of what had happened.

The company said the person who accessed the data claimed to have obtained 1.6 million contacts but it refuted that claim because it did not have that many on its database.

It said third-party platform forensic investigators said this number related to duplicate entries.

"We recognise the trust our clients place in us and regret any concern this incident may cause. Since becoming aware of the incident, our focus has been on containing the issue, understanding exactly what occurred, and working with independent cyber security specialists to protect client information. We remain committed to transparency and will continue to provide updates as deemed necessary," said New Zealand managing director Mark Harris.

In an email to clients, it said there could be some cases where information stored within an open-text notes field could be deemed sensitive and have been accessed. It said anyone affected in that way would be contacted directly.

World.title: Rates rises to be capped at 4 percent
World.content:
The government is moving ahead with its plans to cap the amount councils can increase rates by to a maximum of 4 percent, but won't be able to pass the legislation until next term.

Local Government Minister Simon Watts says the legislation would put "a brake on excessive increases and [give] ratepayers greater certainty", but confirmed the average amount households would save is only $34 a year.

"For too long, ratepayers have been hit with steep and unexpected rates increases, adding pressure to household budgets at a time many New Zealanders are already feeling the squeeze," Watts said.

The changes would also "sharpen the focus on delivering the services communities expect councils to get right, like fixing the potholes, collecting rubbish and running our pools and parks".

Asked if councils had said the policy was achievable and whether the services that communities need can be paid for with this policy, Watts only said that having a "core set of areas of focus" versus was going to be easier for councils.

"As a result of that, then we would expect that that would provide benefits also in terms of the ability for them to reduce spending in particular areas."

Watts said the legislation would be passed "in effect next term", given the limited amount of time before the House rises ahead of the election. If passed, it would come into effect on the 1st July 2029.

He maintained it was "government policy" and had support from National's coalition partners. It comes after those coalition partners have specified they won't support a ban on social media, despite that legislation being announced as government policy.

"With respect, the policy that I'm announcing today is government policy and the coalition partners have been supportive alongside all members of that cabinet," Watts emphasised.

"It has the support of government."

Asked why he wasn't able to get the legislation across the line earlier, in order to pass it before the election, Watts said he'd been working through a comprehensive process and taken time to consider the complex legislation.

On user charges, Watts said they weren't part of the rates cap model. For people going to a public pool or library, it was up to local councils to determine those costs.

"I don't, as Minister of Local Government, get involved in setting charges for how much you pay to go to your local pool."

But he didn't say whether those charges might increase as a result of councils receiving less revenue from rates.

But on Monday, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon had said rates caps were "very important, so you don't have increases in fees and charges".

Watts had to correct that on Tuesday, saying Luxon was referring to the context in which Treasury refers different costs. He said Luxon was referring to what Treasury refers to as "administrative costs", that includes rates.

"The rates cap will not apply to fees and charges on councils; they are explicitly excluded," Watts repeated, saying Luxon had subsequently clarified the comments.

Local Government New Zealand (LGNZ) said in response to the announcement that councils couldn't be expected to deliver "more infrastructure, support growth and meet communities' expectations with fewer levers".

"The maths just doesn't add up and something will have to give," President Rehette Stoltz said.

Stoltz also referenced local government only getting 10 percent of the country's tax take, but being responsible for about a third of all public infrastructure investment in New Zealand.

An Infometrics report for LGNZ in 2025 found the average New Zealand household pays 10 times more towards government taxes than in council rates.

"Introducing a 4 percent cap when councils' costs are increasing at a much higher rate will hamstring already-constrained councils' ability to maintain investment in the services and infrastructure that people rely on them to provide."

Watts disagreed with that, saying everyone had their view.

LGNZ also referenced estimates by officials the rates cap would only save households $34 a year.

Watts confirmed the figure, but said it would depend on the different councils, on average though the number was correct.

"$34 is a savings for households, which is not immaterial. But the important thing here is around certainty," Watts said, and households knowing what was coming in future rates increases.

Stoltz also said the announcement came "hot on the heels" of the National Party ruling out an accommodation levy, which she called a "key tool" that could have helped take the burden off ratepayers.

She said the government was not addressing the drivers of costs, and rather "making things worse by passing on the costs of government reforms to councils and ratepayers."

As part of the announcement, Watts confirmed councils would be able to apply for exemptions from the 2-4 percent band if they were responding to "events such as natural disasters that go beyond what a council can reasonably be expected to plan for", and "where a council can demonstrate prudent financial management and a justified need to operate above or below the target range".

To qualify for the latter, councils would need to carry out community consultation before applying.

"We recognise there will be limited circumstances where councils need greater flexibility, such as recovering from a natural disaster or responding to events outside their control," Watts said.

"Exemptions will not be granted lightly and will only be available in exceptional circumstances where there is strong justification."

The caps will take full effect from 1 July 2029, but long-term plans prepared before then will need to consider the target range of 2-4 percent.

The target range will be reviewed every six years.

Water services, such as those provided by Watercare in Auckland and Tiaki Wai in Wellington, will be exempt.

An independent regulator will be established to monitor compliance, assess exemption applications, and support councils through the transition and provide guidance.

Political reaction

ACT leader David Seymour said a 4 percent rates rise sounded "pretty good", after facing 7.9 percent the past year as an Aucklander.

He said it also signalled a move from councils doing "whatever they like" to being treated like utilities, like "electricity or fibre companies, where the returns are regulated".

David Seymour. RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

"Of course, it's not a silver bullet," he added. "It will only work if councils face less cost from overregulation," and it was important to get things like the resource management laws, temporary traffic management laws, and health and safety reform completed before the rates cap came into force.

Asked about user charges increasing to cover council costs, Seymour said they could "certainly try that".

"But ultimately they also are accountable to their voters and their ratepayers," and he expected a "very stern reaction" if councils did that.

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters was also in support, saying the party thought there was a need for a rates cap.

"If you look at some of the squanderous spending by local governments, something has to be done about it."

He said ordinarily NZ First wouldn't like to say that, but "because it's got so gross, as opposed to some responsible councils, then I think it has to be done".

Greens co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said the "maths don't math" with this government.

Chlöe Swarbrick. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

She said National had decided to rule out the bed tax, just weeks after signing onto that with local government across the country. She said that meant regular ratepayers were going to have to foot the bill for the infrastructure that was necessary in towns and cities across the country.

"Now they're proposing that there's going to be a rates cap. It just doesn't add up, but clearly numbers aren't this government's strong suit."

Labour hadn't yet formed a position on it - despite the 4 percent figure being signalled by the government for months now, with leader Chris Hipkins saying he wanted to see legislation first.

Hipkins said he recognised nobody liked paying higher rates, and rates bills had been going up significantly, but he also recognised local government had to fund the services "we all rely on".

World.title: Teen aquatic diver wins bronze for Fiji at World Junior Diving Champs
World.content:
Maori Pomeroy Farrell, a 17-year-old little-known aquatic diver, has put Fiji on the global map at the World Junior Diving Championships in Croatia.

Maori, who has links to Dama village in Bua and Levuka Vakaviti in Ovalau, claimed a bronze medal at in the Boys' 3-metre springboard event, finished third with a total score of 490.50 points, to claim a bronze medal at the event.

It is the first-ever medal won by Fiji at an aquatic world meet.

Germany's Finn Awe won gold with 560.60 points, while Matvei Pomoshnikov of Russia took silver with 542.00 points.

World Aquatics said in a short post on the achievement on their social media platforms "Maori Pomeroy-Farrell claims bronze at the , becoming the first-ever Fijian athlete to win a medal at a World Aquatics competition. A landmark moment for Fiji diving and a huge achievement on the world stage."

Maori held off challengers from Mexico, Lithuania, Germany and the United States to clinch the bronze medal.

The teenager is also scheduled to compete in the boys' under-18s one metre dive.

His dad Dan Farrell said the family are proud of Maori's achievement and believe his strong performance has now put Fiji on the world map in the sport.

"History for Fiji!," he said.

"Maori charged through a field of 43 international competitors, entering the 12-man final in 12th position.

"Then he turned it up a notch, fighting like a Fijian warrior and charging all the way to bronze, channeling the strength of his vanua, from Dama, Bua, to Levuka, Ovalau, his vuvale and all of Fiji stand proudly with him as he makes history for his nation on the world stage."

Maori, whose family had to relocate from Canada to Mexico so that he could train and compete in the sport he now loves, is the first to represent Fiji in the sport at the world meet.

World.title: NRL changes rules to allow Jai Arrow to 'play' 100 games for Souths
World.content:
Jai Arrow will make cameo appearances in the final two rounds of the regular season in order to reach 100 games for South Sydney.

In one of the feel-good stories of the NRL season, the forward who retired with motor neurone disease in May has been approved to start on the field in rounds 26 and 27.

Arrow will then be substituted out in the opening seconds before any active involvement in play.

It came after the Rabbitohs made an appeal to the NRL to grant the former Queensland representative an on-field swansong while still able to walk and run.

The initiative gives Arrow two final chances to farewell an NRL career that featured a grand-final appearance in 2021 and 12 State of Origin caps.

The NRL has granted Souths special dispensation to name Arrow as an extra player on today's team list and an extra substitution in their rotation.

Arrow vows to help others fight MND Former NRL player Jai Arrow says he is determined to raise money and awareness for Motor Neurone Disease until a cure is found.

The matches, against Gold Coast and the Sydney Roosters, will bring Arrow's tally to 180 career games and 100 for the Rabbitohs.

Arrow will lead the team out on both occasions and sit on the interchange bench in Souths kit after being substituted out.

The Titans and Roosters have both approved the plan, as have the Rugby League Players Association.

"We are very grateful to Peter [V'landys] and the NRL, and Clint [Newton] at the RLPA, for supporting our proposal," Souths chief executive Blake Solly said.

"We believe this will provide great inspiration for everyone watching the game from the stadium or at home, showing that MND will not hold Jai, or anyone else, back from achieving what they want to achieve in life."

The NRL world has rallied around Arrow since his shock diagnosis and immediate retirement in May.

The league threw Arrow "the world's biggest birthday party" on the day Souths beat Newcastle in July, rolling out a birthday cake in the shape of the 31-year-old's jersey and presenting him with a commemorative jersey.

Fundraising efforts have already passed $1 million in support of Arrow, who is the father of a young daughter.

Players from all clubs have shown their support by marking tries with arrow celebrations throughout the month of July.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: McVeigh to canvass Hird return as icon urges Bombers fans to unite
World.content:
New Essendon coach Mark McVeigh says he will speak to James Hird about returning to the club in a different capacity after a second failed bid to be coach.

McVeigh was unveiled on Tuesday in a press conference that was also attended by a number of Essendon's current players.

Both he and club president Andrew Welsh indicated their desire to have Hird involved.

"I'd love to see James as a part of the club going forward. He's such a fantastic football person," Welsh said.

"I feel there's significant value James can bring, not just tokenistic, but real value to our club and our playing group.

"Certainly, part of my messaging was that Mark and I would want to catch up with him when the time is appropriate."

While Welsh said a pair of calls to Hird had gone unanswered on Monday night, McVeigh said he had shared a conversation with his former captain.

"I love James Hird, he's one of my best mates. It was difficult to go through the process against a good friend," he said.

McVeigh (right) called Hird (left) one of his "best mates" after beating him to the Essendon job. (Getty Images: Ryan Pierse)

"I don't fear those people [Hird's supporters], I actually embrace how they feel, and I understand it, to be fair.

"He's been a constant in my life since I was 17 years of age. We spoke this morning, and the way he spoke of how proud he was of this moment for me, it hasn't broken us, we're still together, but I understand and embrace the feelings of the people that love James Hird, because I do too."

McVeigh, Welsh and club CEO Tim Roberts called for unity at the club amid rumours of a potential board challenge from unimpressed Hird fans.

"I don't ask for your patience, I ask for your re-alignment to our club," McVeigh said.

"I sit here year after year, and we get people coming out of the shadows that want to challenge the board," added Welsh.

"I can tell you since I've been here that this club has never been more united.

"These people want to keep living in the shadows and keep on trying to destabilise our club, we don't jump at shadows.

"We're a strong club and we'll continue to make sure that we make the right decisions on behalf of our members and our teams and our staff to get this club moving forward again."

Tim Watson (pictured) has called for unity at Essendon after Mark McVeigh's signing. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

The plea for unity came as Essendon legend Tim Watson has the club's passionate supporters to "put [their] weapons down".

"There's got to be a unification of the club now," he told SEN on Tuesday morning.

"People have to put down their weapons and get behind this appointment of a former player — somebody who has been passionate about the football club.

"This is part of the healing process that needs to take place. Ultimately, it's a much bigger thing than the emotion that might be associated with it now. There is an enormous amount of work to do.

Live Moment Look back at Mark McVeigh's first press conference as Essendon's new senior coach. McVeigh says Bombers 'won't live in the past' Pretty good way to end the press conference from the new Essendon coach. He receives another round of applause from those in attendance before walking off the podium. Welsh with another clue on Hird returning I reckon it's going to be a full-court press on the Dons trying to get Hird to say yes to some kind of role within the club. "We have great people that we want to get back involved with the club in meaningful ways," Welsh says. "I look at this as a point that we can re-align that passion." McVeigh with an insight into his game plan McVeigh explains what areas he's going to try and fix on-field. "In the phases of the game, we can't focus on one. If you look at the numbers, we're the bottom of the table in a lot of areas. "I do want them to be brave, I do want them to play with flare, but we do need to fix up our defence. "They [the players] need to come back prepared physically and ready to learn. "The system we'll put in place, you need to understand, otherwise you'll get found out. "When we get all three phases going in the right direction, Essendon will fly." Show more

"Congratulations to him. He's been an Essendon man all his life. He's loved this football club, that was clear in the days that he played.

"He's had a great development profile if you look at where he's been and what he's been doing. He's been part of elite coaching departments [at GWS and Sydney]."

McVeigh has signed a three-year contract with Essendon and was the unanimous choice of the Essendon board.

World.title: Piastri searching for answers as teammate re-enters F1 title picture
World.content:
Oscar Piastri's "disappointing" end to the Dutch Grand Prix has left the Australian and his McLaren team searching for answers, while his teammate has roared back into the Formula 1 title picture.

Last weekend in Zandvoort was shaping to be a good weekend for Piastri.

The Australian was matching the pace at the front through qualifying, and after a terrific second start in the grand prix following Max Verstappen's heavy crash, Piastri was on course for a first podium finish since Miami in May.

Piastri struggles after slow pit stop, Norris wins as Verstappen crashes Reigning world champion Lando Norris has doubled his grand prix win tally in 2026, producing a pair of brilliant overtakes to win the Dutch Grand Prix.

Piastri had performed a breathtaking overtake on Mercedes driver George Russell to move into third and was not far off the pace set by leaders Kimi Antonelli and teammate Lando Norris, despite being on a harder compound tyre.

But a slow first pit stop knocked Piastri back behind Russell and out of third place, and it only got worse from there.

Piastri, who won the Dutch Grand Prix in 2025, fell right off the pace and finished a distant sixth as Norris surged to victory.

Piastri was running third until a slow pit stop knocked him out of the podium position at Zandvoort. (Reuters: Benoit Tessier)

The sudden pace drop-off has left Piastri with plenty of questions that he and the team will want answers to.

"The first stint felt reasonable, but from the second stint onwards, the pace was simply not there, and it became a real struggle," he said.

"We will review the entire weekend and analyse to understand why we experienced such a significant performance drop-off.

"A slow pit stop didn't help, but the fundamental issue was the lack of pace, which is something we'll work on ahead of Monza.

"That's the priority now, to dig into the data with the team to find the root cause and ensure we can move forward in a more positive direction for the upcoming races."

Piastri's situation is a far cry from where he was at the conclusion of last year's Dutch Grand Prix, when he claimed his seventh grand prix win of the season and was the championship leader.

But while Piastri is seeking answers to get back to the front of the grid, Norris is threatening to stay there.

'The fight's still on': Norris re-enters the F1 title picture

McLaren entered the 2026 season having won the previous two constructors' championships, and with Lando Norris as reigning drivers' champion.

Reigning Formula 1 drivers' champion Lando Norris has won the past two grands prix. (Reuters: Benoit Tessier)

But with a new era of regulations, McLaren's 2026 season started poorly.

Piastri crashed on his way to the grid in Melbourne and he and Norris did not start in Shanghai due to car issues.

Norris then had back-to-back retirements in Montreal and Monaco, meaning he failed to finish three of the opening six grands prix.

But the reigning world champion has returned to winning ways, triumphing in Hungary before the mid-year break and then again last weekend in the Netherlands.

With back-to-back wins and growing confidence in his season, Norris has re-emerged as a drivers' championship contender.

F1 drivers' championship standings after Dutch Grand Prix 242 — Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes

183 — George Russell, Mercedes

183 — Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari

159 — Lando Norris, McLaren

155 — Charles Leclerc, Ferrari

With 10 or 11 rounds remaining this season, depending on conflict in the Middle East, Norris is sitting fourth in the standings, 83 points behind leader Kimi Antonelli.

It is a huge gap, but recent history shows it is not an impossible feat.

At the conclusion of last year's Dutch Grand Prix, Max Verstappen was 104 points behind then-leader Piastri with nine rounds remaining.

Verstappen surged towards the end of the season while Piastri slumped. Verstappen fell two points shy of Norris in the standings, but finished a stunning 11 points ahead of Piastri.

Having seen what is possible, Norris has made this year's title fight a four-way race with Antonelli, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton.

Norris's message to his team over the radio after taking the chequered flag on Sunday certainly sounded like the Briton believed his championship hopes are far from over.

"Let's keep pushing. Thank you for the hard work. Let's keep bringing upgrades, let's keep bringing performance, please," he said.

"The fight's still on."

Out of the car, Norris was quick to point out that there is a long season still ahead of the drivers and that he was not getting ahead of himself with an 83-point deficit.

"One race at a time. A lot of people say it now, but it is the truth of it. There's no point in thinking that far ahead," he said after winning on Sunday.

"There are plenty of things we can do better, and we need to do better if we want to fight for a championship.

"We have to keep working hard. There's still plenty of races, plenty of opportunity for everyone."

Norris's deficit to Antonelli was 101 points prior to the weekend in Hungary, but the McLaren champion has reduced that by 18 with two tremendous weekends.

However, the 83-point gap is significant and Antonelli has extended his overall championship lead.

Entering the Dutch Grand Prix weekend, the young Italian's lead over Hamilton was 50 points, and 59 over Russell.

After the weekend, his lead is 59 points over both Hamilton and Russell.

F1 heads to Monza for the Italian Grand Prix in two weeks, one of the fastest tracks on the calendar and vastly different to the tight and twisting circuits in Hungary and the Netherlands where Norris has won this year.

World.title: 'A dangerous individual': Ex-snooker champ convicted of child sex abuse
World.content:
Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been convicted of sexually abusing two primary school children in Scotland in the 1990s and early 2000s.

Dott, 49, was found guilty of abusing a girl from 1993-96 and a boy from 2006-10 after a five-day trial at the High Court in Glasgow. The judge ordered Dott to be held in custody ahead of his sentencing on September 29.

The woman, now in her 40s, testified that Dott sexually abused her on multiple occasions, "caressing" her bottom over her clothing, exposing himself and touching her with parts of his body, including his penis.

The man, now in his late 20s, said he was abused on multiple occasions, with Dott touching him inappropriately, kissing him and performing sexual acts.

Dott with his wife Elaine after winning the snooker world championship in 2006. (Getty Images: Rui Vieira)

"Dott is a dangerous individual, and I hope this conviction provides some measure of comfort to those impacted by his crimes," Detective Inspector Gary Smillie from Police Scotland said.

Snooker's governing body suspended Dott in April 2025 after he was charged in the case. The Scot was ranked number 56 in the world at the time and dropped from the rankings after the season.

On Monday, the World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association revoked Dott's membership following an emergency board meeting. The WPBSA also said it wrote to the World Snooker Tour to request his immediate removal from the WST Hall of Fame.

Dott won the World Snooker Championship in 2006 and was a runner-up twice.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Zak Butters trade rumours dominate Port Adelaide's turbulent season
World.content:
It's been a tumultuous year for Port Adelaide.

Its newly-appointed coach Josh Carr had to navigate a new system with an injury riddled list; using 39 of its 44-listed players and finishing the season with 15 unavailable.

He also had to build chemistry and belief despite a contract decision overshadowing his campaign.

Its vice-captain and dual All-Australian Zak Butters has dominated headlines all season as one of the biggest free-agents available this off-season; and has now confirmed the worst-kept secret in football that he has requested a trade to Victoria.

"I've made a decision to head home. It's obviously been one that I've wrestled with for a while now. It's been a tough decision and one that I haven't taken lightly," Butters said on Monday.

"Although I've loved my time in Adelaide … I'm probably at a stage in my life where I'd like to get back around some family and friends and enjoy some more time with them."

Butters denied reports in June that he had begun telling those close to him he was eager to move east after a trip back home during the round 12 bye; another chapter in a compendium of updates on the dual Showdown medallist's future.

So why was the club so protective of Butters when he had a foot out the door?

There are two key foundations of any negotiation in any industry. Value and relationships.

Growing speculation

As the weeks progressed and the speculation grew, the four-horse race between Richmond, Geelong, Collingwood and the Western Bulldogs intensified as the coverage evolved into a public bidding war; increasing Butters' contract terms and giving the Power fuel for higher trade demands.

Every story has a source … and every source has an agenda.

Zak Butters to leave Port Adelaide Star Port Adelaide midfielder Zak Butters has informed the Power he wants to return to Victoria.

Player agents are looking to maximise demand and clubs want their outgoing stars to leave at a high price.

Relationships between the two parties are also incredibly important in future dealings. Clubs are constantly trying to find the balance between fair compensation and long-term favours.

For Port Adelaide this was the case two years ago when Dan Houston was desperate to move to Collingwood but the Magpies didn't have the capital for a reasonable return.

The Power settled for Picks 13, 29 and 36 plus forwards Jack Lukosius and Joe Richards in exchange for its dual All-Australian defender and a future first round pick.

It was a move that was widely panned at the time but hasn't done much damage given rising key forward Jack Whitlock was taken at 29 and Joe Richards is developing into a handy midfield option.

But Dan Houston and Zak Butters are different cases.

The Power is hoping to maximise its draft haul in moving its triple best-and-fairest winner given it has rarely had early selections in recent years leading to a gulf in young talent depth.

It also has a litany of upcoming academy and father-son draftees it will need to match bids on, such as expected number one pick Dougie Cochrane and Zemes Pilot.

Matthew Richardson spoke about the Butters trade rumous in May. (ABC News: Marco Catalano)

Back in May, Port chief executive Matthew Richardson flagged on ABC Sport that the club would match any bid on Butters to force a trade given the star is a restricted free agent.

"There will be offers that we can match and we will match. It does give the club a fair bit of control in what happens," he said.

The issue is Butters current suitors have a diverse availability of picks at their disposal and the Power's best option Richmond doesn't quite align with the values Butters claimed he was eyeing when I asked him back in March what would dictate his decision.

"I think you're stupid if you don't want to win premierships," he said.

"I want to win. Family is important as well … but you can't look too far ahead."

THE CONTENDERS (As of current ladder position, all four clubs have all future picks available) Geelong: 17, 35, 53, 71

Western Bulldogs: 10, 28, 46

Collingwood: 16, 34, 63, 66, 70

Richmond: 2, 20, 38, 56

While Port navigates its way through the 20 out-of-contract players it has held fire on due to the Butters decision, there will be time for Josh Carr to reflect on his inaugural season at the helm.

Season highlights

Despite double ups with four sides who missed finals; the Power managed seven wins in 2026 and had a clear narrative throughout; it could match it with the best but could rarely beat them.

Its campaign ended with an equal league record five losses by five-points or less and eight by as much as 14-points.

A Showdown win over Adelaide in June was the highlight, plus its April upset over Geelong; but its only road wins were against fellow bottom four sides West Coast and Richmond.

It finished 16th for ball movement from D50 to F50 but defensively was a powerhouse until the final month where 10-goal losses to the Lions, Swans and Demons blew out the team's average points against to 89, dropping it down from a Top 4 side into 10th.

The other positive was its clearance work. Despite missing Connor Rozee for the majority of the campaign, and Zak Butters for the final month, the side finished second for clearance differential, blooding future stars in Jase Burgoyne, Joe Richards and Miles Bergman on ball.

Port Adelaide won seven games in the 2026 season. (ABC Riverland: Catherine Heuzenroeder)

From a list perspective it was the only side not to have a player named in the AFL's 22-under-22 squad and some of the long-term signings from the Hinkley era like Todd Marshall and Brandon Zerk-Thatcher barely featured.

Former Port midfielder and four times Showdown medallist Josh Francou believes 2026 was a free hit for Josh Carr.

"It has been a difficult campaign … the way they're defending the ground is a real plus for them but they struggle to move the ball," he said.

"Next year things start to ramp up on Josh Carr and he's got to get it right."

Despite all the adversities, it feels like Josh Carr has laid the foundation for success but a critical off-season awaits as he looks to reshape the list and keep his stars healthy for the 2027 campaign.

World.title: Cyclists run for cover as hailstorm forces La Vuelta stage cancellation
World.content:
A torrential hailstorm in the French Pyrenees forced the abandonment of the third stage of the Vuelta a España on Monday.

With 15 kilometres remaining of the 174-km route from Gruissan to Font-Romeu, the skies darkened as the peloton neared the top of the Col de Mont-Louis and huge hailstones began bouncing off the tarmac and pelting the riders.

Mats Wenzel (Kern Pharma) and Lorenzo Fortunato (XDS Astana) were 25 seconds ahead of the peloton when the elements intervened, as race leader and favourite Tadej Pogacar was seen indicating to the peloton to pull off the course.

Bedraggled riders were then seen getting off their bikes and shuffling into a hotel for shelter.

Shortly afterwards, race organisers, ASO, announced the stage would not resume, leaving fans frustrated at the finish where thick layers of hail blanketed the road.

Slovenia's Pogacar (UAE Emirates-XRG) retained his overall lead of nine seconds from Belgium's Wout van Aert (Dutch Visma-Lease a Bike) with Britain's Matt Brennan 10 seconds back.

Earlier it had been warm and sunny on the flat approaches to the mountainous finish with no sign of the chaos to come as a five-man breakaway group stayed out ahead.

Pogacar, bidding to complete his Grand Tour collection by winning the Vuelta for the first time, was always near the front of the pack with his team setting the pace.

Sadly, his expected challenge for the stage victory fell foul of the weather in an anticlimactic finish.

He will get his chance to underline his superiority again on Tuesday, though with stage four featuring three first-category climbs as the race starts and finishes in Andorra la Vella.

Reuters

World.title: From almost drowning as a child to the pinnacle of surf lifesaving
World.content:
Under an expansive blue sky and bathed in the type of sunshine that typifies Queensland's mocking parody of winter, the ocean at Surfers Paradise is made to look incredibly inviting, even on a Thursday morning in August.

But the crashing of waves into the hard-packed sand offers a reminder that beyond the beauty of the scene, the power of the ocean remains a potent force.

Australian Iron Series athlete Tiarnee Massie knows about this more than most.

The 24-year-old is a third-generation surf lifesaver at Maroochydore Surf Life Saving Club on Queensland's Sunshine Coast.

Not only that, but she is the reigning and defending Iron Series champion and will wear the yellow number 1 seed bib when the series gets underway in October with the Coolangatta Gold.

Tiarnee Massie will look to once again win the overall title when the series finishes at Surfers Paradise early next year. (Getty Images: Iron Series/Chris Hyde)

Her story could have been very different, though.

"I think I was nine months old," Massie tells ABC Sport on the Gold Coast.

"I was at home and my older sister was playing in the pool with her friends.

"Someone left the pool gate open and I found myself in the pool and drowning at the bottom of the pool."

The scenario is one that is all too painfully familiar for far too many Australian families.

The 2025 National Drowning Report, published by Royal Life Saving Australia and Surf Life Saving Australia, identified 15 fatalities of children aged four or younger, eight of which occurred in a swimming pool.

In total, the report noted that there were 357 drowning deaths over the past 12 months, a 27 per cent increase on the 10-year average.

Tiarnee Massie is aware she could have become a statistic for Australia's downing deaths. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

"My mum was actually on the phone and she had this gut instinct that something was wrong, so she hung up and she came out and she found me in the water," Massie says, knowing how fortunate she is to not be a contributing statistic to the nation's drowning tally.

"She started doing resuscitation and she saved my life that day."

That near-death experience didn't seem to do Massie any long-term harm.

Even in the short term it seems the young Massie was relatively unperturbed by the experience — she tells ABC Sport she was back in the water the very next day.

"It didn't affect me at all," Massie says.

"But it certainly affected my mum," she adds with an infectious and earnestly cheeky grin.

"Still now, when she's watching me in the ocean, she just can't watch. She's actually fainted a few times.

"She's got demons there, but she knows that I'm capable and she knows that I love it.

"I have the best family who support me. They are always coming to all of my competitions, we stay together and to be able to share these incredible experiences and moments with them, it's a dream come true."

Tiarnee Massie says her mum sometimes struggles watching her race. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

That day sparked something in Massie's mother too, who has gone on to become a CPR trainer at the Maroochydore Surf Club, joining a club that her uncle, Ashley Massie, competed for in surf lifesaving competitions.

"She never was involved [in surf lifesaving] to the extent of being a trainer until the moment that I drowned in the pool," Massie says.

"You don't know if you are someone that deals well in those situations until you're literally in the situation.

"You know, you can do all the training, but unless you actually are in that situation, you don't know whether you can do it. And my mum did it."

And incredibly, that ability to remain calm under the intolerable pressure of a life or death situation, clearly passed on to her daughter.

"I was 15, I was on a family holiday in Thailand and we were out surfing with my friends and I actually noticed that this man was struggling in the water," Massie says.

"My mum signalled me from the beach saying he's in trouble and my friend and I went over and helped him and we saved his life that day."

Competing is serious for Tiarnee Massie, but so too is the bigger picture of saving lives. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

The magnitude of that moment may have passed the then-teenage Massie by somewhat: "I was so young that I actually didn't understand the importance of what I did, I was just doing what I was trained to do," Massie says.

"I was doing what I knew how to do, I was in the ocean, I understand the ocean and I didn't understand that he couldn't."

The enormity soon struck home when the man she saved wrote her a letter.

"Later on he wrote a letter to myself and my friend, Grace, saying how grateful he was for us saving his life and that we have changed his life forever and all of this incredible stuff," she says.

"It was from that moment on that I realised how important the work that we were doing is.

"You know, I may be training to be the best ironwoman in the ocean, but most importantly, I'm training to be the best person to save a life on the beach.

"I think that is so rare in sport and that is such a special gift that we have as surf lifesavers. We are literally training to save someone's life."

Tiarnee Massie (right) will lock horns with number two seed Lily O'Sullivan (left) in the Iron Series. (Supplied)

Massie will start the defence of her title at the Coolangatta Gold, an event she came into as favourite last year, only to suffer the heartache of a broken paddle on the ski leg.

Despite that disappointment, Massey was still able to claim the series title.

Now she looks forward to honouring that yellow jersey over the course of the Iron Series, with events taking place in Coolangatta, Thirroul, Newcastle and the season final at Surfers Paradise on February 7.

"I feel so honoured to be wearing the yellow jersey this season," Massie says.

"I have looked up to every woman and man before me who has worn this jersey and to be actually in those yellow togs with the number one on them is such an honour.

"I'm just so grateful, I did all the hard yards as a young girl and stuck it out through the highs and lows of sport and all the triumphs and failures and I finally got to achieve my dream of becoming the Iron Series champion."

World.title: England drop fast bowler Carse after nightclub incident
World.content:
England fast bowler Brydon Carse has been dropped from the squad for the second Test against Pakistan following an investigation into an incident at a club in Derby, the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) says.

"Following a referral from the ECB, the Cricket Regulator has confirmed that they will investigate events on Saturday night in Derby," the ECB said in a statement.

Bazball's complex legacy Brendon McCullum deliberately set out to make England's men's Test team a less complicated team to play cricket for. After four years of Bazball's highs and lows, it leaves a very complicated legacy.

"Brydon Carse will no longer be available for selection for the second men's Test while this investigation is ongoing and the full facts are obtained."

Carse, who did not play in the opening Test victory at Headingley, will be replaced by Sonny Baker.

Videos circulated on social media appearing to show the 31-year-old Durham bowler in handcuffs being spoken to by police officers outside a venue.

According to reports, Carse was not arrested, and no charges were brought.

BBC reported that Derbyshire Police confirmed a man in his 30s was arrested, but then de-arrested shortly afterwards.

"A man in his 30s was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly in Derby city centre on Saturday night, 22 August," a police statement said, according to the BBC.

"However, the man was de-arrested shortly afterwards, having agreed to leave the area."

It has been a busy summer for England's Cricket Regulator, the body set up to investigate alleged breaches of the ECB's code of conduct.

In June it concluded an investigation into former Test captain Ben Stokes and fast bowler Gus Atkinson after a nightclub incident following the first Test against New Zealand.

Both were left out of the second Test before the regulator ruled that there was insufficient evidence to establish that any regulatory breach occurred.

The latest investigation came less than a week after England's returning Test captain, Joe Root, spoke of the players being "really good role models and human beings" following a series of incidents and accusations of a drinking culture.

Controversy has followed England in recent times, with off-field issues during last winter's tours, including Harry Brook being fined £30,000 ($57,200) following an altercation in Wellington, as well as reports of drinking during a mid-Ashes series trip to Noosa.

Stokes eventually announced his retirement from international cricket while Brendon McCullum was sacked as Test coach, with Root confirming that the team had done away with the curfews under new coach Stephen Fleming.
